Spanish restaurants had reintroduced it to the United States as a chilled punch by the late 1940s, and it became widely known after the Spanish Pavilion served it at the 1964 New York World's Fair. Since 2014 EU labeling rules have reserved the plain name for sangria made in Spain and Portugal.

name: Batanga
description: Tequila and cola with a salted rim, stirred — by decree of its late inventor — with a well-worn kitchen knife. Humble ingredients, sacred technique.
funFact: Don Javier Delgado Corona invented it in 1961 at La Capilla in the town of Tequila and stirred every Batanga with the same knife he used to cut limes, tending his bar into his nineties.

ingredients.item: Mexican cola (from a glass bottle if possible)

steps: Rub a lime wedge around the rim of a highball glass and roll the rim in coarse salt.
Fill the glass with ice, then add the tequila and fresh lime juice.
Top with cola, pouring gently to keep the fizz.
Stir once, tradition says with a kitchen knife, from the bottom up to combine.
Serve with the spent lime wedge dropped in.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on the salted rim

originStory: Don Javier Delgado Corona created the Batanga in 1961 at La Capilla, his cantina in the town of Tequila in Jalisco, mixing tequila, lime and cola over ice in a salt-rimmed glass and stirring each one with the long knife he used to cut limes. The name is usually said to come from a customer's nickname. Don Javier tended bar at La Capilla into his nineties and died in 2020, and the bar remains a destination for visitors to the town.

name: Cantarito
description: Tequila and a citrus grove sharing a rustic clay cup. The vessel sweats, the drink stays cool, and Jalisco road trips suddenly make sense.
funFact: It is named for the little porous clay cup it's served in, which chills the drink through evaporation — devotees insist the cup drinks better with years of use.

steps: If you have a clay cantarito cup, soak it in cold water for a few minutes; otherwise use a highball glass, optionally with a salted rim.
Fill the cup with ice and add the tequila, lime, orange, and grapefruit juices with a pinch of salt.
Stir briefly to combine and dissolve the salt.
Top with grapefruit soda and give one gentle stir.
Garnish and serve immediately while the clay is still cool.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel and a grapefruit or orange wedge

originStory: The Cantarito comes from the tequila country of Jalisco, where it is sold at roadside stands and fairs, and no one has documented who first made it. Its name means little jug, after the unglazed clay cup it is served in, which keeps the mix of tequila, citrus juices, salt and grapefruit soda cool as moisture evaporates through the clay.

name: Carajillo
description: Espresso fortified for active duty. On its Mexican tour it drafts vanilla-citrus Licor 43, foaming over ice into a caffeinated nightcap.
funFact: Folk etymology traces the name to 'coraje' — courage — from Spanish soldiers in colonial Cuba who spiked their coffee before duty.

steps: Pull a fresh double shot of espresso and let it sit while you prepare the glass.
Fill a rocks glass with large ice cubes and pour in the Licor 43.
Slowly pour the hot espresso over the ice so it floats in a dark layer on top.
Serve as is for the layered look, or stir once to integrate; for a frothy top, shake liqueur and espresso hard with ice for 10 seconds and strain over fresh ice instead.

originStory: The Carajillo is Spanish, though no one knows exactly where or when it began. One popular but unproven explanation says Spanish soldiers in colonial Cuba fortified their coffee with rum or brandy for courage, coraje, which became carajillo, while a Catalan story credits customers in Barcelona who ordered it with the words que ara guillo, I'm off now. In Mexico it took a new form, espresso shaken or poured over ice with Licor 43, the Spanish vanilla and citrus liqueur.

name: Coquito
description: Puerto Rico's coconut Christmas elixir, thick as a lullaby and spiced with cinnamon. Appears in December, vanishes by Three Kings Day.
funFact: The name means "little coconut," and Puerto Rican families guard their recipes so fiercely that coquito tasting contests are a holiday institution.

steps: Add the coconut cream, coconut milk, sweetened condensed milk, rum, and ground cinnamon to a blender.
Blend on high for 1-2 minutes until completely smooth and slightly frothy.
Pour into a bottle or pitcher and refrigerate at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, so it thickens and the flavors marry.
Shake the bottle well before serving, since the coconut fat separates as it chills.
Serve in small chilled glasses with a dusting of cinnamon on top.
recipe.garnish: Dusting of ground cinnamon and a cinnamon stick

originStory: Coquito is a Puerto Rican Christmas tradition with no single inventor, usually seen as an island version of the eggnog-style holiday drinks of Europe, with coconut and Puerto Rican rum giving it a character of its own. Recipes are passed down in families, and the season runs from about Thanksgiving to Three Kings Day, when the Coquito Masters contest at El Museo del Barrio in New York celebrates it every year.

name: Kalimotxo
description: Equal parts red wine and cola — the Basque Country's shrug at wine snobbery. Somehow far more than the sum of its cheap, brilliant parts.
funFact: As the story goes, it was christened at a 1972 Basque port festival when vendors rescued a batch of off wine by cutting it with Coca-Cola.

steps: Chill both the wine and the cola thoroughly beforehand.
Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in equal parts red wine and cola.
Stir once gently to combine without killing the fizz.
Add a lemon wedge and serve immediately.

originStory: Wine and cola had been mixed in the Basque Country before, but the Kalimotxo got its name in 1972 at the Puerto Viejo fiesta in Algorta, near Bilbao. As the story goes, friends running a drinks stall found their wine had turned and rescued it with Coca-Cola, and the name joins the nicknames of two of them, Kalimero and Motxongo. Simple and inexpensive, it spread through Basque fiestas and then across Spain.

name: Michelada
description: Beer that went to battle and came back seasoned: lime, hot sauce, and a salted rim turn a lager into brunchtime armor.
funFact: One popular origin story credits Michel Ésper, a regular at a San Luis Potosí sports club, whose custom beer-and-lime order became "Michel-ada" — Michel's lemonade.

ingredients.item: Coarse salt or Tajín (for the rim)

steps: Rub a lime wedge around the rim of a chilled pint glass and roll the rim in coarse salt or Tajín.
Fill the glass with ice, then add the lime juice, hot sauce, and Worcestershire sauce.
Stir briefly to combine the seasonings.
Slowly pour in the cold lager, tilting the glass to preserve the head.
Serve with the rest of the bottle on the side for topping up as you drink.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on the salted rim

originStory: The michelada has two origin stories. The more specific one credits Michel Ésper, a member of the Club Deportivo Potosino in San Luis Potosí, who in the 1960s asked for his beer with lime, salt and ice; other members began ordering Michel's lemonade, or Michel-ada. The other explanation is purely linguistic, reading the name as mi chela helada, my cold beer, in Mexican slang. Either way, the drink grew from a simple beer with lime and salt into a spicier, sauce-laden version that varies from region to region across Mexico.

name: Queen's Park Swizzle
description: A Trinidadian tower of crushed ice, demerara rum, and mint, capped by a rust-red stratum of Angostura. Requires a swizzle stick and forearm commitment.
funFact: Born at Port of Spain's Queen's Park Hotel in the 1920s, it was praised by Trader Vic as "the most delightful form of anesthesia given out today."

steps: Gently press the mint leaves with the demerara syrup in the bottom of a highball glass to release their oils, without shredding them.
Add the rum and lime juice, then pack the glass with crushed ice.
Insert a swizzle stick (or barspoon) and spin it briskly between your palms, moving up and down, until the outside of the glass frosts over.
Top with more crushed ice, mounding it slightly above the rim.
Dash the Angostura bitters generously over the ice cap so it forms a red layer, and garnish.
recipe.garnish: Bouquet of slapped mint over the bitters-stained ice cap

originStory: The Queen's Park Swizzle was created in the 1920s at the Queen's Park Hotel in Port of Spain, Trinidad, a grand hotel facing the Queen's Park Savannah, when Prohibition was sending Americans to the Caribbean in search of a legal drink. The hotel's bar built it on demerara rum, mint and the Angostura bitters made on the island, swizzled with a stick traditionally cut from a Caribbean tree, Quararibea turbinata. Trader Vic singled it out for praise in his 1946 book, and the drink outlived the hotel, which closed in 1996.

name: Sgroppino
description: A Venetian slush of lemon sorbet whipped with prosecco and vodka. Half dessert, half palate cleanser, entirely committed to elegance.
funFact: Its name comes from Venetian dialect for untying a little knot — it was traditionally served between courses to loosen the palate at Venetian banquets.

steps: Chill a champagne flute, a small bowl, and a whisk in the freezer for 10 minutes.
In the cold bowl, whisk the lemon sorbet with the vodka until it loosens into a smooth cream.
Add the prosecco a little at a time, whisking gently after each pour until the mix is velvety and frothy but still pourable.
Pour into the chilled flute.
Garnish and serve immediately with a small spoon, before it separates.
recipe.garnish: Twist of lemon zest or a small mint leaf

originStory: The Sgroppino comes from Venice, where it has long been served between courses or at the end of a meal, though its precise origins are not recorded. The name comes from the Venetian verb sgropar, to untie a knot, a nod to its place after a rich meal, and the classic version is lemon sorbet whisked with prosecco, the sparkling wine of the surrounding Veneto.

name: Terremoto
description: Chile's 'earthquake': sweet young pipeño wine capped with a scoop of pineapple ice cream. The ground feels perfectly stable until you stand up.
funFact: Santiago lore says foreign journalists covering the 1985 earthquake named it for its ground-shifting effects — and a second round is called a réplica, an aftershock.

ingredients.item: Pipeño (or another sweet, young white wine)

steps: Chill a large tumbler or pint glass; no ice is needed, the ice cream does the chilling.
Pour in the cold pipeño, leaving room at the top.
Float a generous scoop of pineapple ice cream on the wine.
Drizzle the grenadine over the ice cream (or substitute a float of fernet for the drier, Santiago-bar version).
Serve with a straw and a long spoon, stirring as little or as much as you dare.
recipe.garnish: None traditional; a pineapple wedge if you like

originStory: Terremoto means earthquake, and several old Santiago bars claim the drink, among them La Piojera and El Hoyo. The best-known story, told at El Hoyo, says German reporters covering the 1985 earthquake tried the mix of sweet pipeño wine and pineapple ice cream, and one remarked that this was the real earthquake; La Piojera tells its own version, and neither is confirmed. Pipeño itself is a young, rustic wine traditionally stored in barrels called pipas, which gave it its name.

name: Ti' Punch
description: Martinique's minimalist ritual: grassy rhum agricole, a coin of lime, and a slick of cane syrup. No ice unless you ask, no apologies either way.
funFact: Caribbean custom dictates "chacun prépare sa propre mort" — each prepares his own death — so the bartender hands you the bottle and you mix your own.

ingredients.item: Rhum agricole blanc (100 proof if you can find it)
Lime disc (a coin of peel with a little flesh)

steps: Cut a small coin of lime, mostly peel with a thin edge of flesh, from the side of a lime.
Squeeze the lime disc over a small tumbler and drop it in.
Add the cane syrup and muddle it briefly with the lime coin.
Pour in the rhum agricole and stir a few seconds with a small spoon until the syrup dissolves.
Serve neat at room temperature in the traditional style, or add a single small ice cube if you must.
recipe.garnish: The lime disc in the glass

originStory: Ti' Punch is short for petit punch, small punch, in the French and Creole of the French Caribbean, and it belongs to Martinique, Guadeloupe and their neighbors rather than to any single inventor. It is defined by rhum agricole, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice rather than molasses, a style that took hold on Martinique as falling sugar prices pushed planters toward rum in the late 19th century. Hosts traditionally set out rum, limes and cane syrup and let each guest mix their own.

name: Appletini
description: A neon-green Jolly Rancher of a drink from the height of the 'tini era. Tastes of sour apple candy; contains no measurable apple.
funFact: It debuted at Lola's in West Hollywood in 1997 as the "Adam's Apple Martini," named for the bartender who created it.

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer or fill it with ice water while you mix.
Add the vodka, sour apple schnapps, and lemon juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until the tin is frosty.
Empty the martini glass and double-strain the drink into it through a fine mesh strainer.
Garnish and serve straight up.
recipe.garnish: Thin slice of green apple on the rim

originStory: The Appletini began as the Adam's Apple Martini at Lola's, a West Hollywood restaurant, in 1996. By the usual account, owner Loren Dunsworth was encouraged to add a signature Ketel One drink, and a bartender named Adam mixed the vodka with DeKuyper Sour Apple Pucker and a splash of sweet and sour mix, giving it his own name. Shortened to Appletini, it became an emblem of the martini-glass craze of the late 1990s and 2000s.

name: Fuzzy Navel
description: Peach schnapps and orange juice in unapologetic harmony. Soft, sweet, and named after a pun rather than a body part, honest.
funFact: The name is a double pun — fuzzy for the peach, navel for the orange — and the drink helped make 1980s peach schnapps one of the fastest-selling new liquors in US history.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the peach schnapps.
Top with cold orange juice.
Stir well to combine.
Garnish with an orange slice and serve with a straw.

originStory: The Fuzzy Navel arrived with DeKuyper Peachtree Schnapps, which National Distillers launched in 1984 as the first peach schnapps on the American market. Peach schnapps and orange juice became its signature serve, and the name is a double pun, fuzzy for the skin of the peach and navel for the orange. Bartending writer Ray Foley has said he came up with it at the company's request, while other accounts credit the brand's advertising agency with the name.

name: Harvey Wallbanger
description: A Screwdriver crowned with a golden float of herbal Galliano. Its groovy name and cartoon mascot did most of the heavy lifting in the 1970s.
funFact: A 1970s Galliano marketing campaign built the drink around a sandal-wearing cartoon surfer whose slogan was "Harvey Wallbanger is the name. And I can be made!"

steps: Fill a highball glass to the top with fresh ice cubes.
Pour the vodka over the ice, then top with the orange juice and give it a brief stir to combine.
Float the Galliano on top by pouring it slowly over the back of a bar spoon so it sits as a golden layer.
Garnish and serve with a straw, letting the drinker stir the float in as they sip.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a maraschino cherry

originStory: The Harvey Wallbanger was largely a marketing creation: in 1969 McKesson Imports, which brought Galliano into the United States, built a campaign led by marketing director George Bednar around a cartoon surfer named Harvey and a Screwdriver topped with the golden Italian liqueur. Bartending instructor Donato 'Duke' Antone is often credited with the recipe, but the popular story that he invented it in 1952 for a Californian surfer is considered implausible by historians. The ads made it one of the most famous drinks of the 1970s.

name: Midori Sour
description: A radioactive-green melon sour beamed straight from a 1980s dance floor. Sweet, kitschy, and completely unashamed of either.
funFact: Midori means 'green' in Japanese, and Suntory launched the liqueur in America with a 1978 party at Studio 54.

steps: Add the Midori, lemon juice, and simple syrup to a cocktail shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until the tin is frosty.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
If you like it lighter and fizzy, top with a splash of soda water.
Garnish and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wheel and a maraschino cherry (or a honeydew melon ball)

originStory: Midori, the bright green melon liqueur made by the Japanese company Suntory, was launched in the United States in 1978 with a party at Studio 54 in New York; its name is simply the Japanese word for green. The Midori Sour, the liqueur mixed with citrus or sour mix, became its signature drink without any one bartender being credited for it, and its color made it a fixture of nightclub bars in the decade that followed.

name: Mudslide
description: A milkshake that took a wrong turn into the liquor cabinet. Vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream engulf everything in delicious sediment.
funFact: It was reportedly invented in the 1970s at the Wreck Bar at Rum Point on Grand Cayman, where it remains the house specialty.

steps: Optionally drizzle chocolate syrup around the inside of a chilled hurricane or rocks glass.
Add the vodka, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds until well chilled and slightly frothy.
Strain over fresh ice in the prepared glass.
For a frozen version, blend everything with a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a cup of ice instead of shaking.
Garnish and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Chocolate syrup drizzle; whipped cream and chocolate shavings optional

originStory: The Wreck Bar at Rum Point on Grand Cayman claims the Mudslide, created in the 1970s. The story goes that a customer asked for a White Russian, and the bartender, with no cream on hand, reached for Baileys Irish Cream instead, which had reached the market only a few years earlier. The combination of vodka, coffee liqueur and Irish cream stuck, and the Wreck Bar still serves it as the house specialty. Frozen, blended versions later spread through American restaurants.

name: Rusty Nail
description: Scotch sweetened by Drambuie's honeyed herbs, sipped slowly in leather-chair lighting. The official nightcap of ring-a-ding-ding.
funFact: Drambuie, its defining half, is tied to a legend that Bonnie Prince Charlie gave the secret recipe to the MacKinnon clan after the failed 1745 Jacobite rising.

steps: Add the Scotch and Drambuie to a mixing glass filled with ice.
Stir gently for 20-30 seconds until well chilled and lightly diluted.
Strain into a rocks glass over one large ice cube.
Express a lemon twist over the surface, then drop it in or rest it on the rim.
Sip slowly; adjust to equal parts Scotch and Drambuie if you prefer it sweeter.

originStory: The Rusty Nail got its name in the United States in the early 1960s, and New York's 21 Club is often linked with the drink; in 1963 Gina MacKinnon, who headed the Drambuie company, publicly endorsed the name. The pairing of Scotch and Drambuie was older, served as the B.I.F., after the British Industries Fair, in 1937 and under other names since. Drambuie itself is tied to a legend that Bonnie Prince Charlie gave the recipe to the MacKinnon clan after the failed Jacobite rising of 1745.

name: B-52
description: A three-layer stratigraphy of coffee liqueur, Irish cream, and orange liqueur. Drink it fast or set the top alight; geology was never this festive.
funFact: A popular origin story credits Alberta bartender Peter Fich, who named his layered creations after favorite bands — this one for the B-52s.

steps: Pour the coffee liqueur into a shot glass as the bottom layer.
Hold a bar spoon upside down just above the surface and slowly pour the Irish cream over its back so it floats in a distinct second layer.
Repeat with the orange liqueur over the spoon to form the clear top layer.
Serve immediately while the three layers are sharp; drink in one go or sip through the strata.
recipe.garnish: None (the three clean layers are the presentation)

originStory: The usual story credits Peter Fich, head bartender at the Banff Springs Hotel in Alberta in the 1970s, who named his new drinks after favorite bands, albums and songs; this one honored the B-52's rather than the bomber. A customer who owned restaurants in Alberta put it on his menus, which led some to place its birth at the Keg Steakhouse in Calgary in 1977. A rival claim credits a bartender at Maxwell's Plum in New York, and neither story is well documented.

name: Baby Guinness
description: A trompe-l'oeil shooter: coffee liqueur topped with a float of Irish cream so it resembles a miniature pint of stout, foam collar and all.
funFact: Despite the name and the perfect two-tone pour, it contains no Guinness at all.

steps: Pour the coffee liqueur into a shot glass, filling it about two-thirds of the way.
Hold a bar spoon upside down just above the liqueur and pour the Irish cream slowly over its back so it settles into a creamy head.
Let it sit a few seconds so the 'foam collar' sharpens into a miniature pint of stout.
Serve immediately and drink in one go.
recipe.garnish: None (the Irish cream head is the garnish)

originStory: The Baby Guinness, a float of Irish cream over dark coffee liqueur, has no recorded inventor and takes its name from its look, a miniature pint of the Dublin stout, though it contains no Guinness at all.

name: Buttery Nipple
description: A dessert-counter shooter of butterscotch schnapps under a cool cream float. Zero sophistication, one hundred percent compliance.
funFact: The layering is pure physics: sugar-dense butterscotch schnapps sinks while the lighter Irish cream floats serenely on top.

steps: Chill the butterscotch schnapps (fridge or a quick stir over ice, strained) for a smoother shot.
Pour the schnapps into a shot glass, filling it about two-thirds full.
Slowly pour the Irish cream over the back of a bar spoon so it floats on top; the denser schnapps stays below.
Serve immediately and drink in one smooth go.

originStory: The Buttery Nipple, a layered American shooter of butterscotch schnapps under Irish cream, has no documented inventor or date.

name: Green Tea Shot
description: Irish whiskey and peach schnapps masquerading as a health beverage. Named purely for its jade hue — no leaves were steeped in its making.
funFact: It contains no tea whatsoever — the name comes entirely from the drink's pale green color.

ingredients.item: Sour mix (or equal parts lemon juice and simple syrup)

steps: Add the whiskey, peach schnapps, and sour mix to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 8-10 seconds until very cold.
Strain into a chilled shot glass, leaving a little room at the top.
Top with a splash of lemon-lime soda for the signature fizz.
Drink in one go while it's ice cold.
recipe.garnish: None (a thin lemon wedge on the rim is optional)

originStory: The Green Tea Shot, an American bar shooter of Irish whiskey, peach schnapps and sour mix, has no documented creator and contains no tea, taking its name from its pale green color.

name: Jägerbomb
description: A depth charge of German herbal liqueur plunged into an energy drink. The splash is part of the ceremony; the regret is complimentary.
glassware: Shot glass dropped in a pint glass
funFact: Jägermeister means "master hunter," and the glowing stag on its label honors St. Hubertus, the patron saint of hunters.

ingredients.item: Jagermeister (well chilled, ideally from the freezer)

steps: Pour the energy drink into a sturdy pint or highball glass, filling it about a third of the way.
Fill a shot glass with the ice-cold Jagermeister.
Drop the full shot glass straight into the glass of energy drink — glass and all.
Drink immediately in one continuous go while it fizzes.
Mind your teeth on the shot glass as you finish.

originStory: No one has documented who first dropped a shot of Jägermeister, the herbal liqueur from Wolfenbüttel in Germany, into a glass of energy drink to make the Jägerbomb.

name: Kamikaze
description: Vodka, orange liqueur, and lime in equal thirds — a citrus dive-bomb with no survivors expected. Clean, sharp, and gone in one motion.
funFact: Add a splash of cranberry, serve it up in a stemmed glass, and the 1970s Kamikaze becomes the blueprint of the Cosmopolitan.

steps: Add the vodka, triple sec, and lime juice — equal thirds — to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds until frosty.
Strain into a chilled shot glass.
For a full-size cocktail, double everything to 1 oz each and strain into a chilled coupe.
Drink in one clean motion.

originStory: The Kamikaze, an equal-parts mix of vodka, triple sec and lime, has no documented inventor or date, and its name is probably taken from the Japanese word, meaning divine wind, used for the suicide pilots of the Second World War.

name: Lemon Drop Shot
description: Vodka-lemonade compressed into candy form, with a sugared rim as the wrapper. Puckers first, forgives quickly.
funFact: It was created in the 1970s at Henry Africa's in San Francisco, widely described as America's first "fern bar."

steps: Rub a lemon wedge around the rim of a shot glass, then dip the rim in sugar to coat it.
Add the vodka, lemon juice, and simple syrup to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds until well chilled.
Strain carefully into the sugar-rimmed shot glass without disturbing the rim.
Shoot it, then bite the lemon wedge if you kept one on the side.
recipe.garnish: Sugared rim and a small lemon wedge

originStory: The Lemon Drop was created in the 1970s by Norman Jay Hobday, owner of Henry Africa's in San Francisco's Russian Hill, widely described as America's first fern bar, the plant-filled style of bar that flourished in that decade. Named after the lemon drop candy, the vodka, lemon and sugar drink was first served up in a cocktail glass, and by the early 1990s bartenders were also pouring it as a shot.

name: Mind Eraser
description: A stratified vodka-and-coffee contraption drained through a straw from the bottom up. Does exactly what the label promises.
funFact: House rules require draining it in one continuous pull from the bottom — coffee liqueur first, fizzy water last — making it a carbonated Black Russian in a hurry.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice cubes.
Pour the coffee liqueur first so it settles at the bottom.
Gently pour the vodka over the ice as the middle layer — do not stir.
Slowly top with chilled soda water to form the fizzy top layer.
Drop in a straw that reaches the bottom and drink in one continuous pull, from coffee liqueur up through the soda.

originStory: The Mind Eraser, a layered American highball of vodka and coffee liqueur topped with soda water, has no documented inventor or date.

name: Pickleback
description: A whiskey shot immediately chased by cold pickle brine, which erases the burn like it never happened. Chemistry-adjacent magic in two small glasses.
funFact: Bartender Reggie Cunningham poured the first one at Brooklyn's Bushwick Country Club in 2006, using brine from a jar of McClure's pickles stored at the bar.

steps: Chill the pickle brine in the fridge ahead of time — cold brine is essential.
Pour the whiskey into one shot glass and the brine into a second, matching shot glass.
Shoot the whiskey first, in one go.
Immediately chase it with the full shot of pickle brine and let it wipe out the burn.
recipe.garnish: None (a small dill pickle spear on the side is a nice touch)

originStory: Bartender Reggie Cunningham is credited with the Pickleback, first poured in 2006 at the Bushwick Country Club, a bar in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, that kept a jar of pickles from McClure's, a local company. The story goes that a customer asked for a shot of the brine to follow her whiskey, and Cunningham tried the pairing and began serving it. By 2011 visitors had carried it to bars in London.

name: Vegas Bomb
description: A whisky-peach-cranberry payload dropped into an energy drink. Detonates on contact with bachelor parties.
glassware: Shot glass dropped in a pint glass
funFact: Skip the energy-drink plunge and the shot inside goes by its own poker-table name: the Royal Flush.

steps: Stir or briefly shake the whisky, peach schnapps, and cranberry juice with ice, then strain into a shot glass.
Pour the energy drink into a sturdy pint glass, filling it about a third of the way.
Drop the full shot glass straight into the energy drink.
Drink immediately in one continuous go.
Skip the drop and sip the strained shot on its own and you have a Royal Flush.

originStory: The Vegas Bomb, a shot of Canadian whisky, peach schnapps and cranberry juice dropped into an energy drink, has no documented inventor, though its name points to Las Vegas.

name: Washington Apple
description: An orchard compressed into a shot glass: whisky, sour apple, and cranberry doing a crisp autumn impression all year round.
funFact: It salutes Washington State, grower of most of America's apples — yet its traditional whisky is Canadian.

steps: Add the whisky, sour apple schnapps, and cranberry juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled shot glass.
For a full cocktail, use 1 oz of each ingredient and strain into a chilled coupe over the same spec.
Garnish and drink while ice cold.
recipe.garnish: Thin green apple slice on the rim (optional for the shot)

originStory: The Washington Apple, an American shooter of Canadian whisky, sour apple schnapps and cranberry juice, has no recorded inventor or date, and its name salutes Washington State, which grows most of the country's apples.

name: Amaretto Sour
description: Almond liqueur brightened with lemon into something between marzipan and lemonade. Long dismissed as a starter drink, lately rebuilt with respect.
funFact: Bartender Jeffrey Morgenthaler famously declared in 2012 that he makes the world's best Amaretto Sour by adding cask-proof bourbon and egg white — a spec many bars now follow.

ingredients.amount: 0.5 oz / 15 ml (about half an egg white)

steps: Add the amaretto, fresh lemon juice, simple syrup, and egg white (if using) to a shaker with no ice and dry shake hard for 10 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake again for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Strain over fresh ice into a rocks glass.
Let the foam settle for a moment, then garnish.
recipe.garnish: Lemon wheel and a brandied cherry

originStory: The Amaretto Sour was introduced in 1974 by the American importer of Amaretto di Saronno, the almond-flavored liqueur from Saronno near Milan, as a simple two-to-one mix of amaretto and lemon juice to sell the brand to American drinkers. It caught on, and through the 1980s most bars made it with premixed sour mix, which earned it a reputation as a sweet starter drink. In 2012 Portland bartender Jeffrey Morgenthaler published a rebuilt version with fresh lemon, egg white and a measure of cask-proof bourbon, and many bars now follow his approach.

name: Aviation
description: Gin, maraschino, lemon, and a whisper of crème de violette tinting the glass the pale gray-blue of a cloudy sky. Delicate, floral, and easy to overdo.
funFact: Crème de violette vanished from the American market for decades, so generations of bartenders made colorless Aviations until imports resumed in 2007.

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer.
Combine the gin, maraschino, crème de violette, and fresh lemon juice in a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until frost forms on the tin.
Double strain into the chilled coupe so no ice shards cloud the pale sky-blue color.
Keep the violette light — more than a bathtub-gin whisper turns it soapy.
recipe.garnish: Brandied cherry dropped to the bottom of the glass

originStory: Hugo Ensslin, head bartender at the Hotel Wallick in New York, created the Aviation and printed it in his 1916 book Recipes for Mixed Drinks: gin, lemon, maraschino and crème de violette. The name presumably reflects the excitement around flight in those years, and the violet liqueur gave the drink a sky-colored tint. When Harry Craddock included it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book he left out the violette, and as the liqueur vanished from American shelves, generations of bartenders followed his colorless version until crème de violette returned to the market in 2007.

name: Bee's Knees
description: Gin, honey, and lemon — a Prohibition-era formula in which the honey did double duty as flavor and camouflage. Named with era-appropriate slang for 'the best.'
funFact: During Prohibition, honey and lemon conveniently masked the harsh bite of bathtub gin; one popular attribution credits Frank Meier of the Ritz Paris with the recipe.

ingredients.item: Honey syrup (3:1 honey to warm water)

steps: Make honey syrup by stirring 3 parts honey into 1 part warm water until fully dissolved; let cool.
Chill a coupe.
Add gin, honey syrup, and fresh lemon juice to a shaker with ice and shake hard for 12-15 seconds.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.

originStory: The Bee's Knees belongs to the Prohibition years of the 1920s, and its name is the era's slang for something excellent. Its inventor is uncertain: a 1929 newspaper item credited Margaret Brown, the Titanic survivor remembered as the Unsinkable Molly Brown, while others point to Frank Meier, who ran the bar at the Ritz in Paris from 1921. Honey and lemon are often said to have masked the harsh taste of bathtub gin, a plausible explanation that nobody has proved.

name: Blood and Sand
description: Scotch, cherry liqueur, sweet vermouth, and orange juice in improbable equal-parts harmony — one of the only classics brave enough to mix Scotch with juice.
funFact: It was named after the 1922 Rudolph Valentino bullfighting film 'Blood and Sand' and preserved for posterity in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book.

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the Scotch, cherry liqueur, sweet vermouth, and fresh orange juice to a shaker with ice — equal parts, per the classic 1930 Savoy spec.
Shake for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist, expressed over the top, plus an optional cherry

originStory: Blood and Sand takes its name from the 1922 film in which Rudolph Valentino played a doomed matador, and the red cherry liqueur and orange juice are often read as a nod to the bullring. Its creator is unknown, but the recipe was preserved in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, compiled at the American Bar of the Savoy hotel in London, and after decades of obscurity craft bartenders revived it.

name: Brandy Crusta
description: Cognac, curaçao, maraschino, and lemon dressed in a full sugared crust and an extravagant ribbon of lemon peel. The peacock ancestor of the Sidecar.
funFact: Joseph Santini's 1850s New Orleans creation is credited with introducing elaborate citrus garnish to the cocktail — the entire glass rim is 'crusted' in sugar.

ingredients.amount: About 2 tbsp on a small plate

steps: Prepare the glass: rub a lemon wedge around the outside of the rim of a small wine glass, then roll the rim in superfine sugar to form a wide, even crust. Chill the glass.
Cut a long, wide ribbon of lemon peel in one continuous spiral and coil it inside the glass so it lines the rim.
Add the cognac, curaçao, maraschino, lemon juice, and bitters to a shaker with ice.
Shake for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain carefully into the prepared glass without disturbing the sugar crust.
recipe.garnish: The sugared rim and a long spiral of lemon peel coiled inside the glass

originStory: Joseph Santini created the Brandy Crusta in the 1850s at his New Orleans bar, the Jewel of the South. The name comes from the crust of sugar around the rim of the glass, set off by a long spiral of lemon peel lining the inside. Jerry Thomas published it in his landmark 1862 bar guide, giving it national reach. Its mix of brandy, orange curaçao and lemon is widely seen as the ancestor of the Sidecar, and a New Orleans bar that took the name Jewel of the South revived both the name and the drink in 2019.

name: Caipirinha
description: Cachaça muddled with whole lime and sugar in the glass it is served in. Brazil's national cocktail: rustic by design, lethal by volume.
funFact: One popular legend traces it to a São Paulo folk remedy for the Spanish flu made with lime, garlic, and honey — over time the garlic left and the cachaça stayed.

ingredients.amount: Half a lime, cut into 4 wedges
Cracked or cubed, to fill the glass

steps: Add the lime wedges and sugar directly to a sturdy rocks glass.
Muddle firmly to press out the juice and lime oils and dissolve the sugar — press, don't pulverize the pith.
Fill the glass with cracked ice and pour in the cachaça.
Churn with a spoon (or cap and give one short shake back into the glass) until the outside frosts.
Serve in the same glass with a short straw.
recipe.garnish: The muddled lime wedges in the glass; add a fresh lime wheel if you like

originStory: The Caipirinha grew up in the interior of São Paulo state. One popular account dates it to around 1918, when a folk remedy of lime, garlic and honey circulating during the Spanish flu was mixed with cachaça, and over time the garlic and honey gave way to sugar and ice. Others trace it to 19th-century landowners in the Piracicaba sugarcane region, who served it at gatherings. The name is a diminutive of caipira, a term for country people from rural São Paulo, and Brazilian law now defines the drink as cachaça with lime and sugar.

name: Clover Club
description: Gin, raspberry, lemon, and egg white shaken into a rosy cloud. Pretty in pink but pre-Prohibition to the bone.
funFact: It was named for a Philadelphia club of lawyers, writers, and industrialists who met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel from the 1880s onward — hardly the crowd its color suggests.

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add gin, raspberry syrup, fresh lemon juice, and egg white to a shaker with no ice and dry shake hard for 10-15 seconds to whip the foam.
Add ice and shake again for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe and let the rosy foam cap settle before garnishing.
recipe.garnish: Three raspberries on a pick, laid across the foam

originStory: The Clover Club cocktail takes its name from the Clover Club, a Philadelphia gathering of lawyers, writers and businessmen founded in 1882 that met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel. Recipes for its mix of gin, lemon, raspberry and egg white appeared in print from around 1908, and it spread to the smart bars of New York before fading after Prohibition; a 1939 drink book dismissed it outright. Revived in the craft era, it lent its name to Julie Reiner's Clover Club bar in Brooklyn, opened in 2008.

name: Corpse Reviver No. 2
description: Gin, Cointreau, Lillet, and lemon over an absinthe rinse — a member of the Victorian family of hangover 'cures' and comfortably the best of them.
funFact: Harry Craddock's 1930 'Savoy Cocktail Book' warns that 'four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again.'

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe: add the absinthe, swirl to coat the inside, and dump (or spray the glass with an atomizer).
Add the gin, Cointreau, Lillet Blanc, and fresh lemon juice to a shaker with ice — equal parts.
Shake for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the absinthe-rinsed coupe.
Heed the Savoy's warning: stop before the fourth.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist or a cocktail cherry

originStory: Corpse revivers were a loose 19th-century family of pick-me-up drinks, but the No. 2 is fixed in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, compiled at the American Bar of the Savoy hotel in London: equal parts gin, Cointreau, Kina Lillet and lemon juice with a dash of absinthe. The drink fell from view for decades until craft bartenders revived it in the early 2000s, and it is now the best-known of its family.

name: Cosmopolitan
description: A blush-pink shard of the 1990s: citrus vodka, cranberry, lime, and orange liqueur served up with maximum poise. Dismissed as a fad, it simply never left.
funFact: Its origin is disputed among several American bartenders, but nobody disputes what made it a global icon: Carrie Bradshaw ordering round after round on 'Sex and the City.'

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer.
Add the citrus vodka, Cointreau, cranberry juice, and fresh lime juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds — you want it ice cold with a slight frothy blush.
Double strain into the chilled martini glass.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist — flame it over the surface for the full 90s effect

originStory: Several bartenders claim the Cosmopolitan: Neal Murray said he created it in 1975 at the Cork & Cleaver in Minneapolis by adding cranberry to a Kamikaze, John Caine is credited with popularizing a version in San Francisco, and historian Gary Regan credited Cheryl Cook in South Beach, Miami, in the mid-1980s. The version most bars use was refined in the late 1980s by Toby Cecchini at the Odeon in New York, with Absolut Citron, Cointreau, cranberry and fresh lime. Madonna and then Carrie Bradshaw of Sex and the City made it a global icon.

name: Daiquiri
description: Rum, lime, and sugar shaken to a snowy chill — nothing more is needed and nothing less will do. Often mistaken for its frozen, blended descendants.
funFact: It takes its name from Daiquirí, a beach and village near Santiago de Cuba, where American mining engineer Jennings Cox is credited with mixing it around 1898.

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer.
Add the rum, fresh lime juice, and simple syrup to a shaker with plenty of ice.
Shake very hard for 12-15 seconds — the Daiquiri wants real dilution and a snowy chill.
Double strain into the chilled coupe so it pours crystal clear with a fine frost.
recipe.garnish: Thin lime wheel on the rim

originStory: The daiquiri is named for Daiquirí, a beach and mining village near Santiago de Cuba, where American mining engineer Jennings Cox is credited with mixing rum, lime and sugar around 1898. Those ingredients were already familiar in Cuba, but the name stuck to Cox's version. US Navy officer Lucius Johnson brought it to the Army and Navy Club in Washington in 1909, and in Havana, Constantino Ribalaigua of El Floridita refined it in the 1920s and 1930s, creating the frozen variations Ernest Hemingway favored.

name: Gimlet
description: Gin and lime cordial, sharp and to the point — named, fittingly, after a small boring tool. A naval ration that retired ashore and never left.
funFact: Rose's lime cordial, patented in 1867, preserved lime juice without alcohol for the Royal Navy — the same lime rations that earned British sailors the nickname 'limeys.'

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the gin and lime cordial to a mixing glass filled with ice.
Stir for 20-30 seconds until thoroughly chilled and slightly diluted — with cordial (no fresh juice) the drink stays silky when stirred.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Prefer it brighter? Swap in a shake and adjust cordial to taste — the naval classic is simply gin and cordial, sharp and to the point.

originStory: The gimlet first turns up by name in 1928, described as gin, a spot of lime and soda, but its roots lie in British maritime lime rations. In 1867 Lauchlan Rose of Leith patented a way to preserve lime juice without alcohol, the same year a Merchant Shipping Act required lime juice aboard British merchant ships, and the story goes that naval officers took to mixing it with gin. The name may come from the small hand drill; a tale crediting navy surgeon Sir Thomas Gimlette goes unmentioned in his obituaries.

name: Hemingway Daiquiri
description: A bone-dry daiquiri sharpened with grapefruit and maraschino, built to a novelist's exacting and immodest specifications. Also answers to 'Papa Doble.'
funFact: Ernest Hemingway, wary of sugar, asked Havana's El Floridita for his daiquiri with no sugar and double rum — the resulting 'Papa Doble' was named in his honor.

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the rum, fresh grapefruit juice, maraschino, and fresh lime juice to a shaker with ice — no sugar, as Papa demanded.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
Expect it bone-dry and bracing; add a bar spoon of simple syrup only if it's too austere for your taste.

originStory: Ernest Hemingway became a regular at Havana's El Floridita in the 1930s, when head bartender Constantino Ribalaigua Vert had made the bar famous for its daiquiris. Hemingway took his without sugar, and the version the bar built for him, sharpened with grapefruit and maraschino, came to be called the Papa Doble after his nickname. El Floridita still trades on the connection, with a bronze statue of the writer leaning on the end of the bar.

name: Jack Rose
description: Applejack, grenadine, and citrus in a blushing pre-Prohibition sour. Orchard fruit with a literary pedigree and a slightly shady name.
funFact: Jake Barnes drinks a Jack Rose in a Paris hotel bar in Ernest Hemingway's 'The Sun Also Rises' (1926).

ingredients.item: Applejack (bonded if you can find it)

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the applejack, fresh lemon (or lime) juice, and grenadine to a shaker with ice — use a proper pomegranate grenadine, not neon syrup.
Shake for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
recipe.garnish: Thin apple slice or a lemon twist

originStory: The Jack Rose appears in print by 1905, when the National Police Gazette credited a New Jersey bartender, Frank J. May, with creating it. Its name has drawn several theories: a Newark restaurateur named Joseph P. Rose, the pink Jacqueminot rose, or simply applejack plus the drink's rosy colour, the likeliest of them; the drink predates the career of the gambler Bald Jack Rose. Hemingway gave it literary fame in 1926, when Jake Barnes drinks one in a Paris hotel bar in The Sun Also Rises.

name: Last Word
description: Equal parts gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino, and lime — an improbable herbal truce that tastes inevitable. Extinct for decades, now everywhere that matters.
funFact: Born at the Detroit Athletic Club around Prohibition, it was forgotten until Seattle bartender Murray Stenson unearthed it from a 1951 recipe book in 2004 and set off a global revival.

steps: Chill a coupe.
Add the gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino, and fresh lime juice to a shaker with ice — strict equal parts is the whole trick.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds; this drink needs the chill and dilution to knit the herbal truce together.
Double strain into the chilled coupe.
recipe.garnish: Brandied cherry or a lime twist

originStory: The Last Word was on the menu of the Detroit Athletic Club by 1916, its inventor unknown, and the vaudeville performer Frank Fogarty carried it to New York later that decade. It survived in print in Ted Saucier's 1951 book Bottoms Up but was otherwise forgotten until the early 2000s, when Seattle bartender Murray Stenson found the recipe and put it on the menu at the Zig Zag Café. From there it spread across the country and inspired a family of equal-parts cocktails, the Paper Plane among them.

name: Lemon Drop
description: Citrus vodka, lemon, and sugar shaken into hard-candy form and served up with a sugared rim. Sweet, sour, and unashamed of either.
funFact: It was created in the 1970s at Henry Africa's in San Francisco, one of the original 'fern bars' that pioneered dating-friendly, plant-filled saloons.

ingredients.amount: About 2 tbsp on a small plate

steps: Rub a lemon wedge around the rim of a martini glass and roll the rim in superfine sugar; chill the glass.
Add the vodka, triple sec, fresh lemon juice, and simple syrup to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until ice cold.
Double strain into the sugar-rimmed glass without wetting the crust.
recipe.garnish: Sugared rim and a lemon twist or wheel

originStory: The Lemon Drop is usually credited to Norman Jay Hobday at Henry Africa's in San Francisco in the 1970s. His bar is often described as the first of the fern bars, singles bars filled with plants and Tiffany-style lamps, a model that spread across the country. Named after the hard lemon candy it imitates, the drink began as sweetened vodka and lemon served up, and it travelled with the vodka boom of the following decades.

name: Margarita
description: Tequila sharpened with lime and orange liqueur behind a crust of salt. A perennial contender for the most-ordered cocktail in the United States.
funFact: 'Margarita' is Spanish for 'daisy,' and the drink is structurally a tequila Daisy — a 19th-century sour template of spirit, citrus, and liqueur.

ingredients.amount: 1 shaker full, plus fresh cubes for the glass

steps: Rub a lime wedge around the outer rim of a chilled margarita or rocks glass, then roll the outside edge in kosher salt. Set aside.
Add the tequila, orange liqueur, and lime juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds, until the tin is frosty.
Strain over fresh ice into the salt-rimmed glass (or fine-strain it straight up).
Garnish with a lime wheel on the rim and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel and a kosher-salt rim

originStory: Mexico's news agency Notimex and many experts have said Francisco 'Pancho' Morales has the strongest claim; he said he mixed the first margarita at Tommy's Place in Ciudad Juárez on 4 July 1942. Rival claims include Carlos 'Danny' Herrera's Rancho La Gloria in Baja California, a story since challenged, and the Dallas socialite Margarita Sames, who dated hers to 1948 in Acapulco, though Jose Cuervo was already advertising margaritas by 1945. Historian David Wondrich sees it as a tequila version of the daisy, and margarita is Spanish for daisy.

name: Paper Plane
description: Equal parts bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, and lemon folded into perfect bittersweet symmetry. One of the few 21st-century drinks already treated as canon.
funFact: Sam Ross devised it in 2008 for Chicago's The Violet Hour and named it after M.I.A.'s song 'Paper Planes,' which was playing on repeat at the time.

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.
Add the bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, and lemon juice to a shaker filled with ice — the drink lives or dies on the equal-parts measure, so jigger carefully.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds.
Double-strain (Hawthorne plus fine strainer) into the chilled coupe, no ice.
Serve as-is; optionally perch a tiny folded paper plane on the rim as a nod to the name.
recipe.garnish: None traditional; optionally a tiny folded paper plane clipped to the rim

originStory: Sam Ross created the Paper Plane in 2008 for a menu at The Violet Hour in Chicago, naming it after M.I.A.'s song Paper Planes, which he was listening to often at the time. The first version used Campari, but Ross soon switched to Aperol for a lighter, rounder drink. Built in equal parts, a nod to the Last Word, it was passed from bartender to bartender and became one of the few drinks of its era already treated as a modern classic.

name: Penicillin
description: Blended Scotch with lemon and honey-ginger syrup under a smoky float of Islay malt. Medicine-cabinet branding, world-class execution.
funFact: Sam Ross created it at New York's Milk & Honey in 2005, and it spread to bar menus worldwide purely by word of mouth — the definitive modern classic.

ingredients.item: Peaty Islay Scotch (e.g. Laphroaig), to float

ingredients.amount: 1 shaker full, plus 1 large cube for the glass

steps: Make honey-ginger syrup ahead: simmer 1 cup honey, 1 cup water, and a 6-inch knob of thinly sliced ginger for 5 minutes, steep off heat, then strain and chill.
Add the blended Scotch, lemon juice, and honey-ginger syrup to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds and strain into a rocks glass over one large ice cube.
Float the Islay Scotch by pouring it slowly over the back of a bar spoon so it rests on the surface — do not stir it in.
Garnish with a piece of candied ginger on a pick and serve.
recipe.garnish: Candied ginger on a cocktail pick

originStory: Australian bartender Sam Ross created the Penicillin at Milk & Honey in New York in 2005, building a sour on blended Scotch with lemon and a honey-ginger syrup, then floating a smoky Islay malt on top. He originally made it with Compass Box whiskies for both the base and the float. It never needed an advertising campaign: bartenders who tasted it took it back to their own menus, and within a few years it was being served around the world.

name: Pisco Sour
description: Grape brandy, lime, and sugar under a snowdrift of egg-white foam dotted with bitters. The subject of a genial but eternal custody dispute between Peru and Chile.
funFact: Credited to American expat bartender Victor Morris in 1920s Lima, it is honored in Peru with a national Pisco Sour Day on the first Saturday of February.

steps: Add the pisco, lime juice, simple syrup, and egg white to a shaker WITHOUT ice and dry-shake hard for 15 seconds to build the foam.
Open the shaker, fill it with ice, and shake again for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled old fashioned glass, holding back the ice so the foam settles into a smooth white cap.
Let the foam set for a few seconds, then dot 3 drops of Angostura bitters on top.
Optionally drag a toothpick through the drops to marble them, and serve straight away.
recipe.garnish: 3 drops of Angostura bitters dotted (or swirled) on the egg-white foam

originStory: The pisco sour as it is known today was developed in Lima in the early 1920s at Morris' Bar, which American bartender Victor Vaughen Morris opened in 1916; the oldest known mention of the drink appeared in the magazine Hogar in 1920. Mario Bruiget, who began working for Morris in 1924, is credited with adding egg white and Angostura bitters. Chile's rival claim, crediting a steward named Elliot Stubb in Iquique, appears to rest on a source describing the whiskey sour, and Peru marks National Pisco Sour Day each February.

name: Sidecar
description: Cognac, orange liqueur, and lemon balanced on a sugared rim — the sour family in evening wear. A relic of 1920s Paris that never went out of style.
funFact: It is supposedly named for an army captain who was chauffeured to his Paris bar of choice in a motorcycle sidecar.

steps: If using the classic sugar rim, rub a lemon wedge around the outer rim of a chilled coupe and roll the edge in superfine sugar; let it dry while you mix.
Add the cognac, Cointreau, and lemon juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds, until the tin frosts over.
Double-strain into the chilled, sugar-rimmed coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface, drop it in or rest it on the rim, and serve.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist, with an optional sugared rim

originStory: The Sidecar's first printed recipes appeared in 1922, in Robert Vermeire's Cocktails and How to Mix Them and Harry MacElhone's Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, which credited Pat MacGarry of Buck's Club in London. Paris has its own claims, from the Ritz to MacElhone's own Harry's New York Bar, and a popular story names an American army captain in wartime Paris who rode to his favourite bar in a motorcycle sidecar. The name is usually taken to come from that attachment, common at the time.

name: Ward 8
description: A rye sour rounded with orange and grenadine — Boston machine politics rendered in liquid form, right down to the premature victory lap.
funFact: Legend says it was mixed at Boston's Locke-Ober in 1898 to toast Martin Lomasney's election win in the Eighth Ward — the night before the votes were actually counted.

steps: Chill a cocktail glass in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.
Add the rye, lemon juice, orange juice, and grenadine to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds.
Double-strain into the chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with an orange slice and cherry flag on a pick and serve.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and maraschino cherry on a pick (a 'flag')

originStory: The usual story says the Ward 8 was first mixed at Boston's Locke-Ober restaurant in 1898 to celebrate Martin Lomasney's election to the state legislature from the city's Eighth Ward, a political machine stronghold, with the toast raised the night before the votes were counted. Historians treat the tale with caution, but the name stuck to this rye sour with orange and grenadine, which appears in cocktail books from the early twentieth century onward.

name: Whiskey Sour
description: The archetype of the sour family: whiskey, lemon, and sugar in perfect three-point balance, optionally cushioned with a cloud of egg-white foam.
funFact: Its best-known variations earned names of their own: shaken with egg white it is often called a Boston Sour, and a float of dry red wine on top turns it into a New York Sour.

ingredients.item: Egg white (optional, for a silky foam)

ingredients.amount: 1 shaker full, plus fresh cubes for the glass

steps: If using egg white, add all ingredients to a shaker WITHOUT ice and dry-shake hard for 15 seconds to build the foam; otherwise skip to step 2.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for 12-15 seconds, until well chilled.
Strain over fresh ice into a rocks glass (or serve it up in a chilled coupe if you prefer).
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry; if you used egg white, a few dashes of Angostura on the foam look and taste great.
Serve immediately, while the foam is still tall.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and maraschino cherry; Angostura dashes on the foam if made with egg white

originStory: Sours grew out of the punch tradition of mixing spirits with citrus and sugar. The oldest known mention of a whiskey sour by name is in an 1870 Wisconsin newspaper, though Jerry Thomas's 1862 bartender's guide had already printed sours made with brandy and gin. Shaken with egg white it is often called a Boston Sour, and with a float of dry red wine it becomes a New York Sour. The template of spirit, citrus and sugar went on to shape the daiquiri, the margarita and the sidecar.

name: Aperol Spritz
description: A sunset-orange aperitivo of Aperol, prosecco, and soda built for golden-hour piazzas. Bitterness with training wheels, in the best possible way.
funFact: The spritz traces back to 19th-century Austrian soldiers stationed in the Veneto, who asked for local wine 'gespritzt' — splashed — with water to tame it.

ingredients.amount: Enough large cubes to fill a wine glass

steps: Fill a large wine glass generously with ice — more ice keeps it colder and less watery.
Pour in the chilled prosecco first (this keeps the Aperol from sinking into a syrupy layer).
Add the Aperol, then top with a splash of soda water.
Give one gentle stir with a bar spoon to marry the layers without killing the bubbles.
Slide in the orange half-wheel and serve with a straw or spoon-side stir.

originStory: The spritz began with Habsburg soldiers and officials in the nineteenth-century Veneto, who found the local wines strong and asked for them spritzed with water. Between the 1920s and 1930s Venetian bars began adding local bitter aperitifs, and Aperol, made in nearby Padua, became the basis of the most famous version; prosecco replaced still wine in the 1970s. The Aperol Spritz joined the International Bartenders Association's official list in 2011 and spread worldwide over the following decade.

name: Bellini
description: White peach puree lifted by prosecco into a pale-pink Venetian daydream. Insists on white peaches; yellow ones are considered a diplomatic incident.
funFact: Giuseppe Cipriani of Harry's Bar named it in 1948 because its pink glow reminded him of robes in paintings by the Renaissance master Giovanni Bellini.

steps: Make the puree: blend ripe peeled white peaches until smooth (a teaspoon of lemon juice keeps the color bright) and chill thoroughly — no ice goes in this drink, so everything must be cold.
Pour the white peach puree into a chilled champagne flute.
Slowly add the prosecco in stages, pausing as the foam rises.
Stir gently once with a bar spoon, lifting from the bottom, to blend the puree evenly.
Serve immediately, ungarnished, while the fizz is lively.
recipe.garnish: None traditional; a thin white peach slice on the rim if you like

originStory: Giuseppe Cipriani, who had founded Harry's Bar in Venice, gave the Bellini its name in 1948, mixing white peach purée with prosecco during the summer peach season. He named it after the fifteenth-century Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini, because its pink glow reminded him of the colour of a saint's robe in one of Bellini's paintings. The drink became the signature of Harry's Bar and travelled with the Cipriani name to restaurants around the world.

name: Champagne Cocktail
description: A bitters-soaked sugar cube dissolving at the bottom of a flute of champagne, releasing a slow ribbon of spiced bubbles. Victorian glamour, still operational.
funFact: It appears in Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide and later earned Hollywood immortality — Victor Laszlo pointedly orders champagne cocktails in 'Casablanca.'

steps: Chill a champagne flute and open a well-chilled bottle of champagne.
Set the sugar cube on a napkin and saturate it with 3-4 dashes of Angostura bitters.
Drop the soaked cube into the bottom of the flute.
Slowly top with champagne — pour gently down the side, as the cube makes it foam aggressively.
Express the lemon twist over the surface, drop it in, and serve while the cube is still streaming bubbles.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist, expressed and dropped in

originStory: The Champagne Cocktail was already a known American drink by 1862, when Jerry Thomas printed it in his pioneering bartender's guide, and it remained a staple of hotel bars through the Victorian era and beyond. Many later recipes added a splash of brandy or cognac to the original of sugar, bitters and wine. It also turns up in Casablanca, where Victor Laszlo orders champagne cocktails at Rick's café.

name: Death in the Afternoon
description: Absinthe clouding into iced champagne like slow opaline weather. Named after a book about bullfighting by the man who invented it, which explains a lot.
funFact: Ernest Hemingway contributed the recipe to a 1935 celebrity cocktail book with the instruction to 'drink three to five of these slowly.'

steps: Chill a champagne flute in the freezer and make sure the champagne is thoroughly iced — the louche depends on cold.
Pour the absinthe into the chilled flute.
Slowly top with champagne, pouring down the side of the glass, and watch the drink cloud into its milky opalescence.
Stop when it reaches, in Hemingway's words, the proper opalescent milkiness — about 4 oz of champagne.
Serve ungarnished, and pace yourself; this one is far stronger than it looks.
recipe.garnish: None — the opalescent louche is the show

originStory: Ernest Hemingway contributed Death in the Afternoon to So Red the Nose, or Breath in the Afternoon, a 1935 collection of cocktail recipes by well-known writers, and named it after his 1932 book about bullfighting. It is one of the few cocktails credited directly to a novelist, and it pairs two drinks closely associated with France. When absinthe returned to legal sale in the United States and much of Europe, bartenders revived it along with other absinthe classics.

name: French 75
description: Gin and lemon given a champagne afterburner. Elegant enough for a wedding, potent enough to be named after artillery.
funFact: It is named after the French 75mm field gun of World War I, whose recoil the drink's kick was said to resemble; Harry's New York Bar in Paris popularized it.

steps: Chill a champagne flute in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.
Add the gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds and double-strain into the chilled flute.
Slowly top with champagne, pouring down the side so it does not foam over.
Garnish with a long lemon twist draped into the glass and serve immediately.

originStory: The French 75 took its name from the French 75mm field gun of the First World War, and Harry MacElhone, who would soon take over Harry's New York Bar in Paris, recorded an early '75' in 1922, made with calvados, gin, grenadine and absinthe. The familiar mix of gin, lemon, sugar and champagne appeared in the 1927 book Here's How, and The Savoy Cocktail Book spread it under the French 75 name in 1930. New York's Stork Club later made it a fixture in America.

name: Mimosa
description: Champagne diluted with orange juice, or orange juice elevated by champagne, depending on your brunch philosophy. Named for a flower it happens to match in color.
funFact: It appeared at the Paris Ritz around 1925, four years after London's nearly identical Buck's Fizz — the main difference being that the Fizz pours more champagne.

ingredients.item: Champagne (or dry sparkling wine, well chilled)

steps: Chill both the champagne and the orange juice thoroughly — the drink takes no ice, so cold ingredients are everything.
Strain the fresh orange juice to remove heavy pulp for a cleaner texture (optional but nicer).
Pour the champagne into a chilled flute first, tilting the glass to preserve the bubbles.
Slowly add an equal measure of orange juice — pouring juice into wine keeps it from foaming over.
Give one very gentle stir and serve immediately; add an orange twist on the rim if you want a garnish.
recipe.garnish: Optional orange twist or small orange wedge on the rim

originStory: The Mimosa is usually credited to Frank Meier, bartender at the Ritz in Paris, around 1925, a few years after London's Buck's Club introduced the similar Buck's Fizz in 1921. It is named after the mimosa plant, whose bright yellow blossoms the drink's colour resembles. Easy to make with any sparkling wine, it became a fixture of hotel and restaurant brunch menus in the United States in the second half of the twentieth century.

name: Negroni Sbagliato
description: A Negroni in which the gin was 'mistakenly' replaced with prosecco — a happy accident promoted to permanent menu status.
funFact: Sbagliato means 'mistaken' — Bar Basso's Mirko Stocchetto grabbed sparkling wine instead of gin mid-Negroni in 1972, and a viral 2022 interview clip made his error a worldwide order.

ingredients.amount: Enough cubes (or one large cube) to fill a rocks glass

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice — one large clear cube is ideal.
Pour the Campari and sweet vermouth over the ice.
Stir briefly with a bar spoon to chill and combine.
Top with chilled prosecco and give one gentle lift with the spoon to integrate without flattening the fizz.
Garnish with the orange half-wheel and serve.
recipe.garnish: Orange half-wheel (or an expressed orange twist)

originStory: Sbagliato means mistaken, and the story told by Mirko Stocchetto, owner of Bar Basso in Milan, is that in 1972 he reached for a bottle of sparkling wine instead of gin while making a Negroni, and the customer liked the result. Bar Basso has served it ever since in its oversized goblets, and for decades it stayed a Milanese speciality. In 2022 an interview clip in which the actor Emma D'Arcy named it as their drink of choice went viral and made it a request in bars around the world.

name: Seelbach
description: Bourbon, Cointreau, a startling fourteen dashes of bitters, and champagne — a drink whose flavor is genuine even if its history was not.
funFact: Its celebrated 'lost 1917 recipe' was a hoax: in 2016 its true creator admitted he invented the drink at the Seelbach Hotel in 1995 and fabricated the vintage backstory.

steps: Chill a champagne flute in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.
Add the bourbon, Cointreau, and all fourteen dashes of bitters directly to the flute — the dash count sounds absurd, but it is the point of the drink.
Swirl or stir briefly with a bar spoon to combine the base.
Slowly top with chilled champagne, pouring down the side of the glass.
Express the orange twist over the surface, drop it in, and serve.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist, expressed and dropped in

originStory: The Seelbach was presented in 1995 as a rediscovered house cocktail of Louisville's Seelbach Hotel, supposedly a pre-Prohibition recipe, and the story was repeated in cocktail books for two decades. In 2016 its real creator, Adam Seger, who had run the hotel's bar, admitted that he had invented both the drink and its vintage backstory. The recipe has stayed on menus anyway, now with its true history attached.

name: Black Russian
description: The White Russian's darker, leaner elder: just vodka and coffee liqueur over ice. Two ingredients, zero small talk.
funFact: Bartender Gustave Tops created it at Brussels' Hotel Metropole in 1949 for Perle Mesta, the United States ambassador to Luxembourg.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice cubes (or one large cube) and let it chill for a moment.
Pour the vodka directly over the ice.
Add the coffee liqueur.
Stir gently with a barspoon for about 10 seconds to combine and lightly dilute.
Serve immediately in the rocks glass.

originStory: Belgian bartender Gustave Tops created the Black Russian in 1949 at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels, mixing it for Perle Mesta, the American socialite then serving as ambassador to Luxembourg. The name is usually read as pairing vodka, long associated with Russia, with the darkness of the coffee liqueur. Adding cream produced its better-known offspring, the White Russian, which first appears in print in the 1960s.

name: Boulevardier
description: A Negroni that traded gin for bourbon and moved somewhere with worse weather. Richer, rounder, and built for autumn.
funFact: It appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 book and is credited to Erskine Gwynne, an American expat who edited a Paris magazine called The Boulevardier.

ingredients.amount: For mixing, plus one large cube to serve

steps: Fill a mixing glass two-thirds full with ice.
Add the bourbon, Campari, and sweet vermouth.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until well chilled and slightly diluted.
Strain over a large ice cube in a chilled rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: The Boulevardier appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 book Barflies and Cocktails, where he credits it to Erskine Gwynne, an American writer in Paris who published a monthly magazine for expatriates called The Boulevardier. MacElhone's Harry's New York Bar, a gathering place for Americans in the city, was its natural home. The drink was largely forgotten for decades and returned with the cocktail revival of the early twenty-first century, when bartenders went looking for whiskey cousins of the Negroni.

name: Hanky Panky
description: Gin and sweet vermouth given a dark herbal jolt of Fernet-Branca. Proof that a few drops of the right bitter can rename an entire drink.
funFact: Ada 'Coley' Coleman, the Savoy's legendary head bartender, mixed it for actor Charles Hawtrey, who sipped it and declared, 'By Jove! That is the real hanky-panky!'

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer or with ice water while you mix.
Add the gin, sweet vermouth, and Fernet-Branca to a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until thoroughly chilled.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Express the oils from an orange twist over the drink and drop it in.

originStory: Ada Coleman, known as Coley, was head bartender at the American Bar of London's Savoy Hotel from the early 1900s, one of very few women in such a role. She created the Hanky Panky for the actor-manager Sir Charles Hawtrey, a regular who asked for something with punch; after tasting it he is said to have declared it the real hanky-panky, and the name stuck. Her successor Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930.

name: Manhattan
description: Rye and sweet vermouth in stately equilibrium, seasoned with aromatic bitters. The borough it is named for reinvents itself constantly; the drink refuses.
funFact: The famous tale that it debuted at a banquet hosted by Winston Churchill's mother is almost certainly false — she was in England, pregnant with Winston, at the time.

steps: Chill a cocktail glass in the freezer while you mix.
Add the rye, sweet vermouth, and Angostura bitters to a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until well chilled and silky.
Strain into the chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry dropped into the glass.

originStory: The Manhattan was being mixed in New York by the early 1880s, when it first appears in print, and early accounts tie it to the city's Manhattan Club. The popular story that it was created for a banquet thrown by Jennie Jerome, Winston Churchill's mother, falls apart because she was in England at the time, about to give birth to Winston. Rye was the original base, and the drink became the model for a whole family of whiskey and vermouth cocktails.

name: Martinez
description: Old Tom gin and sweet vermouth kissed with maraschino and bitters — the plush Victorian ancestor from which the Martini was ruthlessly streamlined.
funFact: Often called the missing link between the Manhattan and the Martini, it first appeared in print in 1884, and the town of Martinez, California claims it with a commemorative plaque.

steps: Chill a coupe before you begin.
Combine the Old Tom gin, sweet vermouth, maraschino liqueur, and bitters in a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until cold and lightly diluted.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: The Martinez first appears in print in 1884, in O.H. Byron's The Modern Bartender's Guide, and Jerry Thomas's 1887 guide gave it Old Tom gin, vermouth, maraschino and bitters. Its origin is disputed: one story credits Thomas at San Francisco's Occidental Hotel, mixing for a traveller bound for the town of Martinez, while Martinez itself says a local bartender invented it and marks the claim with a plaque. Either way, it is widely seen as a forerunner of the Martini.

name: Martini
description: An austere, glacial aperitif of gin and dry vermouth that rewards precision and punishes hesitation. Its ideal ratio has been argued about for over a century without resolution.
funFact: The Martini grew steadily drier through the 20th century — Winston Churchill reputedly said the only vermouth required was a glance at the bottle across the room.

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer — the colder the better.
Add the gin and dry vermouth to a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir briskly for about 30 seconds until glacially cold.
Strain into the chilled martini glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist expressed over the surface, or 1-3 olives on a pick — never both.

originStory: The Martini's origins are disputed, but it appears by that name in Harry Johnson's bartender's manual of 1888, made with Old Tom gin and vermouth and close kin to the Martinez. Some trace the name to the Martinez, others to the Martini brand of Italian vermouth. Dry versions followed early in the twentieth century, among the first printed by San Francisco bartender William Boothby, and the drink grew steadily drier, inspiring quips about vermouth, including one attributed to Churchill that is probably apocryphal.

name: Negroni
description: Equal parts gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth: bitter, scarlet, and entirely sure of itself. A slow sipper that gradually trains the palate to crave it.
funFact: Legend holds that in 1919 Count Camillo Negroni asked a Florence bartender to stiffen his usual Americano by swapping the soda water for gin.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice — one large cube melts slowest.
Pour in the gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth in equal measure.
Stir gently in the glass for 15-20 seconds until chilled.
Garnish with an orange slice (or an expressed orange twist) and serve.

originStory: The usual story says that around 1919, at the Caffè Casoni in Florence, Count Camillo Negroni asked bartender Fosco Scarselli to strengthen his Americano by replacing the soda water with gin, and Scarselli swapped the lemon garnish for orange to mark the difference. Historians still debate details of the account, including the count's title. The drink spread slowly beyond Italy and became one of the defining cocktails of the craft revival.

name: Old Fashioned
description: The fossil record of American drinking: spirit, sugar, and bitters arranged much as they were two centuries ago. It has survived every fad by simply refusing to evolve.
funFact: In 2015 Louisville, Kentucky declared the Old Fashioned its official cocktail and now celebrates it every June with 'Old Fashioned Fortnight.'

ingredients.amount: 1 cube or 1 tsp (or 0.25 oz / 7.5 ml simple syrup)
1 tsp (if using cube or granulated sugar)

steps: Place the sugar in a rocks glass, saturate it with the bitters and a teaspoon of water, and muddle until dissolved (skip muddling if using simple syrup).
Add the whiskey and stir briefly to combine.
Add one large ice cube.
Stir for 15-20 seconds until chilled and lightly diluted.
Express an orange twist over the surface, rub it around the rim, and drop it in.

originStory: The Old Fashioned descends from the original cocktail, defined in a Hudson, New York, newspaper in 1806 as spirits, sugar, water and bitters. As bartenders added liqueurs and absinthe to their whiskey cocktails later in the century, customers who wanted the plain version began asking for an old-fashioned one, and by the 1880s the name had stuck. Louisville's Pendennis Club claims to have popularised it, and in 2015 the city named it its official cocktail.

name: Sazerac
description: Rye, sugar, and Peychaud's bitters swirled in an absinthe-rinsed glass, served without ice and without hurry. New Orleans in liquid form.
funFact: In 2008 the Louisiana legislature proclaimed the Sazerac the official cocktail of New Orleans — one of very few drinks with a statutory hometown.

ingredients.amount: 1 cube or 1 tsp (or 0.25 oz / 7.5 ml simple syrup)
1 barspoon (~5 ml), to rinse the glass
For mixing only — served without ice

steps: Chill a rocks glass, then rinse it: pour in the absinthe, swirl to coat the inside, and discard the excess.
In a mixing glass, muddle the sugar with the Peychaud's bitters and a small splash of water until dissolved (or just add simple syrup).
Add the rye and fill the mixing glass two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed glass — no ice in the serving glass.
Express the lemon peel over the surface; traditionally it is discarded, but you may perch it on the rim.

originStory: The Sazerac takes its name from Sazerac de Forge et Fils, a cognac sold at New Orleans' Sazerac Coffee House, which opened in the 1850s, and the house cocktail was seasoned with the bitters created by Creole apothecary Antoine Peychaud. Rye whiskey later replaced the cognac, in part because phylloxera devastated French vineyards, and the absinthe rinse became part of the ritual. In 2008 the Louisiana legislature named it the official cocktail of New Orleans.

name: Vesper
