composition.process: The honey is heated with the spices before the spirit goes in, which is what marries them.

originStory: Krupnik is a spiced honey liqueur of Poland and Lithuania, where it is called krupnikas, and it is usually traced to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth of the sixteenth century or earlier.

name: Nalewka
description: Not one spirit but a whole Polish tradition: fruit, nuts or herbs steeped in spirit at home, sweetened, and left for months or years. Every family has recipes, and most of them are better than anything commercial.
funFact: Nalewki were served in Polish manor houses as a mark of hospitality, and old recipes specify ageing times of up to ten years before a bottle was considered ready.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass after a meal, at cellar temperature. Cherry (wiśniówka) and quince are the classics. Cold dulls the fruit, so avoid the freezer no matter what the bottle looks like.

composition.summary: Fruit or herbs macerated in spirit, sweetened and long-rested.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rectified spirit or vodka, often cut with fruit juice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Cherry, quince, sloe, walnut, rose petal, honey

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated only

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Months to years in glass

composition.process: Time is the active ingredient; a young nalewka tastes raw and a ten-year-old one tastes like liqueur.

originStory: Nalewka, from the Polish nalewać, to pour, is the Polish household tradition of steeping fruit, herbs, roots or nuts in spirit, sweetening them and leaving them to mature.

name: Spirytus Rektyfikowany
description: Rectified spirit at 96%, sold in Polish shops as an ingredient rather than a drink. It goes into nalewki, preserves and medicine cabinets. Drinking it neat is possible, inadvisable, and occasionally fatal.
funFact: At 96% it is close to the azeotropic limit of distillation, the point beyond which ethanol and water cannot be separated by distilling alone.

serve.glass: Used as an ingredient, not poured neat
serve.how: This is a base, not a drink. Dilute it or steep fruit and herbs in it to make nalewka, or cut it with water to vodka strength. Neat consumption risks serious injury to the throat and stomach.

composition.summary: Grain or potato spirit rectified to the practical limit of distillation.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain or potato

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Multiple rectification columns

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 95–96%, the azeotrope of ethanol and water

composition.process: Going above 96% requires chemical drying rather than distillation, which is why the number stops there.

originStory: Spirytus rektyfikowany is Polish rectified spirit, sold at about 95 percent and bought mainly as an ingredient for nalewki, fruit liqueurs and preserves.

name: Becherovka
description: Karlovy Vary's herbal bitter, cinnamon-forward and sweeter than most, invented as a stomach remedy in 1807 and never quite shaking the reputation. Locals call it the thirteenth spring, after the town's twelve mineral springs.
funFact: Only two people at a time know the full recipe, and they are the only ones permitted to enter the room where the botanicals are weighed.

serve.how: Cold and neat is the Czech way. The other national serve is the beton: Becherovka lengthened with tonic and a slice of lemon, which turns the cinnamon into something surprisingly refreshing.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit steeped with around twenty botanicals and spring water.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit and Karlovy Vary spring water

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Roughly 20 herbs and spices, cinnamon and clove dominant

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated in linen sacks, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Around two months in oak vats

composition.process: The local thermal spring water is claimed to be essential, which is convenient for a company that cannot move.

originStory: Becherovka began in 1807, when Josef Vitus Becher, a Carlsbad merchant, started selling a herbal bitter he had spent two years testing from a recipe worked out with Christian Frobrig, a visiting physician. It was first sold as English Bitter, and Becher's son Johann Nepomuk built the business into a factory from 1838. After the Second World War the drink took the name Becherovka, and the company says only two people know the full recipe and may enter the room where the herbs are mixed.

name: Fernet Stock
description: The Czech reading of Italian fernet: fourteen herbs, drier and less aggressively medicinal than Fernet-Branca, and drunk in far greater quantity per head. There is a citrus version that Czechs drink mixed with tonic.
funFact: Trieste-born Lionello Stock built the brand in the Adriatic, but it became so thoroughly Czech that most drinkers assume it always was.

serve.how: Cold and neat after a meal. The citrus expression mixed with tonic makes a bavorák, a standard Czech pub order that is far easier going than the original.

composition.summary: Fourteen herbs macerated in spirit, sweetened and rested.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 14 herbs including saffron, gentian, mint and rhubarb

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak

composition.process: Less sugar and more mint than the Italian original, which is why it reads as cleaner rather than sweeter.

originStory: Fernet Stock has been made at Božkov, near Plzeň, since 1927, by the company Lionello Stock had founded in Trieste with Carlo Camis in 1884 and extended into Czechoslovakia after the First World War. The Italian-style bitter took root so thoroughly that most Czechs think of it as their own. A citrus version followed in 1997 and quickly became one of the country's most popular spirits.

name: Tuzemák
description: Sugar-beet spirit flavoured to taste like rum, invented because the Habsburg empire had beets and no cane. EU rules forced it to drop the word rum from the label in 2004; Czechs ignored the change entirely.
funFact: The name means domestic, chosen when the label could no longer say tuzemský rum, which is what everybody still calls it.

serve.temp: room temp, or hot in a drink
serve.how: Mostly it goes into grog: tuzemák, hot water, sugar and lemon, which is the standard Czech cure for a winter cold. Neat it is sweet and simple, and it is the backbone of a great deal of Czech baking.

composition.summary: Sugar-beet spirit flavoured with rum essence and caramel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugar beet, not cane

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rum ether, caramel, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column-distilled, then flavoured

composition.process: It is an imitation by design and has been made openly as one for over a century.

originStory: Tuzemák grew out of the Habsburg empire's taste for rum and its lack of cane-growing colonies: distillers in Bohemia and Moravia made a domestic substitute from sugar-beet spirit flavoured with rum essence and sold it as tuzemský rum, domestic rum. When the Czech Republic joined the European Union, rules reserving the word rum for cane spirit forced a new name, and producers settled on tuzemák. Many Czechs still simply call it rum.

name: Hruškovice
description: Czech and Slovak pear brandy, usually from Williams pears, clear and unaged. The good ones smell so strongly of fresh pear that people assume something has been added, and nothing has.
funFact: Some producers grow the pear inside the bottle by fixing it over young fruit on the branch, then filling around it at harvest.

serve.how: Cool rather than iced, in a small pour after a heavy meal. Over-chilling closes down the pear aroma completely, which is the only reason to be drinking it.

composition.summary: Williams pears fermented whole and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Williams or local pear varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, tight cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass, not wood

composition.process: Pears ferment slowly and unevenly, so the mash is watched more carefully than plum or apple.

originStory: Hruškovice, from hruška, pear, is the pear brandy of the Czech and Slovak fruit-distilling tradition, most often made from Williams pears.

name: Meruňkovice
description: Moravian apricot brandy, the Czech cousin of Austria's Marillenbrand and Hungary's barackpálinka. South Moravia's orchards give a slightly rounder, jammier spirit than the Wachau does.
funFact: Home distilling is legal in Czechia through licensed communal stills, so most villages have one that runs flat out every autumn.

serve.how: Cellar temperature, neat, in a small glass. Czechs drink it before the meal as often as after, and a good one is generous enough on the nose that you can smell it across a table.

composition.summary: Apricots fermented whole and distilled twice in copper.

components.label: Base
components.detail: South Moravian apricots

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double pot distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass or steel

composition.process: A proportion of stones is often fermented with the fruit to deepen the almond note.

originStory: Meruňkovice is the apricot brandy of South Moravia's orchards, a cousin of Austria's Marillenbrand and Hungary's barackpálinka.

name: Czech Absinth
description: Wormwood-forward and usually made without anise, so it does not louche when water is added. Purists refuse to accept it as absinthe at all, and the missing e on the label is where that argument starts.
funFact: The burning sugar cube ritual that tourists associate with absinthe was invented in 1990s Prague and has nothing to do with the French tradition.

serve.how: Dilute three or four parts iced water to one of spirit, poured slowly. Skip the flaming sugar cube, which scorches the herbs and is pure theatre. Without anise it will stay clear rather than turning milky.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit macerated or distilled with wormwood, little or no anise.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, sometimes mint and lemon balm; anise usually absent

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Often macerated and coloured rather than distilled

composition.process: No anise means no louche, which is the clearest way to tell the Czech style from the French.

originStory: Czech absinth as it is sold today dates from the early 1990s, when Radomil Hill, whose family liqueur firm had been founded by Albín Hill in 1920, began producing it. Exports of Hill's to Britain later that decade helped spark a wider absinthe revival, though claims that the firm made absinth before the war remain unproven. Many Czech versions contain little or no anise, so they do not cloud with water, and the ritual of setting fire to a sugar cube is credited to Czech drinkers of the 1990s rather than to the French tradition.

name: Borovička
description: Slovak juniper spirit, drier and rougher-edged than gin because the berries are fermented or distilled directly rather than steeped into finished alcohol. Sharp, resinous and completely unsweetened.
funFact: Slovak, Czech and Hungarian producers all claim versions of it, and the Slovak one holds an EU geographical indication.

serve.how: Cold and neat, in one measure, with a beer alongside. It is a mountain and pub spirit rather than a sipping one, and Slovaks will tell you it is good for a cold, which it is not.

composition.summary: Juniper berries distilled with or fermented into grain spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper berries, sometimes alone

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Berries distilled directly rather than macerated

composition.process: Distilling the berries rather than steeping them gives a greener, harsher juniper than any gin.

originStory: Borovička takes its name from borievka, the Slovak word for juniper, and is Slovakia's juniper spirit, several regional versions of which carry EU geographical indications.

name: Demänovka
description: A herbal liqueur from the Low Tatras built on honey and mountain plants, made in bitter and sweet versions. Named after the Demänovská valley, and about as Slovak as a bottle can get.
funFact: The recipe uses fourteen herbs gathered in the Low Tatras and has been made in Liptovský Mikuláš since the 1950s.

serve.how: Cold and neat after eating. The sweet version is the easier introduction; the bitter one is closer to an amaro and works over ice with tonic if you want it longer.

composition.summary: Fourteen Tatra herbs macerated in spirit with honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 14 herbs from the Low Tatras

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended with honey

composition.process: Honey rather than sugar syrup gives it the weight that separates it from a plain herbal bitter.

originStory: Demänovka is a Slovak herbal liqueur named after the Demänová valley in the Low Tatras, near Liptovský Mikuláš, and made in sweet and bitter versions.

name: Törkölypálinka
description: The pomace version of pálinka, distilled from what is left after the wine press rather than from whole fruit. Grippier and more rustic than fruit pálinka, and protected under the same Hungarian rules.
funFact: Hungarian law protects pálinka so tightly that adding sugar, colouring or flavouring disqualifies a spirit from using the name at all.

serve.how: Slightly cooler than room temperature and never iced; Hungarians are emphatic that freezing pálinka is an insult to it. Small pours, after a meal, and give the glass a swirl first.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and double-distilled in Hungary.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape skins, pips and stems from Hungarian wine regions

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double pot distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Optional; wood-aged versions exist

composition.process: Everything must be grown, fermented, distilled and bottled in Hungary for the name to apply.

originStory: Törkölypálinka is the pomace branch of Hungary's pálinka tradition, distilled from the grape skins and seeds left after winemaking and protected under the same Hungarian rules as fruit pálinka.

name: Unicum
description: Hungary's national bitter: forty herbs macerated and aged in oak beneath Budapest, in a round bottle with a red cross. Blacker and more medicinal than Jägermeister, and considerably less forgiving.
funFact: The Zwack family smuggled the recipe out during the communist years and sold a deliberately falsified version behind the Iron Curtain until they could return in 1989.

serve.how: Cold and neat, before or after a heavy meal. Unicum Szilva, the plum-aged version, is markedly sweeter and the better place to start if bitterness is not your thing.

composition.summary: Over forty herbs macerated and distilled, then aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: More than 40 herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Part macerated, part distilled, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Six months in oak casks in cellars under Budapest

composition.process: The cellar ageing is genuine and the casks are large, so the wood rounds rather than flavours.

originStory: Unicum is traced to 1790, when Dr József Zwack, physician to the Habsburg court, is said to have created the bitter for Emperor Joseph II, who supposedly declared it ein Unikum, a unique thing. The Zwack family built a distillery in Pest, but after the communist takeover the business was nationalised and the family went into exile, while the state produced its own version. After the fall of communism Péter Zwack returned and restored production to the original recipe.

name: Žganje
description: Slovenia's household fruit brandy, made from whatever the orchard gives up: plum, pear, apple, quince. Every farm has a version and no two are alike, which is the appeal and the risk.
funFact: Slovenia permits households to distil their own fruit for personal use, so a great deal of the country's žganje never reaches a shop.

serve.how: Poured at the start of a visit rather than the end, which is the Slovenian custom. Room temperature, small measures, and refusing the second one takes more skill than accepting it.

composition.summary: Farm fruit fermented and pot-distilled, usually unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plum, pear, apple or quince

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot still, often shared between neighbours

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; some rest in oak or ash

composition.process: Quality swings enormously with the maker, since almost all of it is produced outside any commercial standard.

originStory: Žganje, from the Slovene žgati, to burn, is Slovenia's household fruit brandy, distilled from plums, pears, apples or whatever the orchard yields.

name: Brinjevec
description: Slovenian juniper brandy in which the berries are fermented and distilled rather than infused, producing something far closer to a fruit brandy than to gin. Fierce, resinous, and traditionally taken as medicine.
funFact: It takes an enormous quantity of juniper berries to produce a single litre, which is why genuine brinjevec is scarce and frequently faked with flavoured spirit.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, in small measures. Slovenians reach for it when someone has an upset stomach, and it has a long folk reputation as a remedy that the taste does nothing to undermine.

composition.summary: Juniper berries fermented and distilled as the sole base.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Juniper berries, fermented

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still; the berries are the fermentable, not a flavouring

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Because the berry itself is fermented, this is technically a fruit brandy rather than a juniper-flavoured spirit.

originStory: Brinjevec takes its name from brin, the Slovene word for juniper, and is made by fermenting and distilling the berries themselves, which makes it closer to a fruit brandy than to gin.

name: Pelinkovec
description: Wormwood bitter from Slovenia and Croatia, very dark, barely sweetened and considerably more austere than the Italian amari. The name comes from pelin, the local word for wormwood.
funFact: In the former Yugoslavia it was drunk with tonic and a slice of lemon, a serve that has outlived the country it came from.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or long with tonic and lemon, which cuts the bitterness enough to make it an aperitif. It is drier than Jägermeister and should not be treated as a substitute.

composition.summary: Wormwood and herbs macerated in spirit with minimal sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Wormwood, gentian, bitter orange, liquorice root

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

composition.process: Restraint with sugar is what keeps it on the bitter side of a liqueur.

originStory: Pelinkovec takes its name from pelin, the South Slavic word for wormwood, and is the dark wormwood bitter of Slovenia, Croatia and their neighbours.

name: Samogon
description: Russian and Ukrainian home distillate, made from grain, beet, potato or fruit depending on what is cheap. Legal to make for personal use, illegal to sell, and produced in quantities nobody can measure.
funFact: The word means self-distilled, and Soviet anti-alcohol campaigns in the 1980s drove production up rather than down.

serve.how: Cold, neat, with food on the table, which is not optional in the culture it comes from. Quality varies from carefully double-distilled and charcoal-filtered to genuinely dangerous, so provenance matters more than usual.

composition.summary: Home-fermented mash distilled in small improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain, sugar beet, potato or fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot stills, often homemade; quality depends on the cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rarely aged; sometimes infused afterwards

composition.process: A careful maker discards the heads and tails; a careless one does not, which is where the danger lies.

originStory: Samogon, self-distilled, is the home-made spirit of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, distilled from grain, sugar beet, potatoes or fruit.

name: Nastoyka
description: The Russian tradition of infusing spirit with fruit, roots or spice. Pertsovka takes pepper and honey, khrenovukha takes horseradish, and there are versions built on everything from cranberry to birch bud.
funFact: Khrenovukha, the horseradish version, is credited to Peter the Great, who is supposed to have decreed that vodka be infused with it as a matter of policy.

serve.how: Freezer cold, neat, and with food. Pepper and horseradish versions are drunk with fatty or salted dishes; the sweet berry ones come out after the meal instead.

composition.summary: Vodka infused with fruit, roots or spice, sometimes sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Vodka or rectified spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Pepper, honey, horseradish, cranberry, birch, herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused only

composition.process: A nastoyka is infused and dry; a nalivka is the sweeter, fruitier relative.

originStory: Nastoyka, from the Russian word for infusion, is vodka steeped with fruit, berries, roots, herbs or spices, a tradition kept in Russian homes and by commercial distillers alike.

name: Horilka
description: Ukrainian vodka, usually from wheat or rye, and a separate national tradition rather than a translation of the Russian word. The pepper-and-honey version is the one that travels.
funFact: The name comes from the verb to burn, the same root as the English brandy by way of burnt wine.

serve.how: From the freezer, neat, and always with something to eat. Ukrainians pair it with salo, cured pork fat on black bread, and the combination is far better calibrated than it sounds.

composition.summary: Wheat or rye distilled to neutrality and cut with water.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wheat or rye

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column-distilled, charcoal-filtered

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Filtration is where most producers claim their difference, since the base spirit is close to neutral.

originStory: Horilka, from the Ukrainian hority, to burn, is Ukraine's word for strong spirit and its own vodka tradition, often flavoured with honey, pepper, herbs or fruit.

name: Pertsivka
description: Horilka infused with honey and chilli, amber-coloured and warming in the literal sense. Ukraine drinks it against cold weather, and it does the job better than most things sold for the purpose.
funFact: Bottles frequently include whole chillies and peppercorns, which keep infusing and make the last measure noticeably hotter than the first.

serve.how: Cold and neat, with rich or fatty food. The honey softens the front and the chilli arrives afterwards, so drink it in one measure rather than sipping and waiting.

composition.summary: Grain spirit infused with honey, chilli and peppercorns.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wheat or rye horilka

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Honey, red chilli, black peppercorn, sometimes allspice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused, not redistilled

composition.process: Honey goes in first to round the spirit, then the chilli, which continues to extract in the bottle.

originStory: Pertsivka, from perets, pepper, is Ukrainian horilka infused with chilli peppers and often honey, frequently bottled with whole chillies inside.

name: Krambambulya
description: A Belarusian spiced honey liqueur revived from a seventeenth-century recipe, dark and heavily spiced, and drunk hot in a country that has serious winters. The name is borrowed from an old German drinking song.
funFact: The original Krambambuli was a Danzig cherry liqueur; Belarus took the name, dropped the cherries, and built something else around honey and spice.

serve.how: Warmed gently with the spices left in, which is how it is drunk through a Belarusian winter. At room temperature it works as a digestive, and the spicing is heavy enough that a small pour is plenty.

composition.summary: Vodka or spirit blended with honey and a heavy spice load.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain spirit or vodka

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Honey, clove, cinnamon, nutmeg, black pepper, galangal

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended, sometimes gently heated

composition.process: Recipes vary widely because it was a household drink long before anyone bottled it commercially.

originStory: The name Krambambuli first belonged to a red cherry liqueur from a distillery in Danzig, now Gdańsk, and it travelled widely through a German student song. In Belarus it names something different, spirit warmed with honey and spices, which Belarusian tradition links to the gentry of the old Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and producers there now bottle it as a liqueur.

name: Riga Black Balsam
description: Twenty-four botanicals at 45%, sold in an opaque black ceramic bottle since 1752 and tasting like tar, liquorice and bitter root. Latvia's most recognisable export and an acquired taste even there.
funFact: The ceramic bottle is not decorative: it blocks light and holds temperature, which is how the recipe was shipped across the Baltic in the eighteenth century.

serve.temp: cold, or hot in a drink
serve.how: Neat and cold takes some commitment. Latvians more often stir it into hot tea or black coffee, or mix it with blackcurrant juice, which tames the tar without losing the herbs.

composition.summary: 24 plants, roots and berries macerated in spirit with honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 24 including valerian, birch bud, linden blossom, bilberry, ginger

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated in oak barrels, then blended with honey

composition.process: It was formulated as a medicine, and Catherine the Great is said to have credited it with curing her illness in Riga.

originStory: Riga Black Balsam is traced to 1752, when Abraham Kunze, an apothecary in Riga, created a herbal balsam whose recipe is still the basis of the drink. It is now made by Latvijas Balzams from twenty-four ingredients and sold in a dark ceramic bottle, and the company says only its head liquor master and two apprentices know the exact recipe.

name: Trejos Devynerios
description: Three nines, in translation: twenty-seven herbs, roots and spices in a Lithuanian bitter that began life as a pharmacy preparation. Dry, resinous, and not remotely designed to be pleasant.
funFact: It was sold in Soviet pharmacies as a herbal tincture, which meant it could be bought when alcohol itself was rationed.

serve.how: Neat, in a small measure, after eating. Lithuanians also add it to tea with honey when something is going around. It is a bitter in the older medicinal sense rather than a modern amaro.

composition.summary: 27 herbs and roots macerated in spirit, barely sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 27 herbs, roots, seeds and barks

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then blended

composition.process: The number in the name refers to the count of botanicals, three times nine, which had folk-medicinal significance.

originStory: Trejos devynerios, three nines, is a Lithuanian herbal bitter named for the twenty-seven herbs, roots and spices in its blend.

name: Vana Tallinn
description: Estonia's rum-based liqueur, flavoured with citrus oil, vanilla and cinnamon, and sold in enough gift boxes to fund a small country. Sweet, warming, and genuinely good in coffee.
funFact: Created in 1960, it became the standard souvenir of Soviet-era Tallinn and remains the drink most visitors leave the city carrying.

serve.glass: Small cordial glass or coffee cup
serve.how: Neat after dinner, or stirred into black coffee with a little cream floated on top, which is the local habit. The cream version, Vana Tallinn Cream, is a different and much sweeter product.

composition.summary: Rum blended with citrus oils, vanilla and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Jamaican and Cuban rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Citrus oil, vanilla, cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended, not redistilled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40%, 45% and 50% expressions

composition.process: A higher-strength version exists at 50%, which carries the spice considerably better than the standard bottling.

originStory: Vana Tallinn, Old Tallinn, was created in 1960 at the Tallinn distillery now called Liviko, its recipe devised by master distiller Ilse Maar with Bernhard Jürno and Jaan Siimo. The rum-based blend with citrus, vanilla and cinnamon became the classic souvenir of Soviet-era Tallinn and has been made without interruption since. It remained a single product until variants at other strengths appeared in 1999, and it is now sold in dozens of countries.

name: Orujo
description: Galicia's pomace spirit, clear and fiery, and the base of the queimada ritual in which it is set alight in a clay bowl while someone recites a spell against witches. That part is not a tourist invention.
funFact: The queimada conxuro, the spell recited while the orujo burns, was written in the 1950s but draws on genuinely older Galician folk practice.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal, or as the herbal and cream versions that Galician bars keep alongside the clear one. For queimada it is burned with sugar, coffee beans and lemon peel in a clay bowl.

composition.summary: Grape pomace from Galician wine fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Skins, pips and stems, largely Albariño and Mencía

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alquitara or pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; herbal and cream versions are infused after

composition.process: Traditional alquitaras are small enough that distilling was historically done village by village.

originStory: Orujo is the pomace spirit of Galicia, distilled from the skins and seeds left after winemaking, and the base of the queimada, a flamed punch served while a spell called the conxuro is recited.

name: Pacharán
description: Navarrese sloes steeped in anise spirit until the liquid runs deep red, then sweetened. Softer than sloe gin and unmistakably aniseed, it is what northern Spain drinks when the meal is over.
funFact: Navarre protects it by denomination, requiring at least 125 grams of sloes per litre and a minimum steeping period before bottling.

serve.how: Over a couple of ice cubes, after dinner, which is how it is served in every bar in Navarre. It is sweet enough that ice is an improvement rather than a compromise.

composition.summary: Blackthorn sloes macerated in anise-flavoured spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Anisado, an aniseed-flavoured neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Wild or cultivated sloes, minimum 125g per litre

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for one to eight months

composition.process: The sloes must be steeped, never merely flavoured, and the colour comes entirely from the fruit skins.

originStory: Pacharán takes its name from patxaran, the Basque word for sloe, and is Navarre's liqueur of wild sloes steeped in anise spirit, now protected as Pacharán Navarro.

name: Licor 43
description: Forty-three ingredients, vanilla and citrus loudest among them, in a bright yellow Spanish liqueur that tastes far more of custard than of anything herbal. Enormously popular in Spain and largely misunderstood elsewhere.
funFact: The company traces the recipe to a Carthaginian liqueur the Romans tried to ban, which is an excellent story and impossible to verify.

serve.how: Over ice with cold milk poured on top, which is the Barraquito or Leche y Licor 43 and by far the most common Spanish serve. Neat over ice also works, and it goes well into coffee.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with citrus, vanilla and 43 botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: 43 ingredients: citrus fruits, vanilla, herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended, then sweetened

composition.process: Vanilla dominates so thoroughly that most tasters never register the other forty-two.

originStory: Licor 43 was launched in 1946 in Cartagena by the Zamora siblings and their partner Emilio Restoy, who named it for the forty-three ingredients in its recipe. The company links it to a legendary golden elixir of ancient Carthago Nova, the city's Roman name, a story that cannot be verified. The family firm, Diego Zamora, has since made it one of the most widely distributed Spanish liqueurs.

name: Anís
description: Spain's aniseed liqueur, made dulce or seco, and a fixture of village bars and grandmothers' cupboards alike. Anís del Mono has been sold in the same faceted, monkey-labelled bottle since 1870.
funFact: The monkey on the Anís del Mono label was drawn with Darwin's face, a joke about evolution that scandalised Catalonia in 1870.

serve.how: Seco neat and cold; dulce over ice or with a splash of water, which turns it cloudy. It is also drunk with coffee as a carajillo, and in some regions poured directly into it.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit distilled or macerated with green anise and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green anise seed, sometimes star anise and fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sweetened to dulce or seco

composition.process: Anethole from the anise is what clouds the liquid when water is added, the same effect as in ouzo and pastis.

originStory: Anise spirits have been distilled in Spain for centuries, with towns such as Chinchón and Cazalla known for them, but one of the best-known bottles came from Badalona in the second half of the nineteenth century. There the brothers Vicente and José Bosch launched Anís del Mono, whose monkey label is often read as a joke about Darwin, though other explanations exist. A poster competition the firm held at the end of the century produced Ramon Casas's celebrated design.

name: Hierbas
description: The Balearic herb liqueur, strongest in Ibiza and Mallorca, made by steeping local plants in anise spirit. Bottles often carry whole sprigs of rosemary, fennel and thyme still floating inside.
funFact: Ibicencan families each keep their own herb mix, and the island protects Hierbas Ibicencas under its own denomination.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after eating, or over ice in summer. The dulce version is thick and sweet; the seca is drier and closer to a straight herbal anise.

composition.summary: Anise spirit macerated with Balearic herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Anise-flavoured spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Rosemary, thyme, fennel, lemon verbena, juniper, orange leaf

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated; sprigs often left in the bottle

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 20–40% depending on style

composition.process: Leaving the herbs in means the liqueur keeps changing on the shelf, which producers treat as a feature.

originStory: Hierbas is the herbal anise liqueur of the Balearic Islands, made by steeping local plants such as rosemary, fennel and thyme in anise spirit and protected as Hierbas de Mallorca and Hierbas Ibicencas.

name: Ron Miel
description: Canary Islands honey rum: local rum blended with palm or bee honey until it is thick, sweet and only about 20% alcohol. The archipelago's own category, and almost never found off the islands.
funFact: The Canaries grew sugar cane from the fifteenth century and supplied the cuttings that started the industry in the Caribbean.

serve.how: Chilled and neat in a small glass, or over ice. Canarians drink it after dinner and pour it over ice cream. It is sweet enough that anything more than a small measure becomes hard work.

composition.summary: Canary rum blended with honey and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rum distilled in the Canary Islands

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bee honey or palm honey, vanilla, cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: Palm honey, made from boiled palm sap rather than by bees, gives the more traditional version its darker edge.

originStory: Ron miel is Canary Islands rum blended with honey, a regional style from islands that have grown sugarcane since the fifteenth century, now protected as Ronmiel de Canarias.

name: Aguardente Vínica
description: Portuguese wine brandy, and the spirit that stops port fermenting. Most of it never reaches a glass on its own, which is a shame, because the aged bottlings can stand comfortably beside a young cognac.
funFact: Port producers historically used a neutral grape spirit of exactly 77% to fortify their wine, a figure fixed by regulation for decades.

serve.how: Neat after dinner. Aged Portuguese brandies are usually softer and sweeter than French ones, so resist the urge to warm the glass; heat pushes them toward syrup.

composition.summary: Wine distilled and aged in oak in Portugal.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Portuguese wine, often from the Douro or Bairrada

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, from a few years to several decades

composition.process: The unaged, near-neutral version is what goes into port; the aged version is the drink.

originStory: Aguardente vínica is Portuguese wine brandy, best known as the grape spirit added to port to stop its fermentation, and Lourinhã, north of Lisbon, is a region demarcated for brandy alone.

name: Aguardente Bagaceira
description: Portugal's pomace brandy, the rougher country cousin of the wine brandy. Northern Portugal drinks it after coffee, poured straight into the cup once the coffee is finished, a habit called café com cheirinho.
funFact: Café com cheirinho translates as coffee with a little scent, which understates the quantity most people pour.

serve.glass: Small glass, or into the coffee cup
serve.how: A small measure after a meal, or the northern habit of swilling it around the empty espresso cup and drinking it from there. Aged versions in oak are smoother and worth seeking out.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and distilled after the press.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Skins, pips and stems from Portuguese winemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, often in small rural distilleries

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Frequently unaged; velha versions are oak-rested

composition.process: Vinho verde country produces some of the sharpest and most aromatic examples.

originStory: Bagaceira takes its name from bagaço, Portuguese for grape pomace, and is the pomace brandy of Portugal's wine regions, above all the north.

name: Medronho
description: Distilled from the fruit of the strawberry tree, which grows wild across the Algarve and Alentejo hills and ripens a full year after it flowers. Genuinely difficult to make well and frequently made badly.
funFact: The medronho fruit ferments slightly on the tree, which is why deer and birds in the Algarve have a reputation for behaving oddly in autumn.

serve.how: Cool, neat, in a small pour after a meal. Honey-sweetened versions, melosa, are common in Algarve bars. The unadulterated version is the one to look for, and it should smell of the fruit rather than of alcohol.

composition.summary: Wild strawberry-tree fruit fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Arbutus unedo fruit, hand-picked from wild trees

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot stills, often licensed to individual growers

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: The fruit is fragile and must be picked ripe and fermented quickly, which limits the scale of production.

originStory: Medronho is distilled from the fruit of the strawberry tree, Arbutus unedo, which grows wild in the hills of the Algarve and Alentejo, especially around Monchique.

name: Ginjinha
description: Sour cherry liqueur, drunk standing up in tiny Lisbon bars that sell almost nothing else. A shot costs small change, arrives with or without a cherry in it, and is finished on the pavement outside.
glassware: Small shot glass or chocolate cup
funFact: In Óbidos it is served in a small cup made of dark chocolate, which you drink from and then eat.

serve.glass: Small shot glass, or an edible chocolate cup
serve.how: One small glass, standing, com or sem — with or without the steeped cherry at the bottom. Always com, for the record. Room temperature is traditional and chilling it flattens the cinnamon.

composition.summary: Sour ginja cherries steeped in aguardente with sugar and cinnamon.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aguardente or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ginja sour cherries, sugar, cinnamon, sometimes clove

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for several months

composition.process: Some producers crush a portion of the stones with the fruit, which is where the almond note comes from.

originStory: Lisbon credits ginjinha, from ginja, the sour cherry, to Francisco Espinheira, a Galician who steeped the cherries in aguardente with sugar and cinnamon, though accounts differ on whether he was himself a friar or took a friar's advice. The bar at Largo de São Domingos that carries his name dates its beginnings to 1840 and still pours it. In Óbidos it is often served in a small cup of dark chocolate, eaten once the drink is finished.

name: Licor Beirão
description: A seed and herb liqueur from the Beira region, made since 1929 and marketed for decades as the liqueur of Portugal, which it more or less is. Sweet, warmly spiced, and drunk at every temperature.
funFact: Its advertising is a national in-joke; the slogan O licor de Portugal has appeared on billboards positioned to be visible from motorway traffic jams for decades.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a shot glass, or long with tonic and lime as a caipirinha-style Beirão. Portuguese bars also pour it over ice with lemon in summer.

composition.summary: Seeds and herbs distilled in water and alcohol, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Cardamom, anise, eucalyptus, lavender, cinnamon, mint

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double-distilled with the botanicals, then sweetened

composition.process: The seeds come from several continents, and the exact blend has never been published.

originStory: Licor Beirão began in the nineteenth century as a pharmacy preparation in Lousã, in the Beira region, and went on being made in a small factory run by the original maker's son-in-law. It took its name in 1929, when it won a gold medal at the second Beirão Congress in Castelo Branco. In 1940 José Carranca Redondo bought the factory and the secret recipe, and his advertising, proclaiming it the liqueur of Portugal, made it a national brand.

name: Aguardente de Cana
description: Madeiran cane spirit, distilled from fresh juice rather than molasses, which technically makes it an agricole rum. It exists mainly to be turned into poncha, the island's honey-and-lemon cure-all.
funFact: Poncha is stirred with a caralhinho, a grooved wooden stick made for the purpose and found in every bar on the island.

serve.how: Rarely drunk neat. Mixed into poncha with lemon juice and honey and stirred hard with a wooden muddler until it emulsifies, then drunk immediately while still cloudy.

composition.summary: Fresh sugarcane juice fermented and distilled on Madeira.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed Madeiran cane juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column or pot still, unaged

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; some aged expressions exist

composition.process: Cane has been grown on Madeira since the fifteenth century, which predates the Caribbean industry entirely.

originStory: Aguardente de cana is Madeira's cane spirit, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice rather than molasses, protected as Rum da Madeira and best known as the base of poncha.

name: Italian Brandy
description: Wine brandy made across Italy, softer and sweeter than cognac, and long treated as a domestic staple rather than a luxury. Vecchia Romagna and Stravecchio Branca are the names most Italians grew up with.
funFact: Italy could not legally call it cognac after 1948, so producers coined arzente, a word Gabriele d'Annunzio invented, before settling on brandy.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or in coffee as a caffè corretto, which is what most of it is actually used for. Italian brandy tends to be sweeter than French, so it needs less warming.

composition.summary: Italian wine distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Trebbiano and other Italian white wine

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Continuous or pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum one year, quality grades far longer, in Slavonian or Limousin oak

composition.process: Slavonian oak is more neutral than French, which keeps Italian brandy leaning fruity rather than woody.

originStory: Italian brandy grew into an industry in the nineteenth century, and one of its founding houses was set up in Bologna by Jean Bouton, a French distiller who italianised his name to Buton. Italian producers long sold their brandy as cognac, until international rules reserved that name for France, which is how Cognac Buton became Vecchia Romagna. Gabriele d'Annunzio is credited with coining arzente as an Italian alternative, but brandy is the word that stuck.

name: Amaro
description: Not one drink but a whole Italian category: bittersweet herbal digestives, one for nearly every region, ranging from gentle and orange-scented to aggressively medicinal. Montenegro, Averna, Nonino and Braulio are all amari and none tastes like another.
funFact: Most amari began as monastic or pharmacy preparations, and several are still made to recipes written by nineteenth-century chemists.

serve.how: Neat after a meal at room temperature, which is how Italy drinks it. Lighter amari take ice and soda well; heavy ones do not. In cocktails they swap in for vermouth to add bitterness without more alcohol.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit or wine macerated with bitter herbs, roots and peel, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, sometimes a wine base

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, cinchona, rhubarb, wormwood, citrus peel, spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated or infused, then sweetened and rested

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Varies; some rest in oak for years

composition.process: Bitterness comes from roots and barks, sweetness from sugar syrup, and the balance between them defines the house style.

originStory: Amaro, Italian for bitter, covers a family of herbal liqueurs that grew from monastery and pharmacy preparations. Many of the famous names date from the nineteenth century, when men such as Ausano Ramazzotti, a pharmacist in Milan, and Salvatore Averna in Caltanissetta turned recipes into brands. Nearly every region has its own, using local herbs, roots and citrus, and no single first amaro can be named.

name: Mirto
description: Sardinian myrtle liqueur, made from the berries for the dark red version and the leaves for the white. Every Sardinian household makes it, and every restaurant on the island pours it unasked at the end of a meal.
funFact: Myrtle grows wild across the Sardinian maquis, and the berries are picked between November and January when they are fully black.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small chilled glass, after dinner. Warm mirto turns medicinal quickly. The red is sweeter and more common; the white, from the leaves, is drier and harder to find.

composition.summary: Wild myrtle berries or leaves macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Myrtus communis berries (rosso) or leaves (bianco)

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for several weeks, then sweetened

composition.process: The berries are never crushed, only steeped, since crushing releases a harsh tannin.

originStory: Mirto is Sardinia's myrtle liqueur, the red made from the ripe dark berries and the white from the young leaves and shoots of the shrub that grows wild across the island.

name: Strega
description: Seventy herbs and saffron in a bright yellow liqueur from Benevento, a town with a long reputation for witchcraft. Strega means witch, and the branding has committed to it entirely for a hundred and sixty years.
funFact: Local legend holds that a couple who drink Strega together will be united forever, which the company has never once discouraged anyone from believing.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice in summer. It is also poured over gelato and used in Neapolitan baking, where it flavours the sponge in a great many cakes.

composition.summary: About seventy botanicals distilled, then coloured with saffron.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Around 70, including mint, fennel, juniper and Ceylon cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the botanicals, then sweetened

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak vats before bottling

composition.process: The yellow is saffron and nothing else, which is why it is expensive to make.

originStory: Strega was created in 1860 in Benevento by Giuseppe Alberti, whose family business turned a recipe of some seventy herbs and spices, coloured gold with saffron, into a brand. The name means witch, after Benevento's old legends of witches gathering under a walnut tree, and the branding has embraced it ever since. In 1947 Guido Alberti, with the writer Maria Bellonci, founded the Premio Strega, now one of Italy's most important literary prizes.

name: Galliano
description: Vanilla and anise in a bottle so tall it does not fit on most shelves, named after an Italian war hero and built for the American market. Without it there is no Harvey Wallbanger, which may or may not be an argument in its favour.
funFact: The bottle shape is modelled on a Roman column, and its height was a deliberate bid for visibility on crowded back bars.

serve.temp: room temp or in a long drink
serve.glass: Cordial glass, or highball in a drink
serve.how: Neat in a small glass after dinner, or floated on top of a screwdriver to make a Harvey Wallbanger. The higher-strength L'Autentico is drier and better in cocktails than the standard bottling.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit infused with vanilla, anise and herbs, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Star anise, Mediterranean anise, vanilla, juniper, lavender, ginger

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Botanicals distilled separately, then blended with vanilla infusion

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 30% standard, 42.3% for L'Autentico

composition.process: Vanilla is added as an infusion after distillation, since distilling it would strip the character out.

originStory: Galliano was created in 1896 in Livorno by the distiller Arturo Vaccari, who named it after Giuseppe Galliano, an Italian officer who had become famous for defending a fort at Mekele during the First Italo-Ethiopian War. Its vanilla and anise recipe and tall bottle, shaped like a classical Roman column, made it stand out on back bars. It gained international fame in the seventies through the Harvey Wallbanger, a vodka and orange drink topped with a float of Galliano.

name: Frangelico
description: Hazelnut liqueur from Piedmont, with cocoa and vanilla behind it, sold in a bottle shaped like a friar complete with a rope belt. The monastic story is decoration; the hazelnuts are real and local.
funFact: Piedmont's Tonda Gentile hazelnuts are the same variety that goes into the region's other famous product, and they are grown a short distance from where Nutella is made.

serve.how: Over one large cube, or neat at room temperature after dinner. It works well in coffee, and it is the standard nut liqueur in a Nutty Irishman or an espresso martini variant.

composition.summary: Toasted hazelnuts infused into neutral spirit with cocoa and vanilla.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Toasted Piedmont hazelnuts, cocoa, vanilla, coffee

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Nuts steeped, then the infusion distilled and blended

composition.process: Toasting before infusion is what turns the nut note from raw and green to roasted.

originStory: Frangelico was launched in 1978 in Canale, in Piedmont, a region known for its Tonda Gentile hazelnuts. Its name draws on a legend, promoted by the makers, of a hermit monk called Fra Angelico who lived in the Piedmont hills and devised liqueur recipes, and the bottle imitates a friar's habit, complete with a cord at the waist. The brand has passed through several owners and has belonged to Campari since 2010.

name: Tsipouro
description: Greek pomace spirit, made with or without anise depending on where you are standing. Thessaly and Epirus drink it unanised and cold with a table full of small plates, which is most of the point.
funFact: Monks on Mount Athos are credited with formalising the distillation in the fourteenth century, and monasteries there still produce it.

serve.how: Cold, in small glasses, alongside mezedes rather than after them. A tsipouradiko will keep bringing food with each round, which is the correct way to spend an afternoon in Volos.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and distilled, sometimes with anise.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape pomace from Greek winemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, once or twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; oak-aged versions exist

composition.process: Adding anise is a regional choice rather than a rule, and northern Greece mostly leaves it out.

originStory: Tsipouro, the pomace spirit of mainland Greece, is traditionally credited to Orthodox monks on Mount Athos in the fourteenth century. It became the farm spirit of Thessaly, Epirus and Macedonia, where families distil after the grape harvest, with or without anise depending on the region. Regional names, including tsipouro of Tyrnavos, are protected under EU rules.

name: Tsikoudia
description: Crete's pomace spirit, always without anise, always poured at the end of a meal whether you asked for it or not. Cretans call it raki, which causes endless confusion with the Turkish drink it resembles not at all.
funFact: Refusing the complimentary tsikoudia at the end of a Cretan meal is close to a social offence, and it usually arrives with a plate of fruit.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in tiny glasses, poured for the whole table at once. It is a communal drink and drinking it alone is regarded as slightly odd. Rakomelo, warmed with honey and cinnamon, is the winter version.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and single-distilled on Crete.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cretan grape pomace

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in a copper kazani

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 37–60%, village versions running higher

composition.process: Autumn distilling is a social event on Crete, with the still running all night and food cooked over the fire.

originStory: Tsikoudia takes its name from tsikouda, the Cretan word for the pomace left after pressing grapes, and is Crete's unflavoured pomace spirit, protected as a geographical indication.

name: Mastiha
description: Made from the resin of mastic trees, which produce it only on the southern half of Chios and nowhere else on earth despite centuries of attempts to transplant them. Pine-like, faintly sweet, and completely distinctive.
funFact: Mastic is harvested by scoring the bark and letting the resin drip onto swept ground, a method unchanged since antiquity and protected by UNESCO.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass after dinner. It also works over ice with soda and a strip of lemon, and Greek bartenders use it in place of a herbal liqueur in gin drinks.

composition.summary: Mastic tree resin distilled or infused into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or tsipouro

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mastiha resin from Pistacia lentiscus var. Chia

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Resin distilled or macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: The trees only weep usable mastic on Chios, an agricultural mystery nobody has fully explained.

originStory: Mastiha is a liqueur flavoured with mastic, the resin of trees that yield it in quantity only in the southern villages of Chios, where the know-how of cultivating it is recognised by UNESCO.

name: Metaxa
description: Not quite a brandy: aged wine distillate blended with muscat wine and a botanical infusion, which puts it in a category of one. Greece's best-known spirit abroad, and consistently mislabelled as brandy on every back bar.
funFact: Spyros Metaxas created it in 1888, and the star rating on the label denotes years of ageing, running from three stars up to the Private Reserve.

serve.glass: Snifter, or rocks glass with a large cube
serve.how: Neat at room temperature for the older expressions; the three and five star take ice and tonic well. Greeks also drink it long with cola, which the higher stars do not deserve.

composition.summary: Aged wine distillate blended with muscat wine and rose petal infusion.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Savatiano, Sultanina and Black Corinth wine distillate

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Muscat wine from Samos plus a botanical infusion including rose petals

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double-distilled, aged, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Three to thirty years in French Limousin oak

composition.process: The muscat wine is added after ageing, which is why it reads sweeter and more floral than any true brandy.

originStory: Metaxa was created in 1888 by Spyros Metaxas, a merchant from a silk-trading family, who blended aged wine distillate with muscat wine and a botanical infusion, producing a spirit that sits outside the usual definition of brandy. Its emblem, the Salamis warrior, was inspired by an ancient medallion reportedly found while his distillery in Piraeus was being built. The stars on the label indicate the age and grade of the blend.

name: Kumquat Liqueur
description: Corfu's speciality, made from a fruit the British introduced to the island in the nineteenth century and which took to it completely. Bright orange, sweet, and sold in every shop on the island.
funFact: Kumquats reached Corfu with British botanists during the protectorate years, and the island now grows more of them than anywhere else in Europe.

serve.how: Cold and neat after a meal, or over ice with soda in summer. The clear version is distilled and drier; the orange one is a sweeter maceration and the one most visitors take home.

composition.summary: Corfiot kumquats macerated or distilled into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Whole Corfu kumquats, skin and all

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for the orange version, distilled for the clear

composition.process: The peel is where nearly all the flavour lives, which is why the fruit goes in whole.

originStory: Kumquat liqueur is a speciality of Corfu, where the kumquat tree is credited to Sidney Merlin, a British botanist who lived on the island, and where the fruit is also made into preserves and sweets.

name: Zivania
description: Cypriot pomace and wine spirit, clear, unaged and traditionally very strong. Protected by the EU since 2004, and used on the island as a disinfectant, a chest rub and a drink, in roughly that order of frequency.
funFact: Village zivania has historically been distilled well above bottling strength, and it is still used in Cypriot households to treat wounds and joint pain.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in small glasses with meze. Cypriots serve it with dried fruit and nuts through winter. The commercial bottlings sit around 45%; the village stuff does not, and should be approached carefully.

composition.summary: Grape pomace and local wine distilled together.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pomace of Xynisteri and Mavro grapes, plus dry wine

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; it must be colourless

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 45% commercially, far higher in villages

composition.process: Blending wine back into the pomace before distilling is what separates zivania from a straight pomace brandy.

originStory: Zivania's origins are unclear: some trace it to the end of the fifteenth century, when Venice ruled Cyprus, and others credit monks from Mount Athos with bringing the method. It is distilled from grape pomace mixed with local dry wine made from Xynisteri and Mavro grapes, and its name is protected under EU rules for Cyprus alone.

name: Filfar
description: A Cypriot orange liqueur whose recipe is claimed to be Venetian and centuries old, made from local bitter oranges and spice. Sweet, thick and unmistakably island-made.
funFact: The recipe is said to have been found in a Venetian manuscript on Cyprus, though the modern product dates from the 1940s.

serve.glass: Small cordial glass or rocks glass
serve.how: Cold and neat, or over ice with soda. It substitutes for triple sec in a Margarita and brings more spice than the French orange liqueurs do.

composition.summary: Cypriot oranges and spices macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Cypriot bitter orange peel, cinnamon, clove and herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

composition.process: Local bitter oranges give more peel oil and less sugar than sweet varieties would.

originStory: Filfar is a Cypriot orange liqueur, and its makers trace the recipe to an old Venetian manuscript found on the island, a claim that cannot be checked.

name: Bajtra
description: Prickly pear liqueur from Malta, made from a cactus that arrived as a colonial import and has since taken over every rubble wall on the islands. Deep pink, faintly floral, and unlike anything else in the Mediterranean.
funFact: Prickly pear hedges were planted across Malta as field boundaries, and the fruit was for centuries a peasant food rather than a luxury.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after dinner. It is also good over ice with prosecco on top, and Maltese bars use it to colour and sweeten summer spritzes.

composition.summary: Prickly pear fruit macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Opuntia ficus-indica fruit, hand-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, strained and sweetened

composition.process: The fruit is covered in fine barbed spines, so harvesting is done at dawn while dew holds them down.

originStory: Bajtra is the Maltese word for prickly pear, the cactus fruit from the Americas that grows along the islands' rubble walls, and the liqueur is a modern product made from its ripe fruit.

name: Rakija
description: The household spirit of the whole Balkan peninsula, distilled from whatever fruit the region grows and offered to any guest who comes through the door. Not to be confused with Turkish rakı, which is a different drink entirely.
funFact: Homemade rakija is so widespread that several Balkan states have had to write specific exemptions into their tax codes for household distilling.

serve.how: Poured on arrival rather than after dinner, and refusing the first glass is not really an option. Room temperature for a good one; chilling is a way of hiding a rough one, and everyone knows it.

composition.summary: Fruit fermented and pot-distilled, usually twice, without additives.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plum, grape, apricot, quince, pear or apple

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, commonly double-distilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often unaged; oak-rested versions turn golden

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–55%, higher in home production

composition.process: The fruit is fermented on its own sugars with no water added, which is why a bad harvest makes bad rakija.

originStory: Rakija, the fruit brandy of the Balkans, takes its name from the Arabic araq by way of the Turkish rakı, and distilling it is generally thought to have spread across the peninsula during the Ottoman centuries. Every country and region has its fruit: plum in Serbia and Bosnia, grapes along the Adriatic, apricots, pears and quinces in the orchards in between. The Serbian tradition of making šljivovica, plum rakija, is inscribed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.

name: Travarica
description: Rakija steeped with wild herbs, which along the Dalmatian coast means sage, rosemary, juniper and whatever else grows on the karst. Served as a welcome drink and credited with settling everything from nerves to digestion.
funFact: Franciscan monasteries along the Adriatic have made herbal rakija for centuries, and several still sell their own blends at the gate.

serve.how: Room temperature, poured on arrival with dried figs or cheese. The herbs are usually left in the bottle, so the last glass is noticeably more medicinal than the first.

composition.summary: Grape or fruit rakija macerated with wild Mediterranean herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Lozovača or fruit rakija

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Sage, rosemary, juniper, mint, wormwood, St John's wort

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, sometimes redistilled

composition.process: Herbs are picked in early summer when the oils are highest and steeped for weeks in the sun.

originStory: Travarica, from trava, herb or grass, is grape rakija infused with wild herbs, the traditional welcome drink of the Dalmatian coast and its hinterland.

name: Biska
description: Istrian mistletoe rakija, a recipe that local tradition attributes to the Druids and that nobody has ever managed to date. Bitter, green and unlike any other Balkan infusion.
funFact: Mistletoe is toxic in quantity, and traditional preparation involves specific handling of the leaves that has been passed down rather than written down.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature, in the small measures Istrian hosts pour without asking. It is bitterer than most travarica and works better before a meal than after.

composition.summary: Grape rakija macerated with mistletoe and herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Istrian grape rakija

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Mistletoe, plus local herbs and sometimes honey

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, occasionally redistilled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 40%

composition.process: The mistletoe is harvested from oak or apple trees, and which host tree it grew on is said to change the result.

originStory: Biska is an Istrian mistletoe rakija closely associated with Hum, the tiny hilltop town in central Istria, and local tradition attributes the recipe to the Celtic Druids, though nobody has managed to date it.

name: Lozovača
description: Grape rakija, made from pomace or whole grapes, and the coastal counterpart to the plum brandy of the interior. Cleaner and sharper than šljivovica, and the usual base for herbal infusions.
funFact: Coastal Balkan households make loza where inland households make plum brandy, a split that follows the line where grapes stop growing well.

serve.how: Slightly cool, neat, before or during a meal rather than after. It carries less weight than plum rakija, which makes it the better match for fish and lighter food.

composition.summary: Grapes or grape pomace fermented and double-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Whole grapes or pomace

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none

composition.process: Using whole grapes rather than spent pomace gives a markedly more aromatic spirit, and costs considerably more.

originStory: Lozovača, from loza, the vine, is grape rakija made from pomace or whole grapes, the spirit of the wine-growing coast and hills of Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro.

name: Kajsijevača
description: Apricot rakija, most of it from the orchards around Serbia's Danube plain. Softer and more perfumed than plum, and generally the bottle a Serbian household keeps back for people it wants to impress.
funFact: Serbia's apricot orchards are concentrated around Vojvodina, and a late frost there can wipe out the year's rakija along with the fruit crop.

serve.how: Just below room temperature so the apricot carries. Serbs will pour it as a welcome drink, and a good one smells like an orchard from across the room.

composition.summary: Apricots fermented whole and double-distilled in copper.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Serbian apricots, typically from Vojvodina

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double pot distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Some stones are fermented with the fruit, which supplies the marzipan note without any added flavouring.

originStory: Kajsijevača, from kajsija, apricot, is apricot rakija, one of the fruit brandies of Serbia's household distilling tradition.

name: Dunjevača
description: Quince rakija, and the one Serbian households bring out for the guests who matter. Quinces are hard, astringent and barely edible raw, but they distil into something extraordinarily floral.
funFact: Quinces were traditionally kept on wardrobes and windowsills in Serbian homes as a natural air freshener before any of them reached a still.

serve.how: Cool but not cold, neat, in a stemmed glass that holds the aroma. This is the rakija to sip slowly rather than take in one, and it is usually reserved for occasions.

composition.summary: Quinces fermented and double-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ripe quince, fermented whole

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, twice, with a narrow cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass

composition.process: Quince yields very little spirit for its weight, which is why it is the most expensive rakija a household makes.

originStory: Dunjevača, from dunja, quince, is quince rakija, one of the most prized of Serbia's fruit brandies.

name: Medovača
description: Rakija sweetened with honey, usually plum or grape as the base, and often infused with herbs alongside. The Balkan answer to krupnik, and the version most likely to be pressed on a guest who has said no to everything else.
funFact: Honey was the region's main sweetener long before sugar arrived, so honeyed rakija predates most of the fruit liqueurs made alongside it.

serve.temp: room temp, or warmed in winter
serve.glass: Small glass, or a warmed cup
serve.how: Room temperature after a meal, or gently warmed when the weather turns. The honey makes it far easier going than straight rakija, which is exactly why it gets poured for guests who are struggling.

composition.summary: Fruit rakija blended with honey and sometimes herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plum or grape rakija

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Local honey, occasionally herbs and spice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: The honey is usually stirred into warm rakija so it dissolves without cooking off the aroma.

originStory: Medovača, from med, honey, is rakija sweetened with honey and often infused with herbs, made across Serbia and the western Balkans on a plum or grape base.

name: Kruškovača
description: Pear rakija from Bosnia and its neighbours, often made from the Williams pear and occasionally bottled with a whole pear grown inside the glass. Delicate by Balkan standards, which is not saying a great deal.
funFact: The pear-in-the-bottle trick involves fixing an empty bottle over a fruiting branch in spring and leaving it there all summer.

serve.how: Cool rather than cold, neat, in a stemmed glass. Over-chilling shuts down the pear completely, which is the whole reason to choose this over plum.

composition.summary: Pears fermented whole and double-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Williams or local pear varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass

composition.process: Pears ferment unpredictably and go to vinegar quickly, so the mash needs closer attention than plum.

originStory: Kruškovača, from kruška, pear, is pear rakija from Bosnia and its neighbours, usually made from the Williams pear.

name: Loza
description: Montenegro's grape rakija, clear and unaged, distilled along the coast and around Lake Skadar. Poured at every occasion that has any weight to it, and a good many that do not.
funFact: Vranac, Montenegro's main red grape, supplies much of the pomace, which gives the local loza a slightly darker, more tannic edge than Croatian versions.

serve.how: Neat, at the start of a meal, with a plate of pršut and cheese. Montenegrins drink it before food rather than after, and in quantities that assume you will be sitting for a while.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Vranac and Krstač pomace

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Home production remains widespread, and village loza routinely runs well above the commercial strength.

originStory: Loza, the vine, is Montenegro's grape rakija, distilled after the harvest along the coast and in the vineyards around Lake Skadar.

name: Mastika
description: An anise and mastic liqueur from North Macedonia and Bulgaria, sweeter and thicker than ouzo, with the resin note doing most of the work. Strumica is the town most associated with it.
funFact: The Balkan version leans harder on mastic resin than the Greek liqueur does, and the two developed separately despite the shared name.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or with a splash of water, which turns it cloudy. It is a before-dinner drink in the Balkans, taken with salty meze rather than at the end of a meal.

composition.summary: Grape or grain spirit distilled with anise and mastic resin.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape or grain spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mastic resin, anise, sometimes fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with botanicals, then sweetened

composition.process: The resin gives a pine-and-cedar note that separates it immediately from a plain anise spirit.

originStory: Mastika is an anise spirit of North Macedonia and Bulgaria, named after mastic resin, and despite the shared name it is a different drink from the mastiha liqueur of Chios.

name: Menta
description: Bright green Bulgarian peppermint liqueur, sweet and cooling, and drunk by teenagers and grandmothers with equal enthusiasm. Frequently mixed with mastika, which produces a combination best described as decisive.
funFact: Mixed half and half with mastika it becomes a mastika-menta, a Black Sea coast standard that tastes exactly as strange as it sounds.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or over ice with soda in summer. It is also poured over ice cream. As a digestive it works better than most, since the mint is doing something genuine.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with peppermint and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Peppermint oil or macerated mint leaves

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and sweetened, then coloured

composition.process: The colour is added; a mint distillate on its own comes out clear.

originStory: Menta is Bulgaria's bright green peppermint liqueur, made by steeping mint in spirit and often mixed with mastika.

name: Țuică
description: Romania's plum spirit, distilled once and therefore softer and lower in strength than the double-distilled palincă. It arrives at the start of a Romanian meal, often warmed, and frequently before you have taken your coat off.
funFact: Romania grows more plums than almost anywhere in Europe, and the great majority of the crop goes into țuică rather than onto a plate.

serve.how: At the start of a meal, room temperature or gently warmed with black pepper in winter. Single distillation keeps it lower in strength, so the glasses come more often than they would with palincă.

composition.summary: Plums fermented and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Romanian plums, chiefly the Vinete variety
