components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single pass in a copper cazan

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes rested in mulberry or oak casks

composition.process: A single distillation leaves more fruit and more weight than the twice-run palincă.

originStory: Țuică is Romania's plum spirit, distilled once from fermented plums in the villages of the Carpathian foothills and Transylvania.

name: Palincă
description: The double-distilled Transylvanian version of țuică, running to 60% in village production and made from plum, apricot or pear. Related to Hungarian pálinka by history and by border changes, and defended fiercely by both.
funFact: Transylvanian villages run communal stills each autumn, and the queue for them is a social event that lasts most of October.

serve.how: Room temperature, neat, in small measures. Never chilled, and never in one gulp if it is a good one. Transylvanians pour it before eating and keep the bottle on the table throughout.

composition.summary: Fruit fermented and distilled twice to a high strength.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plum, apricot, pear, apple or cherry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double distillation in copper

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes rested in mulberry wood

composition.process: Mulberry casks, used in parts of Transylvania, give a distinctive golden colour and soft spice.

originStory: Palincă is the double-distilled fruit spirit of Transylvania, stronger than the once-distilled țuică, and it shares its name and much of its history with Hungarian pálinka.

name: Vișinată
description: Romanian sour cherry liqueur, made at home by steeping the fruit in spirit and sugar through the summer and opening it at Christmas. Deep red, sweet, and considerably stronger than it lets on.
funFact: The cherries left at the bottom of the jar are eaten afterwards and are, by that stage, close to a dessert in their own right.

serve.how: After a meal, at cellar temperature, with a couple of the steeped cherries in the glass. Romanian households serve it at Christmas and Easter, and it is usually homemade rather than bought.

composition.summary: Sour cherries macerated in spirit with sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Țuică or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sour cherries, sugar, sometimes cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for two to three months

composition.process: A few stones are usually left in, which contributes the almond note as they steep.

originStory: Vișinată, from vișină, sour cherry, is a Romanian household liqueur made by steeping sour cherries with sugar in spirit through the summer.

name: Afinată
description: Bilberry liqueur from the Carpathians, made from the small wild berries that carpet the mountain forests in late summer. Darker and more tart than the cherry version, and harder to make because the picking is slow.
funFact: Wild bilberries are picked by hand with combs in the Carpathians, and a full day's work yields a surprisingly small bucket.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal. It is darker and drier than vișinată, so it suits a chocolate dessert better than a sweet one. Mountain guesthouses pour it as a matter of course.

composition.summary: Wild bilberries macerated in spirit with sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Țuică or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Wild Carpathian bilberries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for several weeks

composition.process: Wild berries carry more tannin than cultivated ones, which is why it finishes drier than it starts.

originStory: Afinată, from afină, bilberry, is a Romanian liqueur made by steeping wild bilberries from the Carpathian forests in spirit with sugar.

name: Skanderbeg
description: Albania's aged grape brandy, named after the fifteenth-century national hero who held off the Ottomans for twenty-five years. Sweet, soft and considerably better than its obscurity outside Albania suggests.
funFact: Albania's vineyards are among the oldest in Europe, with evidence of winemaking on the coast going back several thousand years.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature after dinner, or with a Turkish coffee alongside, which is the Albanian habit. The older bottlings carry real oak and reward a warmed glass.

composition.summary: Albanian wine distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Albanian grapes, largely from the coastal plain

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Five to ten years in oak

composition.process: Long oak ageing and a touch of sweetening put it closer to a Spanish brandy than a French one.

originStory: Skanderbeg is an Albanian grape brandy named after Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg, the fifteenth-century lord who led Albanian resistance to the Ottoman Empire and remains the national hero.

name: Chacha
description: Georgian pomace brandy, made in a country that has been fermenting grapes for eight thousand years and treats the leftovers with the same seriousness as the wine. Clear, powerful, and poured at every supra.
funFact: Georgia protected chacha as a national product in 2011, and the town of Batumi built a 25-metre tower that was supposed to dispense it from a public tap.

serve.how: Neat at a Georgian table, in glasses raised for each of the many toasts a tamada will propose. Aged chacha turns golden and is drunk more slowly. Do not drink it without food; the supra assumes otherwise.

composition.summary: Grape pomace, often from qvevri winemaking, fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pomace of Rkatsiteli, Saperavi and other Georgian varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, once or twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; oak-aged versions exist

composition.process: Qvevri fermentation leaves skins in long contact with the wine, so the pomace is more exhausted and the spirit drier.

originStory: Chacha is the pomace brandy of Georgia, distilled from the grape skins and stems left after winemaking in a country with one of the world's oldest wine traditions.

name: Armenian Brandy
description: Ararat valley grapes distilled and aged in Caucasian oak, and the one spirit of the former Soviet Union with a genuine international reputation. Softer and more floral than cognac, with a distinct note of dried fruit.
funFact: Churchill is widely said to have been sent cases of it after tasting it at the Yalta conference, a story Armenia has never had any reason to correct.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, after dinner. Armenians drink it through a meal rather than after one, and toast constantly. The older expressions are worth taking slowly; the three star is not.

composition.summary: Armenian white wine distilled twice and aged in Caucasian oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Voskehat, Garan Dmak and other Ararat valley grapes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double pot distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Three to twenty years in Caucasian oak

composition.process: Local oak is tighter-grained than Limousin, which slows extraction and gives a softer, nuttier profile.

originStory: Armenian brandy began in 1887, when the merchant Nerses Tairyants opened a wine and brandy factory in Yerevan. In 1899 he sold it to the Russian industrialist Nikolai Shustov, whose brandies won fame across the Russian Empire, and the Yerevan Brandy Company now makes the Ararat range. A popular story holds that Winston Churchill was sent cases of it by Stalin after tasting it at Yalta, but it rests on anecdote rather than documents.

name: Oghi
description: Armenian fruit spirit, most distinctively from mulberry or cornelian cherry, and made in villages across the country. The mulberry version is the one Armenians press on visitors and claim will cure anything.
funFact: Mulberry oghi is treated as a folk medicine in Armenia, and is still recommended within families for colds and stomach trouble.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature with food on the table, in the small measures that Armenian hospitality refills constantly. Mulberry is the classic; apricot and cornelian cherry are both worth finding.

composition.summary: Fruit fermented and pot-distilled, often at village scale.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Mulberry, cornelian cherry, apricot or plum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, usually twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Normally unaged

composition.process: Mulberries ferment fast and yield little, which is why the mulberry version is the most expensive.

originStory: Oghi is the Armenian word for fruit spirit, distilled in villages across the country from mulberries, cornelian cherries, apricots, grapes and other fruit.

name: Tutovka
description: White mulberry spirit from the Caucasus foothills, clear, high-strength and intensely fruity. Azerbaijan makes the best-known version, though the tradition runs across the whole mountain region.
funFact: Mulberry trees were planted across the Caucasus for silkworm cultivation, and the fruit became a distilling crop almost by accident.

serve.how: Neat, at or just below room temperature, with food. It is a village spirit rather than a bar one, and the good bottles come from families rather than distilleries.

composition.summary: White mulberries fermented and distilled, usually twice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: White mulberries, hand-gathered

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, double-distilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Mulberries are shaken onto sheets rather than picked, since they bruise and ferment within hours.

originStory: Tutovka, from tut, the word for mulberry across much of the Caucasus and Central Asia, is spirit distilled from fermented mulberries in Azerbaijan and the surrounding mountains.

name: Southern Comfort
description: Whiskey, peach and spice, first mixed in a New Orleans bar in 1874 by a bartender who was tired of serving rough whiskey and decided to fix it rather than replace it. For decades it contained no whiskey at all; it does again now.
funFact: Martin Wilkes Heron originally called it Cuffs and Buttons, a joke on the fancier name of a rival drink, before settling on something more marketable.

serve.how: Over ice with a squeeze of lime, or long with lemonade. It is sweet enough that neat service is heavy going. In cocktails it does the work of both whiskey and sugar, which is why an Alabama Slammer needs neither.

composition.summary: Whiskey blended with peach, citrus and spice, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: American whiskey, reinstated in the 2010s after years of neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Peach, orange, vanilla, cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended and infused after distillation

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 20–35% depending on market

composition.process: The original was a way of making cheap New Orleans whiskey drinkable, which is exactly what it still tastes like.

originStory: Southern Comfort was created in 1874 by Martin Wilkes Heron, a bartender at McCauley's Tavern in New Orleans, who blended whiskey with fruit and spices to improve the rough spirit of the day. He first called it Cuffs and Buttons before settling on its present name, and after moving to Memphis he bottled it under the slogan none genuine but mine. For decades the recipe used neutral spirit as its base, and whiskey returned to it after Sazerac bought the brand in 2016.

name: Ōkolehao
description: Distilled from the baked root of the ti plant, first made in Hawaii around 1790 by a shipwrecked Australian convict who saw what the islanders were fermenting and fetched a still. The name means iron bottom, after the shape of the pots.
funFact: Ti root was baked in the same underground imu ovens used for cooking pigs, which is where the faint smoke in traditional okolehao came from.

serve.how: Neat or over a single cube. Modern craft bottlings are clean enough to sip; older-style ones are earthier and work better in a tiki build where the root note can sit under lime and pineapple.

composition.summary: Baked ti root fermented and distilled, sometimes with cane or rice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cordyline fruticosa root, baked to convert its starch

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still; originally an improvised ship's still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes oak-aged

composition.process: Baking the root in an underground oven converts inulin to fermentable sugar, the same principle as roasting agave.

originStory: Ōkolehao is credited to William Stevenson, an escaped British convict who reached Hawaii in the 1790s and began distilling the fermented, baked root of the ti plant. The name means iron bottom, after the iron try pots from sailing ships that served as stills. It found new popularity in Hawaii during the Second World War, when grain spirits were rationed, and faded as imported spirits returned.

name: Canadian Rye
description: For most of a century Canadian whisky was called rye regardless of what was in it. A wave of distillers has since made the label honest, producing whiskies with real rye in the mash and the spice to prove it.
funFact: Canadian law lets distillers add up to 9.09% of another spirit, including wine or bourbon, which is why the category has so much latitude in flavour.

serve.glass: Glencairn neat, rocks glass on ice
serve.how: Neat for the rye-forward bottlings, which carry enough spice to hold up. On ice or in an Old Fashioned for the blends. Canadian rye's dill note makes it a distinctive base in a Manhattan.

composition.summary: Rye distilled and aged separately, then blended to a house style.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rye, or rye blended with corn, wheat and barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column and pot, each grain distilled separately

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in Canada, in barrels no larger than 700 litres

composition.process: Distilling each grain separately and blending afterwards is the Canadian method and the source of its flexibility.

originStory: Canada's whisky industry took shape in the nineteenth century, when millers such as Gooderham and Worts in Toronto and Hiram Walker in Windsor began distilling their grain. Adding rye to a largely wheat or corn mash gave the whisky its spice, and rye became the popular name for Canadian whisky whatever the recipe. Canadian rules allow a small share of other spirits or wine in the blend, and some distillers now make it from mashes of rye alone.

name: Screech
description: Newfoundland's rum, which is Jamaican in origin, bottled on the island, and surrounded by more ceremony than most spirits three times its price. The screech-in ritual involves kissing a cod and reciting a phrase in dialect.
funFact: The name is said to come from an American serviceman's reaction to his first mouthful during the Second World War, which was audible from outside.

serve.glass: Shot glass, or rocks glass with cola
serve.how: Neat as a shot during a screech-in, or long with cola the rest of the time. It is a dark, sweet rum without much complexity, and pretending otherwise is not part of the tradition.

composition.summary: Caribbean rum shipped in bulk and bottled in Newfoundland.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Jamaican molasses rum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled in the Caribbean, blended and bottled in St John's

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Aged before shipping

composition.process: Newfoundland traded salt cod to the Caribbean for rum for centuries, which is how a Jamaican spirit became a Canadian institution.

originStory: Screech grew from Newfoundland's salt cod trade with Jamaica, which sent rum north in exchange for fish. When the Newfoundland government took control of liquor sales in the twentieth century it began bottling the rum under its own label, and a popular story says the name came from an American serviceman's reaction to his first taste during the Second World War, though screech was already slang for rough spirit. The screech-in, a mock ceremony for visitors involving a cod and a recitation, keeps it central to island hospitality.

name: Maple Liqueur
description: Canadian whisky sweetened with maple syrup, which sounds like a novelty and turns out to be a genuinely good pairing. Quebec makes most of it, and Quebec makes most of the world's maple syrup, so the logic holds.
funFact: Quebec produces around seventy per cent of the world's maple syrup and maintains a strategic reserve of it in warehouses, which has been robbed at least once.

serve.how: Over ice, or poured into black coffee on a cold day. It is also good over vanilla ice cream and works in an Old Fashioned in place of both the whisky and the sugar.

composition.summary: Canadian whisky blended with pure maple syrup.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Canadian whisky

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Pure maple syrup, typically Quebec grade

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: Real syrup rather than maple flavouring is what separates the good bottles from the souvenir ones.

originStory: Maple liqueur is a modern Quebec product, blending Canadian whisky or neutral spirit with maple syrup from the province that makes most of the world's supply.

name: Charanda
description: Michoacán's protected cane spirit, distilled at altitude from cane grown in volcanic soil. Older than most Caribbean rum traditions and almost entirely unknown outside Mexico, where it has held a denomination since 2003.
funFact: The name comes from a Purépecha word for reddish soil, referring to the volcanic ground the cane grows in around Uruapan.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, the way you would approach a good rhum agricole. The mineral edge comes from the soil and gets lost under mixers, so save the mixing for the aged expressions.

composition.summary: Michoacán sugarcane, juice or molasses, fermented and distilled at altitude.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cane grown between 300 and 1,800 metres in Michoacán

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Blanco, oro and añejo expressions

composition.process: Distilling at altitude lowers the boiling point, which producers say gives a lighter, more aromatic spirit.

originStory: Charanda comes from the country around Uruapan in Michoacán, where sugarcane was planted after the Spanish conquest, and it takes its name from the Cerro de la Charanda, a hill near the city where the region's first distillery is said to have stood. In Purépecha the word means red-coloured earth. Early in the twenty-first century charanda received a Mexican denomination of origin, and it is rarely seen outside Mexico.

name: Comiteco
description: A Chiapas spirit made from fermented agave sap rather than roasted hearts, fortified and aged. It nearly died out entirely in the twentieth century and survives now through a handful of producers around Comitán.
funFact: Unlike tequila or mezcal it uses aguamiel, the sap tapped from a living agave, which is the same liquid that ferments into pulque.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature. It is sweeter and rounder than mezcal, closer to a light rum in weight, and the aged versions drink comfortably after a meal.

composition.summary: Agave sap fermented, distilled and blended with piloncillo, then aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aguamiel from Agave americana, tapped from living plants

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, then blended with unrefined cane sugar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, typically one to three years

composition.process: Because the plant is tapped rather than harvested, it keeps producing sap for months before it dies.

originStory: Comiteco takes its name from Comitán de Domínguez in Chiapas, where distilling is said to have arrived with Dominican friars in the colonial period, and it is made from aguamiel, the sweet sap tapped from living agaves, rather than from roasted agave hearts. Tax changes and a shortage of agave nearly ended commercial production in the twentieth century, leaving only artisanal makers. Producers around Comitán have since revived it, and it remains rare outside Chiapas.

name: Kahlúa
description: Coffee liqueur built on Veracruz arabica and Mexican cane spirit, made since 1936 and responsible for a disproportionate share of the world's dessert cocktails. Without it there is no White Russian and no Espresso Martini worth drinking.
funFact: The name comes from a Nahuatl phrase said to mean house of the Acolhua people, chosen by the founders for its local resonance.

serve.how: Over ice, or with cold milk or cream poured over it. In cocktails it is the sweet coffee half of a White Russian, an Espresso Martini or a Mudslide. Neat it is very sweet and best kept short.

composition.summary: Rum and neutral cane spirit blended with coffee extract, vanilla and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Mexican cane spirit and rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Veracruz arabica coffee, vanilla, caramel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Coffee extracted and blended after distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: The rum component is aged before blending

composition.process: The coffee is extracted rather than distilled, which keeps the roast character that distillation would strip.

originStory: Kahlúa was first produced in Veracruz in 1936, blending local arabica coffee with sugarcane spirit, with Pedro Domecq behind its production. The name is usually explained as Veracruz Nahuatl for house of the Acolhua people. Jules Berman, who first imported it into the United States, became known as Mr Kahlúa, and its American success made it a staple of mixed drinks such as the Black Russian and the White Russian.

name: Rompope
description: Egg, milk, sugar and cinnamon fortified with rum or cane spirit, invented in the convent kitchens of Puebla by nuns who had eggs to spare. Mexico's answer to advocaat, and a fixture of Christmas and every birthday in between.
funFact: The Santa Clara convent in Puebla is credited with the original, and the recipe was reportedly kept from the nuns themselves except for the one permitted to make it.

serve.how: Cold and neat in a small glass, or poured over ice cream and flan. Mexicans drink it at Christmas and on Day of the Dead, and it is also spooned onto desserts rather than drunk.

composition.summary: Egg yolk, milk and sugar cooked together and fortified with spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rum or cane aguardiente

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Egg yolk, milk, sugar, cinnamon, vanilla, sometimes almond

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: None; the custard is cooked then fortified

composition.process: Cooking the custard before fortifying is what keeps it stable, and why homemade versions do not last long.

originStory: Rompope is traditionally credited to the nuns of the Santa Clara convent in Puebla, who are said to have made it in the seventeenth century with rum or cane spirit, milk, sugar, egg yolks and cinnamon. Its name is usually linked to rompón, a Spanish eggnog that reached Mexico. It is now bottled commercially across the country and is a fixture of Mexican Christmas celebrations.

name: Xtabentún
description: A Yucatán liqueur of anise and fermented honey, the honey coming from bees that feed on the xtabentún morning glory. Mayan in origin, and the flower it depends on is mildly psychoactive to the bees if not to anyone else.
funFact: The Maya made a fermented honey drink called balché long before the Spanish arrived with anise and distillation, and the modern liqueur is a fusion of the two.

serve.how: Neat after a meal, or the local way: a shot of xtabentún poured into a cup of strong Yucatecan coffee. It also works over ice with soda when the Mérida heat makes anything else unthinkable.

composition.summary: Fermented honey blended with anise-flavoured rum or cane spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rum or cane spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Honey from xtabentún flowers, plus anise

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Honey fermented, then blended with the anise spirit

composition.process: The flower only grows in the Yucatán scrub, which is what ties the liqueur to the peninsula.

originStory: Xtabentún takes its name from the Maya word for a morning glory that blooms across Yucatán and whose nectar feeds local bees. Long before the Spanish arrived, the Maya made balché, a ceremonial fermented drink of honey and tree bark, and the modern liqueur is usually seen as its descendant, with anise and distillation brought by Europeans. Distilleries in Yucatán still make it from honey, anise and rum.

name: Damiana
description: A Baja California herb liqueur sold in a bottle shaped like an Incan fertility goddess, which tells you exactly what it has been marketed on for a century. Herbal, sweet, and the traditional base of the original Margarita, if you believe Baja.
funFact: Damiana has a long folk reputation as an aphrodisiac in Mexico, and the bottle shape has never been an accident.

serve.how: Over ice, or swapped in for triple sec in a Margarita, which is how Baja bars insist the drink was originally made. Neat it is sweet and herbal, closer to a chamomile liqueur than anything bitter.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit infused with damiana leaf and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Turnera diffusa leaf, plus honey and herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened

composition.process: The shrub grows wild across the Baja peninsula and has been used in Mexican folk medicine since well before the Spanish.

originStory: Damiana is a Mexican herbal liqueur made from the leaves of Turnera diffusa, a shrub native to Baja California and other parts of Mexico.

name: Guatemalan Rum
description: Distilled from virgin cane honey rather than molasses and aged at over two thousand metres, where the thin cool air slows maturation dramatically. Ron Zacapa's solera system is what put the country on the map.
funFact: The high-altitude warehouse where Zacapa ages sits at 2,300 metres, and the ageing is slow enough that the solera numbers refer to years in the system rather than the youngest spirit.

serve.glass: Snifter or rocks glass with one cube
serve.how: Neat, or over a single large cube. These are sweet, heavily solera-aged rums, so treat them as you would a dessert spirit rather than a mixing rum. A twist of orange lifts the butterscotch.

composition.summary: Virgin cane honey fermented and column-distilled, then solera-aged at altitude.

components.label: Base
components.detail: First-press cane honey, not molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera system in ex-bourbon, sherry and Pedro Ximénez casks at 2,300m

composition.process: Altitude and cool mountain air slow evaporation, which is why the spirit can sit in wood for so long without drying out.

originStory: Guatemala's modern rum industry is closely tied to the Botrán family, five brothers from Burgos in Spain who founded Industria Licorera Quezalteca in 1939, the start of what became Industrias Licoreras de Guatemala. In 1976 the company created Ron Zacapa to mark the centenary of the town of Zacapa, distilling from virgin sugarcane honey, a concentrated cane juice, rather than molasses. Its rums, aged in the highlands of Quetzaltenango, gave Guatemalan rum an international reputation.

name: Quetzalteca
description: Guatemala's everyday aguardiente, sold plain or in a run of fruit flavours, and named after the city of Quetzaltenango. It is on every shelf in the country and appears at every fiesta, wake and market day.
funFact: The fruit expressions, particularly tamarind and rosa de Jamaica, outsell the plain version in much of the country.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or mixed with fruit juice. It is an inexpensive, uncomplicated spirit and is drunk as one. The tamarind and hibiscus versions are the ones worth trying if you find them.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit, sometimes infused with fruit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Guatemalan sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, to a high strength then cut

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: The flavoured versions are infused after distillation, which is where most of the range now sits.

originStory: Quetzalteca takes its name from Quetzaltenango, in Guatemala's western highlands, and is the country's everyday clear cane aguardiente, sold plain and in fruit flavours.

name: Honduran Aguardiente
description: Cane spirit with a touch of anise, of which Yuscarán is the name every Honduran knows. Cheap, clean and everywhere, and named after a colonial silver-mining town in the southern hills.
funFact: Yuscarán the town was built on silver, and the distillery that carries its name has outlasted the mines by well over a century.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or with lime and soda. It is a working spirit rather than a sipping one, and Hondurans drink it in company rather than alone.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit lightly flavoured with anise.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Honduran sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: A light touch of anise

composition.process: The anise is subtle enough that it reads as sweetness rather than as an aniseed spirit.

originStory: Honduran aguardiente is a clear cane spirit, often with a light anise note, and its best-known name, Yuscarán, comes from a colonial silver-mining town in the department of El Paraíso.

name: Cususa
description: Nicaraguan clandestine cane moonshine, distilled in the northern hills in improvised stills and sold with no label of any kind. Illegal, widespread, and occasionally very good.
funFact: Production is concentrated in the mountains around Estelí and Jinotega, where the sugar mills and the terrain both work in the distillers' favour.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and only from a source you trust. Quality is entirely dependent on whether the maker cut the heads and tails properly, and there is no label to tell you.

composition.summary: Cane juice or panela fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane juice or raw panela

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Homemade pot stills, often single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–60%, unmeasured

composition.process: Because it is unregulated, strength and safety vary enormously from one batch to the next.

originStory: Cususa is the unlicensed cane spirit of Nicaragua's northern highlands, distilled in improvised stills and sold without labels.

name: Guaro
description: Costa Rica's state-produced cane spirit, deliberately kept low in strength and near-neutral in flavour so that it mixes with anything. Cacique is the national brand and has been a government monopoly product since 1850.
funFact: The state liquor factory was set up partly to stamp out home distilling, and the resulting monopoly funded public works for over a century.

serve.glass: Shot glass, or highball for a chiliguaro
serve.how: Cold shots, or in a chiliguaro: guaro with tomato juice, lime, hot sauce and salt, which is the national shot and far better than the description suggests. It also mixes cleanly with any fruit juice.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit distilled to near neutrality and cut to 30%.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Costa Rican sugarcane molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, heavily rectified

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Keeping it neutral is a deliberate design choice: it was made to be mixed, not tasted.

originStory: Guaro, short for aguardiente, is Costa Rica's cane spirit, and its production has been controlled by the state since the mid-nineteenth century, when the government nationalised it and set up a national liquor factory to stamp out illegal distilling. The Fábrica Nacional de Licores still makes Cacique, the dominant brand, as a light, near-neutral spirit designed to mix. Guaro remains the base of the country's simple mixed drinks, from the guaro sour to the chiliguaro.

name: Seco Herrerano
description: Panama's national spirit: sugarcane distilled three times to a clean, light, almost vodka-like spirit. Herrera province makes it, Panamanians drink it with milk, and almost nobody outside the country has heard of it.
funFact: Seco con leche, seco mixed with milk over ice, is a genuinely popular Panamanian serve and tastes considerably better than it reads.

serve.how: Over ice with coconut water, or the national serve of seco, milk and ice. It substitutes for vodka or white rum in almost anything, being cleaner than the first and lighter than the second.

composition.summary: Sugarcane juice fermented and triple-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh Panamanian sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Triple-distilled in column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Three distillations strip out nearly all the cane character, which is what distinguishes it from rum.

originStory: Seco Herrerano comes from Pesé, in Panama's Herrera province, where the Varela family business dates its beginnings to 1908. The family's company, Varela Hermanos, distils local sugarcane three times into a clean, light spirit that took the province's name and became Panama's national drink, while the same firm later built a reputation abroad with aged rums. A popular local serve, seco con leche, mixes it with milk over ice.

name: Belizean Rum
description: Rum from Belizean molasses, of which One Barrel is the best known: a light, vanilla-heavy rum that has won more awards than a country of four hundred thousand people has any right to.
funFact: Travellers Liquors began as a roadside bar outside Belize City where the owner sold rum he had blended himself, and grew from there.

serve.how: Over ice, or long with soda and lime. The one-barrel style is light and vanilla-forward, which makes it a good daiquiri rum and an easy sipper over a single cube.

composition.summary: Belizean molasses fermented and column-distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses from Belizean sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: One year and upward in oak

composition.process: Belize's sugar industry is concentrated in the north, and the distilleries sit alongside the mills.

originStory: Sugarcane and rum were part of life in Belize through its years as British Honduras, but the modern Belizean rum story belongs to one family business. In 1953 the Perdomo family opened a small bar called Travellers on the edge of Belize City and began blending rum to sell over its counter. The bar grew into Travellers Liquors, the country's leading rum house, and One Barrel, its aged blend, became the Belizean rum most visitors know.

name: Rum Popo
description: Belize's Christmas eggnog liqueur, built on local rum with condensed milk, egg and nutmeg. Made at home in December in quantities that assume a large family and a long holiday.
funFact: Every Belizean family has its own ratio, and the arguments about how much rum belongs in it are a fixed part of the season.

serve.how: Cold from the fridge in a small glass, dusted with fresh nutmeg. It is thick and very sweet, so a small pour goes far. Homemade versions keep only a few days.

composition.summary: Local rum blended with egg, condensed milk and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Belizean rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Egg yolk, condensed and evaporated milk, nutmeg, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: None; blended and chilled

composition.process: The condensed milk does the work that cream does in northern eggnog, and keeps better in the heat.

originStory: Rum popo is Belize's Christmas drink, a household mix of rum, condensed or evaporated milk, egg and nutmeg, made to share with visitors through the season. It belongs to the family of eggy holiday drinks that runs from Mexico's rompope to Puerto Rico's coquito, and the name looks like a cousin of rompope, though nobody has recorded how it came about. No one is credited with inventing it, and every family recipe differs a little. Bottled versions have since carried it onto shop shelves.

name: Ron Ligero
description: The Cuban style, codified in the 1860s when Facundo Bacardí filtered and aged his rum into something light enough for a mixed drink. Every clean, dry white rum in the world descends from that decision.
funFact: Cuban law requires even white rum to be aged and then filtered back to clarity, so the colourless bottle in front of you has still spent time in oak.

serve.how: This is a mixing rum by design. A daiquiri with lime and sugar, or a mojito, is what it was built for. Neat, the aged expressions are dry and elegant, but the white is not meant to be sipped.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented, column-distilled, aged and charcoal-filtered.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cuban sugarcane molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, to a light spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years even for white, then filtered clear

composition.process: Filtering after ageing removes the colour but leaves the softness, which is the whole trick of the Cuban style.

originStory: The light Cuban style is usually dated to 1862, when Facundo Bacardí Massó, a Catalan merchant in Santiago de Cuba, bought a small distillery with his brother José. His work with selected yeast, charcoal filtration and ageing in oak gave a rum soft enough to drink young and mix freely, and other Cuban houses followed the same path. The Bacardí family left the island after the revolution, but the ligero style stayed, and Cuban producers still age even their white rums in oak before filtering them back to clarity.

name: Rhum Barbancourt
description: Haitian rum made from fresh cane juice and distilled twice in the Charentais method its founder brought from Cognac in 1862. It sits between agricole and Caribbean rum and belongs entirely to neither.
funFact: Dupré Barbancourt was a Frenchman from the Charente who applied cognac's double pot distillation to Haitian cane, a method the distillery still uses.

serve.how: Neat or over a single cube for the aged expressions, which have real cocoa and dried fruit depth. The younger bottling makes an exceptional daiquiri, since the cane juice base brings grass the molasses rums lack.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented and double pot-distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed Haitian sugarcane juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Charentais double distillation in copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Limousin oak, four to fifteen years

composition.process: Double pot distillation is a cognac technique, and it gives a rounder spirit than the single-column agricole method.

originStory: Rhum Barbancourt was founded in Haiti in 1862 by Dupré Barbancourt, a Frenchman from the Charente, who applied his home region's double distillation, the method behind cognac, to Haitian cane juice; the house still works that way. He and his wife, Nathalie Gardère, had no children, so the business passed to her nephew Paul Gardère and has stayed in the Gardère family since. Paul's son Jean later moved the distillery to the Domaine Barbancourt near Damien, on the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac.

name: Mamajuana
description: A Dominican bottle packed with tree bark, roots and herbs, filled with rum, red wine and honey, and left to steep. Taíno in origin, spiked with European ingredients after contact, and credited locally with curing everything.
funFact: The Taíno originally drank the herb infusion as a tea; rum and wine were added after the Spanish arrived, and the bottle has been refillable ever since.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, and the bottle keeps going: when it empties you top it up with more rum and let it steep again. The first fill is the harshest, and it improves for years afterwards.

composition.summary: Bark, roots and herbs steeped in rum, red wine and honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Dominican rum, with red wine and honey

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bejuco bark, anise, star anise, agave, cinnamon and a dozen more

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused only; the bottle is refilled repeatedly

composition.process: The dry bark is cured first with rum that is then discarded, since the first extraction is bitter and harsh.

originStory: Mamajuana's roots are usually traced to the Taíno, who steeped barks, roots and herbs, with Spanish settlers later adding wine and then rum. The name comes from damajuana, the Spanish word for a demijohn, the big wicker-covered bottle the mixture was kept in, itself from the French dame-jeanne. In the mid twentieth century Jesús Rodríguez of San Juan de la Maguana is credited with popularising it, and the story goes that under Trujillo its sale was restricted to people with a medical licence.

name: Barbados Rum
description: Pot and column stills blended together to a balance nobody else quite matches, from the island that has the strongest claim to inventing rum in the 1650s. Elegant where Jamaica is loud.
funFact: Mount Gay holds a deed from 1703, which makes it the oldest rum brand still in production anywhere in the world.

serve.glass: Rocks glass with one large cube
serve.how: Neat or over a single cube for the aged bottlings. The balance of pot and column makes it the most versatile rum on the shelf: good enough to sip, characterful enough to hold up in a Daiquiri or a Rum Old Fashioned.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented and distilled in both pot and column stills, then blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Barbadian sugarcane molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot and twin-column, blended together

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Tropical ageing in ex-bourbon oak, two years and up

composition.process: Blending the two still types is the house method, and the ratio is what defines each distillery's style.

originStory: Barbados has a strong claim to rum's beginnings. By the 1650s the island's sugar planters were distilling the by-products of cane into a fierce spirit, and a description of the island from that decade calls it rumbullion and kill-devil, the likely root of the word rum. Mount Gay traces itself to a deed of 1703 for an estate in the parish of St Lucy, the basis of its claim to be the oldest rum brand still made. The name honours Sir John Gay Alleyne, who managed the estate.

name: Trinidad Rum
description: Light, dry column-still rum, cleaner and less sweet than most of the Caribbean, and shaped by a distillery better known for its bitters. Trinidad rum is the quiet workhorse of the region.
funFact: Angostura's distillery produces both the island's rum and the bitters, though the bitters recipe uses no Angostura bark and never has.

serve.how: Neat or over ice. The dryness makes it a good rum for anyone who finds Caribbean rum too sweet, and it holds its shape in a Rum Punch better than richer styles do.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented and column-distilled to a light spirit, then aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Multi-column continuous still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak, tropically aged

composition.process: Distilling to a high strength strips out congeners, which is where the dryness comes from.

originStory: Rum on Trinidad grew up with the island's sugar estates under Spanish and then British rule, and for much of the twentieth century several distilleries worked there. The industry consolidated over time: the state-owned Caroni distillery, now prized by collectors for its heavy rums, closed when the national sugar company was wound down, leaving the Angostura works in Laventille as the island's main producer. Angostura is better known for its bitters, named after the Venezuelan town where they were first made.

name: Angostura Aromatic Bitters
description: Invented in Venezuela in 1824 by a German army surgeon treating stomach complaints, made in Trinidad since 1875, and present behind essentially every bar on earth. The oversized label was a printing error nobody ever corrected.
funFact: The label is famously too big for the bottle because two brothers each did half the job without checking with the other, and the family decided it had become recognisable.

serve.glass: Used as a seasoning, not poured
serve.how: A few dashes into an Old Fashioned, a Manhattan or a Pisco Sour, where it works the way salt works in cooking. Also dashed into soda water for an upset stomach, which was its original purpose.

composition.summary: A concentrated botanical tincture on a high-strength spirit base.

components.label: Base
components.detail: High-strength neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian and a secret blend; despite the name, no angostura bark

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended to a concentrate

composition.process: Only a handful of people know the recipe, and the company keeps them from travelling together.

originStory: Angostura bitters began in 1824 in the Venezuelan town of Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar, where Johann Gottlieb Benjamin Siegert, a German surgeon serving in Simón Bolívar's army, compounded them as a tonic for the troops. They took the town's name and contain no bark of the angostura tree. After Siegert's death his sons moved the business to Port of Spain, Trinidad, in 1875. The company says the oversized label came from two brothers who redesigned bottle and label separately, and that a competition judge persuaded them to keep it.

name: Shrubb
description: Rhum steeped with dried bitter orange peel and spice, made in Martinique and Guadeloupe for Christmas and now sold year-round. Drier and more bitter than any orange liqueur, because the rum underneath is agricole.
funFact: Traditionally the orange peel was dried on rooftops through the year specifically so there would be enough for the Christmas batch.

serve.how: Neat at Christmas, or over ice. It also works in place of curaçao in a Mai Tai, where the agricole base adds a grassy edge that the standard build lacks entirely.

composition.summary: Rhum agricole macerated with bitter orange peel, spice and cane syrup.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rhum agricole, white or aged

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sun-dried bitter orange peel, vanilla, clove, cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened with cane syrup

composition.process: Sun-drying the peel concentrates the oil and adds a bitterness fresh peel does not have.

originStory: Shrubb is a Christmas tradition of the French Antilles, made in Martinique and Guadeloupe by steeping rhum with dried orange peel, sugar and spice. Nobody is credited with inventing it; it began as a household preparation for the festive season, with each family keeping its own recipe. The name is generally traced to the English shrub, a family of cordials built from fruit and spirit that was common across the colonial Caribbean. Agricole houses such as Clément later bottled their own versions, carrying it beyond the holidays.

name: Black Seal Rum
description: Bermuda's black rum, blended on the island since 1806 and once sold from the barrel into whatever bottle a customer brought, sealed with black wax. Without it a Dark 'n Stormy is just ginger beer.
funFact: Gosling's holds a trademark on the Dark 'n Stormy, making it one of very few cocktails that legally requires a specific brand.

serve.how: Poured over ginger beer and ice, floated rather than stirred so it sits in a dark layer on top. That is the Dark 'n Stormy, and it is the reason the bottle exists. Neat it is heavy and very sweet.

composition.summary: Caribbean rums blended in Bermuda to a dark house style.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses rums sourced across the Caribbean

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled elsewhere, blended and aged in Bermuda

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Aged in charred American oak before blending

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40% standard, 47% for the overproof

composition.process: Bermuda grows no cane; the island's contribution is the blend, which has stayed in one family for seven generations.

originStory: Gosling's began in 1806, when James Gosling, son of a London wine merchant, was bound for Virginia with a cargo of wines and spirits; the story goes that his ship's charter ran out and he landed in Bermuda instead. He opened a shop on the island, and around 1860 the family began blending rum. The firm later filled champagne bottles from the officers' messes of the Bermuda garrison and sealed them with black wax, and customers asking for the black seal rum gave it its name.

name: Rivers Royale
description: Grenadian cane juice rum at 69 to 75%, made at a distillery that still runs its cane crusher off a water wheel installed in 1785. Raw, hot and utterly uncompromising, and the island drinks it neat.
funFact: River Antoine has been running since 1785 and is widely considered the oldest functioning water-propelled distillery in the Caribbean.

serve.how: Neat in tiny measures, which is how Grenadians take it, or cut heavily with water or coconut water. At 75% it cannot legally be carried on an aircraft, so it is genuinely a drink you have to go there for.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented wild and pot-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh cane juice from the estate's own fields

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Wood-fired copper pot stills; cane crushed by water wheel

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Wild fermentation in open stone tanks gives the funk, and the wood fire gives the rest.

originStory: Rivers rum comes from the River Antoine estate in St Patrick, on Grenada's north-east coast, where the distillery has worked since 1785. The estate's cane is still crushed by a water-driven wheel, and the juice is fermented and distilled much in the old way, which is why River Antoine is widely called the oldest functioning water-powered distillery in the Caribbean. The rum, sold as Rivers and Rivers Royale, takes its name from the estate, and most of it never leaves Grenada.

name: Nutmeg Liqueur
description: Made from the spice on Grenada's national flag, using both the nutmeg and the red mace that wraps it. The island produces a substantial share of the world's supply and puts it into everything, including this.
funFact: Grenada is the only country whose flag features a food crop, and Hurricane Ivan destroyed around ninety per cent of its nutmeg trees in 2004.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice cream. It also does good work in a rum punch, where a spoonful adds the spice note that grated nutmeg gives on top of the drink.

composition.summary: Nutmeg and mace steeped in rum or neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grenadian rum or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Nutmeg and its outer mace, plus cane sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened

composition.process: Mace carries a lighter, more floral note than the nut, and using both gives the liqueur its range.

originStory: Grenada's nutmeg liqueurs follow the spice itself. Nutmeg is native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia, and the usual account credits Frank Gurney with planting Grenada's first trees in the mid nineteenth century. The crop took so well that the island became known as the Spice Isle and put a nutmeg on its flag at independence. Local makers steep the nut and the red mace that wraps it in rum or spirit and sweeten the result; no single producer is credited with the first bottle.

name: Saint Lucian Rum
description: One distillery on the island runs a Coffey still, two pot stills and a John Dore, which gives it more stylistic range than most whole countries manage. The results run from light and clean to thick and estery.
funFact: Saint Lucia Distillers operates four different still types on one site, which is unusual anywhere and rare in the Caribbean.

serve.how: Neat for the aged expressions, which carry real depth. The pot-still-heavy bottlings hold up in a Mai Tai or a Rum Old Fashioned; the lighter ones make excellent daiquiris.

composition.summary: Molasses and cane juice distilled across four still types, then blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses, with some cane juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Coffey still, two pot stills and a John Dore

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, port and sherry casks, tropically aged

composition.process: Having four stills means the blender is building from components rather than adjusting one spirit.

originStory: Modern Saint Lucian rum starts in 1931, when Denis Barnard built a distillery at Dennery on the island's east coast. In 1972 the Barnards joined the Geest company, which ran the only other working distillery, at Roseau, to form Saint Lucia Distillers; their first joint rum, Denros, took its name from the two sites. The company, known for Chairman's Reserve, now makes its rums at Roseau in both a column still and copper pot stills, an unusually varied set-up for one Caribbean distillery.

name: English Harbour Rum
description: Antiguan column-still rum, aged beside the old Royal Navy dockyard the brand is named for. Lighter and drier than its neighbours, and the extra-aged releases are among the Caribbean's most underrated bottles.
funFact: English Harbour was Nelson's Caribbean base, and the dockyard is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

serve.how: Neat for anything aged five years and up. The younger expressions mix cleanly with ginger or lime. Tropical ageing means a ten-year-old here has done the work of a much older continental spirit.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented and column-distilled, then tropically aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak in tropical conditions, five to twenty-five years

composition.process: Tropical ageing loses far more to evaporation each year, which is why old Caribbean rum is scarce and expensive.

originStory: Antigua Distillery was founded in 1932 by a group of merchants and rum shop owners, many of Portuguese descent, who pooled their blending and ageing know-how into one company. Its aged rum, English Harbour, came much later and is named for the sheltered naval port on the island's south coast, where the Royal Navy kept its Caribbean dockyard and a young Horatio Nelson was stationed. The restored Nelson's Dockyard is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the distillery's older Cavalier rum remains a fixture on the island.

name: Cachaça Envelhecida
description: Aged cachaça, and the reason to take the category seriously. Brazilian producers use native hardwoods — amburana, jequitibá, bálsamo — that give flavours no oak barrel in the world can produce.
funFact: Amburana wood gives a pronounced cinnamon and tonka bean note, which is why aged cachaça often tastes spiced without anything having been added.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, the way you would drink an aged rum. Using a good envelhecida in a caipirinha is not a crime, but the wood notes fight the lime, so the unaged version is better there.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice distilled and aged in Brazilian hardwood casks.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed sugarcane juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least one year in casks of amburana, jequitibá, bálsamo, ipê or oak

composition.process: Brazilian law recognises around thirty native woods for ageing, each with its own flavour signature.

originStory: Cachaça has been distilled from fresh cane juice in Brazil since the sixteenth century, when Portuguese settlers set up the first sugar mills on the coast. Ageing it in wood came later and was long informal, with producers using whatever casks or native timbers were to hand. Brazilian rules now reserve the word envelhecida for cachaça with at least half its volume aged a year or more in wood, with premium and extra premium grades above it. Native woods such as amburana help set the category apart.

name: Tiquira
description: Cassava spirit from Maranhão in Brazil's north, made by fermenting the same root that has to be processed carefully to remove its natural cyanide. Sometimes tinted purple by steeping it over a local leaf.
funFact: Indigenous communities in the region were fermenting cassava long before the Portuguese arrived with distilling equipment.

serve.how: Neat and cold in a small glass. It is a regional spirit, rarely found outside Maranhão, and served with the same directness as any village distillate. The purple version is coloured, not flavoured.

composition.summary: Cassava root cooked, fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cassava (manioc) root

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, after the starch is converted

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: The root must be cooked thoroughly first, both to convert starch and to drive off its natural toxins.

originStory: Tiquira comes from Maranhão in northern Brazil, where cassava has long been the staple root. Indigenous peoples of the region fermented cassava into drinks such as cauim well before the Portuguese arrived; distillation came with colonisation, and tiquira grew from that meeting of a native ferment and a European still. Nobody is credited with its invention, and the origin of the name is not documented. It remains a regional spirit, made mostly by small producers in Maranhão and rarely seen elsewhere in Brazil.

name: Licor de Jenipapo
description: Genipap liqueur from Brazil's northeast, made from a fruit whose unripe juice stains skin blue-black and was used by indigenous peoples as body paint. Ripe, it makes something dark, sweet and faintly medicinal.
funFact: Jenipapo juice produces a deep blue-black dye on skin that takes over a week to wear off, which is why it was used for ceremonial painting.

serve.how: Cold and neat after a meal. It is thick and sweet, so a small pour is enough. Northeastern Brazilians treat it as a digestive and it appears at festas alongside the local cachaça.

composition.summary: Ripe genipap fruit macerated in cachaça and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cachaça or neutral cane spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ripe Genipa americana fruit, sugar, sometimes clove

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for weeks, then sweetened

composition.process: Only fully ripe fruit is used; unripe jenipapo is astringent and stains everything it touches.

originStory: Licor de jenipapo is a festival liqueur of Brazil's northeast, made by steeping the ripe fruit of the genipap tree in cachaça or spirit with sugar. The tree is native to tropical America, and long before the liqueur existed indigenous peoples used its unripe juice as a blue-black body paint that lasts on the skin for days. The liqueur has no recorded inventor; it is a home and small-producer tradition, closely tied to the June festivals of São João in Bahia.

name: Enguindado
description: Chilean aguardiente steeped with sour cherries, drunk during the September independence celebrations and rarely at any other time. Sweet, red and considerably stronger than the fruit suggests.
funFact: It appears almost exclusively around the Fiestas Patrias in September, alongside the terremoto and chicha that dominate the same week.

serve.how: Cold, in a small glass, with the steeped cherries at the bottom. Chileans drink it at fondas during the September holidays, and the cherries are eaten afterwards.

composition.summary: Sour cherries macerated in aguardiente with sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Chilean aguardiente or pisco

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Guindas, the local sour cherry, plus sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for several weeks

composition.process: The cherries keep infusing in the bottle, so a jar opened late in the season is sweeter and deeper.

originStory: Enguindado takes its name from the guinda, the sour cherry, which is steeped in aguardiente with sugar and often cinnamon or cloves until the spirit turns deep red. It is a homemade tradition of the Chilean countryside rather than anyone's invention, and families keep their own proportions and steeping times. Cherry trees reached Chile with Spanish settlement, and steeping fruit in local aguardiente follows the pattern of other Chilean country liqueurs. It comes out on festive occasions, the September independence holidays among them.

name: Singani
description: Bolivia's national spirit: Muscat of Alexandria grown above 1,600 metres and distilled to a clear, intensely floral brandy. The altitude stresses the vines, which concentrates the aromatics, and the result tastes like almost nothing else.
funFact: The director Steven Soderbergh discovered it filming in Bolivia and spent years importing it into the United States, where it initially had no legal category to sit in.

serve.how: Chilled and neat, or in a chuflay: singani with ginger ale and lime over ice, which is the Bolivian standard. The floral aroma is the point, so a wine glass serves it better than a shot glass.

composition.summary: High-altitude Muscat of Alexandria fermented and distilled to clear spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Muscat of Alexandria grown above 1,600 metres

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, no water added afterwards

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; rested in steel or glass

composition.process: Bolivian law fixes the minimum altitude, since the vines' response to thin air is what makes the spirit.

originStory: Singani has been distilled in the Bolivian highlands since the sixteenth century, when Spanish missionaries and settlers planted vines in the southern valleys to supply the silver boom at Potosí. Bolivian law now requires Muscat of Alexandria grapes and high-altitude vineyards, with Tarija the centre of production. The origin of the name is debated. The film director Steven Soderbergh met singani while filming in Bolivia, launched Singani 63 and lobbied US regulators to recognise it as a distinct spirit.

name: Viche
description: Artisanal cane spirit from Colombia's Pacific coast, made by Afro-Colombian communities in stills built from whatever is available. Recognised as national cultural patrimony in 2021 after generations of being treated as contraband.
funFact: Viche is the base for a whole family of preparations — arrechón, tomaseca, curao — each traditionally credited with a specific medicinal or restorative purpose.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or in one of its infused forms. Arrechón, blended with milk, honey and herbs, is the best-known preparation and considerably easier going than the raw spirit.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented and distilled in artisanal stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed Pacific coast sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Handmade copper or improvised stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; infused versions are common

composition.process: The 2021 law recognising viche was written to protect it as ancestral knowledge, not just as a product.

originStory: Viche is the cane spirit of the Afro-Colombian communities of the Pacific coast, in Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Cauca and Nariño. Its tradition was carried by the descendants of enslaved Africans brought to the region, with methods handed down within families over generations. For a long time it was sold informally and treated as contraband, until a national law recognised viche as heritage of the Black communities of the Pacific. It is also the base for steeped preparations such as arrechón, tomaseca and curao.

name: Chirrinchi
description: The Wayúu people's spirit, distilled in the desert of La Guajira on the Colombian and Venezuelan border. Made from panela and used ceremonially as much as socially, in a region where little else grows.
funFact: Chirrinchi is used in Wayúu funerary and negotiation rituals, where offering it carries obligations beyond simple hospitality.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. It is a ceremonial and social spirit within Wayúu communities rather than a bar product, and the commercial bottlings that exist are recent.

composition.summary: Panela fermented and distilled in the Guajira desert.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Panela, unrefined cane sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper or improvised stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Water is scarce in La Guajira, which shapes both the fermentation and the scale of production.

originStory: Chirrinchi is the spirit of the Wayúu, the indigenous people of the La Guajira peninsula, whose lands straddle the border between Colombia and Venezuela. It is distilled from fermented panela or cane sugar in small home stills, a technique that reached the peninsula through colonial contact and was taken into Wayúu custom. No inventor or date is recorded. Its importance is social: chirrinchi is offered at wakes and gatherings and has a place in the customary negotiations that settle family agreements and disputes.

name: Cocuy
description: Venezuela's agave spirit, made from Agave cocui in Falcón and Lara, and the only agave distillate outside Mexico with a protected denomination. Roasted in earth pits like mezcal, and tasting broadly similar.
funFact: Cocuy was made illegally for most of the twentieth century and only received Venezuelan denomination of origin protection in 2001.

serve.how: Neat and unchilled in a small wide glass, sipped rather than shot, exactly as you would treat mezcal. The wild-harvested versions carry more mineral and less sweetness.

composition.summary: Agave cocui hearts roasted, fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave cocui, largely wild-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, then small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: The plant takes eight to ten years to mature, and overharvesting has been a genuine conservation concern.

originStory: Cocuy is made from Agave cocui, which grows in the dry hills of Falcón and Lara in north-western Venezuela. Peoples of the region are said to have roasted the plant long before the Spanish arrived; distilling came after contact, and the spirit grew up as a rural craft. A change in the law in the nineteen-seventies pushed artisanal cocuy underground, and only a later reform made it legal to sell again. Cocuy from Pecaya, in Falcón, holds a denomination of origin.

name: Pájaro Azul
description: Aguardiente from Ecuador's Bolívar province, infused with herbs and reputedly a few less orthodox ingredients depending on who is making it. Blue bird, in translation, and the name is a warning as much as a brand.
funFact: Guaranda's version is the most famous, and the recipe reportedly varies from producer to producer in ways nobody documents.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, usually at carnival in Guaranda where it is the drink of the festival. It is strong and rough by design, and pacing matters more than technique.

composition.summary: Cane aguardiente infused with herbs and other additions.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane aguardiente

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Local herbs, anise, and unlisted regional additions

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then infused

composition.process: Recipes are held locally and vary enough that no two producers make quite the same thing.

originStory: Pájaro azul is an aguardiente of Bolívar province in Ecuador's central highlands, made around Guaranda and Guanujo by steeping cane spirit with herbs, citrus leaves and spices. Some recipes are said to include chicken or other meat during distillation, and each producer guards its own version. The name, blue bird, has several local explanations and no settled one. It has become a fixture of the Carnaval de Guaranda, where it is poured along the parade routes.

name: Grapa Argentina
description: Pomace brandy brought to Argentina by Italian immigrants and made ever since in Mendoza and the wine provinces. Rougher and more rustic than Italian grappa, and drunk in cafés rather than after dinner.
funFact: Italian migration to Argentina was heavy enough that grappa, pizza and a distinct dialect all arrived together and stayed.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, often with coffee. Argentine cafés serve it as a mid-morning fortifier as readily as an after-dinner drink, which is an Italian habit that crossed the Atlantic intact.

composition.summary: Grape pomace from Argentine wine fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pomace from Malbec, Torrontés and other Argentine grapes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; some oak-rested

composition.process: Mendoza's scale means the pomace supply is enormous, and much of it is distilled rather than composted.

originStory: Grappa reached Argentina with the great wave of Italian immigration in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when millions of Italians settled in Buenos Aires and the wine provinces. Families who had made pomace brandy at home in northern Italy kept doing so in Mendoza and San Juan, distilling the skins and seeds left after winemaking. Spelled grapa locally, it has no single founder, and today it is made both by large wineries and by small producers keeping family stills going.

name: Caña
description: Argentine sugarcane spirit, frequently infused with herbs, of which Caña Legui is the name that survives. Once the working drink of the countryside, and still sold with a heavy dose of gaucho nostalgia.
funFact: Caña Legui's advertising has leaned on rural and gaucho imagery for so long that the bottle is a period piece in its own right.

serve.how: Neat, or with a splash of soda. In the countryside it is drunk straight and cold in winter. The herbal versions are sweeter and read closer to a light liqueur than a cane spirit.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit, often infused with herbs and lightly sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane from northern Argentina

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Herbs and botanicals in the traditional styles

composition.process: Tucumán and Salta grow the cane, and the spirit was historically a northern rather than a pampas product.

originStory: Caña, cane spirit, has long been made in Argentina, above all from cane grown in the north-west around Tucumán, and it gave the countryside a cheap everyday spirit. It became a staple of the pulpería, the rural store and bar, and part of gaucho lore, and no single founder is credited with it. Caña also carries a folk custom shared with Paraguay: on the first of August many people take a little steeped with rue to mark the arrival of the month.

name: Hesperidina
description: A bitter orange-peel aperitif invented in Buenos Aires in 1864 and patented so early that Argentina created a trademark law partly to protect it. Sweeter and gentler than an Italian bitter, and unmistakably Argentine.
funFact: Melville Sewell Bagley registered it in 1876 as Argentina's first trademark, having built anticipation by chalking the single word Hesperidina on walls across the city before launch.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and an orange slice, which is the standard Buenos Aires aperitif serve. It also works in place of sweet vermouth in a spritz, being lower in alcohol and higher in orange.

composition.summary: Bitter orange peel macerated in spirit, sweetened and rested.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bitter orange peel, herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

composition.process: The wall-chalking campaign that launched it is credited as one of the first modern teaser advertisements anywhere.

originStory: Hesperidina was created in Buenos Aires in 1864 by Melville Sewell Bagley, a young American from Maine who worked at the La Estrella pharmacy and experimented with bitter orange peel. Before the launch he is said to have painted the single word Hesperidina on walls around the city. When imitations followed, Bagley pressed for a trademark law, and Hesperidina is generally cited as Argentina's first registered mark. The name comes from hesperidium, the botanical term for a citrus fruit.

name: Grappamiel
description: Uruguayan grappa cut with honey, which turns a rough pomace spirit into something warming and easy. Drunk through the winter and sold in every Uruguayan supermarket alongside the yerba mate.
funFact: Uruguay's Italian-descended population is proportionally even larger than Argentina's, which is why grappa took root there so completely.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, or warmed slightly in winter. Uruguayans drink it against the cold coming off the Río de la Plata, and it does the job. Also good poured into coffee.

composition.summary: Grape pomace spirit blended with honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Uruguayan grappa from wine pomace

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Honey, sometimes with spice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: The honey rounds off the pomace spirit's edges without disguising it entirely.

originStory: Grappamiel is grappa sweetened with honey, a Uruguayan habit that grew out of the Italian immigration of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Italian families who distilled grape pomace at home kept doing so in Uruguay, and honey softened the rough spirit through the cold, damp winters of the Río de la Plata. Nobody is credited with the first bottle; it was a household mixture long before brands took it up, and it is still a fixture of Uruguayan bars.

name: Caña Paraguaya
description: Paraguay's national spirit, distilled from sugarcane grown across the country and drunk in enormous quantity. Often aged in native woods, which gives it colour and a distinctly local spice.
funFact: Paraguayans mix it with coconut water and lemon to make caribe, a drink that is close to a national institution during Carnival.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or mixed into caribe with coconut water and lime. Aged versions in native hardwood are worth drinking on their own and are increasingly bottled for export.

composition.summary: Paraguayan sugarcane fermented and distilled, sometimes wood-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Paraguayan sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often in native hardwood casks

composition.process: Paraguay grows a great deal of organic cane, much of which goes into caña rather than sugar.

originStory: Paraguay has grown sugarcane since the colonial period, and caña, the spirit distilled from it, became the country's national spirit long before anyone branded it. It was made on estates and in small rural stills, and some producers rested it in casks of native woods, which gave colour and a local spice. No founder is recorded. Paraguayans also keep the custom of caña con ruda: on the first of August a little caña steeped with rue is taken to mark the start of the month.

name: Borgoe
description: Surinamese rum, made in the only Dutch-speaking country in South America from cane grown along the coastal plain. Light, clean and almost entirely unknown outside the Netherlands and the Guianas.
funFact: Suriname's distillery draws on a sugar industry that dates to Dutch plantation agriculture in the seventeenth century.

serve.how: Over ice with cola or soda, which is how it is drunk in Paramaribo and Amsterdam alike. The aged expressions take a single cube neat and carry more vanilla than the age statement suggests.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented and column-distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Surinamese sugarcane molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, from one to eight years

composition.process: Most of the output goes to the Netherlands, where the Surinamese diaspora keeps the brand alive.

originStory: Borgoe is usually said to have been introduced in 1982 to mark a century of the central sugar factory at Mariënburg, the old Dutch plantation in Commewijne, and its name is taken as a local form of the plantation's. Suriname's sugar and rum trade goes back to Dutch plantation agriculture of the seventeenth century. The rum is made by Suriname Alcoholic Beverages, which also bottles the white rum Black Cat, and Borgoe is its signature name at home and in the Netherlands.

name: Potstill Brandy
description: South African brandy made to rules stricter than cognac's: at least thirty per cent pot-distilled, three years minimum in oak, and no shortcuts permitted. The country has been quietly winning international brandy awards for decades.
funFact: South Africa's first brandy was distilled aboard a ship in Table Bay in 1672 by a cook who described the result, in the log, as unimpressive.
