serve.how: Neat at room temperature. South Africans also drink it long with cola as a brandy and Coke, which is a national habit and not one to be sniffy about, though the pot-still bottlings deserve better.

composition.summary: Chenin and Colombard wine pot-distilled and aged in French oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Chenin Blanc and Colombard from the Western Cape

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, minimum 30% of the blend

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak casks under 340 litres

composition.process: The three-year minimum applies to every drop, not just the youngest component, which is stricter than most brandy law.

originStory: South African brandy is dated to 19 May 1672, when an assistant cook aboard the Dutch ship De Pijl, anchored in Table Bay, distilled Cape wine into brandy. Distilling spread to the farms of the Cape, but the modern quality categories took shape in the twentieth century, when the industry set rules for pot stills and maturation in oak. Potstill brandy is the strictest, made almost entirely from copper pot-still spirit and aged at least three years, and houses such as KWV and Van Ryn's are known for it.

name: Witblits
description: White lightning, in Afrikaans: unaged grape spirit distilled on Cape farms and traditionally sold in whatever bottle came to hand. Clear, fierce and increasingly made with real care by producers who used to hide it.
funFact: Witblits was farm-distilled for generations under a system of home-production rights, and only became a legally recognised category relatively recently.

serve.how: Cool and neat in small measures, which is how Cape farmers take it. The better modern bottlings are clean enough to drink like a good eau-de-vie; the farm stuff is not, and does not pretend to be.

composition.summary: Grapes or pomace fermented and pot-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cape grapes or wine pomace

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often on the farm

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; it must be clear

composition.process: Ageing it in wood makes something else entirely, which is why the category is defined by the absence of colour.

originStory: Witblits, Afrikaans for white lightning, descends from the copper pot stills that Dutch and Huguenot settlers brought to the Cape in the seventeenth century. As farming spread inland, farmers distilled unaged spirit from wine and grape leftovers for their own use, and the name stuck to the clear, high-strength result. Twentieth-century liquor laws made unlicensed distilling illegal for many years, but later reforms allowed licensed production, and a number of farm distilleries now make and sell it openly.

name: Mampoer
description: South African farm fruit brandy, made from peach, apricot, marula or prickly pear depending on the season. The name is said to come from a Pedi chief, and the drink has a reputation for potency that it earns.
funFact: Herman Charles Bosman's short stories made mampoer a fixture of South African literature long before it was legally regulated.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, at room temperature. Peach and apricot are the classics. Like witblits, quality is entirely down to the maker, and the good stuff smells of the fruit rather than of alcohol.

composition.summary: Farm fruit fermented and pot-distilled without additives.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Peach, apricot, marula, prickly pear or plum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, small farm batches

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Mampoer is distilled from whole fruit while witblits comes from grapes, which is the distinction between the two.

originStory: Mampoer grew out of the same Cape pot-still tradition as witblits but moved inland with the trekboers, who distilled whatever fruit their farms gave them: peaches, apricots, plums, marula or prickly pear. The popular explanation for the name links it to Mampuru, a Pedi leader, though historians treat that as folklore rather than proven. Like witblits, it was long caught up in the restrictions on home distilling. Herman Charles Bosman's stories of the Groot Marico made mampoer a fixture of South African writing.

name: Amarula
description: Cream liqueur made from the marula fruit, which is fermented and distilled before the cream goes in. The elephants on the label refer to a widely repeated story about them eating fallen fruit and getting drunk, which is mostly a myth.
funFact: Marula fruit is gathered from wild trees by rural communities rather than farmed, since the trees are protected and notoriously difficult to cultivate.

serve.how: Over ice, or poured over ice cream. It also goes into coffee well. Serve it properly cold; at room temperature the cream flattens and the fruit disappears underneath it.

composition.summary: Marula fruit fermented, distilled, oak-aged, then blended with cream.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Marula fruit spirit, distilled from the fermented fruit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Fresh cream and sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Fruit fermented and distilled before blending

components.label: Aging
components.detail: The spirit spends two years in oak before the cream is added

composition.process: Unlike most cream liqueurs the base is a genuine fruit distillate rather than neutral spirit.

originStory: Amarula began in 1983, when the Southern Liqueur Company in South Africa launched a spirit distilled from fermented marula fruit; the cream liqueur followed in 1989 and soon became the brand. The marula, a wild tree of southern Africa also known as the elephant tree, gives the brand its name and its label, since elephants eat the fallen fruit, though the popular idea that the fruit intoxicates them is largely a myth. The fruit is gathered from wild trees by rural communities.

name: Van der Hum
description: A Cape tangerine liqueur made since the seventeenth century, built on brandy and flavoured with naartjie peel and spice. One of the oldest continuously made liqueurs outside Europe.
funFact: The name translates roughly as what's-his-name, apparently because the Dutch settler who first made it could not be recalled by the person who named it.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice. It is also used in Cape cooking, particularly in desserts and with dried fruit. A splash in a brandy Old Fashioned is a very good idea.

composition.summary: Cape brandy infused with naartjie peel and spices.

components.label: Base
components.detail: South African brandy

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Naartjie (tangerine) peel, nutmeg, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended, then rested

composition.process: The naartjie is a Cape citrus variety, and using its dried peel rather than the juice is what keeps it dry.

originStory: Van der Hum is a Cape liqueur of brandy flavoured with naartjie peel and spices, and the earliest mention usually cited dates from 1861. How much older it is nobody knows, and the name is a puzzle: one explanation makes it Mr What's-his-name, because rival claimants could not agree who invented it, while another credits a Dutch sea captain. Naartjie is the South African word for a tangerine, and KWV is among the houses that still make it.

name: Cape Gin
description: South African gin built on fynbos, the shrubland flora of the Cape that exists nowhere else on earth. Buchu, rooibos, honeybush and kapokbos give it a dusty, herbal quality no European gin can imitate.
funFact: The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms and the only one contained entirely within a single country.

serve.glass: Large copa with plenty of ice
serve.how: With a neutral tonic and a rosemary sprig or grapefruit peel, so the fynbos comes through rather than being buried. Skip the cucumber and lime; they flatten exactly the botanicals you are paying for.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with juniper and Cape fynbos botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain or grape spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper plus buchu, rooibos, honeybush, kapokbos, wild rosemary

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour baskets for delicate botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Grape-based neutral spirit is common here, since the Cape has more wine than grain.

originStory: Fynbos gin is usually credited to Lorna Scott, who founded the Inverroche distillery at Still Bay on the southern Cape coast and is widely regarded as the first to make gin from fynbos, using plants from the surrounding hills and dunes. Fynbos is the shrubland of the Cape Floral Kingdom, the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms and the only one inside a single country. The idea spread through South Africa's craft distilling boom, and buchu and rooibos became familiar gin botanicals.

name: Mahia
description: Fig or date distillate kept alive for centuries by Moroccan Jewish families, and now made by very few people anywhere. Clear, dry and faintly aniseed, and among the most endangered spirits in this list.
funFact: Most of Morocco's Jewish community emigrated in the mid-twentieth century, and the surviving mahia tradition now runs largely through Israel and France.

serve.how: Cool and neat, in a small glass, with salted food. It is traditionally drunk at celebrations and on Shabbat, and the aniseed versions are the ones most people encounter.

composition.summary: Figs or dates fermented and distilled, sometimes with anise.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Dried figs or dates

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, usually twice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Aniseed in some versions

composition.process: Figs ferment readily but yield little alcohol, so a great weight of fruit goes into every bottle.

originStory: Mahia was the spirit of Morocco's Jewish communities, distilled at home and in small workshops from figs, dates or raisins and often scented with aniseed. Its name is usually glossed as water of life, and it belonged to festivals and family celebrations. No inventor or date is recorded; it was a household craft passed down through generations. When most of Morocco's Jews emigrated in the mid twentieth century, largely to Israel and France, the tradition went with them, and a handful of distillers now keep it going.

name: Boukha
description: Tunisian fig brandy, clear and unaged, developed in the late nineteenth century by the country's Jewish community. Drier and cleaner than most fruit brandies, and drunk cold rather than contemplated.
funFact: The name comes from an Arabic word for vapour, referring to the steam rising off the still.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass, before or after a meal. Tunisians also pour it over melon or fresh figs, which is an excellent use of both.

composition.summary: Mediterranean figs fermented and double-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Dried Tunisian figs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double distillation in pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Only figs and water go in; there is no added sugar or flavouring in a genuine boukha.

originStory: Boukha is the fig brandy of Tunisia's Jewish community, and its best-known house is Bokobsa. The family dates its distilling to 1880, when Abraham Bokobsa is said to have turned a household craft into a business near Tunis. The name is disputed: many sources trace it to a Judeo-Arabic word for vapour, from the steam rising off the still, while the Bokobsa family's own account links it to the word vodka. No one is credited with first distilling figs.

name: Thibarine
description: A date and herb liqueur made at Thibar in northern Tunisia, originally by White Fathers missionaries who planted vines and orchards in the hills. Sweet, spiced and increasingly hard to find.
funFact: The monastery at Thibar ran a substantial agricultural estate under the French protectorate, and the liqueur outlived the mission that created it.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice with a strip of orange peel. It is sweet and heavily spiced, so a small pour does the work. Also good stirred into mint tea, oddly enough.

composition.summary: Date distillate blended with herbs, spices and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Date spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Herbs and spices to a monastic recipe

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then macerated and sweetened

composition.process: The recipe was developed by missionaries who applied European liqueur technique to North African fruit.

originStory: Thibarine comes from Thibar, in the hills of northern Tunisia, where the Missionaries of Africa, known as the White Fathers, established an agricultural estate under the French protectorate at the end of the nineteenth century. The fathers planted vines and orchards, made wine, and produced a liqueur of dates and aromatic herbs macerated in grape spirit. Accounts differ on when the liqueur was first made, and no member of the order is credited with the recipe. It outlived the mission that created it.

name: Zibib
description: Egypt's anise spirit, related to arak and ouzo and clouding the same way with water. The name comes from the Arabic for raisin, which is what much of it is distilled from.
funFact: Egyptian bars serve it with a small jug of water so drinkers can watch the louche happen at the table, which is half the ritual.

serve.how: Poured over ice or cut with two parts water, which turns it milky white. Egyptians drink it with mezze rather than after a meal, and it stands up well to strongly spiced food.

composition.summary: Grape or raisin spirit redistilled with aniseed.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grapes, raisins or dates

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Aniseed, sometimes mastic

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the anise, usually twice

composition.process: Anethole precipitating out of solution when water is added is what produces the cloud.

originStory: Zibib is Egypt's anise spirit, part of the family that includes Levantine arak, Greek ouzo and Turkish rakı. The name comes from zabib, the Arabic word for raisin, since much of it was traditionally distilled from dried grapes and then flavoured with aniseed. No inventor or date is recorded; it developed within the eastern Mediterranean tradition of grape-based anise spirits. Like its relatives it is mixed with water, which turns it milky white, the effect known as the louche.

name: Areke
description: Ethiopian grain spirit distilled from barley, maize or teff and flavoured with gesho, the buckthorn leaf that also bitters the country's beer. Made at home across the highlands and served at every celebration.
funFact: Gesho, Rhamnus prinoides, is Ethiopia's hop equivalent and has been used in brewing and distilling there for centuries.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature, poured for guests at weddings, holidays and mourning gatherings alike. It is a household product, and the strength varies dramatically depending on who made it.

composition.summary: Grain fermented with gesho and distilled in clay or metal stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Barley, maize, teff or wheat

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Gesho leaf, which also drives fermentation

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Simple pot stills, often clay, sometimes twice

composition.process: Double-distilled areke is called dagim and is noticeably cleaner than the single-run version.

originStory: Areke is the household spirit of the Ethiopian highlands, distilled from a ferment of grains such as barley, maize, sorghum or teff and usually bittered with gesho, the buckthorn leaf that also flavours the beer called tella. Families make it in simple clay stills, and a twice-distilled version, dagim areke, is stronger and clearer. No inventor or date is recorded; it is an old domestic craft, largely in the hands of women, tied to holidays, weddings and hospitality.

name: Aragi
description: Sudanese date spirit, distilled quietly and at some risk in a country where alcohol has been prohibited since 1983. Made from the date palms that line the Nile, and the tradition long predates the ban.
funFact: Sudan removed the death penalty for alcohol consumption by non-Muslims in 2020, a change that made the trade marginally less dangerous.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and discreetly. It is a homemade spirit sold through informal networks, and quality varies with the maker's skill and equipment.

composition.summary: Dates fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Nile valley dates

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Simple pot stills, often improvised

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–60%, unmeasured

composition.process: Dates are high in sugar and ferment readily, which is why they became the region's distilling crop.

originStory: Aragi is the date spirit of Sudan, distilled from the fruit of the palms along the Nile, and its name is a local form of the word arak. It was a common household and village spirit before the Islamic laws of Jaafar Nimeiry's government banned alcohol in 1983 and drove it underground. No inventor or date is recorded. A 2020 reform allowed non-Muslims to drink in private, while the ban for Muslims remains, and aragi is still made at small scale, largely outside any licensing.

name: Chang'aa
description: Kenyan maize and millet moonshine, illegal until 2010 and still made mostly outside any regulation. The name means kill me quick, and adulterated batches have killed people, which is precisely why it was legalised.
funFact: Kenya legalised and set standards for chang'aa in 2010 specifically to pull production out of the informal sector, where methanol adulteration had caused mass poisonings.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and only from a licensed producer. The legalised bottled versions are safe; the informal ones are a genuine gamble, and that distinction matters more here than anywhere else in this list.

composition.summary: Maize, millet or sorghum fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Maize, millet or sorghum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Improvised stills, often single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: The legal standard sets a methanol limit, which is the entire point of the regulation.

originStory: Chang'aa is Kenya's traditional distilled spirit, made from fermented maize, millet or sorghum in small home stills, and its name is usually glossed as kill me quickly. Home distilling is generally thought to have spread in the colonial period, when local spirits were banned and production moved into the informal economy. No inventor or date is recorded. Because unregulated batches were sometimes adulterated with methanol, Kenya legalised chang'aa under its Alcoholic Drinks Control Act of 2010, aiming to bring production into the open.

name: Kenya Cane
description: Kenya's licensed cane spirit, clean and light, and the country's answer to white rum. It sits on every bar shelf from Nairobi to Mombasa and is drunk mostly with soda and lime.
funFact: It has been produced since the 1960s and is one of the few East African spirits with genuine brand recognition across the region.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and lime, or with coconut water. It is a light mixing spirit rather than a sipping one, and it substitutes cleanly for white rum in almost anything.

composition.summary: Kenyan cane molasses fermented and column-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses from Kenyan sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None for the white; a coconut-flavoured version exists

composition.process: Kenya's sugar belt around Kisumu supplies the molasses that goes into it.

originStory: Kenya Cane is the licensed cane spirit of Kenya Wine Agencies, the company the Kenyan government set up after independence to bring the import and distribution of wines and spirits under one roof, and which later began making its own. The company has not published a detailed history of the brand's launch, and no individual is credited with creating it. It became a staple of bars across the country as a legal, consistent cane spirit, and its makers have since added flavoured versions and a second cane spirit, Caribia.

name: Waragi
description: Ugandan spirit distilled from bananas, millet or cassava, made across the country in village stills. The name is a corruption of war gin, from the spirit issued to soldiers during the Second World War.
funFact: Banana waragi, made from the local matoke varieties, is distinct enough from the millet version that Ugandans treat them as separate drinks.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures. Village waragi is unregulated and adulteration is a real hazard, so provenance matters. The banana version is fruitier and considerably more approachable.

composition.summary: Bananas, millet or cassava fermented and distilled locally.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Bananas, millet, sorghum or cassava

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Village pot stills, usually single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Banana waragi ferments the fruit itself, while the millet version malts the grain first.

originStory: Waragi is the general Ugandan name for locally distilled spirit, made from bananas, millet, cassava or sugarcane in village stills across the country. The name is commonly said to be a corruption of war gin, from the colonial era, though that etymology is folk history rather than documented fact. Unlicensed distilling was restricted under colonial rule and later brought under licensing, with licensed makers of the raw spirit, called enguli, required to sell it on to a distiller.

name: Uganda Waragi
description: The commercial, juniper-flavoured version of waragi, triple-distilled and sold in bottles and sachets across East Africa. Essentially a Ugandan gin, and by far the safest way to meet the category.
funFact: It is one of East Africa's biggest spirit brands, and the sachet format was eventually banned in Uganda over concerns about street drinking.

serve.how: With tonic and lime like any gin, or with soda. The pineapple and coconut expressions are popular locally. It is lighter on juniper than a London Dry, so it takes a fruitier mixer well.

composition.summary: Triple-distilled spirit flavoured with juniper and botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses or grain neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper and citrus, lighter than a London Dry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Triple-distilled, then flavoured

composition.process: Triple distillation is a deliberate safety and consistency measure given the category's informal reputation.

originStory: Uganda Waragi was first produced in 1965, when the government of newly independent Uganda set up a distillery to turn the country's village spirit into a regulated, bottled product. The Enguli Act of the same year required licensed makers of enguli, the raw local spirit, to sell it to the distillers, where it was redistilled and flavoured with juniper and other botanicals. The state's Uganda Distilleries made it for decades until the brand passed to Uganda Breweries, part of East African Breweries.

name: Konyagi
description: Tanzania's own cane spirit, sold in a distinctive frosted bottle and sitting somewhere between gin and vodka in character. Legally it is neither, which suits a country that treats it as its own category.
funFact: Tanzanians often describe it as neither gin nor vodka but konyagi, and the marketing has embraced that ambiguity for decades.

serve.how: Over ice with soda, lime or coconut water. It is light enough to substitute for either vodka or gin, and locally it is drunk with bitter lemon more than anything else.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit distilled and lightly flavoured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Tanzanian sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: A light botanical touch

composition.process: It sits deliberately between categories, which is a marketing position as much as a technical one.

originStory: Konyagi is usually dated to 1970, when it was introduced by Tanzania Distilleries, the company that still makes it, and within a generation it became the country's most familiar spirit. Made from cane spirit with flavourings and bottled at 35 per cent, it sits between gin and vodka without being either, and Tanzanians simply call it konyagi as if it were a category of its own. Its makers have not explained the name. Tanzania Distilleries is now part of the Tanzania Breweries group.

name: Gongo
description: Tanzanian village moonshine, distilled from maize, millet or whatever is available, and made across the country despite being illegal. Regional names change every few hundred kilometres.
funFact: Tanzania periodically runs crackdowns on gongo production, and just as periodically debates legalising and regulating it instead.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and with the same caution any unregulated distillate deserves. Quality depends entirely on whether the maker discarded the first runnings.

composition.summary: Grain or fruit fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Maize, millet, sorghum or bananas

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Improvised stills, single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–60%, unmeasured

composition.process: Because nothing is standardised, strength and safety vary from one village to the next.

originStory: Gongo is the general Tanzanian name for village-distilled spirit, made from maize, millet, sugarcane or bananas, depending on the region, in improvised stills. It has no recorded inventor or start date; distilling spread informally and stayed outside the law, since unlicensed production is illegal in Tanzania. The name and the base ingredient change from place to place. Governments have alternated between crackdowns and proposals to license and regulate small producers, as neighbouring Kenya did with chang'aa, and the debate continues.

name: Ogogoro
description: Nigerian palm spirit, distilled from the sap of raffia and oil palms after it has fermented in the tree. Banned under colonial rule to protect imported gin, and now being bottled commercially with real ambition.
funFact: The British colonial administration banned it in 1909 partly to protect the market for imported Dutch and English gin, which made it a nationalist symbol.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, or infused with herbs and roots as it often is locally. The new craft bottlings are clean enough to drink like a rhum agricole and mix well with citrus.

composition.summary: Fermented palm sap distilled in pot stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap of raffia or oil palm, fermented in the tree

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills, traditionally improvised

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none

composition.process: The sap begins fermenting the moment it is tapped, so distilling has to happen within a day or two.

originStory: Ogogoro is distilled from palm wine, the fermented sap of raffia and oil palms, and is most closely associated with the Niger Delta, where it was made in home stills. The British colonial authorities banned local distilling, partly to protect revenue from imported gin, and labelled ogogoro illicit gin; made in secret, it became a symbol of resistance to colonial rule. Production became legal after independence, though much of it is still made informally, and new commercial bottlings now present it as a serious spirit.

name: Akpeteshie
description: Ghana's national spirit, distilled from palm wine or sugarcane, and outlawed by the British until independence. The name is said to mean they are hiding, from the years when making it was a criminal act.
funFact: Akpeteshie is poured on the ground as a libation to ancestors at Ghanaian ceremonies before anyone drinks any of it.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, often with a libation poured first. It is also the base for bitters infused with roots and herbs, which is how a great deal of it is consumed.

composition.summary: Palm wine or cane juice fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Palm wine or sugarcane juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or drum pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Legalised at independence in 1957, it went from contraband to national drink almost overnight.

originStory: Akpeteshie took hold in the 1930s in what was then the Gold Coast, when the colonial government had banned local distilling and raised duties on imported spirits. Ghanaians distilled palm wine and sugarcane in secret, and the Ga name, usually explained as they are hiding, recalls that clandestine trade. The spirit became bound up with the independence movement and was legalised after independence. It is still poured on the ground as a libation to the ancestors at ceremonies.

name: Odontol
description: Cameroonian moonshine distilled from palm wine, maize or cane, made across the country under a dozen local names. Also called arki, and produced almost entirely outside any licensing system.
funFact: Cameroon has repeatedly attempted to regulate odontol production, and the trade has repeatedly proved larger than the enforcement.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures. Frequently infused with bark and roots locally. As with any unregulated distillate, the maker's care is the only quality control there is.

composition.summary: Palm wine, maize or cane fermented and distilled informally.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Palm wine, maize or sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Improvised stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Names shift by region — odontol, arki, ha — but the method stays broadly the same.

originStory: Odontol is the name used in Cameroon for home-distilled spirit, made from palm wine, maize or sugarcane in improvised stills, and known in different regions by other names, arki among them. It has no recorded inventor or start date; like neighbouring West African palm spirits it grew up outside the licensed trade, and most of it is still made that way. The origin of the word odontol is not documented. The Cameroonian authorities have tried several times to regulate or suppress production, but village distilling has stayed widespread.

name: Lotoko
description: Congolese spirit distilled from maize or cassava, made throughout the country in improvised stills often built from oil drums and salvaged pipe. Also called pétrole, which is not a compliment.
funFact: The nickname pétrole refers to both the colour and the smell of the roughest batches, and the comparison is not entirely unfair.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and with real caution about the source. Better-made lotoko is clean and grain-forward; badly made lotoko is genuinely hazardous.

composition.summary: Maize or cassava fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Maize, cassava or plantain

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Drum and pipe stills, single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Cassava must be processed carefully first, since the raw root carries natural cyanogenic compounds.

originStory: Lotoko is the home-distilled spirit of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, made from fermented maize or cassava in stills improvised from oil drums and salvaged pipe. No inventor or date is recorded, and the origin of the name is not documented. It is produced and sold largely outside any licensing, and the authorities have periodically tried to ban it, but it is still widely made.

name: Caporroto
description: Angolan artisanal cane spirit, distilled in the interior from sugarcane grown on smallholdings. A Portuguese colonial legacy crossed with local practice, and rarely bottled for export.
funFact: Angola's cane industry dates to Portuguese colonisation, and caporroto emerged alongside it as the smallholder's product rather than the plantation's.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, or with lime and sugar in the Brazilian manner, which the shared Portuguese heritage makes an obvious move. Often infused with fruit locally.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Angolan sugarcane juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none

composition.process: Using fresh juice rather than molasses puts it technically in the agricole family.

originStory: Caporroto is the artisanal cane spirit of Angola, distilled by smallholders in the interior from sugarcane grown on family plots. Sugarcane came to Angola with Portuguese colonisation, and caporroto grew up beside the plantation trade as the small farmer's product rather than the estate's. Its exact beginnings, and the source of its name, are not documented, and it is rarely bottled for sale outside the country. It is mostly made and drunk locally, often at family and village occasions.

name: Nipa
description: Mozambican distillate made from cashew fruit or palm sap, depending on the region and the season. Cashew nipa uses the fleshy apple that most of the world discards to get at the nut.
funFact: The cashew apple is highly perishable and rarely leaves the country it grows in, so distilling it is one of the few ways to use the crop at scale.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. The cashew version has a distinctive astringency that comes from the fruit itself, and locals often cut it with soft drink or fruit juice.

composition.summary: Cashew apple or palm sap fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cashew apple or palm sap

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Cashew apples must be pressed and fermented within a day of picking, which ties production to the harvest.

originStory: Nipa is the name used in parts of Mozambique for spirit distilled from fermented cashew apples. The cashew tree was brought to East Africa from Brazil by the Portuguese, and Mozambique became a major grower; the fleshy apple attached to each nut spoils within days, so fermenting and distilling it is one of the few ways to use it. No inventor or date is recorded, and how nipa got its name is not documented. It is made in small home stills and sold mostly locally.

name: Grogue
description: Cape Verde's cane spirit, distilled from fresh juice pressed in trapiches — animal or engine-driven mills — mostly on the steep terraces of Santo Antão. Grassy, mineral and unmistakably island-made.
funFact: Santo Antão's cane is grown on terraces cut into near-vertical valleys, and much of it is still carried out by hand or donkey.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or as a grogue sour with lime and sugarcane honey. Cape Verdeans drink it at any hour and treat refusing it as slightly eccentric.

composition.summary: Fresh-pressed cane juice fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh sugarcane juice from island terraces

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot stills, often wood-fired

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; aged versions exist

composition.process: Wild fermentation in open wooden vats gives grogue its funk, much as it does clairin in Haiti.

originStory: Grogue is Cape Verde's cane spirit, and the islands' cane distilling is among the oldest in the Atlantic. Portugal planted sugarcane on the archipelago soon after settling it in the fifteenth century, and cane spirit, then simply called aguardente, followed. The name grogue is generally traced to the English word grog. Today most of it comes from Santo Antão and Santiago, where cane grown on steep terraces is crushed in trapiches and distilled in small copper stills.

name: Ponche
description: Grogue cut with sugarcane honey and lime, sometimes with cinnamon or passion fruit added. Cape Verde's sweet counterpart to its own fierce cane spirit, and the version most visitors take home.
funFact: Mel de cana, the cane honey used to sweeten it, is boiled-down juice rather than anything made by bees.

serve.how: Neat, at room temperature or lightly chilled, after a meal. It is thick and sweet, and the passion fruit and coconut versions found on the islands are sweeter still.

composition.summary: Grogue blended with cane honey, lime and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cape Verdean grogue

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mel de cana, lime, cinnamon, sometimes passion fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: Boiled cane juice gives a darker, more molasses-like sweetness than refined sugar would.

originStory: Ponche is Cape Verde's sweet companion to grogue, made by mixing the cane spirit with mel de cana, a thick syrup boiled down from sugarcane juice, and usually lime. It grew out of the same trapiche culture on Santo Antão and Santiago, where syrup and spirit come from the same cane harvest. No inventor or date is recorded, and families and small producers keep their own recipes. Despite the name, mel de cana has nothing to do with bees; it is simply cane juice cooked down.

name: Malagasy Rhum
description: Madagascar distils rum from cane grown on an island that separated from Africa long enough ago to evolve its own everything. The vanilla-infused expressions draw on the world's best supply of the pod.
funFact: Madagascar produces the majority of the world's vanilla, so infusing it into local rum is less a gimmick than an obvious use of what is to hand.

serve.how: Neat or over a cube. The vanilla-infused bottlings are best served cool and neat, where the pod comes through cleanly. Younger cane spirit works well with lime and sugar.

composition.summary: Malagasy cane juice or molasses fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane grown on Madagascar, juice or molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column or pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Some aged; many infused with vanilla or spice

composition.process: Whole vanilla pods are often left in the bottle, continuing to infuse after it reaches the shelf.

originStory: Sugarcane has long been grown on Madagascar, and rum distilling grew with the colonial sugar industry, centred in the north-west and on the island of Nosy Be. The best-known Malagasy brand, Dzama, is credited to Lucien Fohine, who began with a distillery beside the sugar works on Nosy Be and built a range around the island's produce. Madagascar also grows most of the world's vanilla, so vanilla rums and the household rhum arrangé follow naturally from what grows there.

name: Toaka Gasy
description: Malagasy village moonshine, distilled from cane juice or rice in the highlands, technically illegal and universally drunk. The name simply means Malagasy alcohol, which tells you how central it is.
funFact: Toaka gasy production has been prohibited at various points since colonial times, largely to protect tax revenue from licensed distilleries.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, usually poured from an unlabelled bottle. It is a social and ceremonial drink in rural Madagascar, and appears at famadihana, the turning of the bones.

composition.summary: Cane juice or rice fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane juice, sometimes rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Improvised pot stills, wood-fired

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Wood-firing the still is what gives the smoke that distinguishes it from commercial rum.

originStory: Toaka gasy, simply Malagasy alcohol, is the island's village spirit, distilled from fermented cane juice or sometimes rice in small home stills, mostly in the highlands and countryside. No inventor or date is recorded; it is a household craft that has been made for generations. Production has been prohibited or restricted at various times since the colonial era, largely to protect tax revenue from licensed distilleries, and most of it is still made and sold informally, from village to village.

name: Rhum Arrangé
description: Rum steeped with fruit, vanilla and spice, a household craft across Madagascar, Réunion and Mauritius. Every family and bar keeps its own jars, and the good ones improve for years.
funFact: On Réunion the jars sit on bar counters in plain view, and asking what is in one is a reliable way to start a long conversation.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass after a meal. It is sweeter and lower in strength than the rum it started as. Litchi, vanilla, ginger and combava are the classic infusions; the jar keeps developing as it stands.

composition.summary: Local rum macerated with fruit, spice and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Island rum, white or lightly aged

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Vanilla, litchi, ginger, combava, cinnamon, pineapple

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for months, sometimes years

composition.process: Time is the whole method; a jar left for a year tastes nothing like one left for a month.

originStory: Rhum arrangé, arranged rum, is a household tradition of the French-speaking Indian Ocean islands, above all Réunion and Madagascar. Local rum is steeped with fruit, spices, vanilla or herbs and left for months. Nobody invented it; it grew from the rum of the islands' sugar estates and the fruit and spice that grow around them, and every family and bar keeps its own recipes. On Réunion the big jars sit on bar counters in plain view, and some distilleries now bottle their own versions.

name: Takamaka
description: Seychelles rum, named after the tree that lines the islands' beaches and holds the sand together. Made on Mahé from imported and local cane, and the archipelago's only spirit of any scale.
funFact: The takamaka tree is a coastal fixture across the Indian Ocean and was traditionally used for boat-building before it lent its name to a distillery.

serve.how: Over ice with coconut water or soda and lime. The aged expressions take a single cube neat. The coconut version is sweet and works better in a long drink than on its own.

composition.summary: Cane molasses and juice fermented and distilled on Mahé.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, with some local cane juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak for the aged range

composition.process: Tropical ageing on a small island means high evaporation and fast maturation.

originStory: Takamaka rum dates from 2002, when the brothers Richard and Bernard d'Offay founded the Trois Frères Distillery on Mahé. The distillery now works from La Plaine St André, an old plantation estate from the French colonial era. The brand takes its name from the takamaka tree, a coastal tree of the Indian Ocean that shades Seychelles beaches and was traditionally used for boat-building, and it has become the islands' best-known rum.

name: Kachasu
description: Zimbabwean and Zambian maize moonshine, distilled in townships and rural areas from fermented maize meal. Illegal, ubiquitous, and known by a dozen names across southern Africa.
funFact: Also called junta, kachipembe or skokiaan depending on the country, and the last of those became an international hit song in the 1950s.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and with real attention to who made it. Adulteration is common, and unregulated distillation of this kind carries genuine risk.

composition.summary: Maize meal fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Maize meal, sometimes with sorghum or sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Drum stills, single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–60%, unmeasured

composition.process: The mash is soured before distillation, which is where the characteristic tang comes from.

originStory: Kachasu is the home-distilled maize spirit of Zambia and Zimbabwe, made from fermented maize meal, sometimes with sugar or other grains, in improvised stills. It grew up in townships and villages during the colonial period, when Africans' access to European liquor was restricted, and it has stayed largely outside the law. No inventor or date is recorded. A related home brew, skokiaan, gave its title to a tune by the Zimbabwean bandleader August Musarurwa that became an international hit, recorded by Louis Armstrong among others.

name: Ombike
description: Namibian distillate made by Owambo communities from marula fruit, palm fruit or wild berries, using stills of clay and salvaged metal. A genuinely traditional spirit that has survived colonisation and prohibition alike.
funFact: The German colonial administration banned ombike production, and the practice continued unbroken regardless, largely because it was made by women at household scale.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, usually at social gatherings in northern Namibia. Marula ombike carries a distinct fruit note; the palm-fruit versions are earthier and rougher.

composition.summary: Wild fruit fermented and distilled in traditional stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Marula fruit, makalani palm fruit or wild berries

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Clay or improvised metal stills over open fire

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Marula fruits for only a few weeks a year, so the season dictates when the stills run.

originStory: Ombike is a traditional distilled spirit of the Owambo people of northern Namibia, made from fermented marula fruit, makalani palm fruit, wild berries or grain in stills of clay and salvaged metal. It is household production, largely in the hands of women, and no inventor or date is recorded. The spirit has survived colonial restrictions and periods of prohibition and is still made in villages across the north. The origin of the word is not documented, and it is rarely sold beyond local markets.

name: Israeli Single Malt
description: Whisky matured in Tel Aviv's heat and humidity, where a cask loses far more each year than in Scotland and the spirit comes of age in a fraction of the time. Milk & Honey opened the category in 2012.
funFact: Some casks mature in warehouses near the Dead Sea, the lowest point on land, where the air pressure and heat push maturation faster still.

serve.how: Neat, with a few drops of water. Rapid tropical maturation means young whisky here carries heavy wood, so water helps pull the spirit back out from under it.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in Israel's Mediterranean climate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, sherry, wine and pomegranate casks; three years and up

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 46%, non-chill-filtered

composition.process: Annual evaporation runs several times the Scottish rate, which concentrates the spirit fast.

originStory: Israeli single malt is a young category. One of its pioneers is Milk & Honey, founded in 2012 by a group of entrepreneurs in Tel Aviv, with the Scottish whisky consultant Jim Swan advising on production; its first single malt followed a few years later. The hot, humid coastal climate pushes spirit into wood quickly, and the distillery has also matured casks elsewhere in Israel, including near the Dead Sea. Other distilleries have since joined it.

name: Sabra
description: Israeli chocolate and Jaffa orange liqueur, launched in the 1960s in a bottle modelled on an ancient Phoenician oil flask. Sweet, dark, and named after the prickly pear as a nickname for native-born Israelis.
funFact: The bottle shape was based on a two-thousand-year-old Phoenician vessel, and the design was commissioned specifically to look archaeological.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice. It also works poured over ice cream and stirred into coffee. Very sweet, so a small measure is enough.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with chocolate and Jaffa orange.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Cocoa and Jaffa bitter orange

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

composition.process: Jaffa oranges were Israel's signature export crop, which is what tied the liqueur to national identity.

originStory: Sabra was launched in 1963 and is usually credited to Edgar Bronfman Sr. of Seagram, who wanted an identifiably Israeli liqueur. The name is the Hebrew word for the prickly pear cactus, used affectionately for native-born Israelis, and the first version is said to have been flavoured with the cactus fruit. It did not catch on, and the recipe was changed to bitter chocolate and Jaffa orange, the combination that stuck. The bottle is modelled on an ancient Phoenician flask.

name: Aragh Sagi
description: Iranian raisin spirit, distilled illicitly since the 1979 revolution made alcohol illegal. The name translates as dog sweat, which is either self-deprecating humour or an accurate description depending on the batch.
funFact: Iran has one of the world's oldest winemaking traditions, with evidence of grape fermentation in the Zagros mountains going back seven thousand years.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, and privately. Quality ranges from carefully double-distilled to genuinely dangerous, and methanol poisoning from bad batches is a recurring problem in Iran.

composition.summary: Raisins fermented and distilled in home stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Raisins, sometimes dates or grapes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Homemade stills, single or double distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–70%, unmeasured

composition.process: Raisins are legal to buy in quantity, which is precisely why they became the base.

originStory: Aragh is the Persian word for distilled spirit, related to arak, and Iran's grape culture is among the oldest anywhere: jars from Hajji Firuz Tepe in the Zagros mountains hold wine residue some seven thousand years old. Aragh sagi, dog's sweat, is the slang name for the raisin spirit distilled at home in secret since the Islamic Revolution banned alcohol for Muslims. No inventor or date is recorded, and recognised religious minorities may make alcohol for their own use.

name: Indian Molasses Whisky
description: The overwhelming majority of what India calls whisky is distilled from molasses rather than grain, which means most of the world's best-selling whisky brands are not whisky under European law at all.
funFact: Several Indian brands sell more cases annually than the entire Scotch whisky industry, purely on the strength of the domestic market.

serve.how: With soda and ice, which is how India drinks it, or with water. It is sweeter and lighter than grain whisky and is built for long mixing rather than neat contemplation.

composition.summary: Molasses spirit blended with a small proportion of malt whisky.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, usually with some malt whisky blended in

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often minimal; tropical maturation is fast

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 42.8%

composition.process: India taxes and defines whisky domestically, which is why molasses-based spirit can carry the name there.

originStory: Most whisky sold in India belongs to a category shaped by colonial and post-independence excise law: Indian-made foreign liquor, spirits made in India in the style of imported ones. With molasses plentiful and cheap from the sugar industry, distillers built their whiskies on neutral molasses spirit, blended with flavourings and sometimes a share of malt. No single founder is credited. Because European rules define whisky as a grain spirit, most of these brands cannot be sold as whisky there, though several rank among the world's largest whisky brands by volume.

name: Coconut Feni
description: The other Goan feni, distilled from coconut palm toddy rather than cashew apples. Older than the cashew version, since cashews only arrived with the Portuguese, and now much the rarer of the two.
funFact: Toddy tappers climb the palms twice daily and are a vanishing profession in Goa, which is the main reason coconut feni is disappearing.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or with lime soda, which is the standard Goan serve. It is funkier and more savoury than cashew feni, and it takes acid well.

composition.summary: Coconut palm sap fermented and pot-distilled in stages.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Toddy tapped from coconut palm flower stalks

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional pot distillation, typically three runs

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; some rest in earthenware

composition.process: The sap ferments within hours of tapping, so distillation happens the same day.

originStory: Coconut feni is the older of Goa's two fenis. Toddy, the sap tapped from coconut palms, is generally thought to have been fermented and distilled on the Konkan coast before the Portuguese arrived, while cashew trees came only with them, from Brazil, in the sixteenth century. The name is usually traced to the Konkani word for froth. No inventor is recorded. Coconut feni has grown rare as the number of toddy tappers has fallen, and cashew feni now dominates.

name: Mahua
description: Distilled from the flowers of the mahua tree, which fall in spring and are gathered by Adivasi communities across central India. Long dismissed as country liquor, it was reclassified as heritage liquor in 2021.
funFact: Mahua flowers are also eaten and used as a sweetener, and the tree is treated as sacred in several Adivasi traditions.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass. The flavour is floral and strange, closer to a fortified honey than to anything grain-based. The new commercial bottlings are considerably cleaner than the village versions.

composition.summary: Dried mahua flowers fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Flowers of Madhuca longifolia, gathered as they fall

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional clay or pot stills; modern producers use copper

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: The flowers are naturally high in sugar and need no addition to ferment.

originStory: Mahua spirit is distilled from the fleshy flowers of the mahua tree, Madhuca longifolia, which fall in spring and are gathered by Adivasi communities across central India. The flowers have been fermented and distilled for generations, and the tradition has no recorded inventor. Colonial excise laws restricted village distilling, and mahua was long classed as cheap country liquor. More recently Madhya Pradesh has recognised it as heritage liquor, and new brands bottle it for wider sale.

name: Indian Rum
description: Dark, sweet and heavily molasses-driven, of which Old Monk is the icon: a vatted seven-year rum that built a cult following without ever advertising. India drinks an enormous amount of it.
funFact: Old Monk was famously never advertised, relying entirely on word of mouth, and for decades it was among the best-selling dark rums in the world.

serve.how: Neat, over ice, or with cola. Indian winters call for it hot with water and honey. It is sweet and vanilla-forward, so it does not need much help.

composition.summary: Sugarcane molasses fermented, distilled and aged in the Indian climate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Indian sugarcane molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, tropically matured; Old Monk is vatted at seven years

composition.process: India grows more sugarcane than almost anywhere, so molasses has always been the obvious base.

originStory: Rum has been made from Indian molasses since the colonial era, when breweries and distilleries were set up to supply British troops. Its defining brand, Old Monk, came from Mohan Meakin, the company that grew out of a brewery Edward Dyer founded at Kasauli in the Himalayan foothills. Old Monk was launched in 1954, and its creation is credited to Ved Rattan Mohan, said to have been inspired by Benedictine monks. The company famously never advertised it, relying on word of mouth.

name: Tharra
description: Sugarcane moonshine from the northern Indian plains, distilled from fermented cane juice or jaggery in village stills. Illegal, widespread, and the subject of periodic poisoning tragedies when batches are adulterated.
funFact: Mass poisonings from methanol-adulterated country liquor remain a recurring public health emergency across northern India.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and only from a source you trust absolutely. This is one of the entries on this list where the safety caveat is not a formality.

composition.summary: Cane juice or jaggery fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane juice or jaggery

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Village pot stills, single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–60%, unmeasured

composition.process: Adulteration with industrial methanol to boost strength is the cause of most tharra fatalities.

originStory: Tharra is the slang name across northern India, particularly in Punjab and the Hindi-speaking plains, for cheap country liquor, much of it distilled in villages from fermented sugarcane juice, jaggery or molasses. It has no recorded inventor or start date; it grew from long-standing rural distilling and from the colonial excise system that separated licensed country liquor from illicit production. Much of the illicit trade remains unregulated, and methanol-adulterated batches have caused repeated mass poisonings, which keeps it a constant concern for state excise authorities.

name: Indian Gin
description: A genuinely new category: gins built on Indian botanicals — Goan coriander, Himalayan juniper, gondhoraj lime, black pepper from Kerala. India had no craft gin at all before 2017 and now exports it.
funFact: India grows a large share of the world's spices, so the botanical supply chain that most gin producers import from was already domestic.

serve.how: With a light tonic and a wedge of lime or a few crushed pink peppercorns. The spice-forward botanicals are strong enough that a heavily flavoured tonic will bury them.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with Indian and Himalayan botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Himalayan juniper, gondhoraj lime, coriander, pepper, fennel, cardamom

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour infusion

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Sourcing juniper from the Himalayas rather than Europe is what several producers use to define the category.

originStory: India's ties to gin go back to the British Raj, when officers mixed it with quinine tonic, but the country's own craft gin is usually dated to 2017, when Nao Spirits, founded by Anand Virmani and Vaibhav Singh, released Greater Than from a small distillery in Goa. Nao followed with Hapusa, from the Sanskrit word for juniper, and others such as Stranger & Sons joined them, building recipes on Indian botanicals that most gin distillers elsewhere have to import.

name: Ceylon Arrack
description: Sri Lanka's national spirit, distilled from the fermented sap of coconut flowers and rested in halmilla wood. Light, faintly funky and closer to a soft rum than to anything else, and quite unlike Batavia arrack.
funFact: Toddy tappers move between palm crowns on ropes strung fifteen metres above the ground rather than climbing down between trees.

serve.how: With ginger beer and lime, which is the Sri Lankan standard, or over ice with soda. The premium aged bottlings are worth drinking neat, where the halmilla wood shows as a soft spice.

composition.summary: Coconut flower sap fermented and distilled, then aged in halmilla casks.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Toddy from coconut palm flower stalks

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Halmilla wood vats, six months to fifteen years

composition.process: The sap must be distilled within a day of tapping, since it ferments almost immediately in the heat.

originStory: Coconut arrack has been distilled in Sri Lanka for centuries from toddy, the fermented sap of coconut flowers, and it was already an export when the Dutch East India Company controlled the island's coast. Under British rule production was licensed and taxed, and in the twentieth century a few large distillers came to dominate. Toddy tappers still work the palm crowns by hand, often moving between trees on ropes strung high above the ground. The spirit is matured in vats of halmilla, a native timber.

name: Kasippu
description: Sri Lanka's illicit moonshine, distilled from sugar, cane or fermented fruit in the countryside, and by some estimates outselling every licensed spirit on the island combined.
funFact: Estimates of unlicensed alcohol in Sri Lanka regularly put it at over half of all consumption, most of it kasippu.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, from a source you know. It is produced entirely outside regulation and is frequently adulterated, which makes it a genuine risk rather than a novelty.

composition.summary: Sugar, cane or fruit fermented and distilled in hidden stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugar, cane juice or fermented fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Improvised stills, usually single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–60%, unmeasured

composition.process: Production is deliberately mobile, since the stills have to be moved to avoid enforcement.

originStory: Kasippu is the Sri Lankan name for illicit home-distilled spirit, made in rural stills from sugar, jaggery, fermented fruit or other starches, often hidden away in jungle or paddy country. It has no recorded inventor or start date; it grew up as the unlicensed counterpart to the island's licensed arrack trade, cheaper because it escapes excise duty. Police and excise officers run regular raids, and the trade remains a revenue and safety concern.

name: Raksi
description: Nepali millet or rice spirit, distilled at home in stacked clay or metal pots and served warm in the hills. Cloudy, sour and warming, and offered at every festival and family occasion.
funFact: The traditional still is a stack of pots with a cold-water bowl on top, and the condensate is caught in a vessel suspended inside.

serve.how: Served warm, often with a piece of fried egg or meat floated on top at festivals. Strength varies wildly between households, so the first cup is a reasonable guide to pacing.

composition.summary: Millet or rice fermented with a starter cake and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Millet, rice or maize

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Marcha, a wild-yeast starter cake

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Stacked pot still over an open fire

composition.process: Marcha carries both the yeast and the moulds that convert the grain's starch to sugar.

originStory: Raksi is the home-distilled spirit of Nepal's hills, made from fermented millet or rice and, in some places, wheat or maize. It is distilled in a traditional stacked still: a pot of ferment below, a vessel inside to catch the spirit, and a bowl of cold water on top that is changed as it warms. No inventor or date is recorded; raksi belongs to a wider Himalayan tradition of grain spirits, made by many communities for festivals, rites and hospitality.

name: Aila
description: The Newar community's rice spirit, distilled in Kathmandu valley courtyards and central to Newari feasts. Traditionally poured from a clay jug into a leaf cup, and drunk as part of ritual as much as celebration.
funFact: At certain Newari festivals aila is poured directly into the mouth from a clay jug held above the head, without touching the lips.

serve.how: Room temperature or gently warmed, as part of a Newari feast rather than on its own. The first distillate, called thaha, is the strongest and is kept for elders and guests.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with a yeast starter and distilled in traditional stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice, sometimes with millet

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Manapu, a Newari yeast starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Stacked clay or copper pot still

composition.process: Successive fractions are collected separately, and the first is prized well above the rest.

originStory: Aila is the rice spirit of the Newar people of the Kathmandu valley, distilled at home from fermented rice or other grains and woven into Newar ritual life, from feasts to offerings to deities. It belongs to the wider Himalayan family of grain spirits, and it is traditionally poured from an anti, a long-spouted jug, held high above a small clay bowl. No inventor or date is recorded. Some licensed producers now bottle aila commercially, carrying it from household courtyards into restaurants.

name: Ara
description: Bhutan's home-distilled spirit, made from rice, maize, millet or wheat and served hot with butter and a scrambled egg dropped in. That version, called hoentay ara, is a genuine winter staple.
funFact: Commercial production and sale is restricted in Bhutan, so nearly all ara is made at home for family and guests.

serve.how: Heated with butter and a beaten egg stirred through, which sounds alarming and is genuinely good at altitude in winter. Also drunk cold and plain, though far less often.

composition.summary: Grain fermented with a local starter and distilled at home.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice, maize, millet or wheat

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Phab, a Bhutanese yeast starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Simple pot still over a stove

composition.process: Butter and egg are added at serving rather than in production, and the fat carries the warmth.

originStory: Ara is Bhutan's home-distilled spirit, made from rice, maize, millet, wheat or barley according to what each valley grows. It is a domestic craft, largely in the hands of women, offered to guests and used in religious offerings, festivals and family occasions. No inventor or date is recorded; it shares roots with the grain spirits of Tibet and the eastern Himalaya. Because Bhutan restricts the commercial production and sale of home-made ara, nearly all of it is made for the household and for visitors rather than for market.

name: Murree
description: Pakistan's only legal distillery, founded in 1860 to supply the British garrison and still operating in an Islamic republic where most citizens cannot legally buy its products.
funFact: Murree cannot export easily and cannot sell to Muslim Pakistanis, so it operates in one of the strangest commercial positions of any distillery on earth.

serve.how: Neat or with a splash of water. The older single malts are genuinely accomplished and comparable to mid-range Scotch, which surprises almost everyone who tries one.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in Pakistan.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, some locally grown

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and sherry oak, eight to twenty-one years

composition.process: The brewery and distillery survived partition, prohibition and nationalisation by continuing to operate under licence.

originStory: Murree began in 1860 as a brewery founded by the British near Murree, a hill station in the Punjab high and cool enough for brewing before refrigeration. Under Henry Whymper it became one of the leading breweries in British India, and production later moved down to Rawalpindi, where it remains. Since Partition the Parsi Bhandara family has controlled the company, which brews beer and distils whisky, vodka and brandy, sold legally in Pakistan to non-Muslims and foreigners.

name: Bangla Mod
description: Bangladesh's licensed country liquor, distilled from molasses or rice and sold through a small number of permitted outlets. Cheap, strong, and a rare legal product in a country with very tight alcohol laws.
funFact: Bangladesh requires a permit to buy alcohol legally, and country liquor shops operate under a licensing system inherited from colonial administration.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures. It is a functional spirit rather than a refined one, and the licensed version is considerably safer than the unlicensed alternatives circulating alongside it.

composition.summary: Molasses or rice fermented and distilled under licence.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses or rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column or pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: The licensed trade exists partly to displace the far more dangerous informal one.

originStory: Bangla mod, Bengali for country liquor, is the cheap molasses spirit sold under licence in Bangladesh. Its licensed supply comes from Carew & Co, a distillery at Darsana in Chuadanga that began under British rule, was nationalised after independence and now sits inside a state-owned sugar mill. Licensed country liquor shops operate under an excise system inherited from colonial administration, and buyers need a permit. No individual is credited with the drink, and village distilling continues alongside the legal supply.

name: Uzbek Konyak
description: Central Asian brandy made in the Soviet style from grapes grown in the Ferghana valley and around Samarkand. Sweeter and softer than French brandy, and a legacy of Soviet-era winemaking on the Silk Road.
funFact: The Soviet Union built a substantial brandy industry across Central Asia and the Caucasus, and konyak remains the standard local word for it.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, usually with a meal rather than after it, as is the custom across the former Soviet republics. Frequently accompanied by more toasts than is strictly advisable.

composition.summary: Uzbek wine distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grapes from the Ferghana valley and Samarkand region

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, three to twenty years

composition.process: Hot continental summers give very ripe grapes, which is why the resulting brandy runs sweet.

originStory: Grapes have been grown in the Ferghana valley and around Samarkand since antiquity, but Uzbek brandy is a product of the Russian and Soviet era. Russian merchants built wineries in Samarkand in the nineteenth century, and Soviet planners later expanded vineyards and wine combines across Central Asia, where brandy was made in the style of Armenian and Georgian konyak, softer and sweeter than French cognac. No single founder is credited with Uzbek konyak. The Soviet word stuck, and it remains the everyday name for local brandy.

name: Sauce-Aroma Baijiu
description: The jiangxiang style, from Guizhou, and the most expensive baijiu made. Fermented and distilled seven times over a year, it tastes of soy sauce, mushroom and dried meat rather than anything a Western palate calls a spirit.
funFact: The production cycle runs a full year with nine steamings, eight fermentations and seven distillations, and the spirit is then aged for at least three more.

serve.how: Room temperature in a very small cup, with food, and shared. Chinese banquet custom is to toast rather than sip. The umami depth needs food alongside it; drunk alone it can be overwhelming.

composition.summary: Sorghum solid-state fermented with wheat qu in stone pits, distilled seven times.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Red sorghum and wheat qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Seven distillations across a year-long cycle

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware jars, then blended

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 53%

composition.process: 53% is considered the point where water and ethanol molecules bind most tightly, and the style is bottled there deliberately.

originStory: Sauce-aroma baijiu is the style of Maotai, a town on the Chishui river in Guizhou, where sorghum spirit was being made under the Qing dynasty in workshops that later merged into Kweichow Moutai. Its name, jiangxiang, comes from an aroma that recalls soy sauce. The method follows the seasons: sorghum is fermented through a year-long cycle with two additions of grain, nine steamings, eight fermentations and seven distillations, and the spirit then rests for years before blending. Moutai's place at state banquets made it China's most famous spirit.

name: Strong-Aroma Baijiu
description: The nongxiang style from Sichuan, fermented in mud pits that have been in continuous use for centuries and are treated as the distillery's most valuable asset. Pungent, fruity and enormously popular.
funFact: Luzhou Laojiao's oldest fermentation pits date from 1573 and have been running without interruption since, with the microbial culture in the mud considered irreplaceable.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with food. The fruit-and-funk profile is intense on its own but cuts through rich, oily Sichuan food remarkably well. Toast rather than sip.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in aged mud pits, distilled and blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, often with rice, wheat, corn and glutinous rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation in steamer stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The older the mud pit, the more complex the microbial population, and the higher the value of the spirit.

originStory: Strong-aroma baijiu traces its lineage to Luzhou in Sichuan, where the oldest working fermentation pits of Luzhou Laojiao are dated to 1573, in the Ming dynasty, and have been in use ever since. The style, nongxiang, is defined by those mud pits: grain ferments in them for weeks, and the microbial life built up in the clay shapes the spirit's fruity, pungent aroma. Wuliangye, from nearby Yibin, is the style's other great name, and strong aroma is now China's most widely made baijiu.

name: Light-Aroma Baijiu
description: The qingxiang style from Shanxi, fermented in stone jars rather than earth pits, which keeps it clean and floral. The most approachable baijiu for anyone new to the category, and the historical ancestor of Korean soju.
funFact: Fenjiu from Xinghua village is documented as far back as the Northern and Southern dynasties, making it one of the oldest named spirits in China.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food, or lightly chilled if it is your first baijiu. Its cleaner profile also makes it the style most usable in cocktails, where it behaves a little like a funky gin.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in stone jars with barley and pea qu.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, with a barley and pea qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, two fermentations

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware, typically shorter than other styles

composition.process: Stone jars keep the ferment isolated from soil microbes, which is why the style stays clean.

originStory: Light-aroma baijiu is the style of Fenjiu, from Xinghua village near Fenyang in Shanxi, where alcoholic drinks are recorded long before distillation. Xinghua, apricot blossom village, is often linked to a famous Tang poem by Du Mu, though scholars dispute which village the poet meant. The qingxiang method ferments sorghum in buried earthenware jars rather than mud pits, which keeps the spirit clean and floral. Light aroma remains widespread in northern China, where erguotou belongs to the same family.

name: Rice-Aroma Baijiu
description: The mixiang style from Guangxi and southern China, distilled from rice rather than sorghum. The lightest and most delicate of the four classic aromas, and the closest baijiu gets to a soft, sweet spirit.
funFact: Sanhua jiu from Guilin is the best-known example and is traditionally aged in caves cut into the karst hills around the city.

serve.how: Room temperature or lightly chilled, in small cups. It is gentle enough to drink without food, which is unusual for baijiu, and it works well alongside lighter southern Chinese cooking.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with a small qu starter and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice, sometimes glutinous

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Semi-solid-state fermentation, then distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars, sometimes in karst caves

composition.process: A smaller qu starter than the northern styles means less funk and more of the rice.

originStory: Rice-aroma baijiu, mixiang, is the southern Chinese style distilled from rice rather than sorghum, with Guangxi and Guangdong as its heartland. Its most famous example is Sanhua jiu from Guilin, whose makers age the spirit in caves in the karst hills around the city, including Elephant Trunk Hill. Rice distilling in the south is old and largely undocumented, and no single founder is credited.
