originStory: Riga Black Balsam stirred into hot blackcurrant juice is one of the commonest Latvian ways to serve the herbal balsam in winter, a household pairing that no one is credited with.

name: Riga Black Magic
description: Black Balsam shaken with citrus and apple juice — the modern Riga bar's way of making 24 botanicals approachable.
funFact: Latvia's bar scene spent the 2010s reverse-engineering Black Balsam into something that did not taste like medicine, and apple juice turned out to be the ingredient that finally rounded it off.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a thin apple slice.

originStory: Riga Black Magic is a modern Latvian mix of Riga Black Balsam with apple juice, lemon and a little sugar, and no bar or bartender has published a claim to it or to its name.

name: Arak Lemonade
description: Levantine arak lengthened with lemonade and mint — the anise softened into something you can drink through a Beirut summer.
funFact: Lebanese arak is distilled three times and aged in clay amphorae, and the mountain villages that make it argue about grape variety the way Burgundy argues about vineyards.

steps: Gently press the mint leaves in the bottom of a tall glass — bruise, do not shred.
Add the arak and lemon juice.
Fill with ice and top with cold lemonade.
Stir once and garnish with a mint sprig and a lemon wheel.

originStory: Arak with mint lemonade is an informal Lebanese way of turning the anise spirit into a long summer drink, a habit that no one is credited with and that has no recorded origin.

name: Planteur
description: The French Antilles' planter's punch: rhum agricole with mango, guava and passionfruit, softer and more perfumed than its English-speaking cousin.
funFact: Rhum agricole is distilled from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, which is why a Planteur tastes grassy and vegetal where a Jamaican punch tastes of treacle.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice.
Shake for 10 seconds.
Pour into an ice-filled highball glass.
Grate nutmeg over the top and garnish with a lime wheel.

originStory: The planteur is the French Antilles' take on planter's punch, and it takes its name from the planters of the cane estates. What sets it apart is the rum: in Martinique and Guadeloupe that usually means rhum agricole, distilled from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, a style that spread on the islands in the late nineteenth century after a collapse in sugar prices. Recipes differ from bar to bar and family to family, mixing the rum with tropical juices and cane syrup, and no one is credited with the first.

name: Cazuela
description: A clay bowl the size of your head, packed with citrus, tequila and grapefruit soda, drunk through straws by everyone at the table. Sonora's answer to the punch bowl.
funFact: The bowl is the point: cazuelas are served in unglazed or glazed earthenware that keeps the drink cold, and in Hermosillo the bar brings it with the fruit still floating and scissors to cut more.

steps: Rim a large clay cazuela with lime and chilli salt.
Squeeze the orange, lime and grapefruit wedges into the bowl and drop the spent wedges in.
Fill with ice and pour over the tequila.
Top with grapefruit soda and stir once with a long spoon.
Serve in the middle of the table with straws for everyone.
recipe.garnish: The squeezed fruit wedges, left floating

originStory: The cazuela is a Mexican tequila punch named for the wide clay pot it is served in, packed with citrus, ice and grapefruit soda and shared through straws, and no one has documented who first mixed one.

name: Charro Negro
description: The Cuba Libre's tequila-drinking cousin: blanco, cola, lime, salt on the rim if you're doing it properly. Jalisco's default order when the Paloma feels like too much work.
funFact: Named for the charro — the Mexican horseman — and 'negro' for the cola; in Jalisco cantinas it is often built straight into the bottle-sized 'vitrolero' glass and shared.

steps: Run a lime wedge around the rim of a highball glass and roll it in salt.
Fill the glass with ice cubes.
Add the tequila and lime juice.
Top with cold cola and stir once, gently, to combine.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on a salted rim

originStory: The charro negro is a Mexican highball of blanco tequila, cola and lime, and neither its inventor nor the story behind its name is recorded.

name: Chelada
description: Beer, lime, salt, ice. That's it — no tomato, no sauces, no debate. The Michelada stripped back to the two things that actually matter on a hot afternoon.
funFact: Mexicans distinguish sharply between chelada (lime and salt only) and michelada (with tomato juice and sauces); ordering the wrong one in Monterrey will get you corrected, politely.

steps: Rim a chilled schooner or pint glass with lime and salt.
Fill the glass with ice cubes.
Add the lime juice.
Pour the cold lager down the side of the glass to keep the head under control.
Garnish with a lime wedge and top up from the bottle as you drink.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on a salted rim

originStory: Chela is Mexican slang for a beer, and the chelada is the plainest of the country's prepared beers: lager over ice with lime juice in a salt-rimmed glass. The name of its spicier relative, the michelada, has two explanations, one crediting Michel Ésper of the Club Deportivo Potosino in San Luis Potosí, whose beer with lime and salt other members ordered as Michel's limonada, the other reading it as mi chela helada, my cold beer. Names shift by region, and what one city calls a chelada another may call a michelada.

name: La Bandera
description: Not one glass but three: lime, tequila, sangrita — green, white, red, the flag on the bar top. Sip across them in any order and argue about it afterwards.
funFact: The order is a national argument: most drinkers go lime, tequila, sangrita, but purists insist sangrita comes last only to cleanse, never to chase — the tequila is meant to be sipped, not shot.

steps: Pour the lime juice into the first caballito, the tequila into the second, and the sangrita into the third.
Line the three glasses up left to right so they read green, white, red.
Serve at cool room temperature — never over ice, and never mixed.
Sip the tequila slowly, alternating with small sips of lime and sangrita.
recipe.garnish: None — the three colours are the garnish

originStory: La bandera, the flag, is a way of serving tequila rather than a mixed drink: three small glasses side by side of green lime juice, white blanco tequila and red sangrita, the colours of the Mexican flag. Sangrita comes from Jalisco and is usually traced to Guadalajara and Lake Chapala, where the leftover juices of an orange-and-chilli fruit salad were sipped alongside tequila, its red coming from chilli and pomegranate rather than tomato. No one is credited with arranging the three glasses into a flag.

name: Mexican Firing Squad
description: A 1930s Mexico City sour that Charles H. Baker wrote down and the world then forgot for seventy years: tequila, lime, grenadine, a hard lash of Angostura.
funFact: Baker recorded it at La Cucaracha bar in 1937 in his 'Gentleman's Companion', calling it a drink of 'considerable authority' — one of the earliest tequila cocktails documented in English.

steps: Add the tequila, lime juice, grenadine and bitters to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice.
Add a small splash of soda if you want it longer.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

originStory: The Mexican Firing Squad comes to us through Charles H. Baker Jr., the American writer who collected drinks on his travels and recorded this one at La Cucaracha bar in Mexico City in 1937. He printed it in The Gentleman's Companion of 1939, which makes it one of the earlier tequila cocktails in English print, but he did not record who created it or why it carries its stark name. The short recipe, tequila with lime, grenadine and Angostura, returned to menus when bartenders began mining Baker's books for forgotten drinks.

name: Mezcalita
description: The Margarita rebuilt on mezcal, which changes everything: the smoke arrives first, the lime cuts through it, and the agave finishes earthy rather than bright.
funFact: The rim is the tell: real Oaxacan service uses sal de gusano — salt ground with toasted agave worm and chilli — which tastes far better than its description suggests.

ingredients.item: Sal de gusano or chilli salt

steps: Rim a rocks glass with lime and sal de gusano, then set it aside.
Shake the mezcal, lime juice, agave syrup and orange liqueur hard with ice.
Strain into the rimmed glass over a large ice cube.
Garnish with a lime wheel and, if you have one, a dried chilli.

originStory: The mezcalita is the margarita remade with Oaxaca's smoky mezcal, a swap that rose with mezcal's own popularity and that no bartender is credited with first making.

name: Submarino
description: A shot of tequila dropped, glass and all, into a beer. It sinks, it fizzes, it disappears — and then so does your evening.
glassware: Beer stein with a caballito inside
funFact: The same trick appears worldwide — Boilermaker in the US, U-Boot in Germany, Jägerbomb everywhere — but the Mexican version insists the submarine be tequila and the ocean be a light lager.

steps: Pour the beer into a large stein, leaving room at the top.
Fill a caballito shot glass with tequila.
Lower the shot glass carefully into the beer so it sinks upright.
Drink immediately, before the tequila fully diffuses.

originStory: The submarino takes its name from the shot glass of tequila that sinks, glass and all, to the bottom of a light lager, a Mexican party serve with no recorded inventor.

name: Torito
description: Veracruz in a bottle: cane liquor whipped with condensed milk and fruit — peanut, guanabana, mango — until it drinks like a boozy milkshake with a suntan.
funFact: Toritos are sold from coolers along the Veracruz malecón in a dozen flavours; the peanut ('de cacahuate') version is the benchmark, and every vendor claims their abuela's ratio.

ingredients.item: Aguardiente de caña or white rum

steps: Add the milks and the peanut butter or fruit purée to a blender.
Pour in the cane spirit and add the ice.
Blend on high for about 30 seconds until completely smooth and frothy.
Pour into a chilled tumbler and serve immediately, before it separates.
Dust the top with ground cinnamon or crushed peanut.

originStory: The torito, little bull, is a drink of Veracruz on the Gulf coast: cane aguardiente blended with condensed and evaporated milk and a flavouring, classically peanut but also guanábana, mango or coconut. Local accounts trace it to the cane plantations of the Papaloapan basin, where workers mixed their aguardiente with seasonal fruit, though no one is credited with the recipe. In Morelos and the State of Mexico the same name belongs to a quite different drink, made with orange juice, onion and pickled chillies.

name: Vampiro
description: Tequila, grapefruit soda and sangrita in one blood-red glass. Sweet, salty, citric and quietly spicy — the Paloma after it learned to bite.
funFact: The name means 'vampire' — for the colour, not the bite. It is the house drink of the bars around Tlaquepaque, where sangrita is made fresh daily and never contains tomato juice from a can.

steps: Rim a highball glass with lime and chilli salt, then fill it with ice.
Pour in the tequila, sangrita and lime juice.
Top with grapefruit soda.
Stir gently from the bottom once to marble the colours without fully mixing them.
Garnish with a lime wheel and an extra dusting of chilli salt.

originStory: The vampiro is a tequila highball from Jalisco, built with tequila, grapefruit soda, lime and sangrita, the chilli-and-citrus juice the region sips alongside tequila, and the red of the sangrita is the usual explanation for its name. No one has documented who first mixed it. Bottled sangrita became a common shortcut, though purists still make it fresh, and the International Bartenders Association listed the vampiro among its New Era drinks before dropping it from the list.

name: Airag
description: Fermented mare's milk, sour and lightly effervescent. The drink of the steppe, offered to every guest who enters a ger.
funFact: Refusing the bowl outright is a serious discourtesy in Mongolia; the accepted compromise is to touch it to your lips and return it, which satisfies the custom.

ingredients.item: A leather khokhuur bag or wooden churn

steps: Pour the fresh mare's milk into the khokhuur with a cup of the previous batch as starter.
Churn it repeatedly throughout the day — traditionally a thousand strokes or more.
Let it ferment for one to three days, continuing to churn.
Taste until it is sour, faintly fizzy and lightly alcoholic.
Serve cool in a wide bowl, offered with the right hand.

originStory: Airag is the Mongolian name for fermented mare's milk, the drink known further west as kumys, and it is made each summer while the mares are in milk. Fresh milk is poured into a leather bag or wooden vessel with some of the previous batch and churned or stirred over hours or days, so that it sours and takes on a gentle fizz. The Franciscan traveller William of Rubruck described Mongols making it in the thirteenth century, and it is still served at the Naadam festival and offered to guests through the summer.

name: Tongba
description: Fermented millet in a wooden pot, topped with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw. Refill the water and keep going until it stops tasting of anything.
glassware: Wooden tongba pot with a bamboo straw
funFact: It belongs to the Limbu people of eastern Nepal, and the etiquette is specific: you top up the same millet with hot water several times, and it is impolite to stop after one.

ingredients.item: A wooden tongba pot and bamboo straw (pipsing)

steps: Pack the fermented millet into the wooden tongba pot.
Pour in hot — not boiling — water to cover.
Let it steep for about five minutes.
Sip through the perforated bamboo straw, which filters out the grain.
Top up with more hot water two or three times as you drink.

originStory: Tongba is the traditional drink of the Limbu people of eastern Nepal, and its name is really that of its vessel, a wooden or metal pot holding fermented finger millet. The millet is cooked, mixed with a starter the Limbu call khesung and left to ferment; at the table hot water is poured over it, left to steep and drawn up through a straw with a filtered tip. Offering tongba is a mark of respect to a guest, sharing it is part of the Limbu wedding ceremony set out in the Mundhum, and it is also drunk in Sikkim and Darjeeling.

name: Kopstootje
description: 'Little head-butt': a tulip glass of jenever filled to the brim and a beer beside it. First sip taken bent over, hands behind your back.
glassware: Tulip glass and a beer glass
funFact: The jenever is poured to a convex meniscus, so the only way to take the first sip without spilling is to lean down to the glass — hands behind the back is the traditional form.

steps: Chill the jenever thoroughly and fill the tulip glass right to the brim.
Pour a cold pilsner alongside it.
Bend down to the jenever glass, hands behind your back, and take the first sip without lifting it.
Then pick up the glass, finish the jenever, and chase it with the beer.

originStory: A kopstoot or kopstootje, a little head-butt, is a Dutch pairing rather than a mix: a small tulip glass of young jenever beside a glass of beer. Jenever is the juniper spirit of the Low Countries from which English gin descends, and it is traditionally poured so full that it bulges above the rim, so the first sip is taken by bending to the glass without lifting it, a bow that is itself called a kopstootje. No one is credited with the pairing.

name: L&P and Vodka
description: Lemon & Paeroa — New Zealand's own lemony mineral soda — lengthening a shot of vodka. 'World famous in New Zealand', as the bottle says.
funFact: L&P was originally made by mixing lemon juice with mineral water from a spring at Paeroa; the town has a giant L&P bottle on the main road, which is the country's most photographed soft-drink monument.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the vodka and the lemon juice.
Top with cold L&P.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wedge.

originStory: Vodka topped with L&P, the lemony soft drink that began with mineral water from a spring at Paeroa, is an informal New Zealand mix with no recorded inventor or date.

name: Macuá
description: Nicaragua's official national cocktail, decided by public contest: white rum, guava, lemon and orange, tropical without tipping into syrup.
funFact: In 2006 Nicaragua's tourism board ran a nationwide competition to name a national drink; the winner was submitted by a paediatrician from Granada, and the Macuá is named after a local bird.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake for about 12 seconds until the outside of the tin frosts.
Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

originStory: The Macuá was chosen as Nicaragua's national drink in October 2006, in a contest sponsored by the rum maker Flor de Caña with tourism businesses and backed by the national tourism institute. The winning recipe of white rum with guava and lemon was the work of Edmundo Miranda Sáenz, a paediatrician from Granada, who perfected it with his family, and a separate round of the contest named it after the pájaro macuá, a tropical bird of Nicaragua. The newspaper El Nuevo Diario criticised the rule that entries contain at least half Flor de Caña rum.

name: Palm Wine
description: Sap tapped straight from the palm, fermenting as you carry it. Sweet in the morning, sour and sharp by evening — the clock is part of the drink.
funFact: Fermentation begins within hours of tapping, with no yeast added — the wild yeasts are already on the tree. A morning tapping is mild and sweet; the same container by nightfall is sour and considerably stronger.

steps: Tap the sap from the palm into a clean container — traditionally at dawn.
Leave it to ferment naturally; wild yeasts start work within a couple of hours.
Taste as it goes: sweet and lightly fizzy early, dry and sour by the end of the day.
Strain through cloth to remove debris.
Serve at ambient temperature, the same day it was tapped.

originStory: Palm wine is among the oldest drinks of West Africa, made wherever oil, raffia or coconut palms grow, and no one can say when it began. Tappers cut into the tree or its flower stalk and collect the sap, which starts fermenting within hours on its own wild yeasts. It goes by many names, emu in Yoruba and nsafufuo in Twi among them, it is distilled into spirits such as Ghana's akpeteshie and Nigeria's ogogoro, and it gave its name to palm wine music, the guitar style of the bars where it was sold, which helped shape highlife.

name: Karsk
description: Coffee and moonshine, measured by a coin: drop it in the cup, add coffee until it vanishes, add spirit until you see it again.
funFact: The coin trick is a genuine Trøndelag tradition, and the coffee is deliberately brewed weak so that the coin disappears early and the spirit measure ends up generous.

steps: Drop a clean coin into the bottom of a coffee cup.
Pour in weak coffee until the coin just disappears from view.
Add the spirit slowly until the coin becomes visible again.
Stir in sugar if you take it, and drink hot.

originStory: Karsk is coffee laced with spirit, traditionally home-distilled, and though its exact origin is unknown it was popular in Sweden's Bohuslän in the early nineteenth century and spread across Norway later that century, taking deepest root in Trøndelag. Its name comes from the Old Norse karskr, vigorous or lively. Elsewhere the same drink is kaffedoktor or knikt in parts of Norway and kask or kaffekask in Sweden, and in Trøndelag it remains a fixture of rural life.

name: Seco con Leche
description: Panama's national spirit cut with milk over ice — sounds wrong, drinks like a cold, boozy horchata with a sugarcane backbone.
funFact: Seco Herrerano is triple-distilled from sugarcane and is Panama's national spirit; the milk serve — 'seco con leche' — is standard at interior festivals, especially during Carnaval.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice.
Pour in the seco.
Top with cold whole milk.
Stir gently until the glass frosts, and serve straight away.

originStory: Seco con leche, Panama's Seco Herrerano poured over ice with cold milk, is a country habit of Panama's interior with no credited inventor or recorded first glass.

name: Caña con Ruda
description: Cane spirit steeped with rue, drunk in one shot on the first of August. Bitter, herbal and, by tradition, obligatory.
funFact: Guaraní tradition holds that a shot of caña con ruda on an empty stomach on August 1 wards off the illnesses of the coming winter; the custom is shared with Argentina and Uruguay.

steps: Wash and dry the rue sprig thoroughly.
Push it into the bottle of caña and seal.
Leave to macerate for at least a week — traditionally from the previous winter.
On the morning of August 1, pour a single shot and drink it on an empty stomach.
Do not drink more than three: the tradition is specific about this.

originStory: Caña con ruda is less a drink than a rite: every 1 August, Paraguayans take a little cane spirit steeped with rue and lemon, traditionally on an empty stomach, to keep away the misfortunes of August, the harsh tail end of winter. The custom is traced to Guaraní tradition, later remade with ingredients that came with the Spanish, rue from the Mediterranean and cane spirit from the sugar plantations. In Paraguay it is also called carrulim, from caña, ruda and limón, the national culture secretariat has declared it intangible cultural heritage, and the custom is shared in Argentina and Uruguay.

name: Clericó
description: White wine and chopped summer fruit, chilled hard. Sangria's lighter South American cousin, and Christmas dinner across the Southern Cone.
funFact: Because Christmas falls in high summer in Paraguay, the festive drink is served ice cold with fruit — the name traces back to the English 'claret cup' by way of Spanish.

ingredients.item: Mixed fruit (peach, apple, orange, grape), diced

steps: Toss the diced fruit with the sugar and leave for an hour.
Pour over the white wine and refrigerate for at least four hours.
Top with soda water just before serving.
Serve very cold, spooning plenty of fruit into each glass.

originStory: Clericó is the Río de la Plata's version of claret cup, the wine-and-fruit punch that was hugely popular in nineteenth-century Britain, and its name is a Spanish rendering of the English. Claret cup faded in English-speaking countries, but clericó lives on as a tradition in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, made with wine and plenty of chopped fruit and left to chill. Because Christmas and New Year fall in high summer there, it became a drink of those holidays, and in Paraguay it is often eaten with a spoon from the glass.

name: Algarrobina
description: Pisco with carob syrup, condensed milk and egg — dark, sweet and faintly smoky, Peru's dessert cocktail and reputed aphrodisiac.
funFact: Algarrobina is boiled down from the pods of the Peruvian carob tree that grows in the northern deserts; Peruvians credit it, without much evidence and with great confidence, with restorative powers.

steps: Add the pisco, algarrobina, condensed milk and egg yolk to a blender.
Add the ice and blend until thick and uniform.
Pour into a chilled coupe.
Drizzle a little extra algarrobina over the surface and dust with cinnamon.

originStory: The algarrobina cocktail takes its name from its key ingredient, a dark syrup boiled down from the pods of the algarrobo tree of Peru's northern coast, mixed with pisco and milk, and no one is credited with first making it.

name: Capitán
description: The Peruvian Manhattan: pisco and red vermouth, stirred cold. Sipped in the highlands where the nights get serious.
funFact: It belongs to Puno and the Peruvian Andes, where army officers — the 'capitanes' of the name — are credited with the habit of cutting pisco with vermouth against the cold.

steps: Add the pisco, vermouth and bitters to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 to 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry or a lemon twist.

originStory: The capitán, pisco and red vermouth stirred over ice, is a classic Peruvian aperitif, and its origin is told two ways. A popular story credits army officers posted in the cold southern highlands around Puno, the captains of the name, with cutting their pisco with vermouth, while Peruvian sources tie its appearance in the first half of the twentieth century to Italian immigrants and the vermouth they brought into fashion. Neither names an inventor, and an old Lima marinera, the coastal song and dance, pays tribute to it.

name: Chilcano
description: Peru's everyday pisco drink: pisco, ginger ale, lime and bitters over ice. Lighter than a Pisco Sour and far easier to make ten of.
funFact: Peru holds a national Semana del Chilcano every January; the drink descends from the 'chilcano de pescado', a fish broth once drunk as a hangover cure in the port of Chilca.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the pisco and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Dash the Angostura over the surface.
Stir once gently and garnish with a lime wheel.

originStory: The chilcano goes back at least to the start of the twentieth century: Eudocio Carrera Vergara's account of a Lima jarana, a festive party, around 1900 is among the oldest references to it. Peruvian sources see it as an adaptation of the gin and ginger ale of the day, with pisco in place of gin, and it shares its name with chilcano de pescado, a fish broth, though how the drink came to borrow it is not recorded. It lost ground, returned in the 1950s and has since become one of Peru's most popular pisco drinks, with its own Semana del Chilcano each January.

name: Machu Picchu
description: Green, yellow and red in one tall glass, layered to look like the mountain at sunrise. A tourist drink Cusco has fully embraced.
funFact: It exists almost entirely for the photograph — but Cusco's bars have made it well enough for long enough that it has become a genuine local order.

steps: Pour the grenadine into the bottom of a tall glass.
Fill the glass carefully with crushed ice to hold the layers apart.
Shake the pisco with the orange juice and pour slowly over the ice.
Float the crème de menthe on top over the back of a spoon.
Serve with a straw and let the drinker mix it themselves.

originStory: The Machu Picchu is a tall layered drink of Cusco's bars, built in green, yellow and red bands and named for the Inca citadel, and no one has documented who first made it.

name: Gin Pom
description: Ginebra San Miguel with powdered pomelo juice and ice. Cheap, sharp and the most-drunk gin serve in the world's biggest gin market.
funFact: The Philippines drinks more gin than any other country on earth, almost all of it Ginebra San Miguel — and most of that is mixed with a sachet of powdered juice costing a few pesos.

steps: Dissolve the powdered drink mix in the cold water in a pitcher.
Add the gin and stir well.
Pour over ice into tall glasses.
Serve with a calamansi wedge if you have one.

originStory: Gin pom, Ginebra San Miguel mixed with water, ice and a sachet of powdered pomelo drink, is an everyday Filipino way with gin that no one is credited with starting.

name: Weng Weng
description: Every white spirit on the shelf plus whisky, orange juice and grenadine. Named for the noise your head makes afterwards.
funFact: 'Weng weng' is Filipino for dizzy or spinning; the drink is a Boracay beach-bar institution, and most bars cap the order at two per person.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add all five spirits.
Top with orange juice and stir.
Pour the grenadine down the inside of the glass so it sinks to the bottom.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

originStory: The Weng Weng is a strong mixed drink of the beach bars of Boracay in the central Philippines, and nobody has documented who first mixed it or why it carries its name.

name: Mad Dog
description: Vodka, raspberry syrup and Tabasco layered into one shot. Sweet, then red, then suddenly very hot. Polish student legend.
funFact: 'Wściekły pies' is a staple of Polish student bars, where the layering matters: the syrup sinks, the Tabasco floats, and the burn arrives a beat after the sweetness.

steps: Pour the raspberry syrup into the bottom of a shot glass.
Layer the vodka carefully over it with a barspoon.
Dash the Tabasco on top so it sits on the surface.
Drink in one — sipping it is a mistake people only make once.

originStory: Wściekły pies, mad dog, is a Polish bar shot of chilled vodka over raspberry syrup with a few drops of Tabasco, and no one has documented who first poured it or named it.

name: Tatanka
description: Bison grass vodka and cloudy apple juice. Tastes like apple pie and freshly cut hay, which is a stranger compliment than it sounds.
funFact: Also called a Szarlotka, after the Polish apple cake. Żubrówka is flavoured with a blade of bison grass from the Białowieża Forest, and each bottle traditionally contains one.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the Żubrówka.
Top with cold cloudy apple juice.
Stir once and garnish with an apple slice and a light dusting of cinnamon.

originStory: Bison grass vodka with cloudy apple juice is known in Poland as szarlotka, after the apple cake, and abroad as Tatanka, the Lakota word for the bison, but who first mixed it is not recorded.

name: Nikita
description: Beer, pineapple, white wine and vanilla ice cream, blended. It should be a disaster. Madeira has been proving otherwise since the eighties.
funFact: Named after the Elton John song 'Nikita', which was in the charts when a Câmara de Lobos bar owner first blended it in the mid-1980s.

steps: Put the pineapple, ice cream and white wine into a blender.
Add the beer last, to control the foam.
Blend briefly — just enough to combine, or it will overflow.
Pour into a tall glass and serve with a spoon and a straw.

originStory: The nikita, or niquita, comes from the fishing town of Câmara de Lobos on Madeira, where Portuguese sources credit a group of local friends with first blending ice cream, pineapple and sugar with white wine, beer or both. Its name is usually linked to Elton John's song Nikita, a hit in 1985, around the time the drink appeared. It is mixed until creamy with the same wooden stick used for poncha, and it has spread from Câmara de Lobos across Madeira and Porto Santo.

name: Poncha
description: Madeiran cane spirit muddled with honey and lemon using a wooden 'caralhinho'. Sweet, sharp and much stronger than it lets on.
funFact: The stirring tool — a ridged wooden stick called a caralhinho — is specific to Madeira, and the fishermen's original version was drunk as a cold remedy before going out in the morning.

steps: Put the honey and lemon juice into a small tumbler or a jug.
Work them together with a wooden stick or muddler until the honey fully dissolves.
Add the aguardente and the orange juice if using.
Stir vigorously until frothy and serve at room temperature, without ice.

originStory: Poncha is Madeira's own drink, aguardente de cana, the island's sugar-cane spirit, mixed with honey or sugar and lemon juice, and Câmara de Lobos, the fishing town west of Funchal, is its traditional home. Its name is usually linked to punch, though the connection is not documented, and no one is credited with the first. It is mixed in the jug with a wooden stick with a ridged head, spun between the palms and known locally by the cheeky name caralhinho, and fishermen are said to have made it before setting out on cold mornings.

name: Porto Tónico
description: White port and tonic over ice with mint. Portugal's answer to the Gin and Tonic, and arguably the better summer drink.
funFact: Port houses pushed it hard in the 2010s to sell white port, which had been the least-loved category in the Douro — it worked so well it is now the default aperitif in Porto.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Pour in the chilled white port.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once gently and garnish with a mint sprig and an orange slice.

originStory: Porto tónico, white port with tonic over ice, has become a signature aperitif of Porto as the port houses championed it to win white port new drinkers, though no one has a documented claim to the first.

name: Bilí
description: Vieques in a bottle: pitorro steeped for months with quenepas, cinnamon and sugar until the moonshine turns sweet, fruity and deceptively smooth.
funFact: Bilí is a Vieques speciality made with quenepas (Spanish limes) and is traditionally buried or hidden to age — families open bottles at Christmas that were sealed the previous summer.

steps: Put the peeled quenepas, cinnamon, sugar and vanilla into a large sealable jar.
Cover with the pitorro and seal tightly.
Store somewhere dark and cool for at least two months, turning the jar occasionally.
Strain into bottles, leaving the fruit behind.
Serve chilled in small measures.

originStory: Bilí is a speciality of Vieques, the island off Puerto Rico's east coast: rum, traditionally the home-distilled pitorro, steeped with quenepas, the small green fruit also called Spanish lime, along with sugar and spice. No one is credited with the first batch, and recipes are passed down within Vieques families. Quenepas ripen in summer, and the bottles are often put away to rest for months, much as pitorro itself was traditionally buried to mature, and bilí remains closely tied to the island's identity.

name: Chichaíto
description: Two ingredients, no mercy: pitorro and anisette, shaken with ice and served cold enough to hide how strong it is.
funFact: A staple of Puerto Rican Christmas parrandas, where it is carried house to house in a bottle kept in the freezer — the sugar content stops it from freezing solid.

steps: Combine the pitorro and anisette in a shaker with plenty of ice.
Shake hard for 10 seconds to chill and slightly dilute.
Strain into chilled shot glasses.
Serve immediately, ice cold.

originStory: Chichaíto is a Puerto Rican shot of two ingredients, rum, often home-made pitorro, and anisette, served very cold, and no one is credited with inventing or naming it. It belongs to the island's long Christmas season, which runs into January and the Fiestas de la Calle San Sebastián, and to the parrandas, when friends arrive at a house late at night with guitars, güiros and songs and move on from door to door. A cold bottle waiting in the freezer is part of the welcome.

name: Coco Loco
description: Served in the coconut it was made from: rum, coconut cream and whatever tropical juice is closest to hand, blended into holiday shorthand.
funFact: The 'loco' is usually the pour — beach vendors from Luquillo to Loíza free-pour three spirits into the same coconut and stop when it looks about right.

steps: Cut the top off a young coconut and pour the water into a blender.
Add the rums, coconut cream, pineapple juice, lime and crushed ice.
Blend until smooth and slushy.
Pour back into the coconut shell and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Pineapple wedge and a paper umbrella

originStory: The coco loco, crazy coconut, is rum and coconut cream mixed in a freshly opened green coconut and drunk from the shell, a beach serve found across the Caribbean and Latin America that no one is credited with naming.

name: Țuică Fiartă
description: Plum brandy heated with sugar and peppercorns until it steams. Romanian winter, taken standing outside in it.
funFact: The sugar is caramelised in the pan before the țuică goes in, which is what gives it the amber colour; the peppercorns are traditional and genuinely change the finish.

steps: Melt the sugar in a small pan over low heat until it just caramelises.
Add the peppercorns and cinnamon and stir for a few seconds.
Pour in the țuică carefully — it will spit — and warm it through without boiling.
Serve hot in small heatproof glasses.

originStory: Țuică is Romania's plum brandy, much of it distilled in village households, and țuică fiartă, boiled țuică, is its winter form. Sugar is first caramelised in a pot, then the țuică goes in with black peppercorns and is warmed until it steams, the caramel giving it its amber colour. No one is credited with the recipe, which belongs to cold days in the countryside and gatherings around Christmas, and in Transylvania and Maramureș the stronger plum spirit called pălincă or horincă is warmed the same way.

name: Sbiten
description: Honey, spices and herbs simmered together and spiked — Russia's hot drink of choice for four centuries before tea arrived and took over.
funFact: Sbiten was street food in imperial Russia, sold from insulated copper samovar-like urns carried on the back; it was displaced almost entirely by tea in the nineteenth century.

steps: Bring the water and honey to a simmer, skimming any foam that rises.
Add the ginger, cinnamon, cloves and mint and simmer for 15 minutes.
Strain out the solids.
Stir in the wine or vodka off the heat if you want it alcoholic.
Serve very hot in mugs.

originStory: Sbiten is one of the oldest drinks of the Eastern Slavs, a hot brew of honey, water, spices and herbs first mentioned in a Russian chronicle in the twelfth century and given a recipe in the sixteenth-century household manual Domostroy. For centuries it was a winter drink of every class, sold on the streets by sbitenshchiki whose heated kettle, the sbitennik, is counted among the ancestors of the samovar, until tea and coffee pushed it aside in the nineteenth century. Sbiten itself is usually alcohol-free, and the spiked version is made with wine or spirit.

name: Yorsh
description: Vodka poured into beer. Named after a spiny river fish, and about as gentle as one.
funFact: The name comes from the ruffe, a small bristly fish — Russian drinkers use it as a warning label, since the mix is notorious for arriving all at once.

steps: Pour the beer into a mug, leaving room at the top.
Add the vodka directly to the beer.
Stir once, or drop the shot glass in whole for the theatrical version.
Drink promptly.

originStory: Yorsh, beer and vodka in one glass, takes its Russian name from the ruffe, a small spiny freshwater fish, and the mix has no recorded inventor or first use of the name.

name: Bambus
description: Red wine and cola, half and half, over ice. Beloved across the Balkans and defended fiercely by everyone who drinks it.
funFact: The Balkan bambus predates Spain's kalimotxo in local memory by decades, and the two regions have never agreed on who got there first.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the red wine.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and add a lemon slice if you want it sharper.

originStory: Bambus, red wine mixed with cola, is a staple of bars and summer parties across the former Yugoslavia, and no one has documented who first made it or why it is called bamboo.

name: Tatratea Hot
description: Slovakia's herbal tea liqueur, served hot with honey and lemon. Comes in strengths from 22% to 72%, colour-coded by how serious you are.
funFact: The bottles are numbered by ABV — 32, 42, 52, 62, 72 — and the 72% 'Outlaw' edition exists mostly so that people can say they have had it.

steps: Put the honey and lemon slice in a warmed glass mug.
Add the hot water and stir until the honey dissolves.
Pour in the Tatratea and stir once.
Serve hot, with the lemon left in.

originStory: Tatratea Hot serves Slovakia's bottled tea liqueur, named for the High Tatras, warm with honey and lemon, a serve that has no recorded inventor.

name: Dom Pedro
description: Vanilla ice cream blended with whisky or Amarula until it pours. On every South African dessert menu, and ordered by adults without embarrassment.
funFact: It appears on South African menus far more often than it does anywhere else on earth, and ordering one 'with Kahlúa' rather than whisky is a legitimate regional variation.

steps: Let the ice cream soften for a few minutes so it blends smoothly.
Put the ice cream, spirit and cream in a blender.
Blend briefly — you want it thick and pourable, not liquid.
Pour into a wine glass and dust with grated chocolate or nutmeg.
Serve with both a spoon and a straw.

originStory: The Dom Pedro, vanilla ice cream blended with whisky, coffee liqueur or Amarula, is a South African after-dinner fixture, but no one has documented who first made one or where the name came from.

name: Klippies en Coke
description: Klipdrift brandy and Coke, poured heavy. South Africa drinks more brandy-and-cola per head than almost anywhere, and this is why.
funFact: South African brandy is legally required to be pot-still aged at least three years for the premium grades — a rigour largely wasted on a drink that is then filled to the top with cola.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the brandy.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and add a lemon wedge if you like.

originStory: Klippies en Coke, Klipdrift brandy with cola, is one of South Africa's most familiar brandy serves, and no one is credited with the first glass.

name: Springbokkie
description: Green over cream, in the colours of the national rugby jersey: crème de menthe under a float of Amarula. Poured in vast quantities on match day.
funFact: Amarula is made from the fruit of the marula tree, which elephants are famously — and mostly apocryphally — said to get drunk on after eating the fallen fruit.

steps: Pour the crème de menthe into a shot glass.
Float the Amarula over the back of a barspoon so it sits in a clean layer.
Serve immediately, before the layers start to bleed.
Drink in one.

originStory: The springbokkie, little springbok in Afrikaans, is a South African shot in the green and gold of the national rugby team, crème de menthe under Amarula, and no one has documented who first poured it.

name: Makgeolli
description: Unfiltered rice brew, milky and lightly fizzing, poured from the bottle into a shallow bowl. Korea's oldest drink and its most farmhouse.
funFact: Nuruk — a wild-yeast and mould starter cake — does the work that malting does for beer, breaking down the rice starch; makgeolli is traditionally drunk after farm work, and increasingly after rain, by tradition.

steps: Steam the rice and cool it to room temperature.
Mix the rice with the crumbled nuruk and the water in a clean crock.
Cover with cloth and ferment at room temperature for about a week, stirring daily.
Strain through cloth, pressing lightly — makgeolli is meant to stay cloudy.
Refrigerate, and shake the bottle before pouring into shallow bowls.

originStory: Makgeolli is often called Korea's oldest alcoholic drink, a cloudy, lightly sparkling brew of rice fermented with nuruk, a starter cake of wild yeasts and moulds, and its name is usually read as just strained. Long the farmers' drink, it earned the name nongju, farmers' wine. The twentieth century was hard on it, as colonial rule curbed home brewing and rice shortages later led the government to ban rice in brewing for years, so it was made with wheat, but it has since enjoyed a strong revival, often paired with savoury pancakes on rainy days.

name: Somaek
description: Soju dropped into beer, in a ratio people argue about seriously. Korea's most-poured mixed drink, and the engine of the company dinner.
glassware: Beer glass and a soju shot glass
funFact: The golden ratio is contested — three parts beer to one soju is the common baseline, and there are Korean drinking games devoted entirely to pouring it correctly.

steps: Pour the beer into a glass, leaving room at the top.
Add the soju — either poured in or dropped in the shot glass whole.
Cover the top with your palm and tap the glass once on the table to mix it.
Drink promptly, while it is still fizzing.

originStory: Somaek is a contraction of soju and maekju, the Korean word for beer, and it is South Korea's best-known mixed drink, poured at hoesik, the after-work company dinners, and at gatherings of friends. It belongs to the wider Korean family of poktanju, bomb drinks, in which a spirit is mixed into beer, and nobody is credited with the first one; every table seems to have its own preferred proportion.

name: Yogurt Soju
description: Soju, Yakult and lemon-lime soda. Tastes like a children's drink, disappears like one, and is not one.
funFact: Yakult has been sold in Korea since 1971 and is delivered door to door by the 'Yakult ajumma'; the cocktail is the reason Korean convenience stores stock it next to the soju.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the soju and the Yakult.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once and serve immediately — it separates if it sits.

originStory: Yogurt soju, soju shaken with a sweet cultured milk drink such as Yakult and lemon-lime soda, is a recent Korean bar and restaurant mix that no one is credited with inventing.

name: Agua de Valencia
description: Cava, orange juice, gin and vodka in a jug. Tastes like a Mimosa, behaves like something else entirely.
funFact: Invented at Café Madrid in Valencia in 1959, when a group of Basque regulars kept ordering 'Agua de Bilbao' — the house sparkling wine — and the barman offered them a Valencian alternative made with local oranges.

steps: Stir the sugar into the orange juice in a large jug until dissolved.
Add the gin and vodka and stir again.
Top with cold cava and stir once, gently.
Serve immediately in wine glasses over a little ice.
Make it in front of people — half the drink is the theatre of the jug.

originStory: Agua de Valencia was first made in 1959 by Constante Gil at the Café Madrid in Valencia. According to the writer María Ángeles Arazo, a group of Basque visitors used to order agua de Bilbao, their name for the bar's best cava, and one day challenged Gil to offer them something new, so he mixed cava with Valencian orange juice, gin and vodka. For a decade it was known only to a small circle of regulars, and only in the 1970s did it spread into the city's wider nightlife.

name: Leche de Pantera
description: 'Panther's milk': gin or rum, condensed milk and cinnamon, shaken cold. Spanish Legion issue, now a Madrid dive-bar staple.
funFact: The recipe is traditionally attributed to the Spanish Legion, whose founder Millán-Astray is said to have served it to recruits — the modern Madrid version usually swaps the original brandy for gin.

steps: Add the gin, condensed milk, milk and cinnamon to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds until thick and cold.
Strain into a chilled tumbler.
Dust with more cinnamon and serve very cold.

originStory: Leche de pantera, panther's milk, is a cold mix of gin with condensed or fresh milk, sometimes with egg white and cinnamon, and Spanish sources tie it to the Spanish Legion, whose members made it popular in the bars and taverns they frequented. Its exact origin is undocumented and no one is credited with inventing it. It was at its most popular in Spain in the years around the end of the Franco era and lives on as a curiosity of older bars.

name: Queimada
description: Orujo set alight in a clay bowl with sugar, coffee beans and lemon peel while somebody reads a spell over it. Galicia does not do this ironically.
funFact: The conxuro — the incantation read while it burns — invokes the meigas, Galician witches, and asks them to leave. The ritual is old-looking but was largely written in the 1950s.

steps: Pour the orujo into a wide clay bowl and add most of the sugar, the coffee beans and the lemon peel.
Put a ladleful of orujo and the remaining sugar into a separate ladle and set it alight.
Lower the burning ladle into the bowl to ignite the whole surface.
Stir with the ladle, lifting burning liquid and pouring it back, for several minutes until the flame turns low and blue.
Cover to extinguish, then serve hot in small clay cups.

originStory: Queimada is often called Celtic, but the prehistorian Carlos Alonso del Real pointed out that the still and the sugar it needs rule that out. Burnt aguardiente with sugar and coffee was known in Galicia by the early twentieth century, and the ritual as performed today took shape around the 1950s, when Galicians living away from home began making it at gatherings; the potter Tito Freire of Mondoñedo was making the footed clay bowls now used for it by 1955. The famous conxuro, the spell against the meigas, was written in Vigo in 1967 by Mariano Marcos Abalo.

name: Rebujito
description: Manzanilla sherry lengthened with lemon-lime soda over crushed ice — the drink that keeps Seville upright through a week of Feria.
funFact: It is drunk by the jug at the Feria de Abril in Seville and the Feria del Caballo in Jerez, where the sherry comes from — and where sherry purists have made their peace with it.

steps: Fill a tall glass with crushed ice.
Pour in the cold manzanilla.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once and add a mint sprig if you like.
Drink fast — it dies as the ice melts.

originStory: Rebujito, from the Andalusian rebujar, to mix together, is manzanilla or fino sherry lengthened with lemon-lime soda, and it belongs to the spring fairs and pilgrimages of western Andalusia, Seville's Feria de Abril, the Feria del Caballo in Jerez and El Rocío among them. It sits in a long tradition of wine regions stretching their everyday wines with something cool, and the English sherry cobbler is sometimes named as a forerunner. Nobody is credited with inventing it, and it became known beyond western Andalusia towards the end of the twentieth century.

name: Sol y Sombra
description: 'Sun and shade': brandy and anís in equal parts, no ice. A Spanish breakfast that predates any conversation about moderation.
funFact: The name comes from the bullring, where seats are priced by whether they sit in sun or shade; the drink mixes the dark brandy and the clear anís the same way.

steps: Pour the brandy and the anís into a small tumbler.
Stir once to combine.
Serve at room temperature, without ice.
Traditionally taken standing at the bar, with coffee.

originStory: Sol y sombra, sun and shade, is usually said to take its name from the bullring, where seats are sold as sol, in the sun, sombra, in the shade, or sol y sombra, those that start in sunshine and fall into shadow as the afternoon goes on. The drink matches the idea with dark brandy for the shade and clear anís for the sun, served in a small glass. It is an old and widespread Spanish bar order with no known inventor or date, usually taken with coffee or after a meal.

name: Vermut
description: Red vermouth on ice with a splash of soda, an olive and a slice of orange. Sunday noon in Barcelona has a drink and this is it.
funFact: 'Fer el vermut' — to do the vermouth — is a whole social occasion in Catalonia, held late on Sunday morning, and the best bars still draw their vermouth from the barrel.

steps: Fill a tumbler with ice.
Pour in the cold red vermouth.
Add a short splash of soda.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice and a skewered olive.
Serve with crisps and tinned seafood, if you are doing it properly.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a green olive

originStory: Vermouth came to Spain from Turin in the nineteenth century, and Catalonia took to it so thoroughly that Reus, near Tarragona, became a centre of Spanish vermouth-making. Out of that grew fer el vermut, doing the vermouth: a late-morning ritual, above all on Sundays and holidays, of red vermouth over ice with an olive and a slice of orange, often with a splash of soda and a plate of tinned seafood or crisps before lunch. Older bars pour it from the tap, and the habit, which faded in the late twentieth century, has come back strongly in Barcelona.

name: Arrack and Ginger Beer
description: Ceylon coconut arrack with ginger beer and lime — the island's standing highball, and better than it has any right to be.
funFact: Ceylon arrack is distilled from fermented coconut flower sap, tapped by climbers who move between palm crowns on ropes — a job with its own hereditary caste of specialists.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the arrack and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

originStory: Ceylon arrack, distilled from coconut flower sap, with ginger beer and a squeeze of lime has become Sri Lanka's standing highball, though no one is credited with first mixing the two.

name: Glögg
description: Nordic mulled wine with raisins and blanched almonds waiting at the bottom of the cup — you drink it, then eat it with a spoon.
glassware: Small mug or glass with a handle
funFact: Cardamom is the marker that separates Nordic glögg from German Glühwein, and the spoon is not optional — the raisins and almonds are considered part of the serving.

steps: Warm the wine with the sugar, spices and orange peel to about 70°C and hold for 30 minutes; do not boil.
Strain out the whole spices.
Put a spoonful of raisins and almonds into the bottom of each mug.
Add the aquavit to the pot off the heat, then ladle over the raisins and almonds.
Serve hot with a small spoon.
recipe.garnish: Raisins and slivered almonds in the cup

originStory: Glögg takes its name from glödgat vin, heated wine, and hot spiced wine has been drunk in the Nordic countries since at least the sixteenth century. Drinking glögg at Christmas became a Swedish tradition in the nineteenth century, made at home or bought from wine merchants whose bottles carried fanciful labels with tomte, and it spread to Finland at the end of that century. Since the twentieth century it has been served with almonds and raisins in the cup, alongside gingerbread and saffron buns.

name: Grogg
description: Swedish shorthand for spirit plus mixer, poured strong: whisky or vodka with soda or cola, and no further ceremony.
funFact: The Swedish 'grogg' descends from British naval grog — watered rum named after Admiral Vernon's grogram coat — but travelled north and lost the rum along the way.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the spirit.
Top with cold soda water or cola.
Stir once and serve, with a lemon wedge if using soda.

originStory: Grogg is the Swedish word for a spirit topped up with a soft drink or soda, and it descends from grog, the watered rum of the Royal Navy. Admiral Edward Vernon, nicknamed Old Grog for his coat of grogram cloth, ordered in the middle of the eighteenth century that his sailors' rum be diluted with water, and the nickname passed to the mix. In Sweden the word travelled far from rum: a grogg can be vodka with lemon soda or whisky with ginger ale, and the mixers themselves are known as groggvirke, grogg timber.

name: Kafi Fertig
description: Coffee with schnapps, served in a stemmed glass so you can see the colour. Swiss farmhouse fuel with a colour code all its own.
funFact: In parts of central Switzerland the strength is judged by colour: it should be dark enough that a coin dropped in the glass disappears, and no darker.

steps: Put the sugar in a small stemmed glass.
Pour in the hot coffee and stir until dissolved.
Add the schnapps and stir once more.
Serve hot, in the glass, never in a cup.

originStory: Kafi fertig, finished coffee, is the coffee and schnapps of Central Switzerland, a farmhouse and village-inn drink of Lucerne and the surrounding cantons. A measure of fruit spirit, often Träsch distilled from pears and apples, or plum spirit or kirsch, goes into thin, sweetened coffee served in a glass. It goes by many local names, among them Kafi Luz in Lucerne and Kafi Zwetschgen or Kafi Träsch after the spirit, and no one is credited with the first.

name: Boba Cocktail
description: Milk tea, rum and tapioca pearls in a shaker. Taipei's bars took the island's most famous export and put a wide straw in it.
glassware: Tall glass with a wide straw
funFact: Bubble tea was invented in Taichung in the 1980s; Taipei's cocktail bars started spiking it in the 2010s, and the brown-sugar version is now a fixture across East Asian bar menus.

steps: Cook the tapioca pearls and toss them in a little brown sugar syrup while still warm.
Spoon the pearls into the bottom of a tall glass.
Shake the rum, cooled tea, milk and remaining syrup hard with ice.
Strain over the pearls and add fresh ice.
Serve with a wide boba straw.
recipe.garnish: Brown sugar syrup streaked down the glass

originStory: The boba cocktail spikes Taiwanese bubble tea, milk tea with tapioca pearls, with rum or another spirit, a recent bar idea that no single bar is credited with.

name: Konyagi and Tonic
description: Tanzania's own clear spirit with tonic and lime — light, faintly sweet, and poured on every Dar es Salaam terrace at sunset.
funFact: Konyagi occupies an odd legal space — it is bottled at 35% and labelled as a spirit rather than a gin, though it drinks like a light, sweetened one.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the Konyagi and lime juice.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

originStory: Konyagi, Tanzania's best-known locally made spirit, with tonic and a wedge of lime has become its standard long serve, though no one is credited with the pairing.

name: Thai Bucket
description: Thai rum, Red Bull and cola in a child's sand bucket with several straws. Structurally a punch, spiritually a warning.
funFact: Thai Red Bull — Krating Daeng — is uncarbonated, sweeter and more heavily caffeinated than the export version, which is a meaningful part of why the buckets have the reputation they do.

steps: Fill a small plastic bucket with ice.
Pour in the half-bottle of Sangsom.
Add the bottle of Thai Red Bull.
Top with cola and stir with a straw.
Share it — the bucket is designed for four straws, not one.

originStory: The Thai bucket, a small plastic bucket of local spirit, mixer and ice to share, grew up on Thailand's backpacker beaches, above all at Haad Rin on Ko Pha-ngan, and no one is credited with the first.

name: Sorrel
description: Christmas red: hibiscus calyces steeped with clove, ginger and orange peel, sweetened and cut with rum. Tart, spiced and unmistakably festive.
funFact: The sorrel plant is a hibiscus relative that fruits right at Christmas across the Caribbean, which is precisely why the drink became a December tradition from Trinidad to Jamaica.

steps: Put the sorrel, ginger, cloves and orange peel in a large heatproof jug.
Pour over the boiling water, cover, and leave to steep for at least 12 hours.
Strain out the solids and stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Add the rum to taste and refrigerate.
Serve very cold over ice.

originStory: Sorrel is the Caribbean name for roselle, Hibiscus sabdariffa, a plant of African origin whose crimson calyces are steeped to make the drink, and it is thought to have reached the islands with the slave trade. The plant flowers as the days shorten, so its calyces come in around December, which is why sorrel became the Christmas drink of the English-speaking Caribbean, from Trinidad and Tobago to Jamaica. It is steeped with ginger, clove and orange peel, sweetened and often laced with rum, and its relatives include bissap in West Africa and agua de jamaica in Mexico.

name: Boukha and Orange
description: Tunisian fig brandy over ice with fresh orange juice — dry, faintly floral, and the standard way to serve boukha long.
funFact: Boukha has been distilled from Mediterranean figs in Tunisia since the nineteenth century; unlike most fruit brandies it carries no added sugar, which is why it drinks surprisingly dry.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the boukha.
Top with fresh orange juice.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice.

originStory: Boukha, Tunisia's dry fig spirit, lengthened with fresh orange juice over ice is a standard long serve in Tunisia, and no one is credited with the pairing.

name: Aslan Sütü
description: 'Lion's milk': rakı and cold water in equal parts, which turns it milky white. Sipped slowly over a long table of meze, never rushed.
funFact: The order matters: rakı first, then water, then ice — adding ice before water shocks the anise oils and leaves the drink cloudy in the wrong way. Turks call the milky effect the louche, and drinking it fast is considered poor form.

steps: Pour the rakı into a tall narrow glass, filling it about a third.
Add cold water in roughly equal measure and watch it turn opaque white.
Only now drop in one or two ice cubes.
Sip slowly alongside white cheese, melon and meze — rakı is a meal-length drink.
recipe.garnish: None — the meze is the garnish

originStory: Aslan sütü, lion's milk, is the Turkish nickname for rakı mixed with cold water, the way it is nearly always drunk, and no one knows who first called it that. Rakı is grape spirit distilled with aniseed, and water turns it milky white as the anise oils come out of solution, the effect known in English as the louche. It belongs to the long meyhane tradition of Istanbul and the Aegean, where it is sipped slowly over meze and conversation, and the usual advice is water first and ice after.

name: Waragi and Tonic
description: Uganda's juniper-flavoured banana spirit, lengthened with tonic and lime. Sharper and drier than the gin it is usually compared to.
funFact: The name comes from 'war gin', from the colonial era; commercial Uganda Waragi is distilled from bananas or cassava and then flavoured with juniper, which makes it gin-adjacent rather than gin.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the waragi and lime juice.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

originStory: Uganda Waragi, the country's bottled, juniper-flavoured spirit, with tonic and lime is a usual serve in Kampala's bars, a pairing that no one is credited with.

name: Horilka z Pertsem
description: Ukrainian vodka steeped with chilli and honey. Sweet at the front, hot at the back, drunk cold with something salted.
funFact: It is traditionally taken with salo — cured pork fat — on dark bread, a pairing that sounds unlikely and works because the fat blunts the burn.

steps: Put the chillies and peppercorns into a bottle of horilka.
Add the honey and shake until it dissolves.
Leave to infuse for three to seven days, tasting as you go — chillies work fast.
Strain out the solids once it is hot enough for you.
Serve ice cold in shot glasses.

originStory: Horilka is the Ukrainian word for vodka and strong spirits, related to the verb hority, to burn, and horilka z pertsem is horilka bottled with whole chilli peppers, the style best known outside Ukraine. With honey added it becomes medova z pertsem, honey and pepper horilka. Families have long made it at home, commercial brands such as Nemiroff carried it abroad, and it is traditionally drunk cold with a meal, often with salo, cured pork fat, on dark rye bread.

name: Angel Face
description: Equal parts gin, apricot brandy and calvados. Three spirits, no citrus, and a name that undersells it considerably.
funFact: It appears in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book with no story attached — one of many equal-parts drinks from that era that survive on balance alone.

steps: Add all three spirits to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an apple slice or a lemon twist.

originStory: The Angel Face appeared in print in 1930 in The Savoy Cocktail Book, compiled by Harry Craddock at the American Bar of the Savoy Hotel in London: equal parts of gin, apricot brandy and calvados, shaken. The book gives no story or author for it, and none has turned up since. It is one of many balanced equal-parts drinks of the era, and it is on the International Bartenders Association's official list today among the Unforgettables.

name: Atholl Brose
description: Oatmeal steeped in water, strained, then stirred with honey, cream and whisky. A Highland recipe old enough to have won a battle.
funFact: Legend holds that the Earl of Atholl put down a Highland rebellion in 1475 by filling his enemy's well with the mixture and capturing him while he was drinking it.

steps: Soak the oatmeal in the water for at least six hours, then strain through muslin, pressing to extract the creamy liquid.
Discard the oats and stir the honey into the oat liquid until dissolved.
Whisk in the whisky.
Fold in the lightly whipped cream just before serving.
Serve chilled in small glasses; it keeps a couple of days in the fridge.

originStory: Atholl brose takes its name from Atholl, the Highland district of Perthshire, and from brose, the Scots word for oatmeal mixed with liquid. Legend credits the Earl of Atholl, who in 1475 is said to have put down a rebellion by the Lord of the Isles by filling a well with oatmeal, honey and whisky and capturing the rebel leader as he drank from it, though whisky is not recorded in Scotland until later. The drink itself, oatmeal water mixed with honey, whisky and often cream, is a festive Scottish recipe, and the name is also used for the dessert cranachan.

name: Black Velvet
description: Stout and champagne, poured half and half so the black sits under the gold. Invented for a funeral and never quite shook the mood.
funFact: Created at Brooks's Club in London in 1861 after Prince Albert's death, when the steward decided even the champagne should be in mourning.

ingredients.item: Champagne or dry sparkling wine, chilled

steps: Chill both the stout and the champagne well.
Pour the stout into a tall glass and let the head settle.
Pour the champagne slowly over the back of a spoon to layer it on top.
Serve immediately, while the two are still separate.

originStory: The usual story dates the Black Velvet to 1861, when Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's consort, died in December and a steward at Brooks's Club in London decided that even the champagne should be in mourning, mixing it with stout. Its black and white were said to echo the mourning bands of the time, but the drink long outlived its occasion. When cider stands in for the champagne it is known as the poor man's black velvet.

name: Buck's Fizz
description: Two parts champagne to one part orange juice — the older, stronger, more London answer to the Mimosa, and the two have been arguing ever since.
funFact: Created at the Buck's Club in Mayfair in 1921 by barman Malachy McGarry, three years before the Mimosa appeared at the Ritz Paris — the difference is the ratio, and Londoners will tell you so.

ingredients.item: Champagne or dry sparkling wine, chilled

steps: Chill both the champagne and the orange juice thoroughly.
Pour the orange juice into a flute first.
Top slowly with champagne, tilting the glass to preserve the bubbles.
Do not stir — the pour mixes it.

originStory: Buck's Fizz is named after Buck's Club in London, the gentlemen's club founded by Captain Herbert Buckmaster after the First World War, where it is said to have been first served in 1921 by the barman Malachy 'Pat' McGarry, who appears in P. G. Wodehouse's stories. The classic proportion is two parts champagne to one of orange juice, and the club's own recipe is said to hold extra ingredients. The Mimosa, credited to the Ritz in Paris a few years later, is essentially the same drink, and in Britain Buck's Fizz is a fixture of weddings and Christmas mornings.

name: John Collins
description: The Tom Collins made with whiskey instead of gin — lemon, sugar, soda, tall and cold. The original of the family, depending who you ask.
funFact: John Collins was the head waiter at Limmer's Hotel in London in the early 1800s; the gin version took his colleague's name, and the two have been confused with each other ever since.

steps: Shake the whiskey, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

originStory: The Collins began in London as a gin punch associated with John Collins, headwaiter at Limmer's Old House on Conduit Street in Mayfair in the early 1800s, whose name survives in a rhyme about him. In America the drink split in two, and by the 1880s bar manuals such as Harry Johnson's gave a Tom Collins made with sweetened Old Tom gin and a John Collins made with Dutch gin. The names have been used loosely ever since, and in many American bars a John Collins now means the same drink made with whiskey.

name: Paradise
description: Gin, apricot brandy and orange juice. Simple, apricot-forward and one of the few Savoy-era drinks that needs no adjustment at all.
funFact: Apricot brandy in these recipes means an apricot liqueur, not a distilled eau-de-vie — a distinction that ruins the drink for anyone who buys the wrong bottle.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.

originStory: The Paradise first appears in print in 1922, in Harry MacElhone's Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails, as equal parts gin, apricot brandy and orange juice. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 set the version most bartenders follow, two parts gin to one each of apricot brandy and orange juice. Nobody recorded who first mixed it or why it was called Paradise, and the apricot brandy of these recipes means a sweet apricot liqueur rather than a dry distilled spirit.

name: Pink Gin
description: Navy strength gin stained pink with Angostura and nothing else. Two ingredients, no ice, no apology.
funFact: Angostura was issued to Royal Navy officers as a stomach remedy; mixing it into the gin ration was the medicinal excuse that turned into an institution, and Plymouth Gin still trades on the association.

steps: Dash the Angostura into a chilled coupe and roll it around to coat the inside.
Discard any excess bitters, or leave them in for a stronger version.
Stir the gin over ice for 20 seconds, or serve it neat and cold from the freezer.
Strain into the coated coupe and serve without garnish.

originStory: Pink Gin is generally traced to the officers of the Royal Navy in the nineteenth century. Angostura bitters, created by Dr Johann Siegert in the Venezuelan town of Angostura, were carried aboard ship as a supposed remedy for seasickness, and a few dashes in a glass of Plymouth gin, long carried on Royal Navy ships, turned the gin pink. The habit came ashore to British clubs and bars, along with the old choice of keeping the bitters in the glass or swirling them out before the gin goes in.

name: Russian Spring Punch
description: Dick Bradsell's long, fizzing sour: vodka, crème de cassis, lemon and champagne over crushed ice. Modern London's house punch.
funFact: Bradsell — who also gave the world the Espresso Martini and the Bramble — created it in the 1980s at the Soho Brasserie, and it remains the drink London bartenders make when they want to show off without saying so.

steps: Shake the vodka, cassis, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a tall glass packed with crushed ice.
Top with champagne and stir gently once.
Add more crushed ice to cap the glass and garnish with berries and a lemon slice.
recipe.garnish: Fresh berries and a lemon slice

originStory: Dick Bradsell created the Russian Spring Punch in London in the 1980s, for friends who wanted to throw a cocktail party but were short of money. He had each guest bring a bottle of champagne and set out glasses already built with vodka, lemon, sugar, crème de cassis and ice, ready to be topped up. He later explained the name simply: vodka for Russia, and a long fizz of the kind he thought of as a spring drink.

name: Snakebite
description: Lager and cider, half and half, with a shot of blackcurrant if you want it purple. The most-refused drink in British pubs.
funFact: Many British pubs refuse to serve it, citing an urban myth about the mix being unusually intoxicating — the real reason is that it is cheap, strong and popular with students.

steps: Pour the cider into a pint glass first.
Add the lager slowly at an angle to keep the foam down.
Add a dash of blackcurrant cordial if making a Snakebite and Black.
Do not stir.

originStory: Snakebite, equal parts lager and cider, has no recorded inventor, but it was a familiar order in British pubs and student bars by the 1980s, often with a dash of blackcurrant cordial as a Snakebite and Black. A persistent myth holds that it is illegal in the United Kingdom; it is not, though some pubs have house rules against serving it.

name: Snowball
description: Advocaat and lemonade with a squeeze of lime — a yellow, foamy relic of the British Christmas drinks trolley that refuses to die.
funFact: Advocaat is Dutch, but the Snowball is entirely British — a 1960s Christmas fixture that has been ironically revived so many times it is now simply back.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the advocaat and lime cordial.
Top with lemonade and stir briskly until the drink foams pale yellow.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry and, if you are committing to it, a slice of orange.

originStory: The Snowball, Dutch advocaat lengthened with lemonade and a squeeze of lime, is a long-standing fixture of British Christmas gatherings, and no creator or date is on record.

name: Treacle
description: An Old Fashioned with a float of apple juice on top. Bradsell again, and one of the few modern riffs the classicists never argued with.
funFact: Bradsell built it at the Player in Soho as a rum Old Fashioned, then floated cloudy apple juice over the top — the apple reads as freshness on the nose and disappears entirely by the second sip.

steps: Stir the rum, sugar syrup and bitters over ice until chilled and lightly diluted.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Float the apple juice gently over the top so it sits as a distinct layer.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: Dick Bradsell, the bartender behind much of London's cocktail revival, created the Treacle in London in the 1990s as a twist on the Old Fashioned. It is built in the glass, dark rum stirred down with sugar and bitters over ice, and finished with a float of apple juice. He is reported to have used plain clear apple juice rather than the cloudy pressed kind, and the name suits the dark, molasses-rich drink in the glass.

name: Whisky Mac
description: Scotch and green ginger wine, in equal measure, no ice. The drink Scotland reaches for when the weather turns properly hostile.
funFact: Named for Colonel Hector Macdonald, and traditionally made with Stone's Ginger Wine — a British fortified ginger wine that has been made since 1740 and exists almost solely for this purpose.

steps: Pour the Scotch and the ginger wine into a small tumbler.
Stir briefly to combine.
Serve at room temperature — ice is considered a mistake.
Drink beside something warm.

originStory: The Whisky Mac pairs Scotch with green ginger wine, and its name is traditionally explained by a Colonel Hector Macdonald, who is said to have first mixed the two while serving in India under the British Raj. The story is popular but unproven. The usual ginger wine is Stone's, a London brand with eighteenth-century roots, and the mix became a standard winter order in Scottish and British pubs.

name: White Lady
description: Gin, triple sec and lemon, shaken with egg white to a dense pale foam. The Sidecar's gin cousin, and quietly one of the best.
funFact: Harry MacElhone first made it with crème de menthe in 1919, then rebuilt it with gin at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1929 — the second version is the one that survived.

steps: Dry-shake all the ingredients without ice for 15 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Let the foam settle before garnishing with a lemon twist.

originStory: Harry MacElhone made the first drink called the White Lady at Ciro's Club in London in 1919, but it was built on crème de menthe rather than gin. The gin, triple sec and lemon recipe known today has two claimants: MacElhone is said to have rebuilt it with gin at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1929, while the Savoy credits Harry Craddock, who printed the gin version in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930. The early recipes have no egg white, which became a common addition later.

name: Wibble
description: Gin, sloe gin, grapefruit and lemon — pink, brambly and named for what it does to your legs, not your speech.
funFact: Dick Bradsell created it at The Player and said the name came from the fact that 'it makes you wibble, not wobble' — sloe gin was deeply unfashionable at the time and the drink helped rescue it.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.

originStory: Dick Bradsell created the Wibble in 1999 at The Player in Soho for Nick Blacknell, a well-known gin enthusiast, and built it on Plymouth gin and sloe gin with grapefruit, lemon and a little crème de mûre. He named it after Weebles, the roly-poly children's toys of the 1970s, whose advertising promised that they wobbled but did not fall down. It is counted among his modern London classics alongside the Bramble and the Russian Spring Punch.

name: Alaska
description: Gin and yellow Chartreuse, stirred cold. Two ingredients, and the Chartreuse does exactly as much work as you would expect.
funFact: The Savoy Cocktail Book insists that 'so far as can be ascertained this delectable potion is NOT the staple diet of the Esquimaux' — which is roughly all anyone knows about the name.

steps: Combine the gin, Chartreuse and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: The Alaska appears in the 1910s in the bar manuals of Jacques Straub, made with Old Tom gin, yellow Chartreuse and orange bitters. By the time Harry Craddock printed it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 it had become a drier mix of dry gin and Chartreuse, with a joking note that it was not the staple diet of Arctic peoples and had probably first been thought of in South Carolina. No one knows who named it, or why.

name: Between the Sheets
description: A Sidecar with rum added — cognac, rum, triple sec and lemon. Prohibition-era, and it does not pretend to be gentle.
funFact: The name is usually credited to Harry MacElhone at Harry's New York Bar in Paris, though the drink appears in American sources around the same time — it is a Sidecar with the volume turned up.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and discard.

originStory: Between the Sheets has a disputed birth. It is often credited to Harry MacElhone of Harry's New York Bar in Paris, while another account places it at the Berkeley hotel in London in the early 1920s, and a third story places it in French brothels. The equal parts of brandy, rum and triple sec with a dash of lemon that bartenders follow today match the recipe Harry Craddock printed in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930, which makes it a Sidecar with a second spirit added.

name: Bijou
description: 'Jewel': gin, green Chartreuse and sweet vermouth — diamond, emerald and ruby, in equal parts, as the name intends.
funFact: Harry Johnson's 1900 recipe explains the name directly: the gin is the diamond, the Chartreuse the emerald and the vermouth the ruby — three jewels in one glass.

steps: Combine everything in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry and a lemon twist.
