Add the rum, peach liqueur, pineapple juice and syrup.
Add crushed ice and flash-blend for five seconds.
Pour into a tiki mug.
Garnish with a mint sprig and a pineapple wedge.

originStory: The Aku Aku takes its name from Aku-Aku, Thor Heyerdahl's bestselling account of his Easter Island expedition, a title tiki culture borrowed freely, and the blended drink of light rum, peach, pineapple, lime and mint has no recorded creator.

name: Sidewinder's Fang
description: A large, spice-heavy rum and citrus punch, traditionally served with a coil of orange peel arranged to look like a snake.
funFact: The garnish is the name: a long spiral of orange peel draped over the rim, which the bar staff cut in one continuous piece as a small display of knife work.

steps: Shake everything but the soda with crushed ice.
Pour unstrained into a large tiki mug.
Top with soda and more crushed ice.
Cut a long spiral of orange peel and drape it over the rim.
Serve with a straw.

originStory: The Sidewinder's Fang is a mid-century Polynesian-restaurant riff on Don the Beachcomber's Cobra's Fang, a long punch of Demerara and gold rums with passion fruit, orange, lime and falernum, and no single creator is on record.

name: Molokai Mule
description: Rum, ginger, orange and lime — the tiki answer to a Moscow Mule, spiced rather than sharp.
funFact: Ginger runs through tiki from falernum to Doctor Funk; the mule format simply gives it the lead instead of a supporting role.

steps: Shake the rum, ginger syrup and juices with ice.
Pour into a mug packed with crushed ice.
Top with soda water.
Stir once with a swizzle stick.
Garnish with candied ginger and a lime wheel.

originStory: The Molokai Mule is a mid-century tiki drink named for the Hawaiian island of Molokai, and its recipes vary from one source to another, with no creator, bar or date on record.

name: Puka Punch
description: Four rums, honey, passionfruit and grapefruit, served long over crushed ice. One of the heaviest pours in the canon.
funFact: The Tiki-Ti bar in Los Angeles has served it since 1961, and the staff ring a bell and shout when one is ordered — a ritual that has outlasted most of the tiki era.

steps: Shake everything except the overproof rum with crushed ice.
Pour unstrained into a large tiki mug.
Top with crushed ice.
Float the overproof rum over the top.
Garnish with mint and a cherry.

originStory: The Puka Punch is a long, multi-rum tiki punch with passion fruit and honey from the Californian tiki tradition, and no creator or date is on record for it.

name: Tahitian Rum Punch
description: Rhum with lime, grenadine and tropical juice, poured long — the French Polynesian take on a punch, lighter than its American imitations.
funFact: Tahiti gave tiki bars their aesthetic vocabulary and almost none of their recipes — the actual drinking culture of French Polynesia runs to rhum, beer and fruit juice.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 10 seconds.
Pour into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Stir once to bring the grenadine through.
Garnish with a lime wheel and a flower if you have one.
Serve with a straw.

originStory: Tahitian rum punch is a family style rather than a single recipe, rhum with lime and tropical juices sweetened with grenadine and poured long over ice, with no recorded creator or date.

name: Hukilau
description: Rum with passionfruit, lime and a dry curaçao — named for the communal net-fishing that ends with everyone eating on the beach.
funFact: A hukilau is a Hawaiian group fishing method where the whole village hauls a single net; the song about it was a mainland hit in 1948 and the drink followed the song.

steps: Shake all ingredients with crushed ice for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug.
Top with crushed ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel and mint.
Serve with a straw.

originStory: The Hukilau is a tiki rum drink with curaçao and passion fruit, named for the Hawaiian community net-fishing tradition, with no creator, bar or date on record.

name: Vicious Virgin
description: Two rums, falernum, curaçao and lime — a short, dry Beachcomber formula with none of the fruit-juice padding of later tiki.
funFact: The early Beachcomber drinks were markedly drier and stronger than the tiki of the 1960s; the sweetening happened later, as the format spread to restaurants that wanted volume.

steps: Shake all ingredients with crushed ice for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a small tiki mug or coupe.
Add crushed ice to fill.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
Serve immediately.

originStory: The Vicious Virgin is a short, dry rum drink with falernum and curaçao from Don the Beachcomber's Hollywood bar, and the reason for its name is not recorded.

name: Shark's Tooth
description: Demerara rum with lemon, grenadine and soda — a long, red, deceptively simple drink from the same kitchen as the Zombie.
funFact: Donn Beach built dozens of recipes from the same handful of syrups; the difference between many of his drinks is a quarter-ounce of one ingredient, which is exactly what made them hard to copy.

steps: Shake everything except the soda with ice.
Pour into a tall glass packed with crushed ice.
Top with soda water.
Stir once with a swizzle stick.
Garnish with a lime wheel and a cherry.

originStory: The Shark's Tooth is a long, red, soda-topped Demerara rum drink of the mid-century tiki era, one of several recipes to circulate under that name, with no single recorded creator.

name: Cradle of Life
description: Rum, lime, honey and a cinnamon-spiced syrup with a whole egg — one of very few tiki drinks built on an egg.
funFact: Tiki almost never used eggs, which makes this an outlier — the egg gives it a texture closer to a flip than to a punch.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dust with grated cinnamon.
Serve immediately.

originStory: The Cradle of Life is a tiki-style rum drink unusual for its use of a whole egg, associated with the Hollywood tiki scene, but no recipe book, menu or bartender is on record as its source.

name: Slippery Nipple
description: Sambuca under Irish cream, layered so the two stay separate until you drink them. Named with the subtlety of its era.
funFact: The layers hold because Irish cream is less dense than sambuca; add the grenadine last and it sinks through both to sit at the bottom as a red dot.

steps: Pour the sambuca into a shot glass.
Float the Irish cream over the back of a barspoon so it sits cleanly on top.
Drop two drops of grenadine through the centre — they should sink.
Serve immediately, before the layers bleed.

originStory: The Slippery Nipple is a layered shooter of sambuca and Irish cream from the era of cheekily named shots, and no creator, bar or date has been credited.

name: Duck Fart
description: Kahlúa, Irish cream and whisky in three layers. Alaska's contribution to the shooter canon, and the name is not explained.
funFact: It was invented at the Peanut Farm bar in Anchorage in the 1980s, and Alaskans defend both the drink and its name with more energy than either strictly warrants.

steps: Pour the Kahlúa into the bottom of a shot glass.
Float the Irish cream over a barspoon to make the middle layer.
Float the whisky on top the same way.
Serve immediately and drink in one.

originStory: Alaska claims this layered shooter of coffee liqueur, Irish cream and Canadian whisky, and the usual story places its invention at the Peanut Farm, a bar in Anchorage, in the 1980s. That account is widely repeated but thinly documented, and no bartender has been named.

name: Alabama Slammer
description: Southern Comfort, amaretto and sloe gin with orange juice — a shot in some bars, a tall drink in others, sweet in both.
funFact: It spread through American college bars in the 1970s and is usually associated with the University of Alabama, though no one has ever produced evidence for that.

steps: Shake all ingredients briefly with ice.
Strain into a shot glass, or into a tall glass over ice for the long version.
Add a squeeze of lemon if serving long.
Serve cold.

originStory: The Alabama Slammer, Southern Comfort with amaretto, sloe gin and orange juice, is usually linked to the University of Alabama and the early 1970s, though no one has documented the connection or named a creator.

name: Red Headed Slut
description: Jägermeister, peach schnapps and cranberry — herbal and fruity at once, and far more drinkable than its reputation.
funFact: Jägermeister contains 56 botanicals and was formulated in 1934 as a digestif for hunters; its American career as a party shot would have baffled its inventor.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 8 seconds.
Strain into a shot glass or a small rocks glass.
Serve cold, immediately.
For a longer version, pour over ice and top with more cranberry.

originStory: This shooter of Jägermeister, peach schnapps and cranberry juice comes out of American shooter culture, its name a reference to the red colour, and no creator, bar or date is on record.

name: Woo Woo
description: Vodka, peach schnapps and cranberry. A Sex on the Beach with the orange juice removed, and better for it.
funFact: It belongs to a whole 1980s family built on peach schnapps, which the American market had barely heard of before 1985 and then could not get enough of.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 8 seconds.
Strain into a shot glass, or over ice in a highball for a long version.
Garnish with a lime wedge if serving long.
Serve cold.

originStory: The Woo Woo is a simple vodka, peach schnapps and cranberry drink from the American peach schnapps boom, served long or as a shot, with no recorded creator and no documented explanation for its name.

name: Purple Hooter
description: Vodka, raspberry liqueur and lime — bright purple, sharp and gone in one.
funFact: Chambord is made in the Loire from black raspberries and honey to a recipe claiming descent from a seventeenth-century royal liqueur — a grand pedigree for a bar shot.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 8 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled shot glass.
Serve immediately.
A lime wedge on the side is optional.

originStory: The Purple Hooter is an American vodka shooter coloured with black raspberry liqueur and sharpened with lime, and no creator, bar or date is on record for it.

name: Surfer on Acid
description: Jägermeister, coconut rum and pineapple. Sounds alarming and tastes, unexpectedly, like a tropical dessert.
funFact: The coconut and pineapple mask Jägermeister's bitterness almost completely, which is why people who insist they hate Jäger reliably finish this one.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 8 seconds.
Strain into a shot glass or small rocks glass.
Serve cold.
Scale it up over ice for a longer drink.

originStory: Surfer on Acid is an American shooter that pairs Jägermeister with coconut rum and pineapple juice, and no creator, bar or date has been recorded.

name: Scooby Snack
description: Melon liqueur, coconut rum, pineapple and cream, shaken to a pale green froth. A dessert disguised as a shot.
funFact: Midori was launched in the US in 1978 at Studio 54, and the whole family of green shots that followed exists because of that one marketing party.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 10 seconds.
Double-strain into a shot glass.
It should be pale green and foamy on top.
Serve immediately.

originStory: The Scooby Snack is a creamy green American shooter of melon liqueur, coconut rum and pineapple, named after the dog treats of the Scooby-Doo cartoons, with no creator or date on record.

name: Liquid Marijuana
description: Blue curaçao and melon liqueur with coconut rum and pineapple, turning an improbable green. Named for the colour, nothing else.
funFact: Blue curaçao plus yellow pineapple juice makes green — the same colour trick behind half the novelty drinks invented between 1975 and 1995.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 8 seconds.
Strain into a shot glass or over ice in a rocks glass.
The colour should be a clear green.
Serve immediately.

originStory: Liquid Marijuana is an American novelty shooter named only for its green colour, the old trick of blue curaçao meeting yellow pineapple juice, and no creator or date is on record.

name: Three Wise Men
description: Jack Daniel's, Jim Beam and Johnnie Walker in equal measure, neat. No mixer, no ceremony, no mercy.
funFact: Variations swap in Jose Cuervo to make the Four Horsemen, or add Jägermeister for the Five Wise Men — the joke scales in exactly one direction.

steps: Pour all three whiskies into a shot glass.
Do not stir, chill or dilute — the point is that it is undignified.
Serve at room temperature.
Drink in one.

originStory: Three Wise Men is a bar joke rather than a cocktail, one measure each of three whiskies whose labels carry men's names, Jack Daniel's, Jim Beam and Johnnie Walker, and it has no recorded creator or date.

name: Prairie Fire
description: Tequila and Tabasco. Two ingredients, one of which is hot sauce, and no attempt at balance.
funFact: It belongs to the dare category of shots rather than the drinking category, and the capsaicin genuinely does mask the tequila — which is the only reason it works at all.

steps: Pour the tequila into a shot glass.
Add the Tabasco directly on top.
Do not stir.
Drink in one, and have something cold ready.

originStory: The Prairie Fire is a two-ingredient American shot of tequila with enough hot sauce to sting, named for the burn, with no creator, bar or date on record.

name: Cement Mixer
description: Irish cream held in the mouth, then lime juice added. It curdles on your tongue. That is the entire drink.
funFact: The curdling is real chemistry: lime juice drops the pH below the point where casein proteins stay suspended, and they clump instantly — the same reaction that makes cheese.

steps: Pour the Irish cream into a shot glass and the lime juice into a second.
Take the Irish cream into your mouth but do not swallow.
Add the lime juice and hold both for a few seconds.
Swallow, and accept the consequences.

originStory: The Cement Mixer is an American novelty shooter of Irish cream and lime juice, named for the way the acid curdles the cream almost at once, with no creator or date on record.

name: Chartreuse Bomb
description: A shot of green Chartreuse dropped into a glass of cider or beer. Bartender currency, and traded as such.
funFact: Green Chartreuse is still made by Carthusian monks to a recipe held by two of them at a time; supply shortages since 2021 have made bartenders noticeably less willing to bomb it.

steps: Pour the cider into a small glass, leaving room.
Fill a shot glass with green Chartreuse.
Drop the shot glass into the cider.
Drink immediately, before it dilutes.

originStory: Dropping a shot of green Chartreuse into a glass of dry cider is an American bartenders' ritual rather than a recorded recipe, with no creator or date on record.

name: Lemon Drop Martini
description: The Lemon Drop scaled up into a coupe with a sugared rim — sharper and more grown-up than the shot it came from.
funFact: Norman Jay Hobday created the original at Henry Africa's in San Francisco in the 1970s, a bar widely credited with inventing the fern-bar format.

steps: Rim a chilled coupe with lemon and caster sugar.
Shake the vodka, triple sec, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Double-strain into the rimmed coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist on a sugared rim

originStory: The Lemon Drop was invented in the 1970s by Norman Jay Hobday at Henry Africa's, the saloon he ran in San Francisco's Russian Hill neighbourhood. Henry Africa's is widely credited as the first fern bar, and its sugar-rimmed vodka drink, most likely named after the lemon sweet it resembles, became its most enduring creation. The cocktail-glass Lemon Drop Martini and the later shooter both descend from it.

name: Blue Kamikaze
description: A Kamikaze with blue curaçao standing in for the triple sec. Same drink, different colour, considerably more popular.
funFact: Blue curaçao and triple sec are the same liqueur with food colouring added, which means the Blue Kamikaze is chemically a Kamikaze that photographs better.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 8 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled shot glass.
Serve immediately.
Scale up into a coupe for a full-size version.

originStory: The Blue Kamikaze is the Kamikaze of vodka, orange liqueur and lime coloured with blue curaçao, a purely visual change, and no creator or date is on record for either version.

name: Tokyo Tea
description: A Long Island Iced Tea with melon liqueur in place of the cola. Green, enormous and exactly as strong as its parent.
funFact: The Long Island family is defined by five white spirits plus a modifier: cola makes the original, cranberry the Long Beach, blue curaçao the Blue Motorcycle, and melon this one.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add all the spirits, the melon liqueur and the lemon juice.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once from the bottom.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

originStory: The Tokyo Tea is a green offshoot of the Long Island Iced Tea that keeps the white-spirit base and swaps in melon liqueur, and no creator or date is on record for it.

name: Long Beach Iced Tea
description: The Long Island with cranberry instead of cola. Pink rather than brown, and it fools people just as effectively.
funFact: The whole Long Island format exists to look like iced tea, which is why the original uses cola — the cranberry version abandons the disguise entirely and keeps the strength.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the five spirits and the lemon juice.
Top with cranberry juice.
Stir once from the bottom up.
Garnish with a lemon wedge.

originStory: The Long Beach Iced Tea is an offshoot of the Long Island Iced Tea that swaps the cola for cranberry juice, giving up the resemblance to iced tea, and no creator or date is on record.

name: Adios Motherfucker
description: The Long Island turned blue: five spirits, blue curaçao and lemonade. Also sold politely as an AMF.
funFact: Most bars list it as 'AMF' on the menu to avoid printing the full name, which has done nothing at all to stop customers ordering it by the full name.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the four spirits, blue curaçao and sour mix.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once to bring the colour through.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.

originStory: Usually listed on menus as the AMF, this blue offshoot of the Long Island Iced Tea takes its colour from blue curaçao, and no creator, bar or date is on record for it.

name: Irish Car Bomb
description: Irish cream and whiskey dropped into stout. Drink it fast — the cream curdles within seconds, and the name is genuinely unwelcome in Ireland.
funFact: The name references the Troubles and is considered offensive across Ireland; many bars now list it as an Irish Slammer, and asking for it by the original name in Dublin will not go well.

steps: Pour the stout into a pint glass and let the head settle.
Layer the Irish cream and whiskey in a shot glass.
Drop the shot into the stout.
Drink immediately — the cream curdles in about ten seconds.

originStory: Charles Burke Cronin Oat created the drink in 1979 at Wilson's Saloon in Norwich, Connecticut. Two years earlier he had added Irish whiskey to a shot of Irish cream and coffee liqueur and called it the IRA, and when he dropped that shot into a glass of stout the car bomb name followed. The name refers to the violence of the Troubles and is widely considered offensive, especially in Ireland, and many bars now serve the drink as an Irish Slammer.

name: Boilermaker's Daughter
description: A half of bitter with a shot of whisky poured in rather than beside — the gentler British reading of the boilermaker.
funFact: British pubs traditionally poured the whisky into the beer rather than serving them separately, which is the opposite of the American convention and produces a noticeably different drink.

steps: Pour the ale into a half-pint glass.
Add the whisky directly to the beer.
Stir once, gently.
Drink at cellar temperature.

originStory: The Boilermaker's Daughter is a British pub name for Scotch poured into a glass of bitter ale rather than served alongside it, and no creator, pub or date is on record.

name: Sake Bomb
description: A cup of sake balanced on chopsticks over a beer, knocked in by pounding the table. Loud, communal and not remotely traditional.
funFact: Despite the presentation it is an American invention, not a Japanese one — sake and beer are rarely combined in Japan, and the table-pounding would be startling in Tokyo.

steps: Pour the beer into a pint glass, leaving room at the top.
Rest two chopsticks across the rim, parallel.
Balance a cup of sake on the chopsticks.
Pound the table until the sake falls in, then drink immediately.

originStory: The sake bomb, a cup of sake dropped into a glass of lager, is a serve of Japanese-themed restaurants rather than a traditional Japanese one, and no creator, bar or date is on record.

name: Flaming Sambuca
description: Sambuca set alight with three coffee beans floating in it — one each for health, happiness and prosperity.
funFact: The three beans are called 'con la mosca' — with the fly — and the number matters: an even number is considered unlucky across much of Italy.

steps: Pour the sambuca into a heatproof glass and drop in three coffee beans.
Light the surface carefully and let it burn for a few seconds to toast the beans.
Extinguish by covering the glass — never blow on it.
Let the glass cool before touching it, then drink and chew the beans.

originStory: Sambuca is the anise liqueur of Lazio, first sold commercially under that name by Luigi Manzi in Civitavecchia, the port near Rome, in the nineteenth century, and serving it with coffee beans, con la mosca or 'with the fly', is an old Italian custom in which three beans are traditional. Setting the glass briefly alight to toast the beans is a later bar flourish whose origin is not recorded.

name: Gin Alexander
description: The original Alexander, made with gin rather than brandy — juniper against chocolate and cream, and stranger than the version that replaced it.
funFact: The gin version came first and the brandy version took the name; most bars now serve a Brandy Alexander if you order an Alexander, which reverses the history exactly.

steps: Shake all three hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate fresh nutmeg over the surface.
Serve immediately, before it separates.

originStory: The first known Alexander was a gin drink, equal parts gin, crème de cacao and sweet cream, printed by Hugo Ensslin in his Recipes for Mixed Drinks of 1916. Its origin is disputed: the story most often told credits Troy Alexander, a bartender at Rector's in New York, who is said to have made a white drink for a dinner celebrating Phoebe Snow, the railroad advertising heroine in a spotless white dress. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 printed it in London alongside the brandy version that would eventually claim the name.

name: Golden Cadillac
description: Galliano, white crème de cacao and cream — pale gold, vanilla-scented, and named for a car parked outside the bar that invented it.
funFact: Poor Red's Bar-B-Q in California claims it, named for a customer's gold Cadillac; the same bar's Golden Cadillac sales once made it one of the largest single accounts for Galliano in America.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without garnish, or with a light dusting of nutmeg.
Drink while cold and still emulsified.

originStory: The Golden Cadillac is credited to Poor Red's Bar-B-Q in El Dorado, California, in 1952. The story goes that a newly engaged couple asked the bartender, Frank Klein, for a drink to match the gold Cadillac they had just bought, and he shook Galliano with white crème de cacao and cream. It became the house drink, and Poor Red's is still known for it.

name: Pink Squirrel
description: Crème de noyaux, white crème de cacao and cream. Pale pink, almond-scented, and a Wisconsin supper-club fixture.
funFact: Crème de noyaux is made from apricot and peach kernels rather than almonds, and the Pink Squirrel is essentially the only drink keeping the category commercially alive.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve immediately.
In Wisconsin it is often blended with ice cream instead of shaken.

originStory: Bryant Sharp is usually credited with creating the Pink Squirrel in the 1940s at Bryant's Cocktail Lounge in Milwaukee, the bar he ran, which still pours it. The drink takes its colour from crème de noyaux, a liqueur flavoured with apricot and peach kernels, shaken with white crème de cacao and cream, and it remains a Wisconsin supper club favourite, sometimes made with ice cream.

name: Pink Lady
description: Gin, applejack, lemon and grenadine shaken with egg white. Dismissed for decades as a ladies' drink, and considerably tougher than that suggests.
funFact: Its reputation as a soft drink is entirely a marketing artefact of the 1950s — the original is gin and applejack with a whole egg white, which is not a gentle formula.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry.

originStory: The Pink Lady is a pre-Prohibition gin drink coloured with grenadine, and some early recipes add applejack, much like a Jack Rose with gin added. The name is usually linked to The Pink Lady, a Broadway musical hit of 1911, or to its star Hazel Dawn. Later recipes, including the Savoy's, dropped the applejack in favour of gin, grenadine and egg white, and the drink went on to pick up a reputation as a soft, sweet order that its original formula hardly earns.

name: Colorado Bulldog
description: A White Russian topped with cola. The cream and the cola should fight; somehow they broker a truce.
funFact: Adding cola to a cream drink risks curdling if the cola goes in first — pour it last and gently, and the fat stays suspended.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka, coffee liqueur and cream.
Stir gently to combine.
Top slowly with cola, poured down the side of the glass.
Do not stir again.

originStory: The Colorado Bulldog is an American cream drink of vodka, coffee liqueur and cream topped with cola, a relative of the White Russian, with no documented link to Colorado and no creator or date on record.

name: Godmother
description: Vodka and amaretto over a large cube. The Godfather's cleaner sibling, with the Scotch swapped out.
funFact: The 1970s duo format — one spirit, one liqueur, one big cube — produced the Godfather, Godmother, French Connection and Rusty Nail, and all four are still on menus.

steps: Put a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Add the vodka and amaretto.
Stir gently for 10 seconds.
Serve with no garnish, or a lemon twist if it reads too sweet.

originStory: The Godmother is the vodka partner of the Godfather, a two-ingredient drink of vodka and amaretto over ice, and no creator or date is on record for it.

name: Toasted Almond
description: Amaretto, coffee liqueur and cream. A dessert drink that tastes exactly like its name and makes no apology for it.
funFact: Add vodka and it becomes a Roasted Toasted Almond; the 1970s cream-drink family expanded by adding a spirit and lengthening the name.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 12 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Dust with grated nutmeg.
Serve cold.

originStory: The Toasted Almond is an American dessert drink of amaretto, coffee liqueur and cream from the years when amaretto was at its most fashionable, with no creator, bar or date on record.

name: Freddy Fudpucker
description: A Harvey Wallbanger built on tequila instead of vodka — orange juice with a Galliano float, and a name from the same school.
funFact: It is a straight substitution on the Wallbanger, and both drinks exist mainly because Galliano's importer spent the 1970s pushing bars to float it on things.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the tequila and top with orange juice.
Stir once to combine.
Float the Galliano over the back of a spoon.
Garnish with an orange slice.

originStory: The Freddy Fudpucker is the tequila offspring of the Harvey Wallbanger, with Galliano floated on tequila and orange juice, and no creator or date is documented for it.

name: Bay Breeze
description: Vodka, cranberry and pineapple. The Sea Breeze with pineapple in place of the grapefruit, and gentler for it.
funFact: The whole breeze family is vodka plus cranberry plus one other juice — grapefruit makes a Sea Breeze, pineapple a Bay Breeze, and orange a Madras.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka and cranberry juice.
Top with pineapple juice.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

originStory: The Bay Breeze is the pineapple member of the American breeze family of vodka and cranberry highballs, with no creator or date on record.

name: Madras
description: Vodka, cranberry and orange juice over ice. Named for the fabric, not the city, and the least demanding drink in any bar.
funFact: The name comes from madras plaid, whose overlapping red and orange stripes the layered juices were thought to resemble before they are stirred together.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka and cranberry juice.
Float the orange juice on top without stirring.
Serve with a straw and let the drinker mix it.

originStory: The Madras is the orange member of the American breeze family of vodka and cranberry highballs, its name usually explained by the red and orange checks of madras cloth, with no creator or date on record.

name: Angel's Tip
description: Crème de cacao under a float of cream, with a cherry suspended from a pick across the rim. A pousse-café for people in a hurry.
funFact: It belongs to the pousse-café tradition of layered after-dinner drinks, a genre that largely died because it takes a steady hand and nobody has time.

steps: Pour the crème de cacao into a pony glass.
Float the cream carefully over the back of a barspoon.
Spear a cherry on a cocktail pick and rest it across the rim.
Serve immediately without stirring.

originStory: The Angel's Tip is a layered after-dinner drink of crème de cacao under a float of cream, finished with a cherry, from the early twentieth-century pousse-café tradition, and no single creator is recorded.

name: Velvet Hammer
description: Triple sec, crème de cacao and cream — a smoother, orange-scented cousin of the Alexander family.
funFact: Recipes differ wildly — some versions use vodka, some Tia Maria, some Cointreau — which is common for drinks that spread through hotel bars rather than books.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve immediately.
Dust with cocoa if you like.

originStory: The Velvet Hammer is a creamy American after-dinner drink of orange liqueur, crème de cacao and cream whose recipe has never settled, and no creator or date is on record.

name: Bitter Giuseppe
description: Cynar, sweet vermouth, lemon and orange bitters. Almost entirely bitter, served on the rocks, and a genuine test of your palate.
funFact: Stephen Cole created it at The Violet Hour in Chicago, and it is one of very few cocktails where the amaro is the base spirit rather than the modifier.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve as a digestif rather than an aperitif.

originStory: Stephen Cole created the Bitter Giuseppe at The Violet Hour in Chicago in the late 2000s, building a Manhattan-style drink with Cynar, the artichoke amaro, as the base rather than a modifier, stirred with sweet vermouth, lemon and orange bitters. It became one of the most familiar of the low-strength, amaro-led cocktails of its time.

name: Art of Choke
description: Cynar and rum with green Chartreuse, lime and mint, stirred over crushed ice. Bitter, herbal and unlike anything else.
funFact: Kyle Davidson created it at The Violet Hour; the name is a pun on artichoke, which is what Cynar is made from, and on the difficulty of getting people to order it.

steps: Press the mint gently in the bottom of a mixing glass.
Add the remaining ingredients and stir over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint sprig.
Serve with a short straw.

originStory: Kyle Davidson created the Art of Choke at The Violet Hour in Chicago around 2008, splitting the base between white rum and Cynar and adding green Chartreuse, lime, demerara syrup and mint over crushed ice. The name puns on the artichoke behind Cynar, the amaro that carries the drink.

name: Enzoni
description: A Negroni crossed with a gin sour, built on muddled grapes. Bitter, fresh and unexpectedly bright.
funFact: Created at Milk & Honey, the name splices Enzo — the grapes — with Negroni, and it converted a lot of drinkers who thought they disliked Campari.

steps: Muddle the grapes with the simple syrup in a shaker.
Add the gin, Campari, lemon juice and ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a grape on a pick.

originStory: Vincenzo Errico created the Enzoni at Milk & Honey in New York in the early 2000s, crossing the Negroni with a gin sour and using muddled green grapes in place of sweet vermouth. The name joins Enzo, short for Vincenzo, to Negroni, and Errico also created the Red Hook, another of the drinks that came out of Milk & Honey in those years.

name: Fitzgerald
description: A gin sour with Angostura through it. Dale DeGroff's demonstration that two dashes of bitters can rebuild a whole drink.
funFact: DeGroff created it at the Rainbow Room, and it is often used to teach the point that bitters are a structural ingredient rather than a decoration.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.
Serve immediately.

originStory: Dale DeGroff created the Fitzgerald at the Rainbow Room in New York in the early 1990s, a gin sour given depth by a couple of dashes of Angostura and named for the novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald. It has since travelled to cocktail menus around the world.

name: Water Lily
description: Gin, crème de violette, orange liqueur and lemon — pale purple, floral and citric all at once.
funFact: Richard Boccato created it at Little Branch; crème de violette had been unavailable in America for decades and returned in 2007, immediately producing a wave of purple drinks.

steps: Shake all four in equal measure with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve very cold.

originStory: Richard Boccato created the Water Lily at Little Branch in New York in 2007, the year crème de violette returned to American shelves after decades away. It is an equal-parts sour in the mould of the Corpse Reviver No. 2, with gin, orange liqueur, lemon and violette, and its pale violet colour suits the name.

name: Left Hand
description: A Boulevardier with chocolate bitters — a small addition that turns the whole drink darker and rounder.
funFact: Sam Ross created it at Milk & Honey; the chocolate bitters are the only difference from a Boulevardier, and they change it more than the volume suggests they should.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.
Serve cold.

originStory: Sam Ross created the Left Hand at Milk & Honey in New York around 2007, adding the then-new Xocolatl Mole bitters from Bittermens to a stirred drink of bourbon, sweet vermouth and Campari that closely resembles the older Boulevardier. Its partner is the Right Hand, a rum version made by his Milk & Honey colleague Michael McIlroy.

name: Conference
description: Four brown spirits stirred together — bourbon, rye, cognac and calvados — with no citrus and nowhere to hide.
funFact: Named because the four spirits are 'in conference', it comes from Death & Co and is one of the stiffest modern classics in circulation.

steps: Combine all four spirits and the bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 30 seconds — this needs the dilution.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and discard it.

originStory: Brian Miller created the Conference at Death & Co in New York in the late 2000s by splitting an Old Fashioned four ways, between rye, bourbon, cognac and calvados, seasoned with bitters. It became one of the signature drinks of the bar's early years, after Death & Co opened in the East Village at the end of 2006.

name: Bitter Mai Tai
description: A Mai Tai with Campari standing in for half the rum. Bitter, nutty and the drink that made bitter tiki a category.
funFact: Jeremy Oertel created it at Dutch Kills, and it works because orgeat's almond richness is one of very few things that can stand up to Campari without being erased.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 10 seconds.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint sprig and a spent lime shell.
Serve with a straw.

originStory: The Bitter Mai Tai is credited to the New York bartender Jeremy Oertel, who replaced much of the rum in the classic Mai Tai with Campari, keeping a measure of Jamaican rum along with lime, orgeat and orange curaçao. It became one of the defining drinks of bitter tiki, in which an amaro takes the lead role.

name: Cynar Julep
description: Cynar with mint and crushed ice in place of bourbon. A julep at half the strength and twice the bitterness.
funFact: Amaro juleps became a small genre in the 2010s precisely because the format — crushed ice, mint, a straw — makes a bitter liqueur approachable in a way that neat serving does not.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in a julep tin.
Add the Cynar and fill the tin with crushed ice.
Swizzle until the outside of the tin frosts.
Top with more crushed ice and a splash of soda.
Garnish with a generous mint bouquet.

originStory: Dushan Zaric, an owner of the New York bar Employees Only, has described creating his Cynar Julep on a hot July day, when he wanted a long drink to enjoy with food and built a julep on Cynar, the Italian artichoke amaro, in place of bourbon. He added grapefruit, lemon and mint and finished it with a pinch of ras el hanout, the Moroccan spice blend, borrowed from the kitchen's spice rack. Cynar and grapefruit is also a familiar pairing in Argentina, where the amaro is made locally.

name: Ginger Rogers
description: Gin, mint, lime and ginger ale — a long, fresh highball named for the dancer, and much older than most people assume.
funFact: A brandy version of the name predates the gin one by decades, which is why bar books from different eras disagree entirely about what a Ginger Rogers contains.

steps: Press the mint gently in a shaker with the syrup.
Add the gin, lime juice and ice, then shake hard.
Double-strain into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with ginger ale.
Garnish with a mint sprig and a lime wheel.

originStory: The modern Ginger Rogers, a long gin drink with mint, lime and ginger ale, is credited to the San Francisco bartender Marco Dionysos and associated above all with Absinthe Brasserie and Bar, where he served it. The ginger explains the dancer's name, though no one recorded who first thought of it.

name: Morgenthaler Amaretto Sour
description: The Amaretto Sour rebuilt with cask-strength bourbon and egg white — the drink that rescued a punchline.
funFact: Jeffrey Morgenthaler published it in 2012 with the argument that the Amaretto Sour was not a bad drink but a badly made one; the bourbon supplies the backbone amaretto lacks.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with lemon peel and brandied cherries.

originStory: Jeffrey Morgenthaler, the Portland bartender and writer, published his Amaretto Sour in 2012 in a blog post with a characteristically bold title. His argument was that the Amaretto Sour was not a bad drink but a badly made one, usually built from sour mix. He cut the amaretto back, added cask-strength bourbon for structure, and shook it with fresh lemon and egg white. The recipe spread quickly online and is now widely treated as a modern classic.

name: Whiskey Peach Smash
description: Bourbon muddled with fresh peach, lemon and mint over crushed ice — a summer smash that only works in season.
funFact: The smash is the most seasonal cocktail format there is — the fruit has to be ripe, which is why it appears on menus for about eight weeks a year and then vanishes.

steps: Muddle the peach wedges with the syrup and lemon juice.
Add the mint and press gently.
Add the bourbon and ice, then shake hard for 10 seconds.
Double-strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a peach slice and mint.

originStory: The Whiskey Peach Smash is a seasonal take on the old whiskey smash, with ripe peach muddled alongside the lemon and mint, and no creator or bar is on record for it.

name: Tantris Sidecar
description: A Sidecar with green Chartreuse and apricot added — richer, herbal and considerably more complex than the original.
funFact: Created at the Tantris restaurant in Munich, it is one of very few modern classics to come out of Germany and enter the international repertoire.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve very cold.

originStory: The Tantris Sidecar is credited to the New York bartender Audrey Saunders, who named it after Tantris, the celebrated Munich restaurant. It builds on the classic cognac Sidecar with green Chartreuse among its additions, layering herbal depth over the original's sweet-and-sour frame, and recipes for it vary.

name: Mezcal Mule
description: A Moscow Mule with mezcal — smoke against ginger, which turns out to be one of the easier substitutions in the book.
funFact: The mule format survives almost any base spirit, which is why every distillery markets one — but ginger's heat and mezcal's smoke genuinely complement each other rather than merely coexisting.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the mezcal and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

originStory: Jim Meehan created the Mezcal Mule at PDT in New York in 2008, building it with passion fruit, cucumber, agave, lime and ginger beer rather than simply swapping spirits in a Moscow Mule. Simpler mezcal-and-ginger-beer versions have since become a bar standard, and many drinkers now know it only in that form.

name: Bee Sting
description: A Bee's Knees with chilli — honey, lemon and gin with a hot edge that arrives a beat after the sweetness.
funFact: Chilli and honey work together because capsaicin is fat- and sugar-soluble — the honey carries the heat and then blunts it, which is why the burn builds and fades rather than lingering.

steps: Muddle one chilli slice gently in the shaker.
Add the gin, honey syrup, lemon juice and ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a thin chilli slice as garnish.

originStory: The Bee Sting is a modern variation on the Bee's Knees, the gin, honey and lemon sour, with chilli added for heat, and no creator or date is on record for it.

name: Japanese Highball
description: Whisky and soda, built with a precision bordering on ceremony: frozen glass, hard ice, thirteen stirs. Japan turned the simplest drink into a discipline.
funFact: Suntory's 1950s highball campaign was a deliberate rescue of a collapsing whisky market, and it worked so completely that the highball is now the default way Japan drinks whisky.

steps: Freeze the glass and fill it to the top with hard, clear ice.
Pour the whisky over the ice and stir exactly thirteen times to chill it without melting the ice.
Add more ice if the level has dropped, then pour the chilled soda down the side in one steady motion.
Stir once, vertically, lifting the bar spoon straight out to keep the carbonation.
Express a lemon peel over the surface and serve immediately.

originStory: Japan's whisky highball took hold in the 1950s, when Suntory opened a chain of Torys bars across the country, serving its affordable Torys whisky with soda. The highball remained central to Japanese drinking until whisky fell out of fashion in the 1980s. In 2008 Suntory launched a campaign to revive it around Kakubin, its square-bottled blend, and the precise, ritualised serve that followed became famous far beyond Japan.

name: Mizuwari
description: Whisky and still water, one to two and a half, stirred over ice. The most-drunk whisky serve in Japan and the hardest to make well.
funFact: Japan's soft, low-mineral water is part of the point — mizuwari made with hard water tastes noticeably different, which is why the ratio travels badly.

steps: Fill a tall glass to the top with hard ice and let it chill the glass.
Pour in the whisky and stir thirteen and a half times, in the traditional count.
Top up the ice, then add the still water.
Stir three and a half times only — any more and the drink goes flat and watery.
Serve with food rather than on its own.

originStory: Mizuwari, literally 'cut with water', is the Japanese custom of lengthening whisky with cold still water over ice to drink with food, a national habit rather than an invention, with no single creator.

name: Oyuwari
description: Shochu cut with hot water, poured water-first so the two mix by convection alone. Kyushu's winter default.
funFact: The order is not superstition: pouring hot water first and shochu second lets the density difference mix the drink without stirring, which keeps the aroma intact.

steps: Warm a ceramic cup with a little hot water and discard it.
Pour the hot water into the cup FIRST, filling it about three-fifths.
Add the shochu on top and do not stir — the convection mixes it.
Rest for thirty seconds so the temperature settles to about 45°C.
Drink while hot, alongside food.
recipe.garnish: A slice of pickled plum, optional

originStory: Oyuwari, shochu cut with hot water, is a traditional winter way of drinking shochu in Kyushu, a regional custom rather than an invention, with no creator or date on record.

name: Chuhai
description: Shochu and carbonated water with a fruit flavour — sold canned in a hundred varieties and poured fresh in every izakaya.
funFact: The name shortens 'shochu highball'. Canned chuhai is a vast category in Japan, with strong versions at 9% sold in the same fridge as the 3% ones and colour-coded accordingly.

ingredients.item: Fresh fruit or syrup (peach, grape, ume)

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the shochu and the fruit syrup or muddled fresh fruit.
Top with well-chilled soda water.
Stir once, vertically, to preserve the fizz.
Garnish with a slice of the fruit used.
recipe.garnish: A slice of the matching fruit

originStory: Chuhai is a contraction of 'shochu highball', the habit of lengthening shochu with soda and fruit flavouring that is usually traced to the izakaya of postwar Tokyo, where shochu was cheaper than whisky or beer. It became a national phenomenon once Takara launched the first canned chuhai, and ready-to-drink versions now fill convenience-store fridges across Japan in dozens of flavours. No single creator is recorded.

name: Denki Bran
description: 'Electric Brandy' — a brandy, gin, wine and herb blend served at the same Tokyo bar since 1882, when electricity itself was the novelty.
funFact: Kamiya Bar in Asakusa has served it since 1882 and named it for electricity because anything modern and slightly shocking was 'denki' at the time; the recipe is still secret.

steps: Pour the Denki Bran into a small tumbler — no ice, no dilution.
Serve a small glass of cold draught beer alongside.
Sip the Denki Bran, then chase with the beer.
Do not mix the two; the pairing is the tradition.

originStory: Denki Bran is usually dated to 1882, though accounts of the exact year differ. Its creator, Kamiya Denbei, had opened a liquor shop in Asakusa, Tokyo, and in 1912 the premises became Kamiya Bar, which still serves the drink. In the Meiji era electricity stood for everything modern, and new goods were often sold as 'electric', so Kamiya's brandy-based blend became Electric Brandy; its exact recipe remains a secret.

name: Hoppy
description: Shochu topped with Hoppy, a near beer-flavoured mixer from 1948. Order 'naka' for more shochu and 'soto' for more Hoppy.
funFact: Hoppy was launched in 1948 when real beer was unaffordable, as a way to make cheap shochu taste like beer; postwar nostalgia has kept it on Tokyo izakaya menus ever since.

steps: Chill the mug and the Hoppy thoroughly; keep the shochu in the freezer.
Pour the frozen shochu into the mug — this is the 'naka'.
Add the cold Hoppy in one pour from a height to build a head.
Do not stir; the pour mixes it.
Order another 'naka' when the shochu runs out before the Hoppy does.

originStory: Hoppy went on sale in Tokyo in 1948 as a beer-flavoured soft drink, at a time when real beer was expensive and hard to find. Drinkers soon found that it made cheap shochu taste like beer, and the pairing became a Tokyo izakaya fixture that postwar nostalgia has kept alive.

name: Yuzu Sour
description: Shochu or vodka with yuzu juice and soda — sharper and more floral than lemon, and unmistakably Japanese.
funFact: Yuzu is too sour and too seedy to eat, so it is grown almost entirely for its juice and peel — a citrus cultivated purely as a flavouring.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the shochu, yuzu juice and honey syrup and stir to combine.
Top with chilled soda water.
Stir once vertically.
Garnish with a strip of yuzu peel.

originStory: The yuzu sour is a fresh-citrus member of Japan's izakaya sour family, shochu and soda with the juice of yuzu and a little honey, and no single creator or date is on record.

name: Calpis Sour
description: Shochu with Calpis, the cloudy fermented-milk cordial that has been Japan's comfort drink since 1919. Tastes like a yoghurt lemonade.
funFact: Calpis was created in 1919 by a Japanese businessman who had encountered fermented mare's milk in Inner Mongolia; the name blends 'calcium' with the Sanskrit 'sarpis'.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the shochu and Calpis concentrate and stir until fully combined.
Top with chilled soda water.
Stir once, gently — Calpis foams easily.
Serve with no garnish.

originStory: Calpis, the cultured-milk cordial at the heart of this drink, was launched in Japan by Kaiun Mishima in the Taisho era, after he had encountered airag, fermented mare's milk, while travelling in Mongolia. The name joins cal, from calcium, to pis, from sarpis, a Sanskrit word from Buddhist teaching, chosen after consulting the composer Kosaku Yamada among others. Mixed with shochu and soda, Calpis became a staple sour of the izakaya, though no one claims the first glass.

name: Sakerinha
description: A Caipirinha built on sake — the drink of Brazil's Japanese community, and of Japan's Brazilian one.
funFact: Brazil has the largest Japanese population outside Japan, and hundreds of thousands of Brazilian-Japanese later moved back to Japan — the drink travelled in both directions with them.

steps: Muddle the lime wedges with the sugar in a sturdy rocks glass.
Fill the glass with ice.
Pour over the sake.
Stir hard from the bottom up until the glass frosts.
Serve with the spent lime still in the glass.

originStory: The Sakerinha swaps the cachaça of Brazil's Caipirinha for sake, keeping the muddled lime and sugar, and it has no recorded creator or date.

name: Baijiu Sour
description: Baijiu shaken with citrus, honey and egg white — Shanghai's project to make the world's best-selling spirit approachable to outsiders.
funFact: Baijiu outsells whisky, vodka and rum combined by volume, yet almost none of it leaves China — Shanghai's bar scene spent the 2010s working out how to mix it for people who did not grow up with it.

steps: Dry-shake the baijiu, lemon juice, honey syrup and egg white for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dash the bitters across the foam and draw a pattern through them.
Serve immediately.

originStory: The Baijiu Sour gives China's grain spirit the classic sour treatment, shaken with lemon, honey and egg white, and it has many authors and no single recorded creator or date.

name: Cynar Spritz
description: The spritz for people who find Aperol too sweet: artichoke amaro, prosecco and soda, darker and considerably more bitter.
funFact: Cynar is made from thirteen botanicals including artichoke leaves, and in the Veneto it is drunk as a spritz far more often than it is drunk neat.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Pour in the Cynar, then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Stir once, gently, to combine without killing the bubbles.
Garnish with an orange slice and an olive if you are in the Veneto.

originStory: The spritz is usually traced to the Habsburg years in the Veneto, when soldiers and merchants from the north are said to have asked for a splash of water to soften the local wine; bitter liqueurs and prosecco came later. Cynar, the artichoke-based amaro made from thirteen herbs and plants, was launched after the Second World War by the Venetian entrepreneur Angelo Dalle Molle, and swapping it for Aperol or Select gives a darker, more bitter spritz now familiar in the bars of the Veneto.

name: Select Spritz
description: Venice's own spritz, made with Select rather than Aperol — deeper red, more bitter, and the local order since 1920.
funFact: Select was created in Venice in 1920 and remains the city's default spritz base; ordering an Aperol spritz in a Venetian bacaro marks you out immediately as being from elsewhere.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the Select and then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda.
Stir once gently.
Garnish with a green olive — not an orange slice, which is the Padova style.

originStory: Select was created in Venice in 1920 by the brothers Mario and Vittorio Pilla, and it became the city's own bitter for the spritz. The spritz itself is usually traced to the Habsburg years in the Veneto, when visitors from the north are said to have asked for a splash of water to soften the local wine; bitter liqueurs and prosecco came later. In Venice's bacari, the city's small wine bars, many still regard Select as the proper base for a spritz veneziano.

name: Puccini
description: Prosecco over fresh mandarin juice — the winter member of Harry's Bar's painter-and-composer family.
funFact: Harry's Bar named its sparkling drinks after Venetian artists and composers, and made each with whatever fruit was in season — the Puccini belongs to mandarin season in midwinter.

steps: Squeeze fresh mandarins and strain the juice; chill it thoroughly.
Pour the cold juice into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with prosecco, stirring gently with a bar spoon as you pour.
Serve immediately, with no garnish.

originStory: The Puccini is usually credited to Harry's Bar in Venice, where Giuseppe Cipriani created the Bellini, white peach purée with prosecco, and named it after a Venetian painter. The bar went on to pair sparkling wine with other seasonal fruits and other artists: strawberry for the Rossini, pomegranate for the Tintoretto, and fresh mandarin juice for the Puccini, named after the composer of La Bohème and Tosca.

name: Tintoretto
description: Pomegranate and prosecco — the deepest red of the Harry's Bar family, named for the painter who filled the Scuola di San Rocco.
funFact: Tintoretto spent over twenty years decorating the Scuola Grande di San Rocco, often working for nothing to keep rivals out — a level of commitment the drink does not attempt to match.

steps: Juice fresh pomegranate and strain out the solids.
Chill the juice thoroughly before use.
Pour the juice into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with prosecco and stir once with a bar spoon.
Garnish with a few pomegranate seeds.

originStory: The Tintoretto belongs to the family of fruit-and-sparkling-wine drinks that grew up at Harry's Bar in Venice after Giuseppe Cipriani created the Bellini and named it for the Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini. The bar paired other fruits with other artists, and pomegranate went to Tintoretto, the Venetian master whose vast canvases cover the walls and ceilings of the Scuola Grande di San Rocco. It is mixed with prosecco and served in the colder months, when pomegranates are in season.

name: Carajillo 43
description: Licor 43 shaken over espresso until it foams — Mexico's after-dinner drink, and ordered in vast quantities across the country.
funFact: Spain's carajillo is coffee with brandy or rum; Mexico rebuilt it around Licor 43 and shakes it cold, which is now so dominant that the Spanish original is barely known there.

ingredients.amount: cubed, plus one large cube to serve

steps: Pull a fresh espresso and let it cool for a few seconds.
Add the Licor 43 and espresso to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 10 seconds until a thick crema forms.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Serve immediately, while the foam holds.

originStory: The carajillo, black coffee laced with spirit, is an old Spanish café habit, and the stories told about its name are disputed. Mexico remade it around Licor 43, the vanilla-and-citrus liqueur from Cartagena, Spain, named for its forty-three ingredients, shaking it over ice with espresso, and the Carajillo 43 became a fixture of Mexican restaurants and after-dinner tables. No single creator is recorded.

name: Mastiha Spritz
description: Chios mastiha with soda and citrus — resinous, pine-fresh and made from the tears of a tree that grows nowhere else on earth.
funFact: Mastic resin is harvested only in southern Chios — attempts to grow the trees productively elsewhere have consistently failed — and the villages that farm it are collectively called the Mastichochoria.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the mastiha and the lemon juice.
Pour in the prosecco, then top with soda water.
Stir once gently.
Garnish with a lemon twist and a sprig of thyme.

originStory: The Mastiha Spritz is a modern serve that lengthens mastiha, the pine-scented Greek liqueur made from the mastic resin of southern Chios, with soda, lemon and prosecco, and it has no recorded creator or date.

name: Herrengedeck
description: A beer with a glass of sparkling wine beside it — 'the gentlemen's set menu', and a genuine Berlin tradition rather than a joke.
glassware: Beer glass and a sekt flute
funFact: In the West it means beer and sekt; in the former East it usually meant beer and a shot of clear spirit, and Berliners will still tell you which version their side of the city drank.

steps: Pour the pilsner into a beer glass and let the head settle.
Pour the chilled sekt into a separate small flute.
Serve the two side by side, not mixed.
Alternate between them — the sekt resets the palate between mouthfuls of beer.

originStory: The Herrengedeck, literally the gentlemen's set, is a Berlin bar custom of serving a pilsner alongside a glass of sekt, a corner-bar tradition rather than an invention, with no recorded creator or date.

name: Cubanito
description: Havana's Bloody Mary: rum instead of vodka, with lime, Worcestershire and a heavy hand of hot sauce.
funFact: Cuba's answer to the Bloody Mary predates most of the vodka versions, for the simple reason that Havana had excellent rum and almost no vodka.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the rum, lime juice, Worcestershire and hot sauce.
Top with tomato juice and season with salt and pepper.
Roll the drink between two tins rather than shaking, to mix without frothing.
Garnish with a lime wedge.

originStory: The Cubanito is the rum-based Cuban member of the Bloody Mary family, white rum with tomato, lime and spice, and no creator, bar or date is documented for it.

name: Grzaniec
description: Mulled beer or wine with honey, cloves and ginger — Polish winter, served in mountain shelters and Christmas markets alike.
funFact: The beer version — grzane piwo — is the older of the two, and mulling beer was standard across northern Europe long before mulled wine became the Christmas default.

steps: Warm the beer or wine gently with the spices and orange peel — never boil it.
Hold at about 70°C for ten minutes so the spices infuse.
Stir in the honey until fully dissolved.
Strain into a heatproof mug.
Serve hot with a cinnamon stick.

originStory: Grzaniec, from the Polish word for warming, is the mulled beer or wine of Polish winters, spiced with honey, cloves, ginger and cinnamon, a folk tradition with no recorded creator or date.

name: Almdudler Spritzer
description: White wine with Almdudler, the Alpine herb soda that Austria treats as a national institution.
funFact: Almdudler has been made since 1957 from 32 Alpine herbs and is so entrenched that Austrians describe it as the country's second national drink after beer.

steps: Chill both the wine and the Almdudler well.
Pour the wine into a tall glass.
Top with the Almdudler.
Stir once, gently, and serve without ice in the Austrian manner.

originStory: Almdudler, the herbal soda in this spritzer, was created in Vienna by Erwin Klein, who launched it in the late fifties after three years of development and took the name from the old Alpine expression auf der Alm dudeln, roughly to yodel on the mountain pasture. In the wine regions of Lower Austria and Burgenland it became a popular mixer for local red and white wines, and the spritzer that results is a household serve rather than an invention, with no single creator.

name: Dutch Mule
description: Jenever with ginger beer and lime — the mule format handed to the malty grandfather of gin, which changes it entirely.
funFact: Jenever is distilled from malt wine and tastes closer to a light whisky than to London dry gin, which is why it holds up against ginger where gin can disappear.

steps: Fill a copper mug or highball with ice.
Add the jenever and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

originStory: The Dutch Mule hands the mule format of ginger beer and lime to jenever, the malt-wine spirit of the Netherlands and Belgium, and no creator or date is recorded for it.

name: Irish Mule
description: Irish whiskey with ginger beer and lime. The mule's gentlest branch, and the one that goes down fastest.
funFact: Irish whiskey's triple distillation leaves it lighter and smoother than Scotch or bourbon, which is exactly why it disappears into ginger beer so easily.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the Irish whiskey and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge and a mint sprig.

originStory: The Irish Mule applies the mule formula of ginger beer and lime to Irish whiskey, one of many regional versions of the Moscow Mule, with no creator or date on record.

name: Sima
description: Finnish spring mead: lemon, sugar and yeast fermented for a couple of days and bottled with raisins that float when it is ready.
funFact: The raisins are a timer: a few are dropped into each bottle, and when they rise to the surface the fermentation has produced enough carbonation to drink.

steps: Boil the water with both sugars and the lemon slices, then cool to lukewarm.
Stir in the yeast and leave covered at room temperature overnight.
Bottle, adding a teaspoon of sugar and a few raisins to each bottle.
Leave at room temperature until the raisins float, usually two to three days.
Refrigerate and drink within a week, at Vappu if you are doing it properly.
recipe.garnish: The floating raisins and a lemon slice

originStory: Sima is Finland's traditional drink for Vappu, the May Day festival: a lightly fermented lemonade bottled for a few days with raisins, which rise to the surface when it is ready. Older recipes used honey, which is why sima is often described as a mead, though most households now make it with sugar. It is a folk tradition with no single creator, made in homes across the country each spring.

name: Medovukha
description: Honey fermented with water and spices — an East Slavic drink older than distillation, lighter and quicker than true mead.
funFact: Traditional medovukha was fermented for decades; the boiled quick version was developed in the fifteenth century because nobody wanted to wait twenty years for a drink.

steps: Boil the water and honey together, skimming the foam that rises.
Add the spices and hops, simmer briefly, then cool to lukewarm.
Pitch the yeast and ferment in a covered vessel for about a week.
Strain and bottle, then refrigerate for several days to carbonate lightly.
Serve cool in ceramic mugs.

originStory: Medovukha is the honey drink of the East Slavs, mentioned in medieval chronicles long before distilling reached the region and made by fermenting honey with water and spices. Its name comes from med, the Slavic word for honey. Over the centuries it ranged from long-aged honey drinks to quicker boiled versions, and today it is made both at home and commercially, notably around the old town of Suzdal. It is a folk tradition rather than an invention.

name: Uvita
description: Sweet red wine with grape must and spices, warmed and drunk at winter festivals along the Uruguayan coast.
funFact: Uruguay drinks more wine per head than any other country in the Americas, most of it Tannat, and its winter street festivals run on warmed sweet wine rather than beer.

steps: Combine the wine, must, sugar and spices in a pan.
Warm gently to about 65°C without boiling.
Hold for fifteen minutes so the spices infuse.
Strain into small glasses.
Serve warm, with the orange peel.

originStory: The most famous uvita in Uruguay is the house drink of Bar Fun Fun, a nineteenth-century Montevideo bar long tied to the city's tango history, which pours its sweet, wine-based uvita in small glasses from a recipe it keeps to itself. Uvita simply means 'little grape', and the name is also used more loosely for home-made sweet wine drinks with no single creator.

name: Íslenskur Kaffi
description: Strong coffee with brennivín and cream — the Icelandic answer to Irish coffee, with caraway in place of the sweetness.
funFact: Iceland drinks more coffee per head than almost anywhere on earth, and brennivín's caraway edge makes for a markedly drier coffee drink than the Irish version.

steps: Warm a glass mug and add the sugar.
Pour in the hot coffee and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the brennivín and stir once.
Float lightly whipped cream over the back of a spoon.
Drink through the cream without stirring.

originStory: Icelandic coffee is a café and home serve of strong coffee with a measure of brennivín, the caraway-flavoured spirit of Iceland, topped with cream in the manner of Irish coffee, with no creator or date on record.

name: Cà Phê Trứng Rum
description: Hanoi egg coffee with rum stirred through — egg yolk whipped with condensed milk into a meringue that sits on the coffee like a custard.
glassware: Small glass in a bowl of hot water
funFact: Egg coffee was invented in 1946 when a milk shortage in Hanoi led a Metropole bartender to whip egg yolk as a substitute; the café his family still runs serves it in glasses set in hot water.

steps: Brew strong Vietnamese coffee with a phin filter and keep it hot.
Whisk the egg yolk with the condensed milk until pale, thick and roughly tripled in volume.
Stir the rum into the hot coffee in a small glass.
Spoon the egg foam over the top so it floats as a distinct layer.
Stand the glass in a bowl of hot water and serve with a small spoon.

originStory: Hanoi's egg coffee, the base of this drink, is usually credited to Nguyen Van Giang, a bartender at the Metropole hotel, who whipped egg yolk with sugar and condensed milk as a stand-in for fresh milk during a milk shortage in the late forties. He later opened his own café, Cafe Giang, which his family still runs and where the coffee is served in cups set in hot water to keep it warm. Stirring in dark rum is a modern bar addition, with no recorded creator.

name: Nam Manao Soda
description: Thai rum with fresh lime soda and a pinch of salt — the format street vendors have sold for decades, given a measure of Sangsom.
funFact: The salt is not optional in Thai citrus drinks — it suppresses bitterness and lifts sweetness, which is why nam manao tastes rounder than a plain lime soda.

steps: Stir the lime juice, sugar syrup and salt together until the salt dissolves.
Fill a tall glass with ice and add the rum.
Pour in the lime mixture.
Top with cold soda water and stir once.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

originStory: Nam manao soda, fresh lime juice with sugar, a pinch of salt and soda water, is an everyday Thai street drink, and the version lengthened with Thai rum has no recorded creator or date.

name: Palm Wine Punch
description: Fresh palm wine lengthened with citrus, ginger and a little gin — the village drink dressed for a Lagos party.
funFact: Palm wine ferments so fast that it changes character between morning and evening, which is why punches built on it are mixed to order rather than made ahead.

steps: Stir the ginger juice, lime juice and honey syrup together in a jug.
Add the gin and stir again.
Pour in the fresh palm wine last and stir gently once.
Serve over ice, immediately — it keeps fermenting in the glass.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

originStory: Palm Wine Punch lengthens West African palm wine, the fermented sap of the palm, with gin, ginger, lime and honey, a modern party style of Nigeria's cities with no recorded creator or date.

name: Tej Spritz
description: Ethiopian honey wine lengthened with soda and citrus — the berele flask reimagined for a rooftop bar.
funFact: Gesho, the buckthorn that bitters tej, plays the same role hops play in beer — which is why tej takes to a spritz format better than most honey wines would.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the tej, lemon juice and honey syrup.
Top with soda water.
Stir once gently to combine.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.

originStory: The Tej Spritz is a modern serve that lengthens tej, the Ethiopian honey wine bittered with gesho leaves, with soda and lemon, and it has no recorded creator or date.

name: Ceylon Arrack Sour
description: Coconut arrack shaken with lime, jaggery and egg white — the island's spirit given the sour treatment.
funFact: Jaggery — unrefined palm sugar — is the traditional sweetener here rather than cane sugar, and it gives the drink a smoky, caramel depth that simple syrup cannot.

steps: Dry-shake the arrack, lime juice, jaggery syrup and egg white for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dash the bitters over the foam.
Serve immediately.

originStory: The Ceylon Arrack Sour gives Sri Lanka's coconut-sap spirit the classic sour treatment, sweetened with jaggery, a modern serve of Colombo's bars with no recorded creator or date.

name: Chacha Sour
description: Georgian grape marc spirit with lemon, honey and tarragon — the Caucasus answer to a pisco sour.
funFact: Tarragon is a defining Georgian flavour, most famously in the bright green tarkhuna soda, and it turns up in the country's modern bar scene as readily as mint does elsewhere.

steps: Press two tarragon sprigs gently in the shaker with the honey syrup.
Add the chacha, lemon juice and ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a fresh tarragon sprig.

originStory: The Chacha Sour treats Georgia's grape spirit as a sour with lemon and honey and adds tarragon, a defining Georgian flavour, as a modern serve of Tbilisi's bars with no recorded creator or date.

name: Moroccan Mint Cooler
description: Strong green tea with spearmint, sugar and a measure of fig brandy, served long over ice for the heat of the afternoon.
funFact: Moroccan mint tea is poured from a height to aerate it and build a foam head, a technique the cold version keeps purely because the tea tastes flat without it.

steps: Brew strong green tea with a generous handful of spearmint and cool it completely.
Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the fig brandy, sugar syrup and lemon juice.
Top with the cold mint tea, pouring from a height to aerate it.
Garnish with a large mint sprig.

originStory: The Moroccan Mint Cooler is a contemporary bar serve that chills sweet Moroccan mint tea and adds boukha, the fig spirit of neighbouring Tunisia, and no creator or date is on record.

name: Masala Chai Toddy
description: Spiced milk tea with dark rum stirred in — the roadside chai format given a winter measure.
funFact: Indian chai is boiled rather than steeped — tea, milk, sugar and spice all go into the pan together, which is why it tastes nothing like tea with milk added afterwards.

steps: Boil the water with the ginger, cardamom and sugar for two minutes.
Add the tea leaves and boil for another minute.
Pour in the milk and bring back to a boil, then simmer briefly.
Strain into a glass and stir in the rum off the heat.
Serve very hot.

originStory: The Masala Chai Toddy stirs dark rum into Indian masala chai, black tea boiled with milk and spices such as cardamom and ginger, a modern winter serve with no recorded creator or date.

name: Caju Amigo
description: Cachaça and cashew fruit juice — a two-ingredient northeastern staple made from the fruit the cashew nut hangs beneath.
funFact: The cashew nut grows on the outside of the cashew apple, a soft astringent fruit that is too perishable to export — which is why almost nobody outside Brazil has tasted its juice.

steps: Combine the cachaça and cashew juice in a small glass.
Stir briefly to combine.
Serve at room temperature, or over a single ice cube if the day is hot.
Drink in one or two mouthfuls, as a between-meal pick-me-up.

originStory: Caju Amigo, friendly cashew, is a northeastern Brazilian pairing of cachaça with the juice of the cashew apple, a bar custom rather than a recorded invention, with no creator or date on record.

name: Vermut Torrontés
description: Argentine vermouth over ice with soda and an orange slice — the aperitivo hour that Italian immigrants brought and Argentina kept.
funFact: Argentina's vermouth tradition arrived with mass Italian immigration and nearly disappeared in the twentieth century; a wave of small Mendoza producers rebuilt it from the 2010s onward.

steps: Fill a tumbler with ice.
Pour in the cold vermouth.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice and skewered olives.
Serve with something salty alongside.

originStory: The Vermut Torrontés is a modern Argentine serve of local vermouth over ice with soda and orange in the manner of the Buenos Aires vermú hour, its name pointing to the aromatic white Torrontés grape, and no creator or date is on record.

name: Averna
description: Sicily's best-known amaro, made in Caltanissetta to a recipe a Benedictine abbey gave the Averna family in 1868. Softer and more caramelised than the northern amari, with orange peel and liquorice doing most of the work.
funFact: The monks of the Abbazia di Santo Spirito handed the recipe to Salvatore Averna as thanks for his patronage, and the abbey still appears on the label.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over a large cube with an orange twist. It is sweet enough to take ice without collapsing, and it is the friendliest entry point into Italian amari for anyone who finds Fernet punishing.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit infused with herbs, roots and citrus peel, then sweetened with caramel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Bitter orange, lemon peel, liquorice root, juniper, rosemary, myrtle

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and infused, never redistilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested before bottling; caramel added for colour and body

composition.process: The sugar load is high by amaro standards, which is exactly why it reads as dessert rather than medicine.

originStory: In 1868 Salvatore Averna, a Caltanissetta justice of the peace from a family of drapers, began producing an amaro for guests at his home, using a herbal infusion whose recipe Fra Girolamo, prior of the Abbey of Santo Spirito, had given him in 1859 as a token of gratitude. His son Francesco built the family business, King Umberto I honoured him for the amaro in 1895, and in 1912 the company was authorised to carry the royal crest on its labels.

name: Amaro Montenegro
description: Forty botanicals from Bologna, built around orange and vanilla rather than bitter root. Named for a Montenegrin princess who married into the Italian royal family, and the least aggressive amaro on most back bars.
funFact: The blend is built from six separate infusions kept apart until the final marriage, and one botanical is known internally only as the secret ingredient.

serve.how: Over a large cube with an orange wedge, which is how Bologna drinks it. It also does well long with tonic. Low enough in bitterness to work before dinner as easily as after.

composition.summary: Forty botanicals in six separate infusions, blended and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Sweet and bitter orange, coriander, marjoram, nutmeg, vanilla, artemisia

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Botanicals infused separately, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested six months before bottling

composition.process: Keeping the infusions apart until the end lets the blender adjust the balance year to year.

originStory: Stanislao Cobianchi created this Bologna amaro in 1885 and first sold it as Elisir Lungavita. In 1896 he renamed it Amaro Montenegro in honour of Princess Elena of Montenegro, who married Crown Prince Victor Emmanuel, later King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy, that year. Its proprietary blend of forty botanicals includes orange peel, vanilla and eucalyptus, and it is still produced near Bologna, at San Lazzaro di Savena.

name: Ramazzotti
description: Milan's amaro since 1815, invented by a herbalist who sold it beside the opera house as a coffee substitute. Thirty-three botanicals, with orange and star anise loudest, and the bitterness pitched squarely in the middle.
funFact: Ausano Ramazzotti opened a bar next to Milan's opera house specifically so audiences could drink it in the intervals.

serve.how: Neat after eating, or with soda and a lemon twist as a lighter aperitif. The anise makes it a natural substitute for sweet vermouth in a Boulevardier if you want the drink drier and more herbal.

composition.summary: Thirty-three botanicals infused in neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Bitter orange, star anise, cardamom, myrrh, gentian, liquorice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused, blended, sweetened

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Short rest before bottling

composition.process: Star anise rather than wormwood is what keeps it sweet-spiced instead of medicinal.

originStory: Ausano Ramazzotti created his amaro in Milan in 1815, macerating at least thirty-three roots and herbs, and it is often described as the first Italian aperitif not based on wine.
