In 1848 he opened a bar on Via Santa Margherita, a few steps from La Scala, where it could be served by the glass to the city's theatregoers. Pernod Ricard acquired the company in 1985, and production moved from Lainate to Canelli in Piedmont in 1994.

name: Braulio
description: An alpine amaro from Bormio in the Valtellina, made with mountain botanicals and aged in Slavonian oak. Pine, mint and gentian rather than citrus — it tastes like the altitude it comes from.
funFact: Created in 1875 by a pharmacist in a village at 1,200 metres, and still aged in the same cellars beneath the original shop.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after a heavy alpine meal. Locals also pour it over ice with a twist of lemon in summer. The Riserva, aged longer in oak, is worth the premium and drinks almost like a herbal whisky.

composition.summary: Alpine herbs macerated in spirit and matured in Slavonian oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit and mountain water

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, wormwood, yarrow, juniper, mountain pine

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Roughly two years in Slavonian oak barrels

composition.process: Oak ageing is unusual for an amaro at this strength and is what rounds off the pine.

originStory: Braulio has been made in Bormio, in the Valtellina, since 1875, from a recipe of alpine herbs, roots and berries credited to the local pharmacist Francesco Peloni. It takes its name from Monte Braulio and the Braulio valley above the town, where its herbs were traditionally gathered, and it is still produced and aged in oak casks in Bormio.

name: Amaro Nonino Quintessentia
description: Friuli's amaro, built on aged grappa rather than neutral spirit, which puts it in a class of its own. Lighter, brighter and more expensive than its peers, and the reason a Paper Plane tastes the way it does.
funFact: The Nonino family began distilling single-varietal grappa in 1973, a move that dragged the whole grappa category upmarket almost single-handedly.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature so the grappa base shows. In cocktails it is the modifier in a Paper Plane, split evenly with bourbon, Aperol and lemon. Do not bury it under ice; the barrel character disappears.

composition.summary: Herbs and citrus infused into barrel-aged grappa.

components.label: Base
components.detail: ÙE grape distillate and aged grappa

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Bitter orange, gentian, rhubarb, quassia, liquorice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused into aged spirit, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: The grappa base is barrel-aged before infusion

composition.process: Using aged grappa rather than neutral alcohol is the whole point and the whole cost.

originStory: The Nonino family has distilled in Friuli since 1897, when Orazio Nonino set up a still at Ronchi di Percoto. The firm's turning point came in 1973, when Benito and Giannola Nonino released the first commercial grappa made from a single grape variety, Picolit, a move that helped lift grappa's reputation across Italy. Their amaro, Quintessentia, is built on aged grappa rather than neutral spirit, and its role in Sam Ross's Paper Plane made it a bartender's staple far beyond Italy.

name: Meletti
description: A Marche amaro with saffron and violet in the blend, noticeably sweeter and more floral than its neighbours, in a bottle with a bulbous glass stopper that turns up in every Italian grandmother's cabinet.
funFact: Silvio Meletti built the recipe in the 1870s and the company also makes an anisette so well regarded that locals drink it in coffee as anisetta.

serve.how: Neat after dinner or over ice with an orange slice. It is sweet, so it works better as a dessert amaro than an aperitif, and it makes an excellent float on a coffee.

composition.summary: Herbs, saffron and citrus infused and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Saffron, violet, gentian, anise, citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested before bottling

composition.process: Saffron is expensive enough that its presence sets the price of the bottle.

originStory: The Meletti firm of Ascoli Piceno dates from 1870, when Silvio Meletti began producing anisetta, the anise liqueur for which the family is still best known in the Marche. The company's amaro followed, with a blend that includes saffron and violet, and Caffè Meletti, the family's café on Ascoli's Piazza del Popolo, became one of the historic cafés of central Italy. Locals still take the anisetta in their coffee.

name: Sfumato Rabarbaro
description: Chinese rhubarb root smoked over open fire, then infused into an alpine amaro. Tastes of tar, campfire and bitter earth — the most divisive bottle in most bar backbars, and indispensable once you like it.
funFact: The rhubarb is grown in China, dried, then smoked in the Italian Alps — a supply chain that predates the amaro itself by centuries via the Silk Road.

serve.how: Cold and neat in a small pour, or a bar spoon in a Manhattan or Negroni where it adds smoke without peat. A little goes a very long way; treat it as a seasoning as much as a drink.

composition.summary: Smoked rhubarb root and alpine botanicals infused in spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Fire-smoked Chinese rhubarb root, alpine herbs, gentian

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then blended and lightly sweetened

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 20%, low for the intensity

composition.process: Smoking the root over open flame is the single step that makes it unlike any other amaro.

originStory: Sfumato Rabarbaro comes from Cappelletti, a long-established family distillery in Aldeno, in Trentino. It belongs to the rabarbaro family of Italian amari built on rhubarb root, and the smoky character of its Chinese rhubarb gives it its name: sfumato means smoky, and is also the painter's term for soft, hazy shading.

name: Cardamaro
description: A Piedmontese amaro built on wine rather than spirit, flavoured with cardoon and blessed thistle and aged in oak. At 17% it is barely stronger than vermouth, and it drinks like an autumnal sherry with a bitter edge.
funFact: Cardoon is a thistle relative of the artichoke, which puts Cardamaro in the same botanical family as Cynar despite tasting nothing like it.

serve.how: Chilled and neat as an aperitif, or over ice with soda. Because the base is wine it works beautifully in place of sweet vermouth in low-alcohol cocktails, and it should be refrigerated once open.

composition.summary: Moscato wine infused with cardoon and thistle, then oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Moscato wine, lightly fortified

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Cardoon, blessed thistle, other herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused into wine, not distilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Around six months in oak

composition.process: A wine base means it oxidises like wine — keep it cold and finish it within a month or two.

originStory: Cardamaro is made in Canelli, in the Asti wine country of Piedmont, by the long-established Bosca family firm. It is a vino amaro, a bitter built on wine rather than spirit, flavoured with cardoon and blessed thistle and rested in oak. Cardoon is a thistle and a close relative of the artichoke, which puts Cardamaro in the same botanical family as Cynar, though the two taste quite different.

name: Amaro Lucano
description: Made in Basilicata since 1894 by a pastry chef who blended thirty herbs in the back of his shop. Balanced and mid-weight, and for decades the house amaro of the Italian royal family.
funFact: Pasquale Vena was a confectioner, not a distiller, which is often cited as the reason the sugar balance is so precise.

serve.how: Neat after dinner or over ice. It sits between Averna's sweetness and Ramazzotti's spice, which makes it the safest pour when you do not know your guest's taste in amari.

composition.summary: About thirty botanicals infused in neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Bitter orange, wormwood, angelica, elder, gentian

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested before bottling

composition.process: The recipe has stayed inside the Vena family for four generations.

originStory: Pasquale Vena, a pastry chef, created Amaro Lucano in 1894 in Pisticci, in Basilicata, blending more than thirty herbs, and the name comes from Lucania, the ancient name for the region. By around 1900 the Vena family had become official suppliers to the House of Savoy. After the Second World War his sons Leonardo and Giuseppe turned the workshop into a factory, and production later moved to a new plant at Pisticci Scalo.

name: Amaro del Capo
description: Calabria's amaro, made with twenty-nine local herbs and drunk straight from the freezer. Sweeter and more citrus-driven than the northern styles, and enormously popular across southern Italy.
funFact: There is a chilli version, made with Calabrian peperoncino, which is exactly as aggressive as that sounds.

serve.how: The bottle lives in the freezer and the glass should too. It pours thick and cold, which mutes the sugar and lets the liquorice and mint through. Calabrians consider room-temperature service a mistake.

composition.summary: Twenty-nine Calabrian botanicals infused in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Liquorice, bitter orange, mandarin, mint, juniper, chamomile

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

composition.process: Freezer service is not a garnish of a tradition — the viscosity at −20°C is part of the intended texture.

originStory: Amaro del Capo comes from the Caffo family: in 1915 Giuseppe Caffo, a master distiller, founded a distillery at Santa Venerina, on the slopes of Etna, working at first with grape marc and wine by-products. His sons moved the business to Limbadi, in the Calabrian province of Vibo Valentia, and in 1965 the house created Vecchio Amaro del Capo from twenty-nine Calabrian herbs, flowers, fruits and roots, which became its flagship. There is also a version made with Calabrian chilli.

name: Zucca Rabarbaro
description: A Milanese rhubarb amaro from 1845, dark and gently smoky, and the original aperitivo of the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele. Drier than most amari and closer to a bitter than a digestive.
funFact: Zucca held a royal warrant from the House of Savoy and its bar in the Galleria was the fashionable place to be seen in nineteenth-century Milan.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and a lemon twist as an aperitif, which is how Milan drank it for a century. Neat it is dry and faintly smoky; it also improves a Negroni if you swap it for part of the Campari.

composition.summary: Chinese rhubarb root and cardamom infused in spirit and lightly sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Chinese rhubarb root, cardamom, bitter orange

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 16%, low even for an aperitivo

composition.process: Rhubarb root gives the earthy, faintly smoky note that the whole rabarbaro category is built on.

originStory: Rabarbaro Zucca takes its name from Ettore Zucca, who created it in Milan in 1845 by steeping rhubarb root with bitter orange peel, cardamom and other aromatics, so the name has nothing to do with zucca, the pumpkin. It became one of the classic aperitivi of Milan. From the mid-1990s until 2012 its name replaced Camparino on the sign of the historic café at the entrance to the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, and the brand now belongs to ILLVA Saronno.

name: China Martini
description: A cinchona-bark amaro from Turin, pronounced kee-na and named for the quinine tree rather than the country. Bitter, cocoa-toned, and the ancestor of most quinine liqueurs on the shelf.
funFact: Cinchona bark was the original source of quinine, which is why so many nineteenth-century bitters were marketed openly as anti-malarial tonics.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or the Piedmontese winter serve: warmed with a strip of lemon peel. It also works stirred into coffee, where the cocoa note in the bark meets the roast.

composition.summary: Cinchona bark and botanicals infused in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Cinchona calisaya bark, bitter orange, spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused, then sweetened and rested

composition.process: Calisaya bark is the same species that flavours tonic water, at far higher concentration.

originStory: China Martini comes from Martini & Rossi, the Turin vermouth house, and belongs to the china family of Italian bitters, named not for the country but for cinchona bark, china calissaia in Italian, the source of quinine, and pronounced kee-na. It is made from the bark with a mixture of aromatic herbs and essences. Its cinchona recalls how many nineteenth-century bitters were first sold as tonics rather than as drinks.

name: Cocchi Americano
description: A quinine-flavoured aromatised wine from Piedmont, bitter-sweet and citrus-driven. It is the closest thing available to Kina Lillet, which means it is what a Vesper is supposed to be made with.
funFact: Lillet reformulated in 1986 and dropped most of its quinine, which is why bartenders reaching for a period-correct Vesper use this instead.

serve.how: Cold with ice and a slice of orange as an aperitif. In cocktails it is the third of a Vesper, the Lillet stand-in in a Corpse Reviver No. 2, and the white half of a White Negroni. Refrigerate after opening.

composition.summary: Moscato d'Asti wine aromatised with cinchona and botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Moscato d'Asti wine

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Cinchona bark, gentian, bitter orange peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused into wine and lightly fortified

composition.process: Because it is wine-based it oxidises; a bottle left warm for a month is a different drink.

originStory: Giulio Cocchi, a Florentine pastry maker, settled in Asti in 1891 and began making aromatised wines, and by the turn of the century his Barolo Chinato and Aperitivo Americano were exported to London, New York, Africa and South America. The name is usually traced to amaro, bitter, rather than to America. After Lillet reformulated Kina Lillet in 1986 and softened its quinine, bartenders adopted Cocchi Americano as the nearest match for a period Vesper.

name: Bonal Gentiane-Quina
description: A Savoyard aperitif of gentian, cinchona and alpine herbs on a mistelle base, made since 1865 and advertised as the opener of the appetite. Deep, wine-dark and more bitter than it looks.
funFact: It was created by a monk at the Grande Chartreuse and marketed with the slogan ouvre l'appétit — which is why French bars still pour it before a meal rather than after.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or over ice with a lemon twist. It substitutes well for sweet vermouth in a Manhattan or Boulevardier, bringing gentian bitterness where vermouth brings sweetness.

composition.summary: Mistelle base infused with gentian root and cinchona bark.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Mistelle — grape must stopped with spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian root, cinchona bark, alpine herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated into the mistelle, then aged

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak casks before bottling

composition.process: Both signature botanicals are roots and barks rather than leaves, which is why the bitterness is so deep and slow.

originStory: Bonal was created in 1865 by Hippolyte Bonal, who is said to have been raised and trained at the Grande Chartreuse monastery and to have served as the abbey's doctor before settling as a pharmacist in nearby Saint-Laurent-du-Pont. Drawing on the gentian, cinchona and herbs of the Chartreuse mountains, he made a fortified aperitif and sold it with the promise ouvre l'appétit, the opener of the appetite.

name: Byrrh
description: A French quinquina from Roussillon, sold from 1866 as a health tonic through pharmacies because a medicinal label attracted less tax than an alcoholic one. Red wine, mistelle and cinchona, aged in enormous oak vats.
funFact: The Thuir cellars hold the largest oak vat in the world, at over a million litres, built in 1950 and still in use.

serve.how: Cold with ice and an orange slice, as a French café aperitif. It swaps neatly for sweet vermouth in a Manhattan and makes an excellent low-strength highball with soda.

composition.summary: Red wine and mistelle aromatised with cinchona and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Red wine from Roussillon plus mistelle

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Cinchona bark, coffee, cocoa, bitter orange

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, blended, fortified

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Up to three years in oak foudres

composition.process: Selling it through pharmacies as a tonic was a deliberate tax strategy, and it worked for decades.

originStory: Byrrh was created in 1866 in Thuir, in Roussillon, by the brothers Pallade and Simon Violet, travelling drapers turned wine merchants, who blended local wine and mistelle with cinchona and sold it as a tonic wine, at first through pharmacies. By tradition the name comes from the letters B, Y, R, R and H on a colour chart for the fabrics they sold, and it was registered as a trademark in 1873. Since 1950 the Thuir cellars have held an oak vat of about a million litres, often called the largest in the world.

name: Dubonnet
description: Created in 1846 to persuade French Foreign Legionnaires in North Africa to take their quinine, by burying the bitterness in sweet fortified wine. It worked, and it outlived the empire that commissioned it.
funFact: Queen Elizabeth II reportedly drank it with gin and a slice of lemon before lunch, a combination the household referred to simply as the usual.

serve.how: Cold with ice and lemon, or the royal serve: two parts Dubonnet to one part gin over ice. It is sweet and low in strength, so it suits an afternoon better than an evening.

composition.summary: Fortified wine aromatised with cinchona, herbs and spices.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fortified wine

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Cinchona bark, blackcurrant, cocoa, herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused into wine and fortified

composition.process: Sweetening quinine into palatability was a genuine public-health problem in the 1840s, and this was the commercial answer.

originStory: By the usual account, in 1846 the French government sought a way to make quinine palatable to Foreign Legionnaires in North Africa, where malaria was rife, and Joseph Dubonnet, a Paris wine merchant and chemist, answered with a sweet fortified wine infused with cinchona bark, herbs and spices. The aperitif outgrew its medicinal purpose and became a fixture of French cafés. In Britain it found royal admirers: Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother was famously fond of Dubonnet with gin, a taste Elizabeth II was widely reported to share.

name: Amer Picon
description: A bitter orange aperitif invented by a French soldier in Algeria in 1837, again as a quinine delivery system. Reformulated and weakened over the years, and the ghost that haunts a Picon Bière or a Brooklyn cocktail.
funFact: Gaétan Picon dropped it from 39% to 21% and later 18%, which is why old cocktail recipes calling for it never quite work with a modern bottle.

serve.how: The French serve is Picon Bière — a measure in the bottom of a glass of blonde beer, which sounds wrong and is excellent. In cocktails it belongs in a Brooklyn and a Liberal, though modern bottlings need a heavier hand than the original recipes assumed.

composition.summary: Bitter orange, gentian and cinchona infused and sweetened with caramel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit and water

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Dried bitter orange peel, gentian root, cinchona bark

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Oranges macerated and distilled, then blended with the root infusions

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 18%, down from an original 39%

composition.process: It is not officially exported to many markets, which is why bar substitutes for it are a whole cottage industry.

originStory: Gaétan Picon, a distiller trained in Provence who served with the French army in Algeria, created his bitter orange aperitif there in 1837, by the usual account, first calling it Amer Africain. He went on to open distilleries at Philippeville, Constantine, Bône and Algiers, and a bronze medal at the London exhibition of 1862 helped spread the name. In 1872 he returned to France and founded the Marseille factory, and Picon became a staple of French bars, best known stirred into beer as a Picon bière.

name: Salers
description: A gentian aperitif from the Auvergne, made since 1885 from wild roots dug on volcanic uplands. Paler, drier and more austere than Suze, and the one gentian purists tend to reach for.
funFact: The roots are harvested by hand with a two-pronged fork called a fourche du diable, from plants that have grown for at least twenty years.

serve.how: Over ice with a splash of soda or tonic, which is the Auvergne café serve. It is drier than Suze and less sweet than Aveze, so it is the best of the three in a White Negroni.

composition.summary: Wild gentian root macerated and distilled, then lightly sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentiana lutea root, wild-harvested in the Massif Central

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Part macerated, part distilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in vats before bottling

composition.process: Twenty years of root growth per harvest is why gentian aperitifs have never been cheap.

originStory: Salers dates from 1885, when Alfred Labounoux began making a gentian liqueur at Montaignac-Saint-Hippolyte, in Corrèze, and named it after Salers, the old town of the Cantal uplands where wild gentian grows. It is often described as the oldest gentian aperitif still made in France. In 2006 the brand joined the Védrenne family group and moved to Turenne, also in Corrèze, where it is now made under the Distillerie des Terres Rouges name.

name: Avèze
description: The third of the French gentian aperitifs, from the Cantal, sweeter and rounder than Salers and less citrus-forward than Suze. Made from roots dug in the volcanic pastures of the Massif Central.
funFact: All three major gentian aperitifs come from within a hundred kilometres of each other, because that is where the wild plant grows densely enough to harvest.

serve.how: Over ice with tonic or soda, or with cassis as an Auvergnat kir. Its extra sweetness makes it the gentler introduction to gentian for anyone who has bounced off Suze.

composition.summary: Gentian root macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Wild yellow gentian root from the Cantal

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, blended, sweetened

composition.process: More sugar and less citrus than Suze, which is the whole difference between the two.

originStory: Avèze traces back to 1929, when Émile Refouvelet, who kept a delicatessen at Riom-ès-Montagnes, in the Cantal, began selling a gentian aperitif of his own making in his shop. It was sold for years under the name Auvergne before taking the Avèze name in the 1960s. It is made from the roots of yellow gentian, which grows wild in the volcanic uplands of the Massif Central around the town.

name: Peychaud's Bitters
description: Created by a Creole apothecary in 1830s New Orleans, lighter and more floral than Angostura, with anise and cherry where Angostura has clove. Without it a Sazerac is not a Sazerac.
funFact: Antoine Amédée Peychaud served his tonic in a double-ended egg cup called a coquetier, which is one of the more plausible origin stories for the word cocktail.

serve.glass: Used as a seasoning, not poured
serve.how: Three or four dashes in a Sazerac, alongside rye and absinthe. It is softer than Angostura and not a like-for-like substitute — using one where the recipe wants the other changes the drink noticeably.

composition.summary: A concentrated botanical tincture, anise-forward, on a high-proof base.

components.label: Base
components.detail: High-strength neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Anise, gentian, cherry notes; the full recipe is unpublished

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated to a concentrate

composition.process: The bright red colour is added and has no bearing on the flavour.

originStory: Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Creole apothecary from Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, made his aromatic bitters in New Orleans; popular accounts date them to the 1830s, while other sources place them between 1849 and 1857. They became the defining ingredient of the city's Sazerac, and the Sazerac Company makes them today. A popular story says Peychaud served brandy and bitters in an egg cup called a coquetier and that the word cocktail grew from it, but the word was in print before his drinks were, so the tale is treated as legend.

name: Orange Bitters
description: Dried bitter orange peel, cardamom and caraway in a concentrated tincture. It vanished almost entirely after Prohibition and came back only in the 2000s, which is why a century of Martini recipes read strangely without it.
funFact: Pre-Prohibition Martini recipes almost universally called for orange bitters; the drink we now think of as classic is a version that lost an ingredient by accident.

serve.how: A dash or two in a Martini, a Manhattan or an Old Fashioned. It lifts and defines rather than adding obvious flavour — the effect is much more noticeable by its absence when you go back.

composition.summary: Bitter orange peel and spice macerated to a concentrate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: High-strength neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Seville orange peel, cardamom, caraway, coriander, gentian

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then strained and blended

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 28–43% depending on maker

composition.process: Seville peel dried hard carries far more bitter oil than fresh sweet orange.

originStory: Orange bitters, a tincture built on dried bitter orange peel with spices such as cardamom and caraway, were a standard bottle in nineteenth-century bars on both sides of the Atlantic and appear throughout early Martini recipes. After Prohibition they almost disappeared, kept alive in America largely by Fee Brothers of Rochester. Their comeback came when the writer and bartender Gary Regan developed Regans' Orange Bitters No. 6 with the Sazerac Company, just as the classic cocktail revival took hold.

name: Malört
description: A wormwood liqueur brought to Chicago by a Swedish immigrant, and the city's initiation ritual. Relentlessly, uncompromisingly bitter, with a finish that people describe using words like grapefruit rind and burnt plastic.
funFact: Carl Jeppson sold it through Prohibition as a medicinal tonic, reportedly because agents who tasted it accepted immediately that nobody would drink it for pleasure.

serve.how: One shot, and the tradition is to watch the face of whoever is drinking it for the first time. Chicagoans chase it with cheap lager. Bartenders have found genuine uses for a small amount in cocktails, where the bitterness cuts sweetness sharply.

composition.summary: Wormwood macerated in neutral spirit, barely sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Wormwood, the dominant and near-only flavour

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, minimal sweetening

composition.process: It belongs to the Swedish besk tradition, of which it is the most aggressive surviving example.

originStory: Malört is Swedish for wormwood, and Chicago's version follows the Swedish habit of wormwood-flavoured brännvin. Carl Jeppson, a Swedish immigrant, made it in Chicago and during Prohibition sold it door to door as a medicine, and it was officially introduced in the city in 1933, after repeal. The lawyer George Brode later acquired the formula, and its famously harsh taste turned Jeppson's Malört into a Chicago institution and something close to a civic drink.

name: Fernet
description: Not one brand but the bitterest class of amaro: myrrh, saffron, gentian and menthol, minimally sweetened. A category invented in 1840s Milan as a stomach remedy and adopted wholesale by Argentina and San Francisco.
funFact: San Francisco drinks a wildly disproportionate share of the world's fernet, a habit usually traced to the city's Italian community and its bartending scene.

serve.how: Neat after a heavy meal, which is the intended use. Argentina drinks it long with cola in roughly a one-to-three ratio. Bartenders take it as a shot with ginger beer alongside, a pairing known as a handshake.

composition.summary: Bitter herbs and roots macerated in spirit with almost no sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Myrrh, saffron, gentian, rhubarb, chamomile, peppermint

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, blended, minimally sweetened

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often oak-rested for a year or more

composition.process: The low sugar is what defines the class — a sweeter version stops being a fernet.

originStory: Fernet is the bitterest family of Italian amari, and its archetype, Fernet-Branca, was created in Milan in 1845 by Bernardino Branca, who sold it as a stomach tonic. Where the word fernet comes from is uncertain, and the stories of a doctor named Fernet are not documented. Italian emigrants carried the style to Argentina, where fernet with cola became a national institution, and in San Francisco it became a bartenders' calling card.

name: Kümmerling
description: A German herbal bitter sold almost exclusively in small single-serve bottles, like Underberg but sweeter and more anise-driven. A fixture of German festivals and petrol-station counters alike.
funFact: Hugo Kümmerling launched it in 1938 and the small-bottle format was chosen so it could be sold as a single measure rather than by the bottle.

serve.how: Cold, in one go, after eating. It is sweeter and less punishing than Underberg, which is why it has a following among people who find that one too austere.

composition.summary: Herbs and spices macerated in neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Anise, liquorice, gentian and a mix of herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

composition.process: The single-serve format is the product design, exactly as with Underberg.

originStory: Hugo Kümmerling began developing a herbal liqueur in 1921 in Deesbach, in the Thuringian Forest, and settled on its secret formula in 1938. After the war the business left Thuringia, moving to Coburg in Bavaria in 1949 and then to Bodenheim, near Mainz, in 1963, and in the 1950s his son-in-law Johannes Persch built up its industrial production and marketing. The tiny single-measure bottle became its trademark.

name: Killepitsch
description: A Düsseldorf herbal liqueur of ninety-eight herbs, berries and fruits, made to a recipe devised in an air-raid shelter during the war. Deep red, sweet, and drunk in Altstadt bars by the thousand.
funFact: The name comes from Rhineland dialect roughly meaning to knock back and gasp, and the recipe was written down by two friends sheltering from bombing in 1944.

serve.how: Cold and neat, in one, alongside a glass of Altbier — the standard Düsseldorf order. Sweeter and fruitier than Jägermeister, and considerably stronger at 42%.

composition.summary: Ninety-eight herbs, fruits and berries macerated and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: 98 herbs, berries and fruits

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for weeks, then blended

composition.process: Fruit and berry content is what separates it from the root-driven German bitters.

originStory: Killepitsch comes from the Busch family of Düsseldorf. Family tradition says its name was born in an air-raid shelter during the Second World War, in a conversation between Willi Busch and his friend Hans Müller-Schlösser, author of the comedy Schneider Wibbel, about what they would do if they came out alive. It was first served to the public in 1955, through the small window of the family's Et Kabüffke tasting room in the old town, and its recipe of 98 herb, berry and fruit essences is still a family secret.

name: Blutwurz
description: A Bavarian Forest liqueur made from tormentil root, which stains the liquid blood red and gives it a dry, tannic bitterness. Sold in the region as a digestive and a folk remedy in equal measure.
funFact: Tormentil root was used against dysentery for centuries, which is where both the medicinal reputation and the astringency come from.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass after a heavy meal. At 50% it demands slow drinking. In the Bavarian Forest it is offered to guests almost automatically and refusing takes some doing.

composition.summary: Tormentil root macerated in high-strength spirit with herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit at high strength

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Tormentil (Potentilla erecta) root, plus herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated; colour comes from the root

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 50%

composition.process: The tannin content is high enough that it dries the mouth like strong tea.

originStory: Blutwurz, blood root, is named for tormentil, Potentilla erecta, whose cut rhizome turns red and colours the liqueur, a plant with a long history in central European folk medicine. The roots are chopped and macerated with other herbs and spices, giving a strong, dry and astringent spirit that the Bavarian Forest has made its own. A prominent name is Penninger of Hauzenberg, a family distillery founded early in the twentieth century.

name: Genziana
description: An Abruzzese liqueur made by steeping gentian root in wine or spirit, produced at farmhouse scale across the Apennines. Rougher and more rustic than the French gentian aperitifs, and usually homemade.
funFact: Gentian harvesting is regulated across the Apennines, and in some Italian regions digging wild roots requires a permit.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal, in the small pours Abruzzese households offer. Wine-based versions are lower in strength and closer to a bitter vermouth; spirit-based ones are sharper.

composition.summary: Gentian root macerated in wine or neutral spirit and lightly sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: White wine or neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Wild gentian root from the Apennines

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for weeks

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 16–35% depending on base

composition.process: Almost all of it is made domestically, so no two bottles from different families match.

originStory: Genziana is the gentian-root liqueur of the Abruzzo, made by steeping the roots in wine or spirit to farmhouse recipes across the Apennines, a tradition with no single recorded origin.

name: Fernet Vallet
description: A Mexican fernet made to a recipe a French distiller brought to Veracruz in the 1880s. Sweeter and more cinnamon-driven than the Italian style, and long a fixture of cantinas in the south.
funFact: Henri Vallet emigrated from France, set up in Veracruz, and built a fernet that Mexico kept making long after the Italian originals had come to dominate elsewhere.

serve.how: Neat after a meal, or with cola in the Argentine manner. Its extra sweetness and cinnamon make it an easier fernet than Branca, and it works well in a Toronto or a Hanky Panky.

composition.summary: Bitter herbs and spice macerated in spirit, sweeter than the Italian style.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Myrrh, cinnamon, cardamom, gentian, mint

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

composition.process: Higher strength and a heavier hand with cinnamon are the two things that mark it out from Milanese fernet.

originStory: Henri Vallet, a French entrepreneur who came to Mexico in the time of Emperor Maximilian, founded his liqueur company in Mexico City in 1882, though some accounts give a later date, bringing with him the recipes and methods of French bitters. He stayed on after the empire fell, and his Fernet-Vallet and Amargo Vallet became fixtures of Mexican bar culture. The company says the bitters are still made to his original formulas, giving Mexico a fernet tradition of its own.

name: Amaro Sibilla
description: An intensely bitter amaro from the Sibillini mountains of the Marche, made with honey and mountain herbs to a nineteenth-century recipe. Dark, resinous and closer to a medicine than a digestive.
funFact: The Sibillini mountains are named for a mythical sibyl said to have lived in a cave there, and the amaro's label leans on the legend heavily.

serve.how: Neat in a small pour after a heavy meal. The honey rounds the front but the finish is long and genuinely bitter, so it rewards slow sipping rather than a shot.

composition.summary: Mountain herbs and honey macerated in spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, rhubarb, mountain herbs, honey

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended with honey

composition.process: Honey rather than sugar syrup gives a weight the sweeter commercial amari cannot match.

originStory: Amaro Sibilla comes from the Varnelli family of the Sibillini mountains, whose liqueur business dates from 1868, when Girolamo Varnelli, a herbalist at Cupi di Visso, is said to have devised a bitter remedy for the fevers that struck shepherds on their seasonal migrations. The house describes it as still made the old way, with gentian, cinchona and other plants decocted over a wood fire and sweetened with honey. The Varnelli distillery now works at Muccia, in the province of Macerata.

name: Select Aperitivo
description: Venice's answer to Campari, made since 1920 with thirty botanicals and rhubarb root. It is what a spritz is made with in Venice, and Venetians will correct you firmly if you reach for Aperol instead.
funFact: The Venetian spritz predates Aperol's dominance entirely, and Select was created specifically for it in the year the drink took hold in the city.

serve.how: Three parts prosecco, two parts Select, a splash of soda, over ice, with a green olive rather than an orange slice — that olive is the Venetian marker. More bitter than an Aperol spritz and considerably better.

composition.summary: Thirty botanicals infused in neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Rhubarb root, juniper, bitter orange and 27 others

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Part distilled, part infused, then blended

composition.process: Rhubarb root is the backbone, which is why it lands drier than Aperol despite similar sweetness.

originStory: Select was created in Venice in 1920 by the brothers Mario and Vittorio Pilla, whose liqueur firm, Fratelli Pilla & C., set out to take part in the city's revival after the First World War. In 1954 the brand passed to Distilleria Jean Buton, later absorbed into Gruppo Montenegro, which still makes it to the original recipe. Select became a fixture of the city's bars and the traditional bitter of the Venetian spritz.

name: Cappelletti Aperitivo
description: A wine-based red aperitivo from Trentino, coloured with cochineal as Campari once was. Lower in alcohol and gentler than its Milanese rival, with more fruit and less quinine snap.
funFact: It is still coloured with carmine from cochineal insects, a practice Campari abandoned in 2006 and which makes this bottle unsuitable for vegans.

serve.how: Over ice with soda, or as the red third of a Negroni where its lower strength makes a gentler drink. Because the base is wine, refrigerate it once opened and finish it within a month.

composition.summary: Wine base infused with bitter herbs and citrus.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine, lightly fortified

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Bitter orange, gentian, herbs; cochineal for colour

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused into wine

composition.process: A wine base rather than neutral spirit is what keeps it soft where Campari is sharp.

originStory: The Cappelletti business began in Trento in 1909, founded by Giuseppe Cappelletti, and it is still owned by his family, now producing at Aldeno, south of the city, among vineyards and orchards. Its red aperitivo is built on white wine rather than neutral spirit, which keeps it lower in strength than its Milanese rivals. It is still coloured with carmine from cochineal, a practice Campari abandoned in 2006.

name: Petrus Boonekamp
description: A Dutch-origin bitter now made in Italy, dry and root-driven with almost no sweetness. Boonekamp is a whole nineteenth-century category of stomach bitters, of which this is the surviving standard-bearer.
funFact: Petrus Boonekamp created the style in Leiden in 1777; it became generic enough that a dozen distillers sold their own boonekamp through the 1800s.

serve.how: Neat in a small measure after eating. It is drier than almost anything else in this category — there is essentially no sugar to hide behind, which makes it closer to Underberg than to Jägermeister.

composition.summary: Bitter roots and herbs macerated in high-strength spirit, barely sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, angelica, myrrh, bitter orange

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

composition.process: The near-total absence of sugar is the defining feature of the boonekamp style.

originStory: Petrus Boonekamp dates itself to 1777 and to a Dutch maker of that name, while German sources place the first such bitter around 1780 at Leidschendam, made by an apothecary remembered as Boonekamp or Kamp. The name became a byword for a style of magenbitter, above all in Germany, where an 1894 trademark law left it free for any distiller to use. The Petrus Boonekamp brand changed hands several times and now belongs to Italy's Gruppo Caffo 1915.

name: Amaro Ciociaro
description: A Lazio amaro built heavily on bitter orange, softer and more approachable than most, and frequently used as a stand-in for Amer Picon in cocktails that can no longer get the original.
funFact: American bartenders adopted it as the closest available substitute for Amer Picon after the French original was reformulated and largely withdrawn from export.

serve.how: Neat or over ice after dinner. In cocktails it does duty in a Brooklyn or a Liberal, where the orange-and-gentian profile fills the gap Picon left.

composition.summary: Bitter orange and herbs infused in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Bitter orange peel, gentian, clove, cinchona

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

composition.process: The orange dominance is why it substitutes for Picon better than any other amaro.

originStory: Amaro Ciociaro is made by Paolucci Liquori of Sora, in the province of Frosinone, and the company presents it as a family recipe dating back to 1873. Its name refers to Ciociaria, the traditional name for that hill country of southern Lazio. The recipe is secret but built on bitter orange, which is why American bartenders took it up as a stand-in for Amer Picon after the French original was reformulated and became hard to find abroad.

name: Ferro China
description: A nineteenth-century Italian tonic of cinchona bark and iron salts, sold in pharmacies as a treatment for anaemia and now surviving as a bitter digestive. It genuinely tastes faintly of iron.
funFact: It was prescribed to children as a strengthening tonic well into the twentieth century, in doses that would raise eyebrows now.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or the traditional winter serve of warming it with a strip of lemon peel. Italians of a certain generation also stir it into coffee or milk.

composition.summary: Cinchona bark infused with iron salts and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit and water

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Cinchona bark, iron citrate, cocoa, spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

composition.process: The iron is not a flavouring accident; it was the active ingredient the whole product was sold on.

originStory: Ferro China is the Italian family of amari made with cinchona bark and an iron salt, and its founding brand, Ferro-China Bisleri, was patented in 1881 by the Milanese chemist Felice Bisleri. It was sold in its day as a tonic, and the iron still gives it a faint metallic edge. The category faded in the later twentieth century, leaving a handful of makers such as the Roman house Baliva to carry it on.

name: Amaro Nardini
description: Made by Italy's oldest distillery, in Bassano del Grappa since 1779, on a grappa base rather than neutral spirit. Mint-forward and unusually clean, with the grappa giving it a sharpness other amari lack.
funFact: Nardini has been distilling on the Ponte Vecchio in Bassano since 1779, which makes it the oldest continuously operating distillery in Italy.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or the Veneto habit of mixing it half and half with soda as a mezzo e mezzo. The mint is pronounced enough that it reads almost like a digestif and a palate cleanser at once.

composition.summary: Herbs and mint infused into a grappa base.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grappa

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Peppermint, gentian, bitter orange, herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused into distilled grappa

composition.process: A grappa base rather than neutral spirit gives a grip that a neutral base cannot.

originStory: Bortolo Nardini settled in Bassano del Grappa in 1779 and opened a grapperia at the eastern end of the Ponte Vecchio, distilling grappa from pomace in copper stills. Still run by his descendants, the house is often described as Italy's oldest distillery, and the grapperia on the bridge still serves. Its amaro, built on a grappa base rather than neutral spirit, is a later addition to a house built on grappa.

name: Rabarbaro
description: The rhubarb-root class of Italian amaro, distinct enough to be its own category. Chinese rhubarb root gives a dry, earthy, faintly smoky bitterness that no other botanical produces.
funFact: The rhubarb in question is not the garden vegetable but Rheum palmatum, imported dried from China along trade routes that predate the amari themselves.

serve.how: Over ice with soda as an aperitif, or neat after a meal. The class sits drier than the citrus amari and is the natural bridge for someone moving from Campari toward Fernet.

composition.summary: Dried Chinese rhubarb root infused in spirit with supporting botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Rheum palmatum root, cardamom, bitter orange

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, sometimes with smoked root

composition.process: Smoking the root, as Sfumato does, is a variation within the class rather than the norm.

originStory: Rabarbaro is the family of Italian amari built on dried Chinese rhubarb root, Rheum palmatum, a botanical long traded into Europe, with Milan's Zucca the most famous name in the style.

name: Crème de Cacao
description: Cacao bean and vanilla liqueur, made clear (white) or caramel-coloured (dark) from the same base. The crème refers to sugar content, not dairy — there is no cream in it at all.
funFact: EU rules require a crème liqueur to carry at least 250 grams of sugar per litre, which is where the name comes from — the texture, not the ingredient.

serve.how: Rarely drunk neat. White goes into a Grasshopper and an Alexander; dark into a Brandy Alexander or a Twentieth Century. Keep the white version when you need chocolate flavour without muddying the colour of a drink.

composition.summary: Cacao beans and vanilla infused into neutral spirit and heavily sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Roasted cacao beans, vanilla pod

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused or distilled, then sweetened; dark is caramel-coloured

composition.process: Distilling rather than infusing gives the white version, since the colour stays behind in the beans.

originStory: Crème de cacao is a sweet French-style liqueur of cacao beans and vanilla, made clear or dark, its name referring to its high sugar content rather than to any cream.

name: Crème de Banane
description: Banana liqueur, bright yellow and frankly artificial-tasting in its cheap forms, genuinely good in its better ones. A tiki staple and the making of a Banana Daiquiri.
funFact: Isoamyl acetate, the compound that reads as banana, is also produced naturally by fermenting yeast — which is why some Jamaican rums taste of banana with no banana involved.

serve.how: In a Banana Daiquiri with rum and lime, or a bar spoon in a tiki build where it bridges rum and citrus. Neat it is very sweet; the better bottlings made from real fruit are worth seeking out.

composition.summary: Banana infused into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Banana, natural or compounded, plus vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened

composition.process: Real-fruit versions are darker and less neon than the compounded ones, and taste noticeably less like confectionery.

originStory: Crème de banane is a banana liqueur in the French crème tradition and a long-standing tiki and dessert-drink ingredient, with no single recorded inventor.

name: Crème de Mûre
description: Blackberry liqueur, deep purple and tart under the sweetness. Without it there is no Bramble, which is the only cocktail invented in 1980s London that anyone still orders.
funFact: Dick Bradsell built the Bramble at Fred's Club in Soho, drizzling the mûre over crushed ice so it bleeds down through the drink.

serve.how: Drizzled over a gin sour on crushed ice to make a Bramble — pour it last and do not stir, the bleed is the point. It also lifts a Kir if you want something darker than cassis.

composition.summary: Blackberries macerated in neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Blackberries, sometimes with raspberry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, pressed and sweetened

composition.process: Like cassis, it is a maceration rather than a distillate, so the fruit character stays raw and bright.

originStory: Crème de mûre is a French-style blackberry liqueur, the one Dick Bradsell drizzled over crushed ice to finish his Bramble in London.

name: Crème de Noyaux
description: Made from apricot and cherry stones rather than nuts, which gives an almond flavour from a fruit source. Pink, old-fashioned, and the ingredient that makes a Pink Squirrel pink.
funFact: The almond note comes from benzaldehyde in the kernels — the same compound that makes marzipan taste of almond, present here without a single almond involved.

serve.how: A cocktail ingredient rather than a sipper. It is the almond note in a Pink Squirrel and an Old Etonian, and it substitutes for orgeat in drinks where you want alcohol rather than syrup.

composition.summary: Apricot and cherry kernels macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Apricot and cherry stones, cracked

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened and coloured

composition.process: Kernels contain amygdalin, which is why the quantity used is carefully controlled.

originStory: Crème de noyaux is a French-style liqueur that takes its almond flavour from apricot and cherry kernels rather than almonds, and it is what turns a Pink Squirrel pink.

name: Melon Liqueur
description: Bright green muskmelon liqueur, invented in Japan in 1978 and responsible for an entire decade of drinks. Sweet, unmistakable, and rehabilitated in recent years by bartenders who stopped being embarrassed by it.
funFact: Suntory launched it in 1978 and the colour comes entirely from added dye — the melon infusion itself is pale gold.

serve.how: With soda and lime over ice, which is far better than its reputation. In cocktails it makes a Midori Sour or a Japanese Slipper. Cut it with acid; the sugar needs something to push against.

composition.summary: Muskmelon infused into neutral spirit, sweetened and coloured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Yubari and muskmelon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened; colour added

composition.process: Two melon varieties are used, one for aroma and one for body.

originStory: The melon liqueur most drinkers know began in Japan in 1964, when Suntory released it as Hermes Melon Liqueur. Renamed Midori, the Japanese word for green, it was launched in the United States in 1978 with a party at New York's Studio 54, and it was made only in Japan until 1987. Its vivid green colour made it a fixture of the cocktails of the following decade.

name: Black Raspberry Liqueur
description: Black raspberries, blackberries, vanilla and honey infused into cognac, from the Loire. Sold in a round bottle bound like a medieval orb, and rather better than the packaging suggests.
funFact: The recipe is said to descend from a raspberry liqueur served to Louis XIV when he visited the Loire in the seventeenth century.

serve.how: Topped with champagne as a Kir Royale variant, or in a French Martini with vodka and pineapple. Neat over ice it is heavy going — it wants dilution and acid.

composition.summary: Berries infused into cognac with vanilla and honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cognac

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Black raspberry, blackberry, Madagascar vanilla, honey

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused over weeks, then blended

composition.process: A cognac base rather than neutral spirit is what gives it weight behind the fruit.

originStory: The most familiar black raspberry liqueur, Chambord, was developed in 1982 by Norton Cooper at his family's Philadelphia cordial firm, Charles Jacquin et Cie, and is made in the Loire Valley from raspberries, vanilla, citrus peel, honey and cognac. Its makers tie it to a legend that Louis XIV was served a wild-raspberry liqueur on a visit to the Château de Chambord in the late seventeenth century. Brown-Forman has owned the brand since 2006, and Cooper's son Robert went on to create St-Germain.

name: Coconut Rum Liqueur
description: Caribbean rum flavoured with coconut and cut to around 21%. Dismissed for decades as a holiday drink, and quietly indispensable in any tiki bar that wants coconut without opening a fresh nut.
funFact: It was created in 1978 specifically to make Piña Coladas easier to serve at bar speed, which is exactly what it still does.

serve.how: With pineapple juice, or long with soda and lime. In a Piña Colada it replaces both the rum and the cream of coconut in a hurry. Keep it cold; warm it turns cloying fast.

composition.summary: Caribbean rum blended with coconut extract and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Barbadian rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Coconut, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: The rum base is real and aged, which is why it mixes better than a neutral coconut liqueur would.

originStory: The coconut rum most bars know, Malibu, was created in 1978 by Tom Jago of International Distillers and Vintners and was first made in Curaçao, as a way to make piña coladas simpler for bartenders. When it took off, production moved to Barbados, where the rum comes from the West Indies Rum Distillery. Pernod Ricard has owned the brand since 2005.

name: Anisette
description: The sweetest of the anise family, made from green anise seed and heavily sugared. Softer than pastis and lower in strength than ouzo, and a Mediterranean breakfast habit for older generations.
funFact: Marie Brizard began making it in Bordeaux in 1755 from a recipe she was reportedly given by a West Indian sailor she had nursed through illness.

serve.how: With cold water, which turns it milky, or over ice. In Italy and Spain it also goes into coffee. It is sweeter than pastis, so use less of it and more water than instinct suggests.

composition.summary: Green anise seed distilled into neutral spirit and heavily sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green anise seed, sometimes coriander and fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sugared

composition.process: The higher sugar is what separates it from pastis and ouzo more than the botanicals do.

originStory: Marie Brizard, the daughter of a Bordeaux distiller, founded her liqueur house in the city in 1755 with Jean-Baptiste Roger, the husband of one of her nieces, and her anisette made Bordeaux's name in the style. Legend says she nursed a sick West Indian sailor who repaid her with the recipe, a story that cannot be verified. Her anisette found favour at the court of Louis XV, and the founders' descendants were still among the company's leaders ten generations later.

name: Chinchón
description: Spain's protected anise spirit, from the town of Chinchón south of Madrid, made in dry, sweet and extra-strength versions. Distilled from anise grown locally rather than flavoured after the fact.
funFact: The seco especial is bottled at 74%, which makes it one of the strongest commercially available anise spirits anywhere.

serve.how: Dry over ice as an aperitif, sweet after a meal, and the 74% version with considerable respect and a great deal of water. Spaniards also add it to coffee as a carajillo.

composition.summary: Locally grown anise distilled in copper alembics.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Anise grown around Chinchón

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, distilled with the seed

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 35% to 74% depending on style

composition.process: Distilling with the seed rather than adding oil afterwards is what earns it protected status.

originStory: Vines and anise have long been grown around Chinchón, south-east of Madrid, and in 1911 local growers founded the Sociedad Cooperativa Alcoholera de Chinchón to distil and bottle the town's anise on an industrial scale. The name later gained legal protection as a geographical indication for anise spirit. It is made in dry, sweet and extra-strong versions, and the extra-strong seco especial is among the strongest anise spirits sold.

name: Herbsaint
description: New Orleans' anise spirit, created in 1934 as a legal substitute for absinthe when the real thing was still banned. It is what a Sazerac is rinsed with in its home city.
funFact: The name is a contraction of herbe sainte, the Creole French name for wormwood — a fairly transparent nod to what it was standing in for.

serve.glass: Used as a rinse; or a tumbler with water
serve.how: Rinse a chilled glass and discard the excess, then build a Sazerac in it. Neat it takes water like pastis and louches the same way. The Original formula is drier and closer to the pre-war recipe.

composition.summary: Anise and fennel distilled into neutral spirit, wormwood-free at first.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Star anise, fennel, herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the botanicals

composition.process: It was built to satisfy absinthe drinkers under a legal regime that banned the original, and it never lost that job.

originStory: Herbsaint was created in New Orleans in 1934 by J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, who had learned about absinthe in France during the First World War. It was first sold as Legendre Absinthe, although it contained no grand wormwood, and when federal regulators objected to the word it became Legendre Herbsaint, from herbe sainte, the Creole French name for wormwood. The Sazerac Company bought the Legendre firm in 1949, and Herbsaint is the traditional rinse for a New Orleans Sazerac.

name: Kümmel
description: Caraway, cumin and fennel in a clear, sweet liqueur with roots in sixteenth-century Holland and a devoted afterlife in Scottish golf clubhouses, where it is drunk against the shakes.
funFact: It is known in British golfing circles as the putting mixture, on the widely held theory that it steadies the hands.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass, or over ice. It also works in a Silver Bullet with gin and lemon. The caraway is assertive, so it divides a room much as aquavit does.

composition.summary: Caraway and cumin distilled into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Caraway seed, cumin, fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sweetened

composition.process: It shares its botanical backbone with aquavit; the difference is the sugar.

originStory: The earliest known kümmel recipe, attributed to a knight of the Livonian Order, dates from 1503, and a legend credits Lucas Bols with distilling it in the Netherlands in 1575, before he was born. The style flourished in the Baltic: by 1823 Wilhelm von Blanckenhagen was making it on his estate at Allasch, near Riga, and by the mid-nineteenth century Ludwig Mentzendorff was importing kümmel to Britain. In Scottish golf clubhouses it earned the nickname putting mixture, for its supposed effect on the nerves.

name: Cinnamon Schnapps
description: Neutral spirit heavily flavoured with cinnamon, sometimes carrying flakes of gold leaf. Bracing, sweet and hot, and the single most-ordered shot in a great many bars.
funFact: The gold-flake versions descend from Danziger Goldwasser, a sixteenth-century tradition of suspending edible gold in liqueur as a supposed medicine.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer, in one. Cold is essential — warm, the sugar dominates and the cinnamon turns medicinal. It also does real work in hot cider or a mulled drink.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with cinnamon and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Cassia cinnamon oil and extract

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended, not redistilled

composition.process: Cassia rather than true Ceylon cinnamon gives the sharper, hotter note the category is built on.

originStory: Cinnamon schnapps is a sweet, hot cinnamon-flavoured spirit popularised by Swiss and American brands, some suspending gold flakes in the bottle in the manner of the old Danzig Goldwasser.

name: Parfait Amour
description: A violet-purple liqueur of citrus, rose petals, vanilla and almond, made since the eighteenth century and once sold as a love potion. More perfume than drink, and used accordingly.
funFact: It was marketed in the 1700s as an aphrodisiac, which is where the name — perfect love — comes from.

serve.how: A cocktail ingredient rather than a sipper. A bar spoon adds colour and floral lift to a gin sour; more than that and the drink tastes of soap. Sits close to crème de violette but with citrus behind it.

composition.summary: Citrus peel, rose and violet infused into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or brandy

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Curaçao orange peel, rose petals, violet, vanilla, almond

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and sweetened; colour added

composition.process: It is essentially a curaçao with flowers, which is why the citrus is still detectable under the perfume.

originStory: Parfait amour, French for perfect love, is a violet-coloured liqueur of citrus, flowers, vanilla and almond made in France and the Netherlands, with no recorded inventor.

name: Pistachio Liqueur
description: Sicilian pistachios, mostly from Bronte on the slopes of Etna, blended into a cream or clear liqueur. Intensely nutty, and a relatively modern addition to the Italian liqueur canon.
funFact: Bronte pistachios grow in volcanic soil on Etna, are harvested only every other year, and cost several times the price of ordinary pistachios.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after dinner, or poured over gelato. The cream versions separate if frozen, so chill rather than freeze.

composition.summary: Roasted pistachios infused into spirit, often with cream.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bronte pistachios, sugar, sometimes cream and vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then blended

composition.process: Roasting the nuts before maceration is what pushes it from green and raw to rounded.

originStory: Pistachio liqueur is a relatively modern Sicilian speciality made from the pistachios of Bronte, on the slopes of Etna, in both cream and clear styles.

name: Nocello
description: A walnut and hazelnut liqueur from Emilia-Romagna, lighter and less syrupy than nocino, which is made from green walnuts. This one uses ripe nuts, so it reads as toasted rather than bitter.
funFact: Its cousin nocino is made from green walnuts picked at midsummer, husks and all, which is why nocino is bitter and this is not.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, over ice, or poured onto vanilla gelato. It also works in coffee and stands in well for Frangelico when you want walnut rather than pure hazelnut.

composition.summary: Ripe walnuts and hazelnuts infused into neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ripe walnuts and hazelnuts

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: Ripe nuts rather than green ones is the entire distinction from nocino.

originStory: Nocello is made by Toschi, the company Giancarlo and Lanfranco Toschi founded in Vignola, near Modena, in 1945 to preserve the town's famous cherries in spirit. The firm, now based at Savignano sul Panaro, added a traditional nocino in the 1960s and Nocello in the 1980s. Where nocino is made from green walnuts picked in early summer, Nocello is a lighter, sweeter liqueur of walnut and hazelnut.

name: Blood Orange Liqueur
description: Made from Sicilian blood oranges grown on Etna's slopes, with the fruit's characteristic raspberry note intact. Deeper and less bitter than a curaçao, and a genuinely different thing from triple sec.
funFact: Blood oranges get their colour from anthocyanins that only develop when nights are cold, which is why Etna's altitude matters to the crop.

serve.how: Over ice with soda, or in place of triple sec in a Margarita or Sidecar where it brings berry as well as citrus. At 40% it has enough backbone to be sipped neat over a cube.

composition.summary: Blood orange peel and juice distilled and blended into neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sanguinello and Tarocco blood oranges, plus lemon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Peel distilled, juice blended in afterwards

composition.process: Higher strength than most orange liqueurs, which is why it holds up in a stirred drink.

originStory: The most prominent Sicilian blood orange liqueur, Solerno, was launched by William Grant & Sons in the late 2000s and created by Lesley Gracie, the distiller behind Hendrick's Gin. It is made from hand-picked Sanguinello blood oranges grown on the slopes of Etna, together with Sicilian lemons. The fruit's colour comes from anthocyanins that develop when nights turn cold, which is why the volcano's altitude matters to the crop.

name: Bergamot Liqueur
description: Made from the Calabrian bergamot, a citrus grown almost nowhere else and best known for flavouring Earl Grey tea. Floral, bitter and unmistakably perfumed.
funFact: Around 80% of the world's bergamot comes from a narrow coastal strip of Calabria, and the fruit is grown almost entirely for its oil rather than to eat.

serve.how: Cold and neat after dinner, or a bar spoon in a gin sour where it does what a tea infusion would without the tannin. It is bitter enough to work as an aperitif over ice with soda.

composition.summary: Bergamot peel infused into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Calabrian bergamot peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated or distilled, then sweetened

composition.process: The fruit is too sour and bitter to eat, so essentially the entire crop goes to oil and liqueur.

originStory: Bergamot liqueur is a southern Italian speciality made from the Calabrian bergamot, the perfumed citrus grown mostly along a narrow coastal strip of Calabria and best known for flavouring Earl Grey tea.

name: Ratafia Catalana
description: A Catalan liqueur of green walnuts and dozens of herbs, macerated in the sun through summer and traditionally started on the feast of Saint John. Made at home across Catalonia to family recipes.
funFact: The jars are traditionally left outdoors for the whole of summer, so the maceration is driven by sunlight rather than heat from a still.

serve.how: Neat after a meal, at cellar temperature. Catalans serve it with dessert and at village festivals. Sweet and heavily spiced, so a small pour goes far.

composition.summary: Green walnuts and herbs sun-macerated in spirit with sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or aguardiente

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green walnuts, cinnamon, nutmeg, lemon peel, dozens of herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Sun-macerated over months

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 26%

composition.process: Nou de Sant Joan — walnuts picked around 24 June, while the shell is still soft enough to cut.

originStory: Ratafia catalana is a traditional Catalan liqueur of green walnuts and many herbs, macerated in the sun through the summer to family recipes, and its origins are not documented.

name: Palo de Mallorca
description: A Mallorcan bitter of gentian root and cinchona bark, dark as treacle and originally sold as an anti-malarial when the island's wetlands still carried the disease.
funFact: It was drunk to ward off malaria in the Mallorcan marshlands, and survived the disease's eradication purely because islanders had grown to like it.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and a slice of lemon, which is the standard island serve. Neat it is thick and very sweet. Locals also drink it with orange juice.

composition.summary: Gentian and cinchona infused in spirit with caramelised sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Gentian root, cinchona bark, burnt sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused and blended

composition.process: The burnt sugar gives both the colour and most of the body.

originStory: Palo de Mallorca grew out of the Balearic apothecary tradition: cinchona bark reached Spain from Peru in the seventeenth century, when the islands' marshy coasts still bred malaria, and bitter infusions of it, often with gentian, were taken against fever. Sweetened with sugar and caramel to make them palatable and fortified with alcohol, they became a dark bitter liqueur, made commercially since the nineteenth century. Palo de Mallorca is now a protected geographical designation.

name: Guavaberry Liqueur
description: Sint Maarten's national liqueur, made from wild guavaberries that ripen only briefly in the island's hills — a fruit unrelated to guava despite the name. Rum-based, spiced, and a Christmas tradition.
funFact: There is a traditional Christmas carol on the island whose entire subject is going house to house asking for a taste of the family's guavaberry.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or over ice. Islanders drink it at Christmas and mix it with rum punch. The wild fruit is picked from hillside trees rather than farmed, so supply is genuinely limited.

composition.summary: Wild guavaberries steeped in aged rum with spice and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aged Caribbean rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Wild guavaberry (Myrciaria floribunda), cinnamon, clove

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for months

composition.process: The berry has nothing to do with guava; it is a myrtle relative that fruits for a few weeks a year.

originStory: Guavaberry liqueur is Sint Maarten's traditional Christmas drink, made in island homes for generations from rum, cane sugar and wild guavaberries, a fruit unrelated to the guava.

name: Sorrel Liqueur
description: Made from hibiscus calyces — sorrel in Caribbean usage — steeped with rum, ginger and clove. Deep crimson, tart and spiced, and inseparable from Christmas across the West Indies.
funFact: The plant is Hibiscus sabdariffa, the same species that makes agua de Jamaica in Mexico and karkade in Egypt — three continents, one calyx.

serve.how: Cold over ice, or topped with sparkling wine. It is tart enough not to need much cutting. Caribbean households make it fresh each December and the bought version is a year-round stand-in.

composition.summary: Hibiscus calyces steeped with rum, ginger and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Caribbean rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dried hibiscus calyces, ginger, clove, cinnamon, orange peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: It is the calyx that is used, not the flower — the fleshy cup left after the bloom drops.

originStory: Sorrel liqueur bottles a Caribbean Christmas tradition, hibiscus calyces steeped with rum, ginger and clove, and it has no single recorded origin.

name: Ponche Kuba
description: A Caribbean cream liqueur of rum, condensed milk, egg and spice, from Curaçao and hugely popular across Venezuela and the Dutch islands. Thicker and more cinnamon-driven than Irish cream.
funFact: It is a Christmas fixture across the southern Caribbean, where it competes directly with Venezuela's ponche crema for the same place on the table.

serve.how: Cold from the fridge, neat, in a small glass. Shake before pouring. It also goes into coffee, and over ice cream. Refrigerate once opened and finish it reasonably quickly.

composition.summary: Rum blended with condensed milk, egg and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Caribbean rum

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Condensed milk, egg, cinnamon, nutmeg, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended, not distilled

composition.process: Condensed milk rather than fresh cream is what makes it shelf-stable in the tropics.

originStory: By its maker's account, Ponche Kuba dates from 1942, when the Curaçao merchant Jaime Sprock travelled to Cuba and tasted the homemade cream liqueurs islanders called ponche. He combined what he learned into one recipe of rum, milk, egg and spice, named it Ponche Kuba and made it through his firm, J.A.J. Sprock, on Curaçao. It became a Christmas staple across the Dutch Caribbean islands and Venezuela, where it shares the season with the local ponche crema.

name: Licor de Café
description: Costa Rican coffee liqueur, built on cane spirit and Tarrazú beans, drier and more roast-forward than the Mexican coffee liqueurs that dominate the shelf.
funFact: Tarrazú beans grow between 1,200 and 1,900 metres, and the altitude is what gives the acidity that survives into the liqueur.

serve.how: Over ice, or with milk. It is less sweet than Kahlúa, which makes it the better choice in an Espresso Martini where you want coffee rather than sugar. Costa Ricans also add it to hot coffee.

composition.summary: Costa Rican coffee extracted into cane spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Tarrazú arabica coffee, vanilla

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Coffee extracted and blended

composition.process: Less sugar than the Mexican style is the whole difference, and it shows in cocktails.

originStory: Costa Rican coffee liqueur is built on cane spirit and the country's high-grown coffee, notably from Tarrazú, a drier and more roast-led take on the style.

name: Yuzushu
description: Japanese yuzu steeped in shochu or sake, cloudy with pulp and intensely aromatic. Yuzu is barely edible as a fruit — almost all peel and pip — which is exactly why it works as a liqueur.
funFact: Yuzu trees can take a decade to fruit, and the fruit is so pithy that a kilo yields very little juice — which is why it is priced like a spice.
