description: The green style, coloured naturally by steeping herbs in the finished spirit so chlorophyll bleeds in. That colour fades to amber with age, which is how a genuine old bottle is recognised.
funFact: Naturally coloured absinthe turns amber over years as the chlorophyll degrades — a bottle described as feuille morte, dead leaf, is old rather than spoiled.

serve.glass: Absinthe glass with a slotted spoon
serve.how: Three to five parts iced water dripped slowly over a sugar cube on a slotted spoon. The louche should build gradually. No flames — burning the sugar is a 1990s invention that scorches the herbs.

composition.summary: Wormwood, anise and fennel distilled, then steeped with herbs for colour.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral or wine-based spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, green anise, fennel; petite wormwood and hyssop for colouring

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then a second cold steep for natural colour

composition.process: Artificially coloured absinthe stays green forever, which is the giveaway.

originStory: The usual story credits Pierre Ordinaire, a French doctor living in the Swiss Val-de-Travers, with an absinthe elixir in the 1790s, though the Henriod sisters of Couvet are more securely documented making it. Their recipe passed to Major Daniel-Henri Dubied, who in 1798 opened a distillery in Couvet with his son-in-law Henri-Louis Pernod. In 1805 Pernod moved across the border to Pontarlier, and the green, naturally coloured absinthe of France became the drink of Belle Époque cafés until bans in Switzerland in 1910 and France in 1915.

name: Absinthe Blanche
description: The clear style, bottled straight off the still with no colouring step. Swiss in origin, where clandestine producers kept it colourless through the ban so it could pass as something innocent.
funFact: Swiss bootleggers kept it clear precisely because a colourless bottle was easier to explain to the authorities than a vivid green one — the style outlived the reason for it.

serve.how: Iced water dripped slowly, three to five parts to one. Blanche louches to a bright opalescent white rather than a cloudy green, and it tends to be cleaner and more herbal than verte.

composition.summary: Wormwood and anise distilled and bottled without a colouring steep.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, green anise, fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled once with botanicals; no second steep

composition.process: Skipping the colouring step also skips the extra herb tannin, which is why blanche often tastes brighter.

originStory: Absinthe was born in the Val-de-Travers in the late eighteenth century, but the clear style as it is known today is a child of its ban. When Switzerland outlawed absinthe in 1910, the valley's distillers carried on in secret, dropping the colouring step and bottling the spirit straight off the still, since a colourless bottle was easier to explain to an inspector than a vivid green one. Locally it became known as la bleue. Switzerland legalised absinthe again in 2005, and Val-de-Travers producers now make blanche openly, the style having outlived the reason for it.

name: Dill Aquavit
description: The Danish and Swedish variation in which dill leads rather than caraway. Fresher and greener than the classic style, and built for the summer table rather than the winter one.
funFact: Scandinavian aquavit must legally take its dominant flavour from caraway or dill — those two, and no others, define the category in EU law.

serve.how: From the freezer, in small measures, with food rather than before it. Dill aquavit belongs with crayfish and new potatoes in a way the caraway styles do not — it is a summer spirit.

composition.summary: Grain or potato spirit redistilled with dill as the lead botanical.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain or potato neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Dill leading, with fennel, coriander and citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Dill's aromatics are fragile, so it goes in later and gentler than caraway would.

originStory: Aquavit enters the written record in the sixteenth century, when Eske Bille, the Danish lord of Bergenhus castle in Norway, sent 'some water which is called Aqua Vite' to the Archbishop of Norway. Caraway became the defining flavour across Scandinavia, but Danish and Swedish distillers also made versions led by dill, the herb that seasons so much of the Nordic summer table, from crayfish to new potatoes. When the European Union defined the category, it named caraway and dill as the only permitted lead flavours, which makes dill aquavit one of the two pillars of the style.

name: Taffel Akvavit
description: The classic Danish table aquavit, clear and caraway-forward, unaged and bottled at 45%. What Danes mean when they say akvavit without qualifying it further.
funFact: Taffel means table, and the name marks it as the everyday version rather than an aged or special bottling.

serve.how: Freezer cold, in small measures, with the meal. Danish tradition is a beer alongside and a toast before each glass, with eye contact — skipping the eye contact is the part visitors get wrong.

composition.summary: Grain spirit redistilled with caraway and citrus, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Caraway dominant, plus citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Bottling unaged and clear is what distinguishes it from the oak-rested Norwegian styles.

originStory: Taffel akvavit is bound up with Aalborg, in northern Jutland, where Isidor Henius, a distiller from Toruń, made his name with a clean, caraway-led spirit; the brand gives 1846 as its starting date. His Aalborg Taffel Akvavit, nicknamed Rød Aalborg for its red label, became Denmark's best-known akvavit, and in 1881 his business was merged into De Danske Spritfabrikker. Taffel means table, and the name marks it as the everyday bottle for the lunch table rather than an aged or special one.

name: Kruidenbitter
description: The Dutch herbal bitter category, of which Beerenburg is the most famous example. Juniper spirit steeped with gentian, bay and laurel, drunk cold and largely by people who grew up with it.
funFact: Amsterdam spice merchants sold the herb blends over the counter so drinkers could steep their own jenever at home, which is how the category began.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass. Dutch and Frisian drinkers take it before or after food rather than with it, and often alongside a beer.

composition.summary: Jenever or neutral spirit steeped with a fixed herb blend.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Jenever or grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, bay, laurel, juniper berry, and a dozen more

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated rather than redistilled

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation keeps the herbs green and raw rather than polished.

originStory: Dutch kruidenbitters grew from the old habit of steeping herbs and roots in jenever, and the most famous takes its name from Hendrik Beerenburg, an Amsterdam spice merchant on the Stromarkt who sold a herb mixture for customers to steep in their own spirit. The drink found its real following in the northern provinces, above all Friesland, where distillers such as Sonnema later bottled it ready-made. Many other towns and families kept their own kruidenbitter recipes.

name: Horincă
description: The Maramureș variant of Romanian fruit brandy, double or triple distilled to a considerably higher strength than țuică. Made from plums or apples in the far north, and a matter of local pride.
funFact: Names shift by region across Romania — țuică in the south, horincă in Maramureș, pălincă in Transylvania, jinars in parts of the west — for broadly the same tradition.

serve.how: Room temperature, neat, in small glasses, offered on arrival. Northern Romanian households serve it warmed with honey and pepper in winter, which is called a fiartă.

composition.summary: Plums or apples fermented and distilled two or three times.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plums, apples or pears from Maramureș orchards

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double or triple distillation in copper

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes rested in mulberry or oak

composition.process: The extra distillation is what separates it from țuică, and locals consider the strength a point of honour.

originStory: Horincă is the Maramureș name for the fruit brandy distilled across Romania, and the word reflects the region's place on the Ukrainian border: it is related to the Ukrainian horilka, from a Slavic root meaning to burn. Families distil plums or apples in small copper stills, often twice, and the spirit is poured for guests and at weddings and funerals. The same tradition goes by other names elsewhere, țuică in the south and pălincă in Transylvania. No single maker is credited with horincă; it belongs to the villages of the north.

name: Medovina Rakija
description: Honey-fermented rakija from the Balkans — distinct from medovača, which is rakija sweetened with honey after the fact. Here the honey is fermented and distilled, which is a different drink entirely.
funFact: Fermenting honey is the basis of mead, the oldest known alcoholic drink, so distilling it produces something closer to a mead brandy than to a fruit rakija.

serve.how: Room temperature in a small pour after a meal. It is rounder and more floral than fruit rakija, and worth tasting beside a medovača to see the difference between fermenting honey and adding it.

composition.summary: Honey fermented into mead and then distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Honey, fermented with water

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, usually twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes oak-rested

composition.process: Honey ferments slowly and needs nutrient additions, which is why honey distillates are rare everywhere.

originStory: Medovina rakija is a rare Balkan spirit distilled from fermented honey, the base of mead, rather than rakija sweetened with honey afterwards like medovača, and no producer, village or date is credited with it as a style.

name: Macallan 12 Sherry Oak
description: Sherry Cask Single Malt from Scotland. Speyside; matured in seasoned Oloroso casks.
funFact: Macallan 12 Sherry Oak: Speyside; matured in seasoned Oloroso casks

serve.how: Neat, with water added sparingly. Sherry casks carry a lot of tannin, so heavy dilution turns them drying rather than sweeter. Oloroso gives nuts and spice; PX gives raisin and syrup.

composition.summary: Malt whisky matured in ex-sherry European or American oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-oloroso, ex-Pedro Ximénez or ex-fino casks

composition.process: European oak gives more tannin and spice; American oak seasoned with sherry is softer and sweeter.

originStory: The Macallan was founded in 1824 by Alexander Reid, a farmer who took out one of the first licences under the new Excise Act on the Easter Elchies estate, above a ford on the Spey near Craigellachie used by cattle drovers. Its reputation came to rest on sherry casks, which the distillery has made to order in Spain and seasoned with oloroso in Jerez before filling. The 12-year-old took the name Sherry Oak when Macallan added a Fine Oak range alongside it, and in 2018 the house moved into a new distillery built into the hillside.

name: Macallan 18 Sherry Oak
description: Sherry Cask Single Malt from Scotland.
funFact: One of 8 Sherry Cask Single Malt bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat, with water added sparingly. Sherry casks carry a lot of tannin, so heavy dilution turns them drying rather than sweeter. Oloroso gives nuts and spice; PX gives raisin and syrup.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-oloroso, ex-Pedro Ximénez or ex-fino casks

composition.process: European oak gives more tannin and spice; American oak seasoned with sherry is softer and sweeter.

originStory: Macallan's story begins in 1824 with Alexander Reid's licence on the Easter Elchies estate in Speyside, and its long-aged sherry whiskies did much to make its name among collectors. For many years the 18-year-old's label carried the year it was distilled, so each annual release could be told apart. It is matured only in oak casks seasoned with oloroso sherry in Jerez, and Easter Elchies House, the early-eighteenth-century manor on the estate, still appears on the label.

name: Glenfiddich 12
description: Speyside Single Malt from Scotland. The world's best-selling single malt.
funFact: Glenfiddich 12: The world's best-selling single malt

serve.how: Serve a neat dram in a Glencairn at cellar temperature and nose it patiently — apple, honey, and vanilla should rise in sequence, with sherried fruit on richer bottlings. Sip slowly and let it coat the palate; Speyside's elegance is about balance rather than punch. A few drops of water can unfold extra orchard fruit, but many Speysides are perfect exactly as poured.

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–46% ABV

composition.process: Tall stills and generous sherry-cask maturation build the honeyed, orchard-fruit house style.

originStory: William Grant worked for twenty years at Mortlach before building his own distillery in Dufftown, with the help of his children and a single stonemason, using second-hand stills bought from Cardhu. The first spirit ran on Christmas Day 1887. He called it Glenfiddich, Gaelic for valley of the deer, which is why a stag appears on the label. The family firm, still independent, was among the first to promote single malt abroad in the 1960s, when almost all malt whisky disappeared into blends, and the 12-year-old is its signature bottling today.

description: Speyside Single Malt from Scotland.
funFact: One of 21 Speyside Single Malt bottlings catalogued here.

originStory: Glenfiddich has been distilled in Dufftown since 1887, when William Grant's family filled their first casks on Christmas Day. The 15-year-old Solera was created in 1998 by the malt master David Stewart, who borrowed the solera idea from the sherry bodegas of Jerez: whisky aged in bourbon, sherry and new oak casks is married in a large vat of Oregon pine that is never emptied below half, so every batch carries a little of the ones before it. The vat has been topped up continuously since it was first filled.

originStory: Glenfiddich began in 1887 in Dufftown, where William Grant and his family built the distillery stone by stone, and it is still owned by his descendants. The house keeps its own coopers and coppersmiths on site, unusual for a distillery of its size, and has long been bottled in a distinctive triangular bottle. The 18-year-old, once sold as Ancient Reserve, is aged in a mix of oloroso sherry and bourbon casks and married in small batches before bottling, a deeper, longer-aged expression of the same Speyside spirit.

originStory: George Smith had distilled illicitly on his farm at Upper Drummin for years before taking out one of the first licences under the new Excise Act in 1824, with the backing of his landlord the Duke of Gordon, and he is said to have carried a pair of pistols for protection from smugglers who saw him as a traitor. After a fire, production moved to Minmore in 1859. So many distillers borrowed the valley's name that Smith's son went to court, and from then on only his whisky could be called The Glenlivet, while others had to add their own names.

originStory: The Glenlivet traces its licence to 1824, when George Smith became one of the first legal distillers in a remote glen famous for smuggling, where illicit whisky had long been carried over the hills to the Lowlands. The name became such a mark of quality that many Speyside rivals tacked it onto their own, earning Glenlivet the joking title of the longest glen in Scotland. The 18-year-old, matured in a mix of American and European oak, is a longer-aged expression of the same house spirit.

originStory: George Smith's licence of 1824 made Glenlivet one of the first legal distilleries in Speyside, in a glen where illicit stills had been the rule. Nàdurra, Gaelic for natural, was introduced in the mid-2000s as the distillery's take on whisky bottled the old way: at cask strength, without chill filtration, and in its first batches from first-fill bourbon casks. Each batch carries its own strength and batch code, and later releases have varied the wood, including oloroso sherry casks and casks that once held peated whisky.

name: Balvenie DoubleWood 12

originStory: John Smith, a distiller who had managed Macallan, Glenlivet and Glenfarclas, founded Cragganmore in 1869 at Ballindalloch, choosing the site for its spring water and for the new Strathspey railway beside it. originStory: Mortlach was the first legal distillery in Dufftown, founded in 1823 by James Findlater, and the town grew into one of the capitals of Speyside whisky around it. Its stills run a complex, partial triple distillation that the distillery describes as 2.81 times, giving a heavy, meaty spirit nicknamed the Beast of Dufftown. For decades it went mostly into blends, until Diageo relaunched it as a single malt; the 16-year-old Distiller's Dram arrived in 2018.

originStory: Speyburn was built in 1897 by John Hopkins and Company in a narrow glen near Rothes, to a design by Charles Doig. Its owners were determined to fill a cask in Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee year, so distilling began on 15 December in a snowstorm, before the doors and windows had been fitted, and one butt was filled bearing that year's date. Speyburn was also an early user of pneumatic drum maltings. Inver House Distillers has owned it since the early 1990s.

originStory: Brothers Alexander and Donald Johnston founded Laphroaig in 1815 on the south coast of Islay, and the name is usually translated as the beautiful hollow by the broad bay. originStory: Bowmore is the oldest distillery on Islay, founded in 1779 by John Simson, a local merchant, on the shore of Loch Indaal in the village of the same name. The distillery still turns part of its own barley on traditional malting floors and dries it over Islay peat, and its whisky sits between the heavily peated malts of the south coast and the gentler ones of the north. Suntory has owned it since the 1990s.

Its peppery, maritime character made the 10-year-old the island representative when the Classic Malts range was launched in 1988.

originStory: A distillery was licensed at Craighouse on the Isle of Jura in 1810, but it fell into ruin early in the twentieth century. originStory: Ledaig was the original name of the distillery John Sinclair founded in 1798 at Tobermory on the Isle of Mull, and comes from the Gaelic for safe haven. Ledaig has grown into a range of its own, and the 10-year-old is its core release.

serve.how: Serve a dram at cool room temperature in a Glencairn, swirl gently, and nose for heather and dried fruit before the first sip. Because the Highlands span so many styles, taste it on its own terms — some pours lean floral and honeyed, others muscular with a wisp of smoke. A teaspoon of water is the classic move if the malt feels closed; add it gradually and re-nose each time.

originStory: William Matheson licensed Glenmorangie in 1843 at Tain, on the Dornoch Firth, converting a farm brewery at Morangie. He is said to have equipped it with second-hand gin stills, and their descendants are still the tallest in Scotland, with necks over five metres high, which help give the spirit its light, fruity character. The house translates its name as glen of tranquillity. The 10-year-old, matured in American oak, was renamed The Original in the 2000s, and LVMH has owned the distillery since 2004.

originStory: Glenmorangie, licensed at Tain in 1843, made its name with an unusually light spirit from Scotland's tallest stills. originStory: Alexander Matheson founded Dalmore in 1839 on the Cromarty Firth at Alness, and from 1867 it was run by the Mackenzie family. The stag on every bottle comes from the Mackenzie arms and a clan legend that an ancestor saved a Scottish king from a charging stag in the thirteenth century, after which the family was granted the right to bear a stag's head. Whyte and Mackay owns the distillery today, and Richard Paterson, its master blender for decades, is closely associated with the sherry-led house style.

originStory: James Henderson founded Pulteney in 1826 in Wick, Caithness, in Pulteneytown, a planned fishing settlement laid out by the British Fisheries Society and named after its governor Sir William Pulteney. originStory: John Begg built the New Lochnagar distillery on Deeside in 1845, near the mountain of Lochnagar and just across the river from Balmoral. originStory: Auchentoshan, on the north-western edge of Glasgow near the Erskine Bridge, officially dates its founding to 1823, and its name is usually translated from Gaelic as corner of the field. It is the only Scotch distillery that triple-distils all of its spirit, a technique more associated with Ireland, which gives it a light, delicate character typical of the Lowlands. The distillery was badly damaged by bombing during the Clydebank Blitz of 1941, and Suntory has owned it since the 1990s.

originStory: Springbank was licensed in 1828 in Campbeltown, a town that once had around thirty distilleries and called itself the whisky capital of the world. It is one of the very few distilleries in Scotland to carry out every step on site, from malting all its barley on traditional floors to bottling, and it distils its namesake spirit two and a half times. The 10-year-old is its youngest regular bottling.

The site is now Scotland's largest grain distillery and also makes the base spirit for well-known gins and vodkas.

originStory: John Jameson, a Scot from Alloa, came to Dublin and took over the Bow Street distillery, which the brand dates to 1780. After Irish Distillers was formed in 1966, production moved in the 1970s to the new Midleton distillery in County Cork. The family motto, Sine Metu, meaning without fear, still appears on the label.

originStory: Bushmills prints 1608 on its labels, the year King James I granted Sir Thomas Phillips a licence to distil in the district around the River Bush in County Antrim, though the Old Bushmills Distillery Company itself was registered in 1784. The distillery near the Giant's Causeway is one of the oldest licensed distilleries in the world and makes triple-distilled malt whiskey. Original, sometimes called White Bush, blends that malt with grain whiskey and is the house's everyday bottling.

originStory: Bill Samuels Sr. bought the old Burks' Distillery at Star Hill Farm in Loretto, Kentucky, in 1953 and set out to make a softer bourbon, using red winter wheat in place of rye. originStory: Buffalo Trace Kentucky Straight Bourbon was launched in 1999, the year the Sazerac Company renamed its Frankfort distillery after the ancient buffalo trail that crossed the Kentucky River there. Small Batch marries four of the distillery's ten recipes, built from two mash bills and five yeast strains.

originStory: Four Roses traces its trademark to 1888 and Paul Jones Jr., and its Spanish Mission-style distillery near Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, built in 1910, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The distillery makes ten separate bourbons from two mash bills and five yeast strains, and the Single Barrel bottles just one of them, the high-rye OBSV recipe, at 100 proof. For decades Four Roses straight bourbon was sold only abroad, until Kirin bought the brand in 2002 and reintroduced it in the United States.

name: Elijah Craig Small Batch
description: Small Batch Bourbon from USA.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour into a rocks glass neat or over one big cube; small batch is blended for balance, so it rarely needs taming. Nose for vanilla and toasted nuts, then sip for the caramel mid-palate and gentle oak-spice finish that the blender worked to make consistent. It is the reliable house pour: great neat, great in an Old Fashioned, never a wasted dram.

originStory: Heaven Hill launched Elijah Craig in 1986 as a twelve-year-old small batch bourbon, and in 2016 it dropped the age statement to stretch its stocks. It is named after the Reverend Elijah Craig, an eighteenth-century Baptist preacher and early Kentucky distiller, whom legend credits with first charring barrels and so inventing bourbon, a story historians do not accept. Heaven Hill, a Bardstown family company founded in 1935, has distilled at the Bernheim distillery in Louisville since 1999, after a 1996 fire destroyed its Bardstown distillery.

name: Elijah Craig Barrel Proof
description: Cask Strength Bourbon from USA.
funFact: One of 5 Cask Strength Bourbon bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp, with water on standby
serve.how: Pour a smaller-than-usual measure into a Glencairn and approach in stages: nose gently from a distance first, since 60%-plus alcohol will singe an eager nostril. Take a tiny first sip to calibrate, then add water a few drops at a time, tasting between additions until the burnt sugar and dark cherry bloom out of the heat. Finding each barrel's ideal dilution point is the whole sport.

originStory: Elijah Craig Barrel Proof was introduced by Heaven Hill in 2013, an uncut and unfiltered version of its Elijah Craig bourbon, usually around twelve years old and released in three batches a year, each with its own proof and a code showing when it came out. The brand began in 1986 and takes its name from the Reverend Elijah Craig, a Baptist preacher and early Kentucky distiller credited by legend, though not by historians, with charring the first bourbon barrels.

originStory: Heaven Hill introduced Evan Williams in 1957, naming it after a Welsh-born settler whom the label credits as Kentucky's first distiller, working on the banks of the Ohio at Louisville in 1783. Historians have questioned both the date and the claim to be first, but the name stuck, and Evan Williams became one of Heaven Hill's leading bourbons. It is distilled at the Bernheim distillery in Louisville, and the Evan Williams Bourbon Experience stands on the city's Whiskey Row.

originStory: Evan Williams has been a Heaven Hill brand since 1957, named for an eighteenth-century Welsh settler said to have distilled at Louisville. The white-label Bottled-in-Bond follows the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897, a law passed to guarantee unadulterated whiskey: it must come from one distillery and one distilling season, age at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse and be bottled at 100 proof. Heaven Hill, a family company in Bardstown, has long been one of the main keepers of the bonded style.

originStory: George Garvin Brown, a Louisville pharmaceutical salesman, began selling Old Forester in 1870, presenting it as the first bourbon sold exclusively in sealed glass bottles, a guarantee against the tampering common at the time. The name is thought to honour Dr. William Forrester, a Louisville physician, though the second r was later dropped. Brown's firm became Brown-Forman, and Old Forester stayed on sale through Prohibition under one of the few licences to bottle whiskey for medicinal use, so the brand says it has been sold continuously by the same company since it began.

originStory: Old Forester dates from 1870, when George Garvin Brown began selling it in Louisville in sealed bottles, and it kept going through Prohibition under one of the few federal licences to bottle whiskey for medicinal use. The 1920 Prohibition Style, announced in 2016 as part of the Whiskey Row Series, is bottled at 115 proof, meant to evoke the robust bourbon the company sold on doctors' prescriptions in those years. The series retells the brand's history in chapters, each bottling named for a year in that history.

originStory: Henry McKenna, who had emigrated from Ireland, is said to have begun distilling in Fairfield, Kentucky, in 1855, and his name outlived his distillery. Each bottle is marked with its barrel number and the date the barrel was filled.

originStory: Longbranch arrived in 2018 as a collaboration between Wild Turkey and the actor Matthew McConaughey, who had become the brand's creative director in 2016. Developed with master distiller Eddie Russell, it is an eight-year-old Kentucky bourbon refined through charcoal from Texas mesquite and American oak, a nod to McConaughey's Texan roots alongside the brand's Kentucky home. Wild Turkey itself takes its name from a 1940 hunting trip on which an Austin Nichols executive shared the company's bourbon with friends.

Swirl once, nose in short sniffs, and sip slowly, noticing how the wheat trades rye's pepper for bread-dough and red-fruit roundness. Higher-proof bottles reward a teaspoon of water, which unlocks extra honey and vanilla.

originStory: Heaven Hill launched Larceny in 2012 as a wheated bourbon, and its name comes from a story attached to John E. Fitzgerald, whose name lives on in the Old Fitzgerald brand. As the brand tells it, Fitzgerald was a treasury agent with keys to the bonded warehouses who helped himself to the choicest barrels. Old Fitzgerald was a wheated bourbon from the Stitzel-Weller distillery, and Heaven Hill acquired the brand in 1999, building Larceny on the same style of recipe with wheat in place of rye.

originStory: This bourbon comes from the Barton distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, which dates its founding to 1879 and was long associated with the Tom Moore name, and it takes its name from the year Kentucky became a state. It began life as Ridgewood Reserve 1792, became 1792 Ridgemont Reserve after a trademark dispute, and later settled on 1792 Small Batch. The Sazerac Company, which bought the distillery in 2009, renamed it the Barton 1792 Distillery after the bourbon.

A single large cube softens the spice without erasing it. This is also the ideal Old Fashioned bourbon, since the rye kick stands up to sugar and bitters.

originStory: Tom Bulleit, a Louisville lawyer, started the Bulleit brand in 1987, saying he was reviving a high-rye recipe of his great-great-grandfather Augustus Bulleit, a tavern keeper who, according to the family's account, made whiskey from around 1830 until his death in 1860. The bourbon was distilled under contract at first; Seagram bought the brand in 1997, and it passed to Diageo, which opened its own Bulleit distillery near Shelbyville, Kentucky, in 2017.

originStory: Rittenhouse Rye takes its name from Rittenhouse Square in Philadelphia and belongs to the Pennsylvania tradition of rye whiskey that dominated early American distilling. It first appeared after Prohibition, and when the Pennsylvania distilleries closed the brand passed to Heaven Hill, which makes it in Kentucky. Bottled in bond at 100 proof, it was one of the few ryes still widely available when bartenders rediscovered classic cocktails, and it became a familiar bottle for the Manhattan and the Sazerac.

originStory: The Michter's name was coined in the 1950s by Louis Forman, who owned an old distillery at Schaefferstown, Pennsylvania, and named his whiskey after his sons Michael and Peter. Chatham Imports later revived the name, and Michter's whiskeys have been made in Kentucky since the 2000s, with the company opening its own distillery in Shively. US*1 is its core range.

originStory: Rendezvous Rye was among the first releases of High West, which David and Jane Perkins opened in Park City, Utah, in 2007 as the state's first licensed distillery since Prohibition. The whiskey blends older and younger straight ryes sourced from other distilleries, and its name recalls the rendezvous of the Rocky Mountain fur trade, the summer gatherings where trappers met traders. High West, now part of Constellation Brands, has since added whiskey from its own stills in Utah.

name: Pikesville Rye
description: Rye Whiskey from USA.
funFact: One of 11 Rye Whiskey bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers neat and take a small first sip: rye bites first with black pepper and baking spice, then charms with mint and dried fruit as your palate adjusts. A large cube rounds the edges if the spice runs sharp. And if you make one cocktail with it, make a Manhattan, rye is what the drink was born with.

originStory: Pikesville Rye takes its name from Pikesville, Maryland, outside Baltimore, and is one of the last survivors of the Maryland rye style, once a rival to Pennsylvania's in American bars. After Prohibition the brand passed through Maryland producers before Heaven Hill acquired it and moved production to Kentucky. Heaven Hill later relaunched it as a six-year-old bottled at 110 proof, a much stronger whiskey than the version long sold around Baltimore.

originStory: Old Overholt is dated to 1810, when Abraham Overholt took over his family's farm distillery at West Overton, Pennsylvania, and made it into a business. His grandson, the industrialist Henry Clay Frick, later became a partner along with Andrew Mellon, and the whiskey carried the Old Overholt name with Abraham's stern portrait on the label. A medicinal whiskey permit carried the brand through Prohibition, and it is often called America's oldest continuously maintained whiskey brand. Beam has made it in Kentucky since 1987.

originStory: The modern Templeton Rye was introduced in 2006, drawing on the story of the bootleg rye made by farmers around Templeton, Iowa, during Prohibition, which local lore says was a favourite of Al Capone. For years the whiskey was distilled in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, by MGP, and after a class-action settlement in 2015 the labels were changed to say so and to drop claims about a Prohibition-era recipe. The company has since built its own distillery in Templeton to make the whiskey in Iowa.

name: Jack Daniel's Old No. 7
description: Tennessee Whiskey from USA.
funFact: One of 5 Tennessee Whiskey bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers into a rocks glass and sip neat first, looking for the signature banana-and-caramel softness the charcoal mellowing leaves behind. One large cube stretches it into an easy evening drink, and it famously partners with cola in a tall glass when the mood is casual. Notice how the finish is gentler than a comparable bourbon; that is the Lincoln County Process at work.

originStory: Jack Daniel's labels say the distillery was established and registered in 1866 in Lynchburg, Tennessee, though Daniel's biographer argues the business was not registered until 1875. Jasper Newton 'Jack' Daniel learned to distil from the preacher Dan Call and from Nathan 'Nearest' Green, an enslaved man who became the distillery's first master distiller after emancipation. The whiskey is filtered through sugar maple charcoal, the Lincoln County Process. Why it is called Old No. 7 remains unclear, and Brown-Forman has owned the company since 1956.

originStory: Schenley first bottled George Dickel Tennessee Whisky in 1964, from a distillery Ralph Dupps had rebuilt at Cascade Hollow near Tullahoma, close to where Cascade whisky was made in the nineteenth century. George A. Dickel, a German-born Nashville merchant, had sold that Cascade whisky, and the brand keeps the Scottish spelling, whisky without an e. The spirit is chilled before it is filtered through sugar maple charcoal, a Dickel signature, and the distillery now belongs to Diageo.

originStory: Fawn Weaver launched Uncle Nearest in 2017 to honour Nathan 'Nearest' Green, an enslaved man who taught the young Jack Daniel to distil and became Jack Daniel's first master distiller after emancipation. Weaver set out to document his story after reading about him in a 2016 New York Times article, and Victoria Eady Butler, Green's great-great-granddaughter, became the brand's master blender. The 1856 bottling is one of its premium aged whiskeys, and the company opened its own Nearest Green Distillery in Shelbyville, Tennessee.

name: Balcones Texas Single Malt
description: American Single Malt from USA.
funFact: One of 5 American Single Malt bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a standard dram into a Glencairn, swirl gently, and nose in short sniffs with your mouth slightly open to catch malt, chocolate, and orchard fruit. Sip neat first, then add a few drops of water to unlock the toasted-oak depths; many American single malts run above 43% and open beautifully. Compare it mentally to Scotch, the malt DNA is the same but the New World oak speaks louder.

originStory: Chip Tate founded Balcones Distilling in Waco, Texas, in 2008, building stills by hand in a former welding shop beneath a bridge, and named it after the Balcones Escarpment, the fault line that crosses central Texas. Texas Single Malt became one of its core whiskies, matured in a climate whose summer heat works the casks hard. Tate left the company in 2014, and Balcones has since moved into a larger distillery in downtown Waco, where Texas Single Malt is still made.

originStory: Steve McCarthy founded Clear Creek Distillery in Portland, Oregon, in 1985, using fruit from his family's Hood River orchards to make European-style eaux-de-vie. He went on to make an Islay-style whiskey: McCarthy's Oregon Single Malt, made from peated barley imported from Scotland and aged partly in Oregon oak, became one of the early single malts of the American craft era. Hood River Distillers bought Clear Creek in 2014 and continues the whiskey.

name: Mellow Corn
description: Straight Corn Whiskey from USA.
funFact: One of 2 Straight Corn Whiskey bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour neat and taste it as a history lesson: with no new charred oak allowed, the sweet corn and popcorn notes stay front and center the way early American whiskey would have tasted. Sip slowly and notice the honeyed softness and only a whisper of wood on the finish. A single cube is fine, but heavy dilution washes out its delicate grain character.

originStory: Mellow Corn is a rare bottled-in-bond corn whiskey, made by Heaven Hill, the Bardstown, Kentucky, family company founded in 1935. Corn whiskey descends from the frontier spirits of early American settlers: by law it must be at least 80 percent corn, and when aged it goes into used or uncharred barrels, which keep it paler and closer to the grain. As a bonded whiskey it is aged at least four years, comes from a single distilling season and is bottled at 100 proof.

Balcones takes its name from the Balcones Escarpment, the fault line that runs across central Texas past Waco.

name: Bernheim Original Wheat
description: Wheat Whiskey from USA.
funFact: The only Wheat Whiskey bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a generous ounce and a half into a Glencairn and let it sit for a minute or two so the alcohol vapors settle. Nose it gently with your mouth slightly open, then take a small sip and let it coat your tongue before swallowing. Look for the soft fresh-bread and honey sweetness that sets wheat whiskey apart from spicier rye-heavy pours; a few drops of water will open it up if the 45-50% proof reads hot.

originStory: Heaven Hill introduced Bernheim Original in 2005 as a straight wheat whiskey, with winter wheat as its main grain, a style hardly seen on American shelves at the time. It is named after Isaac Wolfe Bernheim, a German immigrant who built a whiskey business in Louisville in the late nineteenth century and created the I. W. Harper brand. Heaven Hill had bought the Bernheim distillery in Louisville in 1999 and makes its whiskeys there, including this one.

name: Fireball
description: Flavored Whiskey from USA.
funFact: One of 2 Flavored Whiskey bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Keep it in the fridge or freezer and serve as a chilled shot, where the cinnamon-candy or honeyed sweetness plays best. Over ice in a rocks glass it drinks like a low-effort dessert; topped with lemonade, apple cider, or ginger beer it becomes an easy porch highball. Do not overthink it, this category is engineered for fun, not contemplation.

originStory: Fireball was developed by Seagram in the mid-1980s as one of a line of flavoured spirits, originally sold as Dr. McGillicuddy's Fireball Whisky and built on Canadian whisky. The Sazerac Company of New Orleans bought the brand and recipe in 1989, and in 2007 gave it its present name and look as Fireball Cinnamon Whisky. Its flavour recalls the hard cinnamon candies known as fireballs, and the brand remains part of the Sazerac portfolio.

Steven, a restaurant and bar owner, had created a peanut butter flavoured whiskey drink for his bar, and its local following led the couple to bottle a peanut butter whiskey of their own. name: Ole Smoky Moonshine
description: Moonshine from USA.
funFact: One of 2 Moonshine bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve it cold, straight from the freezer if you like, in the traditional mason jar; the chill tames the raw ethanol edge and lets the sweet corn flavor through. Sip in small pulls rather than gulps, and taste for the popcorn-like graininess that barrel aging would normally polish away. It also mixes cheerfully with lemonade, sweet tea, or apple cider for a backporch punch.

originStory: Ole Smoky opened in 2010 in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, after a change in state law allowed distilleries in many more counties, and presented itself as the first federally licensed distillery in the history of East Tennessee. Its founders set out to bottle the moonshine tradition of the Great Smoky Mountains, where families had long made unaged corn whiskey out of sight of the revenue men, and sold it in mason jars. Its jars and flavoured moonshines helped popularise legal moonshine across the country.

Piedmont, billed as North Carolina's first legal distillery since Prohibition, worked from the town's old train depot.

originStory: Samuel Bronfman of Seagram created Crown Royal in 1939 as a tribute to King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, whose royal tour of Canada that year was the first by a reigning monarch. It is made at Gimli, Manitoba, on the shore of Lake Winnipeg, and now belongs to Diageo.

Canadian Club received a royal warrant from Queen Victoria and now belongs to Suntory Global Spirits.

originStory: John K. Hall, a winemaker, took over the Kittling Ridge winery and distillery at Grimsby, Ontario, in 1992 and set about making whisky with a winemaker's approach, distilling rye, barley and corn separately and ageing each before blending, much like a meritage wine. Its reception abroad helped change how many whisky drinkers saw Indian single malt. Amrut takes its name from amrit, the Sanskrit word for the nectar of the gods.

Nose for mango-adjacent tropical fruit and barley sugar, then sip and follow the spice into toasted oak. Bottlings often run 46-50%, so keep water handy and add a few drops if the jammy fruit feels buried under heat.

originStory: McDowell's takes its name from McDowell and Co., set up in British India by the Scottish trader Angus McDowell in the nineteenth century. The company passed into Indian hands in the middle of the twentieth century and became the core of the UB Group's spirits business, now United Spirits, part of Diageo. Like most Indian whisky, McDowell's No.1 is a blend built largely on spirit distilled from molasses, and it grew into one of the best-known whisky names in India.

originStory: Kavalan is the whisky of the King Car Group, a Taiwanese food and drinks company, which built its distillery in Yuanshan, Yilan County, in 2005 and ran its first spirit in 2006. The name is the old name for Yilan, taken from the Kavalan people, and the subtropical climate between the sea and the mountains makes the whisky mature much faster than it would in Scotland.

Its Madeira expression, matured in ex-bourbon barrels and finished in Madeira wine casks, became the house's signature.

Classic, matured mainly in ex-bourbon casks with some red wine casks, is the house single malt, and the distillery also ages casks by the Dead Sea, the lowest place on land.

originStory: David Vitale founded Starward in Melbourne in 2007, setting out to make a whisky that reflected Australia rather than imitating Scotland. The distillery leaned on the country's wine industry, maturing its single malt in barrels that had held Australian red wine, and moved from its first home at Essendon Fields to a larger site in Port Melbourne. Nova, aged entirely in red wine barrels such as shiraz, cabernet and pinot noir, became its flagship, and Diageo's Distill Ventures invested in the business.

The distillery's small, single cask releases of Tasmanian barley malt drew international attention, and the French Oak expression is matured in French oak casks that once held Australian fortified wine.

Patel presented it as proof that France, better known for brandy and wine, could make a single malt with its own accent.

originStory: Zuidam Distillers was founded in 1975 by Fred van Zuidam at Baarle-Nassau, in the southern Netherlands, and is now run by his son Patrick. The family began distilling malt whisky in the late 1990s and called it Millstone, after the traditional Dutch windmills that grind its grain. The 10-year-old is one of the range's longer-aged single malts, and the distillery also makes genever and liqueurs in the Dutch tradition.

originStory: Florian Stetter, a trained brewer and maltster, founded Slyrs in 1999 at Schliersee in the Bavarian Alps, an early pioneer of German single malt. The name comes from Slyrse, the old Bavarian name for the Schliersee lake and its monastery. The first release was small and sold locally, and the whisky is made from Bavarian barley, double distilled in copper pot stills and matured in new American oak.

originStory: Säntis Malt comes from Brauerei Locher, a family brewery in Appenzell, Switzerland, which began making whisky in 1999, as soon as Swiss law allowed spirits to be distilled from grain. originStory: Hammer Head began with a stock of single malt distilled in 1989 at the Prádlo distillery near Plzeň, part of the Czech spirits firm Stock, in the last months of Czechoslovakia's communist era. After the Velvet Revolution the casks were left largely undisturbed, the story goes, until the whisky was rediscovered and first released in 2011 as a 20-year-old. The 23-year-old is a later release from the same stock, made from Czech barley and matured in Czech oak.

originStory: Murree Brewery was founded in 1860 at Ghora Gali, near the hill station of Murree, to supply beer to British troops, and later brewed at Rawalpindi. Since the 1940s it has been controlled by the Parsi Bhandara family, and it added whisky to its range, maturing malt in Pakistan. Alcohol has been prohibited for Muslims in Pakistan since 1977, so Murree sells mainly to non-Muslims and foreigners, and it remains one of very few legal distillers in the Muslim world.

name: Tanqueray London Dry
description: London Dry Gin from England.

serve.how: London dry is at its best ice-cold and bracing: stir it into a martini with dry vermouth over plenty of ice, strain into a chilled coupe, and finish with a lemon twist expressed over the surface. For a simpler serve, build a gin and tonic over abundant ice with a wedge of lime. Either way, nose before sipping and let the piney juniper hit first, then hunt for the citrus peel and coriander backbone that follow.

originStory: Charles Tanqueray began distilling gin in Bloomsbury, London, in 1830, as the London dry style was taking shape. His son Charles Waugh Tanqueray built up the business, which merged with Gordon's in 1898, and the gin's squat green bottle is often said to have been inspired by a cocktail shaker, though no one has proved it. Tanqueray became a favourite for the martini and the gin and tonic in America in the twentieth century, and today it is distilled at Cameronbridge in Fife.

originStory: In the early 1860s the pharmacist James Burrough bought a distillery in Chelsea, London, and began making gin and liqueurs. Its botanicals are steeped in the spirit for a day before distillation.

originStory: Alexander Gordon, a Scot, opened a gin distillery in Southwark, London, in 1769, and moved it to Goswell Road in Clerkenwell in 1786. The boar's head on the label comes from the Gordon clan's arms, linked to a legend of a Gordon saving a Scottish king from a wild boar. In 1898 Gordon's merged with Tanqueray, and the gin went on to hold royal warrants and become one of the most familiar names in gin. It is now distilled at Cameronbridge in Fife.

originStory: Sipsmith was founded in 2009 by Sam Galsworthy and Fairfax Hall, with the drinks historian Jared Brown as master distiller, and set up in a small building in Hammersmith, west London, with a copper pot still named Prudence. Licensing a still that small took a long negotiation with HM Revenue and Customs, and the brand presents itself as the first copper pot distillery to open in London in nearly two centuries. Beam Suntory took a controlling stake in 2016, and Sipsmith now distils in Chiswick.

serve.how: At 57%+, this gin rewards cold and dilution: stash the bottle in the freezer, then pour a small measure into a chilled coupe, or stir it into a martini where the extra proof keeps the juniper vivid through the ice. If sipping it straight, add a few drops of water and let it sit a minute before nosing. Notice how the pepper-and-heat edge recedes as it opens, leaving intense juniper and bright citrus oils.

It is bottled at 57.7 percent, and juniper is used more than once in its making to push the pine character to the front. The distillery's copper stills, starting with Prudence, are all given women's names.

originStory: Plymouth Gin has been distilled at the Black Friars Distillery in Plymouth since 1793, in a building dating from 1431 that is reputed to have been a Dominican monastery, and local tradition says some of the Pilgrim Fathers stayed there before the Mayflower sailed in 1620. The port's naval links made Plymouth a long-standing supplier to the Royal Navy, and navy strength, at 57 percent, is usually explained by the old shipboard test: gunpowder soaked with gin of that strength would still ignite.

originStory: Hayman's is run by descendants of James Burrough, the pharmacist who created Beefeater, and the family dates its gin making to 1863, when Burrough began distilling in Chelsea. Taste for the rounded, honeyed edge that softens the juniper; that gentle sweetness is the whole point of the style.

originStory: Christian Jensen, a Dane working in London, set out in the early 2000s to recreate the style of older London gins, inspired, the story goes, by a bottle he tasted in a Tokyo bar. Originally made under contract, the gins are now distilled under a railway arch in Bermondsey, south-east London.

name: Hendrick's
description: Contemporary Gin from Scotland. Cucumber and rose.
funFact: Hendrick's: Cucumber and rose

serve.how: Build a Spanish-style gin tonic: fill a large copa glass to the top with ice, pour in two ounces of well-chilled gin, add a quality tonic slowly down a bar spoon, and garnish to match the botanicals — cucumber for fresh styles, rose petals or grapefruit for floral and citrus-led ones. The big bowl traps the aromatics, so nose the glass before each sip. Taste for what leads: in these modern gins the juniper steps back and the signature botanical should shine.

originStory: Hendrick's was launched in 1999 by William Grant & Sons, created by Lesley Gracie at the company's Girvan distillery on the Ayrshire coast of Scotland. Gracie blends spirit from two very different stills, a Bennett still and a Carter-Head still, and then adds essences of cucumber and Bulgarian rose, an unusual pairing that set it apart from classic London dry gins. With its dark apothecary-style bottle, it is often credited with helping to start the modern gin revival. The name is said to honour a gardener once employed by the Grant family.

originStory: The Botanist was launched in 2010 by Bruichladdich, the Islay whisky distillery, and is distilled slowly in Ugly Betty, a Lomond still rescued from the closed Inverleven distillery. Its recipe adds 22 botanicals hand-foraged on Islay, among them heather, bog myrtle and sweet cicely, to nine classic gin aromatics, and the foraging was guided by the local botanists Richard and Mavis Gulliver. It was devised under Jim McEwan, then Bruichladdich's master distiller.

originStory: The Isle of Harris Distillery opened in the village of Tarbert, in the Outer Hebrides, in 2015. It was set up by Anderson Bakewell, a man with long ties to the island, chiefly to bring steady work to a small community whose young people were leaving. originStory: Monkey 47 was launched in 2010 by Alexander Stein and the distiller Christoph Keller in Germany's Black Forest. Its makers tell of Montgomery Collins, a British airman who settled in the Black Forest after the Second World War, opened a guesthouse called The Wild Monkey and made a gin of his own, and they present the brand as a revival of his recipe. The 47 counts both the botanicals, many gathered locally, including lingonberries, and the strength at which it is bottled.

description: Genever from Netherlands.

Sip slowly and notice how the malty, bready base makes it read halfway between whisky and gin. Richer oude and barrel-aged genevers deserve slightly warmer service so the honeyed malt can open up.

originStory: The Bols family opened their distillery, 't Lootsje, or the little shed, outside the walls of Amsterdam in 1575, and the company calls itself the oldest distilling brand in the world. The Bols Genever sold today was relaunched in 2008 from a recipe the company dates to the early nineteenth century, a malty style aimed at cocktails.

Sip slowly and notice the tart plum and jammy fruit up front giving way to a subtle almond note from the sloe stones.

originStory: Plymouth Gin has been distilled on the same premises in the Barbican quarter of Plymouth since 1793, in a building known as the Black Friars distillery, and the house says its sloe gin follows a recipe from the late nineteenth century. Sloe gin itself is an English country tradition: the hard, sour fruit of the blackthorn, picked from the hedgerows in autumn, is steeped in gin with sugar until the spirit turns a deep ruby red.

originStory: Alexander Gordon, a Londoner of Scottish descent, began distilling gin in 1769, and his London dry recipe went on to become one of the most familiar gins in the world. Gordon's added a sloe gin to the range in 1906, steeping sloes, the small sour fruit of the blackthorn, in gin with sugar in the manner of English country households. The wild boar on the label recalls a legend in which a member of Clan Gordon saved a Scottish king from a charging boar.

originStory: Beefeater began in 1863, when the pharmacist James Burrough, who had bought a distillery in Chelsea the year before, started producing his own gin; the name, adopted later, refers to the Yeomen of the Guard, the ceremonial bodyguards of the British monarch. The distillery has stood in Kennington, south London, since the 1950s. Beefeater Pink adds strawberry to the classic London dry recipe and arrived as pink gin became a craze in Britain in the late 2010s.

originStory: Absolut's name goes back to Lars Olsson Smith, the nineteenth-century Stockholm spirits entrepreneur who introduced Absolut rent brännvin, or absolutely pure brännvin, made by repeated rectification, in 1879, the year from which the brand dates itself. The state monopoly Vin & Sprit revived the name a century later for an export vodka, launched in the United States in 1979 in a clear bottle modelled on an old apothecary flask, with the lettering printed straight on the glass.

It is the luxury expression of the vodka that Vin & Sprit launched for export in 1979.

name: Smirnoff No. 21

serve.how: Store the bottle in the freezer and pour small measures into chilled shot glasses — the cold thickens the texture to a silky, almost viscous pour. Sip rather than slam it, and pay attention to the finish: good grain vodka shows faint cream, white pepper, and mineral notes instead of burn. Serve it alongside salty little bites, Eastern European style, refilling glasses in rounds.

originStory: Smirnoff began in Moscow in 1864, when Pyotr Smirnov founded a vodka distillery that pioneered charcoal filtration and was reportedly a favourite of the Russian court. After the revolution his son Vladimir fled and rebuilt the business abroad under the French-style spelling Smirnoff, and in the 1930s the American rights passed to Rudolph Kunett and then to Heublein, which made it a global brand. No. 21 is the flagship vodka, and Smirnoff is no longer made in Russia.

In 2022, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, SPI renamed its version Stoli.

He worked with François Thibault, a cognac cellar master, who developed the recipe in the Cognac region using soft winter wheat from Picardy and spring water from Gensac-la-Pallue. A frosted bottle with geese in flight completed the pitch, and Frank sold the brand to Bacardi in 2004.

Potato was its first spirit and remains the house signature, made from potatoes grown in the surrounding region and distilled four times. The Dorda family, who run the distillery, later added rye and wheat versions to show how the base ingredient changes a vodka's taste.

Today the Polmos Białystok distillery makes it, with a hand-picked, naturally dried blade of the grass in every bottle.

originStory: Starka, from the Polish word for old, is an aged rye spirit known in Poland and Lithuania since at least the fifteenth century, and later a favourite of the nobility of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Modern Starka is aged in oak with small additions of apple and linden leaves, and Starka 10 has rested for ten years.

originStory: Bacardí began in Santiago de Cuba on 4 February 1862, when Facundo Bacardí Massó, a merchant from Sitges in Catalonia, and his brother José bought a small distillery. Facundo set out to make a lighter, smoother rum by filtering and ageing it, and fruit bats roosting in the rafters gave his wife Amalia the idea for the bat emblem. Carta Blanca, the house's white rum, became a classic base for the Daiquirí and the Mojito; after the revolution the family carried on outside Cuba, chiefly from Puerto Rico.

originStory: J. Wray & Nephew began in 1825, when John Wray opened the Shakespeare Tavern in Kingston and started blending and selling rum. originStory: Mount Gay's oldest surviving deed dates from 1703, and the company calls itself the oldest commercial rum distillery in the world. Eclipse, the house's signature blend, was developed in the early twentieth century and named for the solar eclipse and the passing of Halley's comet in 1910. Rémy Cointreau has been the majority owner since 1989.

originStory: Ron Zacapa was created in 1976 to celebrate the hundredth anniversary of the founding of Zacapa, a town in eastern Guatemala, and its blends were developed by the chemist Alejandro Burgaleta for Industrias Licoreras de Guatemala. The rum is made from concentrated virgin sugarcane honey and aged in a solera system high in the mountains near Quetzaltenango, under master blender Lorena Vásquez. The 23 on the label refers to the solera, which combines rums of different ages, the oldest up to 23 years.

originStory: Flor de Caña, Spanish for sugarcane flower, grew from Nicaragua Sugar Estates, founded in 1890 at Chichigalpa at the foot of the San Cristóbal volcano, which appears on the label. The Italian-born entrepreneur Francisco Alfredo Pellas was its majority shareholder, and rum was first made there in small quantities for employees and partners; the Flor de Caña brand itself was created in 1937. The Pellas family still owns the company, and the 12 Year Old is aged in ex-bourbon barrels.

originStory: Matusalem was founded in Santiago de Cuba in 1872 by the brothers Benjamín and Eduardo Camp, who brought from Spain the solera method of blending used for sherry and brandy. The name is Spanish for Methuselah, the biblical patriarch famed for his long life. After the Cuban revolution the family took the brand into exile, and Matusalem is now produced in the Dominican Republic. Gran Reserva 15 is built on that solera tradition.

The family launched Don Q, named after Don Quixote, Cervantes's errant knight, in 1932, and it became one of the island's best-known rums. Don Q Cristal is the house's white rum, aged and then filtered clear.

name: Rhum Clément VSOP
description: Rhum Agricole from Martinique.
funFact: One of 4 Rhum Agricole bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Drink it the Martinique way: a short pour in a rocks glass at room temperature, ideally as a Ti' Punch — a squeeze of lime disc and a small spoon of cane syrup stirred right in the glass. Neat, swirl gently and breathe in the fresh-cut-grass and green-olive aromas that molasses rums never show. Skip heavy ice on aged expressions; the vegetal character is delicate and fades when over-chilled.

originStory: Homère Clément, a doctor and politician from Martinique, bought the Habitation Acajou estate at Le François in 1887, and the family later turned it to making rhum agricole, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice rather than molasses. The estate, now Habitation Clément, became one of the island's leading rum houses, and its gardens and old cellars are open to visitors. Clément VSOP is aged for at least four years in oak, under the Martinique AOC rules granted to the island's agricole rums in 1996.

originStory: Dupré Barbancourt, from the cognac country of the Charente in France, founded his distillery in Haiti in 1862 and applied the cognac method of double distillation to fresh sugarcane juice. After his death the business passed to his wife, Nathalie Gardère, and her nephew Paul, and the Gardère family has run it ever since, through the 2010 earthquake that destroyed many of its ageing barrels. The Five Star, labelled Réserve Spéciale, is aged for around eight years in oak.

name: Clairin Sajous
description: Clairin from Haiti.
funFact: One of 2 Clairin bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour a modest ounce and a half neat into a rocks glass and let it sit for a minute — wild-ferment cane spirits open up dramatically with a little air. Sip slowly and hunt for the olive-brine savoriness underneath the fresh cane and tropical fruit; every bottling is different, so taste it blind before deciding whether it needs a cube. If the proof runs hot (many are 50%+), a single large cube or a few drops of water tames the fire without muting the funk.

originStory: Clairin is Haiti's rustic cane spirit, made at hundreds of small village distilleries from native cane varieties, wild fermentation and traditional stills. Clairin Sajous comes from Michel Sajous's Chelo distillery at Saint-Michel-de-l'Attalaye, in the north of the country, where he grows his own cane. It reached the wider world in 2014, when the Italian bottler Luca Gargano of Velier released it in a series called The Spirit of Haiti, introducing clairin to bartenders far beyond the island.

originStory: Clairin Communal is a blend of clairins from several small Haitian distilleries, released by Luca Gargano's Velier as a companion to the single-distillery bottlings that first carried clairin abroad in the 2010s. Each component is made in the traditional village way, from native cane varieties fermented with wild yeasts and distilled without filtration. As the name suggests, the blend presents clairin, long drunk almost entirely within Haiti, as a shared national tradition rather than the work of a single still.

originStory: James Gosling sailed from England in 1806 with goods bound for America, but when his ship's charter ran out he put in at Bermuda and set up shop there instead. The family began blending rum in 1860 and soon developed a dark, full-bodied Old Rum, sold first from the barrel and then in Champagne bottles salvaged from the British garrison's officers' messes and sealed with black wax. Customers asked for the black seal rum, and the name stuck. Goslings holds the trademark for the Dark 'n Stormy.

name: Rivers Royale Grenadian
description: Rivers Royale from Grenada.
funFact: The only Rivers Royale bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat in tiny measures, which is how Grenadians take it, or cut heavily with water or coconut water. At 75% it cannot legally be carried on an aircraft, so it is genuinely a drink you have to go there for.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented wild and pot-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh cane juice from the estate's own fields

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Wood-fired copper pot stills; cane crushed by water wheel

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Wild fermentation in open stone tanks gives the funk, and the wood fire gives the rest.

originStory: Rivers rum is made at the River Antoine Estate in St Patrick, in the north-east of Grenada, a sugar estate dating from the late eighteenth century that is often cited as the oldest functioning water-powered distillery in the Caribbean. A water wheel still crushes the cane, the juice ferments in open tanks, and the spirit is distilled in wood-fired pot stills. Rivers Royale is the estate's bottling of this raw cane spirit, sold mostly on the island.

name: Cruzan Single Barrel
description: Gold Rum from US Virgin Islands.
funFact: One of 14 Gold Rum bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: This is an easygoing sipper: pour two fingers into a rocks glass, neat or over a single large cube. Take a small first sip to acclimate, then look for the caramel, vanilla, and ripe banana that the oak has coaxed out of the cane. It is also forgiving in a highball with soda and a lime wedge on hot days.

composition.summary: Molasses rum mellowed by a few years in oak barrels.

components.label: Base

components.label: Distillation

originStory: Cruzan traces its rum to 1760 and Estate Diamond on St Croix, then part of the Danish West Indies, and the Nelthropp family has managed the distillery for eight generations through many changes of ownership. The name echoes Crucian, the word for a native of St Croix. Single Barrel is the brand's premium blend: rums aged from five to twelve years are married and then rested again in new oak, one barrel at a time.

name: Pusser's Gunpowder Proof
description: Overproof Rum from British Virgin Islands.
funFact: One of 2 Overproof Rum bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: At 57%+ this is not a neat-pour spirit for most people — serve a small measure over one large cube, or better yet lengthen it into a highball with plenty of ice in its natural habitat, a tiki mug. If you do taste it neat, take tiny sips and let the ripe banana and burnt sugar punch through the heat; a splash of water reveals surprising fruit. Keep it well away from open flames unless you actually intend the theatrical float.

composition.summary: Molasses rum bottled far above standard strength.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, as with most Caribbean rum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column stills, simply proofed down much less

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often unaged and clear; some aged versions exist

composition.process: Minimal dilution after distillation keeps both the flavour and the fire intact.

originStory: Pusser's was founded in 1979 by Charles Tobias, who won the Admiralty's blessing to recreate the rum the Royal Navy had issued to its sailors until the last daily tot in 1970, and set up blending and bottling on Tortola in the British Virgin Islands. Pusser is naval slang for purser, the officer who issued the ration, and a share of sales goes to a Royal Navy sailors' fund. Gunpowder Proof recalls the old test in which rum poured on gunpowder that still lit was proof it had not been watered.

name: Captain Morgan Spiced
description: Spiced Rum from Jamaica.
funFact: One of 4 Spiced Rum bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Spiced rum is happiest long and cold: fill a highball with ice, pour two ounces, and top with cola or ginger beer plus a lime wedge. The vanilla and cinnamon are built to mingle with a mixer rather than stand alone, though a chilled neat pour works as an easy after-dinner nip. Notice how the clove and caramel bloom on the finish once the initial sweetness fades.

components.label: Base

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Strength

composition.process: The spice blend and added sugar happen post-distillation, which is why brands taste so different.

originStory: The Seagram company created Captain Morgan rum in 1944 and named it after Sir Henry Morgan, the seventeenth-century Welsh privateer who raided Spanish ports and later served as lieutenant governor of Jamaica. Original Spiced arrived in the United States in 1984 and made the brand a household name; Diageo bought it in 2001, and its rum is now made in the US Virgin Islands. In Jamaica, J. Wray & Nephew holds the rights and makes Captain Morgan locally.

Its inky colour and sea-monster branding set it apart on the shelf.

The company launched a spiced navy-style rum with Collins's hula girl artwork on the label, honouring a man whose bold designs helped shape the American traditional style before his death in the 1970s. William Grant & Sons bought the rum business in 2008.

originStory: Malibu was created in 1978 by Tom Jago of International Distillers and Vintners, at first in Curaçao, as a coconut-flavoured rum drink meant to make piña coladas easier to mix. When it took off, production moved to Barbados, where the rum comes from the West Indies Rum Distillery, the column still distillery George Stade built on the beach at Blackrock in 1893. Pernod Ricard has owned the brand since 2005. Despite its Caribbean image, it is named after the California beach town.

name: Stroh 80
description: Stroh from Austria.
funFact: The only Stroh bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Almost nobody drinks the 80% neat, and nobody should. It belongs in Jagertee with black tea, in punch, or over apple strudel. The 38% and 40% versions are drinkable straight, cold, in very small amounts.

composition.summary: Neutral or cane spirit flavoured with vanilla and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rum and neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Vanilla, spice and caramel to a secret formula

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended rather than redistilled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 38%, 40%, 60% and 80% expressions

composition.process: Because it was designed to imitate rum rather than be one, it leans harder on spice than any cane spirit would.

originStory: Stroh was founded in 1832 by Sebastian Stroh in Carinthia, then part of the Austrian Empire, and later moved to Klagenfurt. With no tropical colonies to supply real rum, Austria-Hungary regulated its own Inländer-Rum, or domestic rum, made from local spirit flavoured and coloured to suggest the Caribbean original, and Stroh became its most famous name. Stroh 80 is used mainly as an ingredient, in baking and in hot drinks such as Jagatee, and the name has become a byword for the style in German-speaking countries.

name: Ron Miel Guanche
description: Ron Miel from Spain.
funFact: The only Ron Miel bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Chilled and neat in a small glass, or over ice. Canarians drink it after dinner and pour it over ice cream. It is sweet enough that anything more than a small measure becomes hard work.

composition.summary: Canary rum blended with honey and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rum distilled in the Canary Islands

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bee honey or palm honey, vanilla, cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: Palm honey, made from boiled palm sap rather than by bees, gives the more traditional version its darker edge.

originStory: Ron miel, or honey rum, is a speciality of the Canary Islands, where sugarcane was grown long before the Caribbean rum trade took shape. It is a sweet blend of rum and honey that must contain at least two percent honey, and the Canary Islands government protects the style under the name Ronmiel de Canarias. Guanche takes its name from the Guanches, the islands' indigenous people before the Spanish conquest.

name: Ypióca Ouro
description: Cachaça from Brazil.
funFact: One of 5 Cachaça bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp, neat (unaged) or one cube (aged)
serve.how: Sip artisanal unaged cachaça neat at room temperature in a rocks or small tulip glass, nosing for the fresh-cane, grass, and green-banana brightness that column rum lacks; barrel-aged expressions take a single cube well. And of course, muddle lime and sugar in a rocks glass, add ice and a generous pour, and you have Brazil's caipirinha — the drink this spirit was destined for. Notice how the vegetal cane character stays lively even under citrus.

components.label: Strength

composition.process: Distilling fresh juice rather than molasses is exactly why it refuses to be called rum.

originStory: Ypióca was founded in 1846 by Dario Telles de Menezes, a Portuguese immigrant, at Maranguape in the north-eastern state of Ceará, and it grew into what is described as the oldest continuously active private company in Brazil. The family business expanded into farming and mineral water while keeping cachaça at its heart, and Diageo bought the Ypióca brand in 2012. Ouro, meaning gold, is aged in wooden casks, which give it the colour of its name.

It is distilled from fresh sugarcane juice in Minas Gerais, the inland state with the country's deepest tradition of artisanal cachaça, and briefly rested in French oak before bottling. Bacardi later took over the brand as the caipirinha spread through cocktail menus abroad.

The Campari Group bought the brand in 2011.

originStory: Novo Fogo, Portuguese for new fire, is an organic cachaça from Morretes, a small town in the state of Paraná in southern Brazil, where the Serra do Mar mountains meet the Atlantic rainforest. It reached the United States around the turn of the 2010s, part of a wave of premium cachaças that followed the caipirinha abroad. Silver is the unaged expression, distilled in copper alembics and rested without wood to keep the fresh character of the cane.

name: Avuá Amburana
description: Cachaça Envelhecida from Brazil.
funFact: The only Cachaça Envelhecida bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, the way you would drink an aged rum. Using a good envelhecida in a caipirinha is not a crime, but the wood notes fight the lime, so the unaged version is better there.

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least one year in casks of amburana, jequitibá, bálsamo, ipê or oak

composition.process: Brazilian law recognises around thirty native woods for ageing, each with its own flavour signature.

originStory: Avuá was founded in 2013 by Pete Nevenglosky and Nate Whitehouse, who partnered with master distiller Katia Espírito Santo at her family's small distillery in Carmo, in the hills of Rio de Janeiro state. The cachaça is made in copper alembics from sugarcane grown on the property. Amburana takes its name from one of the native Brazilian woods that cachaça makers have long used for ageing, which gives warm notes of cinnamon and clove.

His sons began distilling rum in the 1930s, and the family still runs the Hacienda San Isidro, where the cane is grown and the rum is made. Abuelo is Spanish for grandfather, and the 12 Year Old is aged in American oak barrels.

name: Guaro Cacique
description: Guaro from Costa Rica.
funFact: The only Guaro bottling catalogued here.

serve.glass: Shot glass, or highball for a chiliguaro
serve.how: Cold shots, or in a chiliguaro: guaro with tomato juice, lime, hot sauce and salt, which is the national shot and far better than the description suggests. It also mixes cleanly with any fruit juice.
