components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still, heavily rectified

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Keeping it neutral is a deliberate design choice: it was made to be mixed, not tasted.

originStory: Guaro is Central America's name for a clear cane spirit, and in Costa Rica its production has been in state hands since the mid-nineteenth century, when the government took it over to curb illegal distilling and set up the Fábrica Nacional de Licores. Since 1980 the factory has sold it as Guaro Cacique, cacique being a Taíno word for a chief, and it is the classic base of the guaro sour.

name: Grogue de Santo Antão
description: Grogue from Cape Verde.
funFact: The only Grogue bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or as a grogue sour with lime and sugarcane honey. Cape Verdeans drink it at any hour and treat refusing it as slightly eccentric.

composition.summary: Fresh-pressed cane juice fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh sugarcane juice from island terraces

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot stills, often wood-fired

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; aged versions exist

composition.process: Wild fermentation in open wooden vats gives grogue its funk, much as it does clairin in Haiti.

originStory: Grogue de Santo Antão is a bottling of Cape Verde's traditional cane spirit from the island most closely tied to it. On Santo Antão, cane grows in steep valleys such as Paul and is crushed in a trapiche, a cane press once turned by oxen, before it is fermented and distilled in small stills. The name grogue is usually traced to the English word grog, and the spirit is also the base of ponche, sweetened with sugarcane molasses.

name: Batavia Arrack van Oosten
description: Batavia Arrack from Indonesia.
funFact: The only Batavia Arrack bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Taste it first neat at room temperature in a small glass or punch cup, taking short sniffs to map its smoky, funky, black-tea strangeness — it is unlike any rum you know. Then honor its history: build a classic punch with lemon, sugar, water, and tea, where its 48-50% funk blooms into dried-fruit richness. A little goes a long way as a seasoning spirit, even a quarter ounce transforming an otherwise ordinary cocktail.

composition.summary: A Javanese cane spirit fermented with red rice cakes and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses, fermented with local red rice cakes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot stills, in the old Javanese manner

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in teak vats in Java before shipping

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 48–50% ABV

composition.process: The rice-cake ferment introduces wild microbes that build its smoky, funky signature.

originStory: Batavia arrack is the cane spirit of Java, named after Batavia, the Dutch colonial name for Jakarta, where it was made from sugarcane molasses fermented with red rice. Shipped home by the Dutch East India Company, it became a favourite base for the punches of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Europe and later for Swedish punsch. Van Oosten is a modern bottling of the style, brought to American bartenders by the importer Haus Alpenz as interest in historic punch recipes revived.

name: Charanda Uruapan
description: Charanda from Mexico.
funFact: The only Charanda bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, the way you would approach a good rhum agricole. The mineral edge comes from the soil and gets lost under mixers, so save the mixing for the aged expressions.

composition.summary: Michoacán sugarcane, juice or molasses, fermented and distilled at altitude.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cane grown between 300 and 1,800 metres in Michoacán

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Blanco, oro and añejo expressions

composition.process: Distilling at altitude lowers the boiling point, which producers say gives a lighter, more aromatic spirit.

originStory: Charanda is the cane spirit of Michoacán, made around Uruapan from sugarcane juice or molasses, and it grew up around the sugar mills the Spanish established in the region. Its name is usually traced to the Cerro de la Charanda, a hill near the city whose Purépecha name is translated as red earth. It has its own Mexican denomination of origin, which ties it to a group of municipalities in Michoacán, and this bottling carries the name of Uruapan itself.

name: Pitorro Casero
description: Pitorro from Puerto Rico.
funFact: The only Pitorro bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve traditional clear pitorro in a small shot glass at cellar temperature, sipping slowly and respectfully — at 40-60% it demands small draws, revealing raw sugarcane and a green funky edge. Fruit-cured 'pitorro curao,' steeped with tropical fruit for months, is best lightly chilled so the infusion stays bright. Around the holidays, do as Puerto Rican families do and fold it into homemade coquito, or toast with it straight at the Christmas table.

composition.summary: Puerto Rico's homemade cane spirit, distilled clandestinely and often infused with fruit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane — guarapo or molasses, depending on the family

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small backyard pot stills, run high and clear

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, or 'curao' — buried underground with fruit for months

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–60% ABV, sometimes higher

composition.process: Burying the jug with fruit and spices for months is the ritual that makes pitorro curao.

originStory: Pitorro is Puerto Rico's moonshine: rum distilled at home, outside the licensed trade, from cane, molasses or sugar, and often steeped with fruit or spices once it comes off the still. It is closely tied to the island's Christmas season, when homemade bottles circulate at parrandas, the musical visits that move from house to house. Nobody is credited with inventing it and the origin of the word pitorro is not documented. Casero simply means homemade, which is how most pitorro has always been made.

name: Patrón Silver

originStory: Casa Herradura dates to 1870, when Félix López registered the agave fields and distillery of the Hacienda San José del Refugio in Amatitán, Jalisco, as a tequila producer. originStory: Tequila Ocho was founded in 2008 by Carlos Camarena, of the family that runs La Alteña distillery in Arandas, and Tomas Estes, a restaurateur who did much to bring tequila to European bars. description: Tequila Blanco from Mexico.
funFact: One of 11 Tequila Blanco bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a couple of ounces into a caballito and sip, do not shoot; blanco is the purest expression of roasted blue agave and rewards patience. Take small sips and look for white pepper, citrus, and green herbs riding over the sweet agave core. A slight chill crisps it up in summer, but avoid heavy icing, which mutes the vegetal brightness.

composition.summary: Unaged tequila distilled purely from cooked blue Weber agave.

components.label: Base

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None, or a brief rest in steel — bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–46% ABV

composition.process: Skipping the barrel entirely leaves the cooked agave with nothing to hide behind.

originStory: Siete Leguas was founded in 1952 by Ignacio González Vargas in Atotonilco el Alto, in the highlands of Jalisco, and is named after the horse of the revolutionary general Pancho Villa; siete leguas means seven leagues. The González family still runs it, from two distilleries, one of which still crushes agave with a stone tahona. For years it also made the tequila sold under the Patrón name, until that brand moved to its own distillery in 2002. The blanco is the house's unaged expression.

name: G4 Blanco
description: Tequila Blanco from Mexico.
funFact: One of 11 Tequila Blanco bottlings catalogued here.

originStory: G4 is made at El Pandillo, the distillery Felipe Camarena, a member of the Camarena tequila family, built in the early 2010s in the Jalisco highlands near Jesús María. He is known for engineering his own equipment, including a mechanical stone crusher nicknamed Frankenstein, and for making tequila with a blend of collected rainwater and spring water. The brand says the name stands for four generations of the family in tequila. The blanco is unaged, bottled to show off the agave and the water.

name: Chinaco Añejo
description: Tequila Añejo from Mexico.
funFact: One of 5 Tequila Añejo bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Treat anejo like a fine whiskey: pour into a snifter, swirl once, and let it rest a few minutes before nosing for caramel, chocolate, and cooked agave. Sip neat and slow, noting how the oak frames the agave rather than burying it. A single large cube is fine on a warm night, but skip crushed ice and mixers, this earned its barrel time.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila aged one to three years in oak barrels.

components.label: Strength

composition.process: Small barrels concentrate wood contact, pushing agave toward caramel and chocolate.

originStory: Chinaco comes from González, in Tamaulipas, one of the few places far from Jalisco inside the tequila denomination, where Guillermo González Díaz Lombardo planted agave and built the La Gonzaleña distillery. In 1983 it became, by most accounts, the first 100 per cent agave tequila imported into the United States, brought in by Robert Denton and Marilyn Smith. The name recalls the chinacos, horsemen who fought the French intervention in nineteenth-century Mexico. Production stopped for some years before the distillery reopened.

name: Del Maguey Vida
description: Mezcal Joven from Mexico.
funFact: One of 4 Mezcal Joven bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a wide, shallow veladora and let it breathe for a minute before nosing. Kiss it rather than gulp it: small sips held on the palate reveal tropical fruit and wet-stone minerality behind the campfire smoke. Traditional accompaniments are orange slices dusted with sal de gusano, not lime and shot glasses.
pair: orange slices with sal de gusano

components.label: Base

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–52% ABV

composition.process: Days of roasting in stone-lined earth pits is the single step that makes mezcal smoky.

originStory: Del Maguey was founded in 1995 by the American artist Ron Cooper, who had come to know family mezcal makers in Oaxaca and began bottling each village's mezcal separately under the name Single Village Mezcal. Vida was added later as a mezcal meant for mixing, made from espadín agave cooked in earthen pits and distilled in small stills by a family producer in the village of San Luis del Río. Its name is Spanish for life. Pernod Ricard became the majority owner of Del Maguey in 2017.

name: Del Maguey Chichicapa
description: Mezcal Espadín from Mexico.
funFact: One of 3 Mezcal Espadín bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, in a wide shallow glass, sipped rather than shot. Orange slices with sal de gusano are the traditional accompaniment in Oaxaca. Never chill it.

composition.summary: Cultivated Espadín agave pit-roasted, crushed and twice pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave angustifolia (Espadín), 6–8 years to maturity

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, tahona-crushed, copper or clay pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually joven, unaged

composition.process: Earth-pit roasting over hot stones is where all the smoke comes from — nothing is added.

originStory: Chichicapa is one of the early Single Village mezcals that the American artist Ron Cooper bottled after founding Del Maguey in 1995, each labelled with the village where it was made rather than with a blend name. It comes from San Baltazar Chichicapam, in the Oaxacan hills, where a family producer roasts espadín in an earthen pit, crushes it with a stone wheel drawn by an animal and distils it twice in a small still. Putting the village on the label was Cooper's way of crediting the place and the maker.

name: Del Maguey Tobalá
description: Mezcal Tobalá from Mexico.
funFact: The only Mezcal Tobalá bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour sparingly, this is scarce juice, and let the glass sit for several minutes; tobala's floral perfume needs air to bloom. Sip in small, slow draws and chase the wild fruit and wet-stone notes that float above the gentle smoke. No ice, no citrus, no mixing: at this rarity you are tasting a plant that took a decade to grow in a mountain canyon.

composition.summary: Mezcal from wild tobalá agave, a small canyon-dwelling species that yields very little.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wild Agave potatorum, harvested from high mountain canyons

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, then twice through small copper or clay stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, so the wild agave stays the loudest voice

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–50% ABV

composition.process: It takes several times more tobalá hearts than espadín to fill a bottle.

originStory: Tobalá is the local name for Agave potatorum, a small wild agave that grows at high altitude in the Oaxacan mountains, often in the shade of oak trees, and that is gathered rather than farmed. Each plant yields little, which has always made tobalá mezcal scarce. Del Maguey, founded in 1995 by the American artist Ron Cooper to bottle the mezcals of individual Oaxacan villages, includes a tobalá made by one of its family producers from wild-gathered plants.

name: Del Maguey Pechuga
description: Mezcal de Pechuga from Mexico.
funFact: The only Mezcal de Pechuga bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Treat this like the ceremonial spirit it is: pour a small measure into a veladora, no ice, no mixing, and share it slowly with people you like. Take tiny sips and hunt for the stone fruit and holiday spice riding under the smoke, with that faint savory roundness from the pechuga itself on the finish. Let the glass sit between sips; it keeps evolving as it breathes.
pair: roast turkey or chicken with mole

composition.summary: Mezcal given a final still run with seasonal fruit, spices, and raw poultry breast.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pit-roasted agave, plus fruit, nuts, spices and raw poultry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: An extra pass with the breast suspended inside the still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged — bottled straight after the pechuga run

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–55% ABV

composition.process: That third distillation over hanging poultry strips harshness and rounds the spirit into ceremony.

originStory: Pechuga is a celebration mezcal from Oaxaca: an already distilled mezcal is run through the still a third time with wild fruits, nuts, rice and spices, while a raw chicken breast, the pechuga that gives the style its name, hangs in the still in the path of the vapours. It was traditionally made in small amounts for weddings, feast days and the end-of-year holidays, when the fruit is in season. Del Maguey, founded by the artist Ron Cooper in 1995, bottles its pechuga from one of its family producers.

funFact: One of 4 Mezcal Joven bottlings catalogued here.

originStory: Ilegal began in 2004 at Café No Sé, the bar the American John Rexer ran in Antigua, Guatemala, where he served mezcal he brought in informally from Oaxaca, and in 2006 he turned it into a brand named for those unofficial beginnings. The mezcal is made from espadín by the Hernández family at their Mal de Amor distillery in Santiago Matatlán, Oaxaca. Bacardi took a minority stake in 2015 and bought the company outright in 2023, and Joven is the unaged expression.

name: Ilegal Reposado
description: Mezcal Reposado from Mexico.
funFact: The only Mezcal Reposado bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Sip it neat from a veladora to catch the honey and vanilla the barrel has draped over the smoke, taking your time between small pours. This is the friendliest on-ramp to mezcal, so if the smoke still reads strong, a single large cube softens it into something almost dessert-like. Notice how the roasted agave core stays intact under the oak polish.

composition.summary: Pit-roasted agave mezcal rested a few months in wood before bottling.

composition.process: A short rest in wood lays vanilla and honey over the smoke without burying it.

originStory: Ilegal Reposado comes from the brand John Rexer started in 2006, after two years of informally bringing Oaxacan mezcal into Guatemala for Café No Sé, his bar in Antigua; the name recalls those unofficial shipments. The mezcal is distilled from espadín by the Hernández family at their Mal de Amor distillery in Santiago Matatlán, Oaxaca, and the reposado is then rested for a few months in American oak, which softens the smoke. Bacardi has owned the brand outright since 2023.

name: Montelobos Espadín
description: Mezcal Espadín from Mexico.
funFact: One of 3 Mezcal Espadín bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, in a wide shallow glass, sipped rather than shot. Orange slices with sal de gusano are the traditional accompaniment in Oaxaca. Never chill it.

originStory: Montelobos was created in the early 2010s by Iván Saldaña, a Mexican biologist who had studied agave scientifically, with the spirits company Casa Lumbre. It is distilled in Santiago Matatlán, Oaxaca, from organically grown espadín roasted in an earthen pit before fermentation, and its name means wolf mountain. Saldaña has also written a book on the science of agave spirits, and the brand presents itself as a bridge between that research and traditional mezcal making.

Elote began as Aquilino's mezcal: espadín redistilled with corn grown on his farm and toasted, a nod to the maize that grows alongside agave in Oaxacan fields. The brand has since added mezcals from several other family producers, each named on the label.

name: Rey Campero Tepeztate
description: Mezcal Tepeztate from Mexico.
funFact: The only Mezcal Tepeztate bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat and unhurried, in small sips. The vegetal, almost savoury profile confounds people expecting smoke and sweetness. It is a spirit to sit with rather than to introduce anyone to the category with.

composition.summary: Wild Tepeztate agave pit-roasted and pot-distilled.

components.detail: Agave marmorata, wild-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

originStory: Rey Campero is made by the Sánchez Parada family in Candelaria Yegolé, in Oaxaca's southern sierra, a village where they have distilled mezcal for generations, and Rómulo Sánchez Parada began bottling it under the Rey Campero name, king of the countryside, in the early 2010s. Tepeztate, Agave marmorata, is a wild agave that grows on steep, rocky slopes and can take a quarter of a century to mature, so the family gathers it rather than plants it, and each batch depends on what the hills provide.

name: Bozal Cuishe
description: Mezcal Cuishe from Mexico.
funFact: The only Mezcal Cuishe bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat, small pours. Drier and more austere than Espadín, and it makes an excellent bridge between the cultivated and wild styles for someone working through a flight.

composition.summary: Wild Cuishe agave pit-roasted and pot-distilled.

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Producers often distil the different karwinskii varieties separately purely to show the differences.

originStory: Cuishe is a wild Oaxacan agave of the karwinskii group, which also includes madrecuixe, barril and tobasiche, and its tall, narrow trunk gives a dry, herbal mezcal. It is gathered from hillsides rather than farmed, and like other mezcals it is roasted in an earthen pit before fermentation and distillation. Bozal bottles it as a single-agave mezcal, made from cuishe alone.

originStory: Los Amantes, the lovers, is an unaged joven mezcal from Oaxaca, the state that makes most of Mexico's mezcal.

name: Alipús San Andrés
description: Mezcal Espadín from Mexico.
funFact: One of 3 Mezcal Espadín bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, in a wide shallow glass, sipped rather than shot. Orange slices with sal de gusano are the traditional accompaniment in Oaxaca. Never chill it.

originStory: Alipús is a line of village mezcals created by the team behind Los Danzantes, a Oaxacan restaurant group that also runs its own distillery in Santiago Matatlán. Rather than blending, each Alipús bottling comes from a single family producer and carries the name of the village where it is made; San Andrés is one of them, an espadín mezcal from the Oaxacan hills. The idea, shared with other single-village labels, is to bring the work of small palenques to a wider market while keeping each maker's style intact.

name: Bacanora Cielo Rojo
description: Bacanora from Mexico.
funFact: The only Bacanora bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour an ounce or two into a veladora and let it sit for a minute or two so the alcohol vapors lift off before you nose it. Sip neat in small draws, rolling the spirit across your tongue to catch the mineral edge and desert-herb notes beneath the light smoke. Skip ice entirely; dilution flattens the wild-agave character that makes bacanora worth hunting down.

composition.summary: Distilled from Sonoran agave, mostly the wild-harvested Agave angustifolia known locally as pacífico.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave angustifolia ('pacífico'), much of it still gathered wild

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, then run through small copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Almost always bottled unaged and clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–48% ABV

composition.process: Roasting the agave hearts in earth-and-stone pits is what lays down that mountain smoke.

originStory: Bacanora is the agave spirit of Sonora, named for the town of Bacanora in the foothills of the Sierra Madre and distilled from wild Agave angustifolia. Families in the sierra made it for generations, but the state outlawed its production for most of the twentieth century, so it survived as a clandestine spirit until it was legalised again late in the century and later given its own denomination of origin. Cielo Rojo, red sky, is one of the brands bottled since legalisation.

name: Sotol Por Siempre
description: Sotol from Mexico.
funFact: The only Sotol bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a small measure neat and give it a minute of air, then nose gently: sotol smells like the high desert after rain, all grass, pine, and mineral. Sip slowly and let it sit on the mid-palate, where the earthy, vegetal side unfolds; it is drier and greener than mezcal, so do not go looking for sweetness. Room temperature keeps those delicate herbal notes alive.

composition.summary: Distilled from the wild desert spoon plant, not agave at all.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wild Dasylirion — desert spoon — harvested across the Chihuahuan Desert

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Roasted, crushed, then run through small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Most is unaged; some producers rest it briefly in oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: The plants are gathered wild from desert hillsides, so the spirit changes with the terrain.

originStory: Sotol is distilled in Chihuahua, Durango and Coahuila from the desert spoon, a Dasylirion plant that looks like an agave but is not one, and it takes years to mature in the wild. Rural families of the Chihuahuan Desert have made it for generations, roasting the plant hearts in pits much as mezcal makers do, and it now has a Mexican denomination of origin covering those three states. Por Siempre, meaning forever, is a sotol bottled in that tradition.

name: Raicilla La Venenosa
description: Raicilla from Mexico.
funFact: The only Raicilla bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve neat at room temperature in a veladora and nose it first: raicilla leads with ripe fruit and wild funk rather than smoke, so expect something closer to a natural wine's aromatics. Sip slowly and let it coat the palate, watching for the green agave brightness underneath the fermented-fruit character. Keep it away from ice and mixers until you have met it on its own terms.
pair: tropical fruit with chile and lime

composition.summary: Western Jalisco agave spirit from mountain and coastal species, cooked without heavy smoke.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Local Jalisco agaves such as maximiliana and inaequidens

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or filipino-style stills, often clay or wood-fired

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged, bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: Many producers cook the agave in above-ground ovens, which is why it reads fruity, not smoky.

originStory: Raicilla comes from western Jalisco, from the coast around Cabo Corrientes and the mountains around Mascota, where it is distilled from local agaves such as maximiliana and angustifolia. The name means little root, and the usual story is that producers called it that in colonial times to avoid the taxes levied on mezcal. La Venenosa, the poisonous one, was started by Esteban Morales to bottle raicillas from individual traditional makers, each labelled with its region and its maestro.

name: Comiteco Balún Canán
description: Comiteco from Mexico.
funFact: The only Comiteco bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature. It is sweeter and rounder than mezcal, closer to a light rum in weight, and the aged versions drink comfortably after a meal.

composition.summary: Agave sap fermented, distilled and blended with piloncillo, then aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aguamiel from Agave americana, tapped from living plants

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, then blended with unrefined cane sugar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, typically one to three years

composition.process: Because the plant is tapped rather than harvested, it keeps producing sap for months before it dies.

originStory: Comiteco is the traditional spirit of Comitán de Domínguez in Chiapas, distilled from fermented agave sap, the aguamiel also used for pulque, often with cane sugar or piloncillo added to the ferment. It has been made in the Comitán area since colonial times. Balún Canán is the old Maya name for Comitán, usually translated as nine stars or nine guardians, and it is also the title of Rosario Castellanos's novel set in the town.

name: Cocuy Pecayero
description: Cocuy from Venezuela.
funFact: The only Cocuy bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat and unchilled in a small wide glass, sipped rather than shot, exactly as you would treat mezcal. The wild-harvested versions carry more mineral and less sweetness.

composition.summary: Agave cocui hearts roasted, fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave cocui, largely wild-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, then small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: The plant takes eight to ten years to mature, and overharvesting has been a genuine conservation concern.

originStory: Cocuy is the agave spirit of northwestern Venezuela, distilled in the states of Falcón and Lara from Agave cocui, whose hearts are roasted in pits much as in Mexican mezcal. For long stretches of the twentieth century much of it was made clandestinely, outside the law, by rural families. Pecayero means from Pecaya, a town in Falcón whose cocuy received a Venezuelan denomination of origin, and the name marks this bottling as coming from that tradition.

name: Hennessy VS
description: Cognac VS from France.
funFact: One of 2 Cognac VS bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Young and grape-bright, VS is the cognac to enjoy casually: neat in a small snifter, over a single large cube, or stretched into a highball with ginger ale or tonic. If sipping neat, warm the glass briefly in your hand, swirl, and look for fresh grape and citrus over young oak. Don't overthink it — this grade was made for mixing and easy evenings, so save the ceremony for older bottles.

composition.summary: The youngest cognac grade: Charente grape brandy aged at least two years.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Thin, acidic white wine, overwhelmingly Ugni Blanc

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Twice through the copper Charentais alembic

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Youngest eau-de-vie at least two years in French oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Bottled at 40% ABV

composition.process: The second pass — la bonne chauffe — is where the distiller cuts the heart of the spirit.

originStory: Hennessy was founded in 1765 by Richard Hennessy, an Irish officer who had served in the French army under Louis XV and settled in Cognac, where he began distilling and exporting brandy. The house introduced star ratings on its labels in 1865, and its youngest blend, long sold as Three Star, is today labelled VS, very special, meaning its youngest eau-de-vie has spent at least two years in oak. Hennessy merged with Moët et Chandon in 1971, and the group became part of LVMH in 1987.

funFact: One of 6 Cognac VSOP bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour an ounce and a half into a snifter or tulip glass at room temperature — skip the flame-warming cliché, gentle hand warmth is plenty. Swirl, nose in two or three passes, and sip slowly, tracking dried apricot into vanilla and baking spice. VSOP straddles both worlds: refined enough to sip neat after dinner, sturdy enough for an elegant Sidecar or a single cube on a warm night.

originStory: Hennessy says the VSOP grade began in 1817, when the Prince Regent of Britain, the future George IV, asked the house for a very superior old pale cognac. The house had been founded in Cognac in 1765 by Richard Hennessy, an Irish officer in the French army, and the initials it adopted became the standard for cognac aged at least four years in oak. Pale is usually explained as meaning cognac sold without added caramel colouring. Hennessy is now part of LVMH, through Moët Hennessy.

name: Hennessy XO
description: Cognac XO from France.
funFact: One of 5 Cognac XO bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Reserve XO for unhurried evenings: pour a small measure into a snifter, let it breathe five to ten minutes, and resist any ice or water. Cradle the bowl, swirl slowly, and nose repeatedly — candied orange, fig, and walnut should deepen with every pass as the rancio character emerges. Sip in tiny draws and let each one sit on the palate; a single pour should comfortably last half an hour.

originStory: Maurice Hennessy created XO, extra old, in 1870, at first as a cognac for his family and friends, and the house says it was the first to carry those letters, which later became an official grade for cognac with long ageing. The blend draws on old eaux-de-vie from several crus, and Hennessy is now part of LVMH, through Moët Hennessy.

originStory: Rémy Martin VSOP was popularised from 1927 by André Renaud, a partner in the house, who built it around Fine Champagne, a blend of eaux-de-vie from Grande and Petite Champagne, the two most prized crus, with at least half from Grande Champagne. Rémy Martin merged with Cointreau in 1990 to form Rémy Cointreau.

originStory: Louis XIII was created in 1874 by Paul-Émile Rémy Martin, who named it in homage to the seventeenth-century French king. It is a blend of very old eaux-de-vie from Grande Champagne alone, many of them aged for decades, and it is sold in a crystal decanter modelled, the house says, on a metal flask found on the site of the sixteenth-century Battle of Jarnac. Each cellar master lays down eaux-de-vie for it that only a successor will use, so every bottle spans several generations of the house's work.

description: Cognac VS from France.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Young and grape-bright, VS is the cognac to enjoy casually: neat in a small snifter, over a single large cube, or stretched into a highball with ginger ale or tonic. If sipping neat, warm the glass briefly in your hand, swirl, and look for fresh grape and citrus over young oak. Don't overthink it — this grade was made for mixing and easy evenings, so save the ceremony for older bottles.

originStory: Martell was founded in 1715 by Jean Martell, a merchant from Jersey who began trading brandy on the banks of the Charente at Cognac, and it is usually counted the oldest of the great cognac houses. The house came to lean on the Borderies, a small cru prized for floral eaux-de-vie, and on fine-grained oak from the Tronçais forest. VS is its youngest blend. Seagram bought Martell in 1987, and Pernod Ricard has owned it since 2001.

originStory: Courvoisier grew from a wine and spirits business that Emmanuel Courvoisier and Louis Gallois ran at Bercy, then just outside Paris, which Napoleon is recorded visiting in 1811. A legend that he took cognac from the house with him into exile on St Helena gave Courvoisier its old slogan, the cognac of Napoleon. Félix Courvoisier and Jules Gallois later moved the business to Jarnac, in the Cognac region, where it is still based. The Campari Group bought Courvoisier in 2024.

originStory: This cognac was introduced in the early 2010s by Alexandre Gabriel, owner of the Ferrand estate in Grande Champagne, working with the drinks historian David Wondrich. They modelled it on a bottle of 1840 cognac from the house of Pinet Castillon, aiming for the strong, fruity style that nineteenth-century bartenders such as Jerry Thomas would have mixed into punches and juleps. It is bottled at a higher strength than most cognac for that reason, and the name points to the year of the bottle that inspired it.

name: Darroze Les Grands Assemblages
description: Armagnac from France.
funFact: One of 3 Armagnac bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a modest ounce and a half into a snifter or small tulip and give it ten patient minutes to breathe — older Armagnacs unfold dramatically with air. Warm the bowl slightly with your hand, swirl slowly, and return to the nose repeatedly as prune, violet, and toffee emerge in waves. Sip in small draws with no ice and no water at first; this is a fireside spirit meant to be interrogated over an hour.

originStory: Darroze is the work of Francis Darroze, whose family ran a well-known restaurant in Villeneuve-de-Marsan in the Landes, and who in the 1970s began seeking out armagnacs from individual small estates, buying and ageing them himself and bottling each under the name of its property. His son Marc Darroze runs the house today. Les Grands Assemblages are its blended range, labelled by age, made by marrying eaux-de-vie from several of those estates rather than from a single one.

Delord 25 is a blend whose youngest eau-de-vie has spent at least twenty-five years in oak, showing how armagnac changes over very long ageing.

name: Boulard Grand Solage
description: Calvados from France.
funFact: One of 3 Calvados bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve an ounce and a half in a snifter at room temperature, swirl once, and breathe in the orchard — baked apple and cider aromas should leap out before you ever sip. Take small sips and note how younger bottlings stay crisp and appley while older ones drift toward butterscotch and spice. Honor the 'trou normand' by pouring a small glass mid-feast, or serve it alongside dessert in place of whisky.

originStory: Boulard was founded in 1825 by Pierre-Auguste Boulard in the Pays d'Auge, the Normandy district whose calvados must be double distilled in pot stills, and it became one of the region's best-known houses. Its cellars at Coquainvilliers age apple brandy in oak casks of many sizes. Grand Solage is the house's blend of young and older calvados, made to be approachable while keeping the cider-apple character of the region, and calvados itself is distilled from cider pressed from local apples and pears.

serve.how: Serve slightly cool but never frozen — an over-chilled pour hides the ripe-pear perfume that makes this eau-de-vie special. Pour a small measure into a tulip glass, warm it faintly in your hand, and nose it in slow passes; a fully ripe Williams pear should materialize before you sip. Take tiny sips as a digestif, letting the clean spice and white-fruit sweetness linger between them.

originStory: Massenez is an Alsatian fruit-brandy house founded in the late nineteenth century in the Villé valley, where the region's orchards have long supplied distillers of eau-de-vie. Poire Williams is a clear brandy distilled from the Williams pear, the variety called Bartlett in North America, and Alsatian houses made it a speciality. Massenez is known for selling it with a whole pear inside the bottle, grown there by slipping the bottle over the young fruit on the tree and leaving it until harvest.

name: Massenez Kirsch
description: Kirschwasser from France.
funFact: The only Kirschwasser bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a small measure into a tulip glass at cellar temperature — freezing it, as some bars do, kills the delicate sour-cherry perfume. Nose gently for the signature whisper of bitter almond from the distilled pits, then sip slowly and let the clean heat carry the stone fruit across your palate. Serve it as a digestif after a rich meal, the traditional Black Forest role it was born for.

components.detail: Black Forest cherries, crushed and fermented with their stones

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Twice through small copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged — rested in glass or steel to stay water-clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–45% ABV

composition.process: Fermenting the pits along with the fruit is what leaves that whisper of bitter almond.

originStory: Kirsch, short for Kirschwasser, cherry water, is a clear brandy distilled from fermented small black cherries, stones included, in the Black Forest, Alsace and Switzerland. Massenez, founded in the Villé valley of Alsace in the late nineteenth century, is among the Alsatian houses that made fruit brandy their whole business. Its kirsch is unaged and colourless, as the style traditionally is, with the faint almond note that comes from the cherry stones.

name: Marc de Bourgogne
description: Marc from France.
funFact: The only Marc bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve after dinner at room temperature in a small pour. Aged marc rewards a warmed glass; young marc does not, and heat only sharpens its edges. It also does honourable work poured into an espresso.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and distilled after the wine press.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Skins, pips and stems from winemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still, often mobile and shared between growers

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Frequently oak-aged, sometimes for decades

composition.process: Because the pomace has already given up its juice, everything left is skin and structure, which is where the grip comes from.

originStory: Marc de Bourgogne is the pomace brandy of Burgundy, distilled from the skins, pips and stems left after the region's grapes have been pressed for wine, and its name comes from marc, the French word for that pressed residue. Growers once distilled it on the estate or with travelling stills, as a way to make use of the pomace. It differs from Italian grappa in usually being aged in oak, which gives it an amber colour and a rounder, earthier character, and it is now a protected geographical indication.

name: Torres 10
description: Brandy de Jerez from Spain.
funFact: One of 4 Brandy de Jerez bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour into a snifter at room temperature and let it rest a few minutes before nosing — the sherry-cask perfume of raisin and fig needs a moment to assemble. Swirl gently and sip slowly, chasing the nutty oloroso richness through to the toffee finish. Its softer 36-40% strength makes it an easy neat sipper after dinner; ice is forgivable on a hot Andalusian-style afternoon but mutes the sherry character.

originStory: Torres began making brandy in 1928, when Juan Torres Casals, second generation of a Penedès wine family, started distilling wine in Vilafranca del Penedès, in Catalonia. The business had been founded in 1870 by the brothers Jaime and Miguel Torres; Jaime had made his fortune in Cuba before returning home to go into wine with his brother. Torres 10 is a Gran Reserva brandy aged in oak, made in Catalonia, far from the sherry country of Jerez.

It is a Brandy de Jerez Solera Gran Reserva, aged in casks that previously held sherry, mainly oloroso and Pedro Ximénez, moving through a solera so that younger brandy is blended with older. It remains one of the most widely known Spanish brandies.

It is one of the few Brandies de Jerez distilled by the house itself, in copper pot stills, from Palomino wine grown around Jerez, before ageing by solera in casks that held the house's sherries.

name: Orujo de Galicia
description: Orujo from Spain.
funFact: The only Orujo bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal, or as the herbal and cream versions that Galician bars keep alongside the clear one. For queimada it is burned with sugar, coffee beans and lemon peel in a clay bowl.

composition.summary: Grape pomace from Galician wine fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Skins, pips and stems, largely Albariño and Mencía

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alquitara or pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; herbal and cream versions are infused after

composition.process: Traditional alquitaras are small enough that distilling was historically done village by village.

originStory: Orujo de Galicia is the pomace brandy of northwestern Spain, distilled from the skins and pips left after winemaking, and its name comes from orujo, the Spanish word for that residue. Galician families long distilled it at home in small copper stills, sometimes with the help of travelling distillers, and it is now a protected geographical indication. It is the base of queimada, a hot drink of orujo, sugar, lemon peel and coffee beans set alight in a clay bowl while a spell against evil spirits is recited, a ritual whose ancient pedigree is disputed.

name: Nardini Grappa
description: Grappa from Italy.
funFact: One of 3 Grappa bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve a small pour — an ounce or so — in a narrow tulip glass, slightly cool for young grappa and closer to room temperature for barrel-aged riservas. Hold the glass at a slight distance when you first nose it; grappa's aromatics are punchy, and short gentle sniffs reveal grape skin, hay, and pear without the alcohol burn. Sip in small amounts as a digestivo after dinner, or tip a splash into your espresso for a classic caffè corretto.

originStory: Nardini was founded in 1779 by Bortolo Nardini, who bought an inn at the end of the wooden bridge over the Brenta in Bassano del Grappa and began distilling there, and the Grapperia Nardini on the bridge is still open. It is often described as the oldest grappa distillery in Italy, and it is still run by the Nardini family. The house is known above all for clear, unaged grappa bottled at fifty per cent, the style it has made since its early days in the Veneto.

Sarpa is the Venetian dialect word for grape pomace, and this grappa is distilled from the pomace of merlot and cabernet in the family's copper pot stills. Jacopo Poli also founded a museum of grappa in nearby Bassano del Grappa, devoted to the history of the spirit and its stills.

description: Grappa from Italy.

originStory: In 1973 Benito and Giannola Nonino distilled the pomace of a single grape variety, picolit, on its own, and in doing so are credited with launching the single-varietal grappa that changed how the spirit was regarded in Italy. The family had been distilling at Ronchi di Percoto, in Friuli, since 1897, when Orazio Nonino built the first still. Il Merlot applies the same idea to merlot pomace, distilled in small batches in copper stills. The family also founded the Nonino literary prize in 1975.

name: Vecchia Romagna
description: Italian Brandy from Italy.
funFact: The only Italian Brandy bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or in coffee as a caffè corretto, which is what most of it is actually used for. Italian brandy tends to be sweeter than French, so it needs less warming.

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging

originStory: Vecchia Romagna comes from the distillery that Jean Bouton, heir to a French distilling family, founded in Bologna in 1820, Italianising his name to Buton. The brand name, old Romagna, was coined in 1939 by Count Achille Sassoli de' Bianchi, after international agreements had reserved the word cognac for France, and the same year brought the triangular bottle that became its signature. Made from Trebbiano grapes, it is one of Italy's most popular brandies and has belonged to the Montenegro group since 1999.

name: Metaxa 7 Star
description: Metaxa from Greece.
funFact: One of 2 Metaxa bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Snifter, or rocks glass with a large cube
serve.how: Neat at room temperature for the older expressions; the three and five star take ice and tonic well. Greeks also drink it long with cola, which the higher stars do not deserve.

originStory: Spyros Metaxa created his spirit in 1888 in Piraeus, the port of Athens, where he had been running a tavern, and he built a distillery there. The emblem on the bottle, a warrior of Salamis, comes from an ancient medallion said to have been found while the distillery was being built. Metaxa is not legally a brandy: aged grape distillates are blended with sweet Muscat wine from Samos and a secret mix of botanicals, and the stars distinguish its blends.

originStory: Metaxa traces itself to 1888, when Spyros Metaxa, born into a family of silk merchants, began making his spirit in Piraeus and founded a distillery there. His recipe blends aged grape distillates with sweet Muscat wine from Samos and a closely guarded mix of botanicals, which places it outside the legal definition of brandy. The stars distinguish the house's blends, and Grand Metropolitan bought the family company in 1989 before Rémy Cointreau took it over in 2000.

name: Tsipouro Tirnavou
description: Tsipouro from Greece.
funFact: The only Tsipouro bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Cold, in small glasses, alongside mezedes rather than after them. A tsipouradiko will keep bringing food with each round, which is the correct way to spend an afternoon in Volos.

components.detail: Grape pomace from Greek winemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, once or twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; oak-aged versions exist

composition.process: Adding anise is a regional choice rather than a rule, and northern Greece mostly leaves it out.

originStory: Tsipouro is the pomace brandy of mainland Greece, distilled from the skins and pips left after winemaking, and tradition credits monks on Mount Athos with making it as early as the fourteenth century, though that story is hard to document. Tyrnavos, in Thessaly, is one of its best-known homes, distilling both plain tsipouro and versions flavoured with anise, and the town marks the autumn distilling season with festivities. Tirnavou simply means of Tyrnavos, which places this bottling in that local tradition.

name: Tsikoudia Crete
description: Tsikoudia from Greece.
funFact: The only Tsikoudia bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in tiny glasses, poured for the whole table at once. It is a communal drink and drinking it alone is regarded as slightly odd. Rakomelo, warmed with honey and cinnamon, is the winter version.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and single-distilled on Crete.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cretan grape pomace

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in a copper kazani

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 37–60%, village versions running higher

composition.process: Autumn distilling is a social event on Crete, with the still running all night and food cooked over the fire.

originStory: Tsikoudia is the pomace brandy of Crete, distilled from the grape skins and pips left after winemaking, and its name is usually traced to tsikouda, the local word for that pressed residue. Every autumn, after the harvest, villages fire up licensed copper stills for a few weeks, and these kazanemata, the distilling days, are social gatherings with food and music. Cretans often call the spirit raki, though it contains no anise, and it is offered chilled in small glasses as a gesture of hospitality.

name: Ararat 5
description: Armenian Brandy from Armenia.
funFact: One of 2 Armenian Brandy bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, after dinner. Armenians drink it through a meal rather than after one, and toast constantly. The older expressions are worth taking slowly; the three star is not.

composition.summary: Armenian white wine distilled twice and aged in Caucasian oak.

components.label: Base

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging

composition.process: Local oak is tighter-grained than Limousin, which slows extraction and gives a softer, nuttier profile.

originStory: Armenian brandy production began in 1887, when the merchant Nerses Tairyan built a winery and distillery in Yerevan, and the Russian producer Nikolai Shustov bought it at the end of the century. The distillery grew into the Yerevan Brandy Company, and its brandies took the Ararat name, after the mountain that looms over Yerevan. Pernod Ricard bought the company in 1998, and the five-year blend is at the core of its range.

originStory: Ararat brandies come from the Yerevan Brandy Company, whose history begins in 1887 with Nerses Tairyan's distillery in Yerevan, later run by the Shustov family of Moscow. The brand takes its name from Mount Ararat, the snow-capped peak that dominates the view from the city and is a national symbol of Armenia. The ten-year-old blend is sold as Akhtamar, after an island in Lake Van with a medieval Armenian church, and Pernod Ricard has owned the company since 1998.

name: Zsindelyes Pálinka
description: Pálinka from Hungary.
funFact: One of 2 Pálinka bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Hungarians insist pálinka be served around 60-65°F, never ice-cold — chilling smothers the pure apricot and orchard-fruit aromatics that are the whole point. Pour a small measure into a tulip glass, nose it patiently, and sip in small amounts, letting the fiery finish bloom after the fruit fades. Traditionally it opens a meal as much as it closes one, always accompanied by a toast: egészségedre.

originStory: Pálinka is Hungary's fruit brandy, distilled from fermented fruit such as plums, apricots, pears and cherries, with no added sugar or flavouring, and its name is usually traced to a Slavic word for burning. Since Hungary joined the European Union, pálinka has been a protected name reserved for spirits made in Hungary from Hungarian fruit, with apricot pálinka also allowed in four Austrian provinces. Zsindelyes, which means shingled, is the Hungarian producer behind this bottling.

originStory: Rézangyal, copper angel, is a Hungarian pálinka brand whose name evokes the copper stills in which fruit brandy is made. Pálinka is a long-standing tradition of the Carpathian Basin, and EU rules reserve the name for fruit brandy distilled in Hungary from Hungarian fruit, with apricot pálinka also permitted in four Austrian provinces. Hungarian law bans added sugar, colouring and flavouring.

name: Slivovitz Jelinek
description: Slivovitz from Czechia.
funFact: The only Slivovitz bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour into a small shot glass or tulip at cellar temperature — Balkan tradition frowns on chilling, which hides the ripe plum and almond notes. Despite the glassware, sip it slowly rather than shooting it; a proper rakija is nursed through conversation, often with a toast of 'živeli!' to open. Notice the earthy plum sweetness up front and the peppery heat that follows, best buffered with food on the table.

composition.summary: Central European plum brandy distilled from fermented plums, skins and all.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ripe plums, traditionally damson-type varieties, fermented whole

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double pot distillation, often at small family stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in glass, or matured in oak or mulberry wood

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: Fermenting on the skins pulls out the deep, jammy plum character that defines it.

originStory: Rudolf Jelínek is the best-known slivovitz maker in the Czech Republic, based at Vizovice in Moravia, where plum brandy has long been made from the region's orchards, and the firm dates its distilling to 1894. After the Second World War the business was nationalised, and it returned to private hands after the fall of communism. Jelínek is also known abroad for its kosher slivovitz, produced under rabbinical supervision. Slivovitz takes its name from the Slavic word for plum, sliva.

name: Chacha Askaneli
description: Chacha from Georgia.
funFact: The only Chacha bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat at a Georgian table, in glasses raised for each of the many toasts a tamada will propose. Aged chacha turns golden and is drunk more slowly. Do not drink it without food; the supra assumes otherwise.

composition.summary: Grape pomace, often from qvevri winemaking, fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pomace of Rkatsiteli, Saperavi and other Georgian varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, once or twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; oak-aged versions exist

composition.process: Qvevri fermentation leaves skins in long contact with the wine, so the pomace is more exhausted and the spirit drier.

originStory: Chacha is Georgia's pomace brandy, distilled from the skins, pips and stems left after winemaking, and chacha is also the Georgian word for that pressed residue. For generations it was made at home in wine villages across the country, especially in Kakheti and western Georgia, and offered with toasts at the supra, the Georgian feast. Askaneli, a Georgian wine and spirits producer, bottles a commercial chacha in that tradition.

name: Pisco Portón
description: Pisco from Peru.
funFact: One of 3 Pisco bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: For sipping, pour into a tulip glass at cellar temperature or just lightly chilled, swirl once, and nose the jasmine-and-white-grape perfume — Peruvian piscos in particular are all about aromatics, having never touched oak. Sip slowly, noticing the floral lift up front and the warm spice on the finish. At home it also earns its keep shaken into a pisco sour or lengthened with ginger ale in a chilcano.

components.label: Base

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Peru distils once to final proof; no water may be added afterward

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Peruvian pisco rests in inert vessels only; Chilean pisco may see oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: Distilling straight to bottling strength means the cut decides everything, with no dilution to fix it.

originStory: Pisco Portón is made at Hacienda La Caravedo in Ica, Peru, a distillery founded in 1684 that is often described as the oldest still working in the Americas. The brand was launched around 2010 with the Peruvian pisco authority Johnny Schuler as its master distiller. Portón means gate. Its piscos follow Peruvian rules: distilled once, to bottling strength, in copper pot stills from fresh grape must, with no water added and no time in wood.

originStory: BarSol is made at Bodega San Isidro in Ica, on Peru's southern coast, a winery and distillery established in 1919, and the BarSol brand was created in the early 2000s to take Peruvian pisco to export markets. Quebranta is the backbone grape of Peruvian pisco, a non-aromatic variety that arose in Peru from vines the Spanish brought in the sixteenth century, and pisco puro made from it is earthy rather than floral. Like all Peruvian pisco, it is distilled to proof and rests without wood.

name: Capel Pisco
description: Pisco from Chile.
funFact: One of 3 Pisco bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: For sipping, pour into a tulip glass at cellar temperature or just lightly chilled, swirl once, and nose the jasmine-and-white-grape perfume — Peruvian piscos in particular are all about aromatics, having never touched oak. Sip slowly, noticing the floral lift up front and the warm spice on the finish. At home it also earns its keep shaken into a pisco sour or lengthened with ginger ale in a chilcano.

composition.summary: South American grape brandy from aromatic muscat-family varieties.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine from Quebranta, Italia, Torontel and other pisco grapes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Peru distils once to final proof; no water may be added afterward

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Peruvian pisco rests in inert vessels only; Chilean pisco may see oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: Distilling straight to bottling strength means the cut decides everything, with no dilution to fix it.

originStory: Capel is a cooperative of grape growers in Chile's Elqui and Limarí valleys, founded in 1938 at Vicuña, and its name is an abbreviation of its original Spanish title, the agricultural pisco cooperative of Elqui. It grew into one of Chile's largest pisco producers, drawing on the grapes of many small growers. Chile and Peru both claim pisco as a national spirit and dispute the right to the name, and Chilean pisco, unlike Peruvian, may be diluted to strength and aged in wood.

name: Laird's Applejack
description: Applejack from USA.
funFact: The only Applejack bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers into a rocks glass, neat if you want the full baked-apple and caramel aroma, or over one large cube to soften the edges. Swirl and nose before sipping — the apple should read clearly under the oak and warm spice. Bonded, higher-proof bottlings also shine in a simple highball with dry ginger ale, a nod to its colonial tavern roots.

composition.summary: American apple brandy, historically freeze-concentrated cider, now distilled and often blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fermented apple cider

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column distilled; the old way was freeze-concentration

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak-matured; blended versions cut apple brandy with neutral spirit

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: Colonial 'jacking' froze cider and threw away the ice — no still, no tax, no mercy.

originStory: Laird & Company holds what it describes as licence number one, granted in 1780, and it is usually counted the oldest licensed distillery in the United States. The family traces its applejack to William Laird, who came to Monmouth County, New Jersey, from Scotland in 1698, and to Robert Laird, who served under George Washington and is said to have shared the family recipe with him. In colonial times applejack was often concentrated by freezing hard cider and removing the ice, and Laird's now distils in Virginia and bottles in New Jersey.

name: Germain-Robin
description: American Brandy from USA.
funFact: The only American Brandy bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour an ounce and a half into a snifter and cup the bowl briefly in your palm — a touch of hand warmth coaxes out the caramel and vanilla. Swirl gently, nose in stages, and sip slowly, looking for the grape brightness that survives beneath the oak. Craft pot-still bottles deserve neat contemplation, while workhorse California brandies are equally happy over a cube or lengthened in a highball with ginger ale.

composition.summary: Grape brandy distilled in the United States, historically from California vineyards.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine from California grapes, often high-yield table varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column stills for the big houses, copper pots for craft producers

components.label: Aging
components.detail: American or French oak, typically a few years

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–45% ABV

composition.process: Abundant California fruit and a free hand with still choice make the category wildly varied.

originStory: Germain-Robin was founded in 1982 by Ansley Coale and Hubert Germain-Robin, who had met the year before when Coale, driving near his ranch outside Ukiah in Mendocino County, California, picked up the Frenchman hitchhiking; Germain-Robin's family had made cognac until their business was sold. The two set up a small alembic still on Coale's land and distilled brandy in the cognac manner, but from fine California wine grapes such as pinot noir. E. & J. Gallo bought the business in 2017.

name: Asbach Uralt
description: Weinbrand from Germany.
funFact: The only Weinbrand bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature after dinner, or in coffee with cream. German bars also serve it long with cola, which is less of a crime than it sounds given how sweet the base spirit already is.

composition.summary: Wine distillate, mostly imported, aged in Limousin oak in Germany.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine, largely from France and Italy

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum six months, quality grades far longer, in small Limousin casks

composition.process: Smaller casks mean faster wood contact, which is where the vanilla and caramel come from.

originStory: Hugo Asbach, a native of Cologne, founded his company at Rüdesheim am Rhein on 11 May 1892, and his aged brandy, Asbach Uralt, very old, became the best-known German brandy. After the First World War, when the Treaty of Versailles reserved the name cognac for France, Asbach coined the term Weinbrand for German grape brandy, and it later became the legal name of the category. The town's Rüdesheimer Kaffee, made with the brandy, became a local speciality, and the brand now belongs to Underberg.

name: KWV 10
description: Brandy de Jerez from South Africa.
funFact: One of 4 Brandy de Jerez bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour into a snifter at room temperature and let it rest a few minutes before nosing — the sherry-cask perfume of raisin and fig needs a moment to assemble. Swirl gently and sip slowly, chasing the nutty oloroso richness through to the toffee finish. Its softer 36-40% strength makes it an easy neat sipper after dinner; ice is forgivable on a hot Andalusian-style afternoon but mutes the sherry character.

composition.summary: Andalusian grape brandy matured by solera in casks that once held sherry.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine from Airén and Palomino grapes

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Both pot stills and columns, blended for character

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera system, in ex-sherry American oak, inside the sherry triangle

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 36–40% ABV

composition.process: The solera fractionally blends young into old forever, so nothing is ever a single vintage.

originStory: KWV was founded at Paarl on 8 January 1918 as a cooperative of Cape winegrowers, the Koöperatieve Wijnbouwers Vereniging, to steady prices and raise quality, and for much of the century it regulated South Africa's wine and spirits trade. Brandy had been distilled at the Cape since the Dutch period, and KWV makes its own at its brandy cellar in Worcester. Its 10-year-old is a pot-still brandy, a South African category reserved for brandy made overwhelmingly in pot stills and aged in small oak casks.

name: Cointreau
description: Triple Sec from France.
funFact: One of 3 Triple Sec bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Triple sec is a workhorse, so let it work: keep it cool and reach for it in margaritas, cosmopolitans, and sidecars, where its clean orange brightness does the heavy lifting. To assess a bottle, sip a small chilled pour from a rocks glass — better versions taste of real orange peel, not candy. A splash in chilled prosecco with a twist makes an effortless aperitif.

composition.summary: A clear orange liqueur made by distilling neutral spirit with orange peel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, sweet and bitter orange peel, sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with the peels, which keeps it clear and bright

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: A wide 15–40% ABV depending on quality

composition.process: Redistilling with the peel — rather than just infusing — is what makes it clean enough to disappear into a margarita.

originStory: Cointreau went on sale in 1875, made by the family firm that the confectioner brothers Adolphe and Édouard-Jean Cointreau had founded in Angers in 1849, and Édouard-Jean's son Édouard is usually credited with the recipe of sweet and bitter orange peels distilled with neutral spirit. It was first labelled as a white curaçao triple sec, and the story goes that the family later dropped the term as rivals copied it. The company merged with Rémy Martin in 1990 to form Rémy Cointreau, and the liqueur is still made outside Angers.

name: Grand Marnier Cordon Rouge
description: Grand Marnier from France.
funFact: The only Grand Marnier bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or on the rocks
serve.glass: Snifter, or a coupe in a drink
serve.how: Neat in a snifter after dinner, or over a single large cube. In cocktails it belongs in a Sidecar or a Cadillac Margarita, where its cognac base adds weight that Cointreau deliberately leaves out.

composition.summary: Cognac blended with distilled bitter orange essence and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cognac, roughly half the blend

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Citrus bigaradia, the bitter orange of the Caribbean

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Orange peel macerated and distilled, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak after blending

composition.process: Using cognac rather than neutral spirit is the whole difference, and it is why the liqueur can be drunk on its own.

originStory: Grand Marnier Cordon Rouge was created in 1880 by Louis-Alexandre Marnier-Lapostolle, who had married into a family running a distillery at Neauphle-le-Château since 1827, by blending cognac with an essence of bitter Caribbean oranges and sugar. The hotelier César Ritz is said to have suggested the name, and Marnier-Lapostolle in turn helped him establish the Ritz in Paris. The liqueur became a fixture of French cooking, notably in crêpes Suzette. The Campari Group took over the family company in 2016.

name: Combier Triple Sec
description: Triple Sec from France.
funFact: One of 3 Triple Sec bottlings catalogued here.

originStory: Combier was founded in 1834 in Saumur, in the Loire Valley, by Jean-Baptiste Combier, a confectioner, and his wife, who began making a liqueur of bitter orange peels at their shop; the house says it was the first triple sec, a distinction other houses also claim. It is still made in the town, in copper stills more than a century old, from orange peels macerated in alcohol before distillation.

name: Pierre Ferrand Dry Curaçao
description: Orange Curaçao from France.
funFact: The only Orange Curaçao bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Richer bottlings sip like a gentle orange brandy: pour it neat or over one large cube in a rocks glass and let the candied peel and warm spice unfold. It is also the backbone of a proper Mai Tai and lends classic cocktails a deeper glow than triple sec can. Notice the bitter laraha-peel edge that keeps all that candied-orange sweetness honest.

composition.summary: Orange liqueur flavoured with dried peel from Curaçao's bitter laraha orange.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Brandy or neutral spirit with sun-dried laraha peel and sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Peels steeped and often redistilled, then sweetened and blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Some richer bottlings rest in oak; many do not

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 25–40% ABV

composition.process: Sun-drying the laraha peel concentrates the bitter oils that give curaçao its depth.

originStory: Pierre Ferrand Dry Curaçao was launched in 2012 by Alexandre Gabriel of Maison Ferrand, who developed it with the drinks historian David Wondrich to recreate the drier, brandy-based orange curaçao that nineteenth-century bartenders used, before sweeter versions took over. It is built on bitter orange peels, including the laraha of Curaçao, steeped in brandy and cognac, and it is labelled Ancienne Méthode, old method. Curaçao takes its name from the Caribbean island where the bitter laraha orange grew from Spanish-planted trees.

name: Bols Blue Curaçao
description: Blue Curaçao from Netherlands.
funFact: One of 2 Blue Curaçao bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: This one is showmanship, so lean in: build it chilled and over plenty of ice in a hurricane glass with lemonade, sour mix, or coconut and pineapple for a Blue Hawaiian. Keep the bottle in the fridge — cold and dilution keep the candied sweetness in check. Close your eyes as you sip and notice it tastes purely of orange; the electric azure is all theater.

composition.summary: Orange peel liqueur from Curaçao, dyed a flamboyant electric blue.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, sugar, dried laraha orange peel, blue colouring

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Peels are steeped and often redistilled, then sweetened and dyed

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 20–25% ABV

composition.process: The colour is pure theatre — everything you taste comes from bitter laraha peel.

originStory: Bols dates itself to 1575, when the family opened a small distillery, 't Lootsje, the little shed, in Amsterdam, and it calls itself the oldest distillery brand in the world. Lucas Bols, born in 1652, was a shareholder in the Dutch East India Company, whose ships brought the spices and peels behind the house's liqueurs, and the company says he made a liqueur from the bitter laraha oranges of Curaçao. Bols sold a blue version in 1912 as Crème de Ciel, cream of the sky, and blue became its best-known curaçao.

name: Senior Curaçao of Curaçao
description: Blue Curaçao from Curaçao.
funFact: One of 2 Blue Curaçao bottlings catalogued here.

originStory: Senior & Co began selling its liqueur from a pharmacy on Curaçao in 1896, and since 1947 it has made it at Landhuis Chobolobo, a colonial manor house in Willemstad. The company bills it as the only curaçao made on the island, from the dried peel of the laraha, a bitter orange descended from the Seville oranges the Spanish planted in 1527, which grew small, bitter and inedible in the dry climate. It sells the same liqueur in several colours, since the colour is added and the flavour stays the same.

name: St-Germain
description: Elderflower Liqueur from France.
funFact: The only Elderflower Liqueur bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve it chilled — a small neat pour in a coupe works as a delicate aperitif, but its natural habitat is the spritz: one part liqueur, two parts prosecco, and a splash of soda over ice. It also slips beautifully into a martini or a glass of dry white wine. Notice the lychee and honeysuckle perfume on the nose and the pear-like softness that improves nearly everything it touches.

composition.summary: A perfumed liqueur made from elderflower blossoms infused in neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, fresh elderflower blossoms and sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused rather than distilled, to keep the floral aroma

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; bottled while the perfume is at its brightest

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 20% ABV

composition.process: The blossoms are picked and processed fast, because the aroma starts fading almost immediately.

originStory: St-Germain was launched in 2007 by Robert Cooper, son of Norton Cooper of the liqueur house Charles Jacquin et Cie, who had been inspired by elderflower drinks he came across in London. It is made from the blossoms of the elder tree, gathered for a few weeks each spring in the Savoie, in the French Alps, and the brand's story has collectors bringing them down by bicycle. The name comes from the Paris neighbourhood of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Bacardi bought the brand in 2013.

name: Chambord
description: Crème de Cassis from France.
funFact: One of 2 Crème de Cassis bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Keep the bottle refrigerated — cassis is fragile and fades once open, so cold storage protects the fruit. The classic home serve is a kir: a small pour in a wine glass topped with chilled dry white wine (traditionally aligoté), or with champagne for a kir royale. Sipped alone over ice, notice the tug-of-war between jammy sweetness and tart, earthy blackcurrant bite.

composition.summary: A Burgundian liqueur of blackcurrants macerated in spirit and heavily sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blackcurrants steeped in neutral spirit, then loaded with sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Never distilled — cold maceration keeps the fresh fruit intact

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; best drunk young while the colour is deep

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 15–20% ABV

composition.process: 'Crème' signals a very high sugar load, which is what makes it syrupy and jammy.

originStory: Chambord was created in 1982 by Norton Cooper at Charles Jacquin et Cie, inspired by a raspberry liqueur said to have been made in the Loire Valley in the late seventeenth century and served to Louis XIV on his visits to the Château de Chambord, which gives it its name. It is a black raspberry liqueur, made in the Loire Valley from raspberries and blackberries with cognac, vanilla, citrus peel and honey, and its round bottle is modelled on a royal orb. Brown-Forman has owned it since 2006.

name: Lejay Crème de Cassis
description: Crème de Cassis from France.
funFact: One of 2 Crème de Cassis bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Keep the bottle refrigerated — cassis is fragile and fades once open, so cold storage protects the fruit. The classic home serve is a kir: a small pour in a wine glass topped with chilled dry white wine (traditionally aligoté), or with champagne for a kir royale. originStory: Lejay-Lagoute, in Dijon, credits its founder Auguste-Denis Lagoute with creating crème de cassis in 1841, by steeping Burgundy blackcurrants in alcohol and sweetening the infusion, and the house presents itself as the original maker. Dijon became the capital of the liqueur, and crème de cassis de Bourgogne is now a protected name. After the Second World War the city's mayor, Canon Félix Kir, served white Burgundy with a little cassis at official receptions, and the drink came to bear his name.

name: Giffard Crème de Violette
description: Crème de Violette from France.
funFact: One of 2 Crème de Violette bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: This is a painter's liqueur — a quarter ounce in an Aviation or a splash beneath chilled sparkling wine turns the glass the color of dusk. To taste it on its own, pour a small, well-chilled measure into a coupe and nose it first: it smells exactly the way violets do. Use a light hand in cocktails; too much and everything tastes like perfume rather than twilight.

composition.summary: A purple liqueur made by macerating violet flowers in sweetened spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit steeped with violet petals, plus sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Maceration and blending; the flowers are too fragile to boil

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, and it fades with light and time

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 16–22% ABV

composition.process: Cold-steeping the petals is the only way to catch a scent this delicate.

originStory: Giffard was founded in 1885 by Émile Giffard, a pharmacist in Angers who created a mint liqueur, Menthe-Pastille, and turned his pharmacy into a distillery to make it. The family has run the house for four generations since, building a range of liqueurs and syrups that includes this crème de violette, a sweet liqueur flavoured with violet flowers in the old French style. Violet liqueur is the ingredient that gives the Aviation cocktail its pale sky-blue colour.

name: Rothman & Winter Crème de Violette
description: Crème de Violette from Austria.
funFact: One of 2 Crème de Violette bottlings catalogued here.
