originStory: Rothman & Winter Crème de Violette reached the United States in 2007 through the importer Haus Alpenz, at a time when no violet liqueur had been widely available there for decades, and it let bartenders make the Aviation as its original recipe intended. Hugo Ensslin's 1916 recipe for that gin cocktail had called for crème de violette, which later editions often dropped. The liqueur is made in Austria from violets steeped in spirit and sweetened.

name: Tempus Fugit Crème de Menthe
description: Crème de Menthe from Switzerland.
funFact: One of 2 Crème de Menthe bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve it seriously cold: keep the bottle in the freezer and pour a small measure into a chilled coupe, or go old-school with a frappe over a mound of crushed ice. It is also the engine of the Grasshopper and the Stinger if you want a proper cocktail. Sip slowly and enjoy the cooling menthol wave — it should feel like an after-dinner mint you can drink.

composition.summary: A sweet mint liqueur made by steeping or distilling mint leaves in spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, mint leaves and a great deal of sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Mint is macerated, sometimes redistilled; green versions are coloured

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 20–25% ABV

composition.process: Corn mint and peppermint bring the cooling menthol; the sugar makes it a crème, not a cream.

originStory: Tempus Fugit Spirits was founded by Peter Schaf and John Troia, two Americans who collected nineteenth-century liqueur bottles and recipes and set out to recreate pre-Prohibition styles that had disappeared from bars. Their crème de menthe, like their crème de cacao, is produced in Switzerland and, the company says, based on a nineteenth-century recipe, made with distilled mint and other botanicals. The company's name is Latin for time flies.

originStory: Get 27 was created in 1796 by the brothers Jean and Pierre Get, who began making a peppermint liqueur in Revel, in the Lauragais south-east of Toulouse; their old distillery is now a cultural centre for the town. The 27 originally referred to its strength, though it is now bottled lower, at 21 per cent. Production later moved to Gémenos and, in 1995, to Beaucaire, and the brand now belongs to Bacardi. Its vivid green colour and cool mint flavour made it a familiar sight in French bars, usually served over crushed ice.

name: Luxardo Maraschino
description: Maraschino Liqueur from Italy.
funFact: The only Maraschino Liqueur bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a small measure at cellar temperature into a cordial glass and treat it as a curiosity-sipper: it is drier and funkier than its candied-cherry name suggests. Most bottles earn their keep a quarter ounce at a time in a Last Word, Martinez, or Hemingway Daiquiri. Nose it first for the almond-and-flowers mystique from the distilled pits, then taste for the sour-cherry funk underneath.

composition.summary: A clear liqueur distilled from marasca cherries, their pits, stems and leaves.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Marasca cherries fermented whole, with pits, stems and leaves

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot-distilled to a clear spirit, then sweetened

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in neutral ash-wood vats that don't add colour

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 32% ABV

composition.process: Distilling the pits and leaves along with the fruit builds that funky almond-and-flowers character.

originStory: Girolamo Luxardo founded his company in 1821 in Zara, now Zadar in Croatia, then part of the Habsburg Kingdom of Dalmatia, after his wife Maria Canevari had made a name with her homemade rosolio maraschino, a liqueur from local marasca cherries. The company distilled the cherries, with their stones and leaves, into a clear liqueur and sold it in straw-wrapped bottles. After the Second World War destroyed the factory, Giorgio Luxardo moved the business to Torreglia, near Padua, where the family grows its own marasca orchards.

name: Luxardo Limoncello
description: Limoncello from Italy.
funFact: One of 3 Limoncello bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Store the bottle in the freezer — the high sugar keeps it pourable — and serve small measures in chilled cordial glasses straight after dinner, Amalfi style. Sip it slowly while it is still glacially cold and slightly syrupy, letting it warm on the tongue. Notice that it is all fragrant zest and no sourness: candied lemon and flowers, never lemon juice.

composition.summary: Southern Italian liqueur made by steeping lemon zest in spirit with sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, lemon zest only, sugar and water

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pure maceration — the zest gives up its oils to the alcohol

components.label: Aging

originStory: Limoncello is the lemon liqueur of southern Italy, made by steeping lemon zest in neutral spirit and sweetening the infusion, and Sorrento, Amalfi and Capri all claim to be its birthplace, each with its own family stories. It was bottled widely for sale only in the late twentieth century. Luxardo, the house Girolamo Luxardo founded in Zara in Dalmatia in 1821 and moved to Torreglia in the Veneto after the Second World War, added a limoncello to a range best known for its maraschino.

originStory: Pallini is a Roman family firm founded in 1875 by Nicola Pallini, and it is still run by his descendants. Limoncello's birthplace is disputed among Sorrento, Amalfi and Capri, and the liqueur was long a homemade drink of the south before firms such as Pallini bottled it for sale across Italy and abroad.

originStory: Disaronno's makers date it to 1525 and tell a legend: the painter Bernardino Luini, decorating a church in Saronno with a fresco of the Madonna, was given a liqueur by the young widow who modelled for him. The documented business belongs to the Reina family of Saronno, whose company, Illva Saronno, made it famous as Amaretto di Saronno before renaming it Disaronno Originale in 2001. Despite its almond flavour it contains no almonds, relying instead on apricot kernel oil, herbs and fruits.

The family dates its liqueur to 1851. Saronno, a town north of Milan, gives its name to the whole amaretto tradition, and Lazzaroni's is one of the town's two historic amarettos, alongside Disaronno.

description: Nocino from Italy.

serve.how: Serve it the Emilian way: a small pour at room temperature in a cordial glass after a heavy meal, though a single small cube or a slight chill suits warmer nights. It is also wonderful drizzled over vanilla gelato or stirred into espresso. Sip slowly and follow the arc from dark walnut and baking spice into coffee-like, bitter-herb depths — farmhouse alchemy in slow motion.

originStory: Nocino is a dark liqueur of unripe green walnuts, steeped with sugar and spices in alcohol for weeks, and tradition, especially around Modena in Emilia-Romagna, says the walnuts must be picked on or around the night of St John, 24 June, while their shells are still soft. Families made it at home each summer to open in winter. Sibona, a Piedmontese distillery at Piobesi d'Alba better known for grappa, bottles a commercial nocino in that tradition.

originStory: Galliano was created in 1896 by Arturo Vaccari, a distiller in Livorno, Tuscany, who named it after Giuseppe Galliano, an Italian army officer celebrated for his defence of a fort at Mekele during the First Italo-Ethiopian War. Its vanilla and anise flavour, golden colour and tall bottle shaped like a classical column made it distinctive, and in the 1970s it became famous in the United States through the Harvey Wallbanger. Its owner, Lucas Bols, presents L'Autentico as a return to the original strength and recipe.

Sip rather than slam, crunching a bean between tastes so the roasty bitterness cuts the syrupy anise sweetness. It also works beautifully as a digestivo splashed into espresso or over ice with a coffee bean garnish.

originStory: Sambuca is the anise liqueur of Lazio, and its commercial history begins in the port of Civitavecchia in the mid-nineteenth century, when Luigi Manzi sold an anise liqueur under that name. The word is usually traced to the Latin for elder, sambucus, though other derivations have been proposed. Sambuca Romana takes its name from Rome and is one of the brands that carried the liqueur abroad; it is often served con la mosca, with coffee beans floating in the glass.

Molinari's Extra is a clear anise liqueur made with star anise and other aromatics. It is often served con la mosca, with three coffee beans floating in the glass.

Illva Saronno, makers of Disaronno, bought the brand from Pernod Ricard in 2009.

originStory: Baileys was launched in 1974 by Gilbeys of Ireland, part of International Distillers and Vintners, as the first Irish cream liqueur. The idea came from a London team, Tom Jago, David Gluckman and Hugh Seymour-Davies, asked to create a new drink for Ireland; combining Irish whiskey with fresh Irish cream also made use of surplus dairy cream. By its creators' account the name was borrowed from a restaurant near their office in Soho, and the R. A. Bailey signature on the label belongs to no real person.

originStory: Advocaat's commercial history is usually dated to 1828, when J. G. Cooymans began making an egg liqueur at his distillery in 's-Hertogenbosch, though its origins are disputed. One theory links it to an avocado drink Dutch colonists met in Brazil, with egg yolk replacing the avocado back home; another derives the name from advocatenborrel, a lawyers' drink. Warninks became one of the best-known Dutch brands of this thick egg liqueur, traditionally eaten with a spoon.

originStory: Verpoorten was founded in 1876 by Eugen Verpoorten, who opened a liquor and colonial goods business in Heinsberg, in the German Rhineland, and began making an egg liqueur. The firm moved to Berlin in 1920 and, after the Second World War, to Bonn, where it has been based since 1952. It is still family-owned, now in its fifth generation, and the company says its recipe of egg yolks, sugar and spirit has not changed since the start.

Its true calling is seasoning rum drinks — try a Corn n' Oil (blackstrap rum, falernum, lime, bitters) in your tiki mug. originStory: Falernum is a Barbadian syrup liqueur of rum, lime, ginger, clove and almond, made on the island since at least the nineteenth century; its name may echo the Falernian wine of ancient Rome, though other stories exist. John D. Taylor's Velvet Falernum, which the brand dates to 1890, took its name from the syrup's thick, velvety texture and became the best-known commercial version. It is now produced in Barbados by R. L. Seale and appears in tiki drinks such as the Zombie.

To taste it on its own, pour a small measure at room temperature and sip slowly — the whole spice rack unfolds in order: allspice, clove, cinnamon, then brown sugar. In winter, stir a barspoon into hot mulled cider and thank Jamaica.

originStory: Allspice dram, also called pimento dram, is a Jamaican liqueur of rum infused with the dried berries of the pimento tree, which grows on the island and is what the English-speaking world calls allspice. Tiki bartenders of the mid-twentieth century used it in their recipes, but it later vanished from most bars outside Jamaica. This bottling is named after St Elizabeth, a parish in southwest Jamaica, and its arrival in the US in the late 2000s let bartenders make those recipes again.

In winter, try it gently warmed with hot water, oyuwari-style. Sip and notice the honeyed sweetness balanced by apricot-like tartness, with the almond note from the ume kernel on the finish.

originStory: Choya began in 1914 with grape growing in Habikino, near Osaka, and the company was founded in 1924 to make wine. In 1959 it began making umeshu, the Japanese liqueur of green ume fruit steeped in spirit with sugar, which households had long made at home each June when the fruit ripens. Ume is usually called a plum in English but is closer to an apricot, and many of the company's bottles carry whole ume fruit inside.

Takara also owns the Tomatin whisky distillery in Scotland.

originStory: De Kuyper Peachtree was introduced in the US in the mid-1980s and touched off the peach schnapps boom, inspiring drinks such as the Fuzzy Navel, peach schnapps with orange juice. The De Kuyper family business began in 1695, when Petrus De Kuyper started making casks in the Netherlands, and by 1752 the family ran a distillery in Schiedam, the centre of Dutch genever. In America the brand had been made under licence since the end of Prohibition, and the company became De Kuyper Royal Distillers in 1995.

name: Midori
description: Melon Liqueur from Japan.
funFact: The only Melon Liqueur bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: With soda and lime over ice, which is far better than its reputation. In cocktails it makes a Midori Sour or a Japanese Slipper. Cut it with acid; the sugar needs something to push against.

composition.summary: Muskmelon infused into neutral spirit, sweetened and coloured.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Yubari and muskmelon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened; colour added

composition.process: Two melon varieties are used, one for aroma and one for body.

originStory: Suntory first sold its melon liqueur in Japan in 1964 as Hermes Melon Liqueur, and in 1978 renamed it Midori, Japanese for green, for its American debut at a party at Studio 54 in New York celebrating the film Saturday Night Fever. Its bright colour suited the cocktail fashions of the following decade, notably the Japanese Slipper, created in Melbourne. In 2013 Suntory reformulated it with less sugar and moved it to a frosted bottle. It is flavoured with Japanese melons, including the Yubari King.

name: Cointreau Blood Orange
description: Triple Sec from France.
funFact: One of 3 Triple Sec bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Triple sec is a workhorse, so let it work: keep it cool and reach for it in margaritas, cosmopolitans, and sidecars, where its clean orange brightness does the heavy lifting. To assess a bottle, sip a small chilled pour from a rocks glass — better versions taste of real orange peel, not candy. A splash in chilled prosecco with a twist makes an effortless aperitif.

composition.summary: A clear orange liqueur made by distilling neutral spirit with orange peel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, sweet and bitter orange peel, sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with the peels, which keeps it clear and bright

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: A wide 15–40% ABV depending on quality

composition.process: Redistilling with the peel — rather than just infusing — is what makes it clean enough to disappear into a margarita.

originStory: Cointreau Blood Orange is a variation on the orange liqueur the Cointreau family first sold in 1875 in Angers, made by adding the peel of blood oranges, with their berry-like edge, to the house's blend of sweet and bitter orange peels. The original Cointreau is credited to Édouard Cointreau, whose father and uncle, both confectioners, had founded the family distillery in 1849. Rémy Cointreau, formed when Cointreau merged with Rémy Martin in 1990, makes both at Saint-Barthélemy-d'Anjou, just outside Angers.

name: Sheridan's
description: Irish Cream from Ireland.
funFact: One of 3 Irish Cream bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Keep the bottle in the fridge and pour it well chilled over ice in a rocks glass, or spike your coffee and crown it with whipped cream. Steer clear of citrus-heavy mixers — the cream will curdle — and refrigerate after opening. Sip slowly and notice the order of arrival: silky cream, then chocolate and vanilla, with the whiskey warmth surfacing only at the finish.

composition.summary: Irish whiskey emulsified with fresh dairy cream, sugar and chocolate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Irish whiskey, fresh dairy cream, sugar and cocoa

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Not distilled as a liqueur — the whiskey is blended in

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; the cream sets a real shelf life

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 17% ABV

composition.process: Homogenising the cream with the spirit is the trick that stops it curdling or separating.

originStory: Sheridan's went on sale in 1994 in a bottle split into two chambers, one holding a dark coffee and whiskey liqueur and the other a white vanilla cream, poured together so the two settle in the glass. The idea came from Pat Rigney, head of research and development for Baileys, who first conceived it in the 1980s, and it is made in Dublin under the name of Thomas Sheridan and Sons. It was part of the wave of Irish cream liqueurs that followed Baileys.

name: Bénédictine D.O.M.
description: Bénédictine from France.
funFact: The only Bénédictine bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour an ounce or two into a snifter at room temperature, cup the bowl in your palm, and give it a slow swirl to release the honey and herb aromatics. Sip it neat as an after-dinner drink, or go classic with a B&B — equal parts Bénédictine and brandy in the same glass. As it warms, count the layers: honey first, then baking spice, then a long herbal finish that hints at the 27 botanicals.

composition.summary: A honeyed French liqueur of twenty-seven herbs and spices on a spirit base.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral and brandy spirit carrying twenty-seven herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Botanicals distilled in separate batches, then blended to recipe

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak before the final blend and sweetening

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40% ABV

composition.process: Distilling the botanical groups separately lets the blender assemble the flavour like an orchestra.

originStory: Bénédictine was created in 1863 by Alexandre Le Grand, a wine merchant in Fécamp, Normandy, who worked with a local chemist from old herbal formulas. He promoted it with a story that it revived a recipe of the Benedictine monks of Fécamp Abbey, attributed to a monk named Dom Bernardo Vincelli in 1510, a tale historians regard as marketing. The D.O.M. on the label stands for Deo Optimo Maximo, to God, most good, most great. Le Grand commissioned the ornate Palais Bénédictine in Fécamp, where it is still made.

name: Izarra Verte
description: Izarra from France.
funFact: The only Izarra bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight and cold after a meal, or poured over crushed ice as they do in Bayonne. The yellow is the gentler of the two and the better introduction; the green is stronger and more aggressively herbal.

composition.summary: Armagnac and plant distillates blended with honey and sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Armagnac

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Reportedly 32 Pyrenean plants for the yellow, 48 for the green

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Plants macerated and distilled, then blended and sweetened with honey

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak

composition.process: Honey rather than sugar syrup gives it the weight that separates it from its Alpine cousins.

originStory: Izarra was created in 1906 by Joseph Grattau, a botanist and pharmacist, in Hendaye in the French Basque Country, and its name is the Basque word for star. In 1912 the business opened a large distillery in Bayonne on the banks of the Adour, which operated there until 1998. Green Izarra is made from seventeen plants and spices, distilled and blended with armagnac and bottled at 48 per cent, while the yellow version is softer, at 40.

name: Génépi Le Chamois
description: Génépi from France.
funFact: The only Génépi bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Do as the ski lodges do: keep the bottle cold and pour a small measure into a cordial glass after a rich meal. It also takes well to a single small cube or a splash of tonic if the wormwood bite runs hot. Sip in small doses and notice the progression from meadow herbs and chamomile to the bittersweet, alpine-scree finish that makes it such a bracing digestif.

composition.summary: An Alpine liqueur made from tiny high-altitude artemisia flowers.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit steeped with génépi (Artemisia) flowers and sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditionally a maceration; some producers distil the herb

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; often the flower stalks sit right in the bottle

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 30–40% ABV

composition.process: The wormwood-family flowers only grow on high scree, which is why the bite tastes so alpine.

originStory: Génépi is the Alpine liqueur of Savoie and the Aosta Valley, made from small, silvery artemisia plants, relatives of wormwood, that grow above the treeline, and its name is the local word for the plants themselves. Mountain families once gathered the wild plants in late summer and steeped them in spirit with sugar at home; today most génépi uses cultivated plants, because wild picking is restricted. Le Chamois takes its name from the chamois, the Alpine goat-antelope.

name: Mastiha Skinos
description: Mastiha from Greece.
funFact: The only Mastiha bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass after dinner. It also works over ice with soda and a strip of lemon, and Greek bartenders use it in place of a herbal liqueur in gin drinks.

composition.summary: Mastic tree resin distilled or infused into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or tsipouro

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mastiha resin from Pistacia lentiscus var. Chia

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Resin distilled or macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: The trees only weep usable mastic on Chios, an agricultural mystery nobody has fully explained.

originStory: Mastiha liqueur is flavoured with the resin of the mastic tree, which is harvested as tear-like drops only in the south of Chios, in the island's mastic villages, and has been traded since antiquity; Chios mastic is a protected product, and Chios mastiha liqueur has its own geographical indication. Skinos was launched as a modern brand of mastiha liqueur for bars and export, and its name is the Greek word for the mastic tree. It is a clear, piney, faintly sweet spirit.

name: Beerenburg Sonnema
description: Beerenburg from Netherlands.
funFact: The only Beerenburg bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass, taken before or after food rather than with it. In Friesland it is also drunk with hot water and sugar as a cure for whatever is going around.

composition.summary: Jenever or neutral spirit steeped with a fixed herb blend.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Juniper spirit or jenever

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, bay, juniper berry, laurel and a dozen more

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated rather than redistilled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 30%

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation keeps the herbs tasting green and raw instead of polished.

originStory: Beerenburg takes its name from Hendrik Beerenburg, an Amsterdam spice merchant who opened a shop on the Stromarkt in 1724 and sold a herb mix for steeping in genever. The habit caught on far more in the northern provinces of Friesland, Groningen and Drenthe than in Amsterdam, and Frisian distillers took the drink up as their own. Sonnema, from Dokkum in Friesland, is one of the best-known of them, making a herbal genever bitter with gentian, bay leaf and other botanicals.

name: Zirbenz Stone Pine
description: Zirbenschnaps from Austria.
funFact: The only Zirbenschnaps bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: After a long walk, at room temperature, in a small glass. Cold flattens the resin note that is the entire reason to drink it. Austrians pour it into hut coffee when the weather turns.

composition.summary: Young stone pine cones macerated in spirit and lightly sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or clear fruit brandy

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green cones of Pinus cembra, the Swiss stone pine

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for weeks; colour and flavour extract together

composition.process: The pink colour leaches out of the cone resin and deepens the longer the maceration runs.

originStory: Zirbenschnaps is an Alpine tradition from Austria and South Tyrol: young cones of the Swiss stone pine, the Zirbe, are picked green in early summer and steeped in spirit, which turns red-brown and takes on a resinous, piney flavour. Families made it at home and mountain inns served their own. Zirbenz is a commercial version, made in Austria from the cones of high Alpine trees and brought to the American market by the importer Haus Alpenz.

name: Enzian Grassl
description: Enzian from Germany.
funFact: The only Enzian bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Cool, neat, in a very small pour after a heavy meal. It is not a beginner's spirit and does not reward gulping. Give it time in the glass, since the earthiness settles into something closer to celery and honey.

composition.summary: Fermented gentian root distilled to a clear, dry spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Gentiana lutea or punctata root, fermented

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still; the root itself is the fermentable

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Unlike gentian liqueurs, the root is fermented and distilled rather than steeped, so there is no sugar to hide behind.

originStory: Grassl was founded in 1602 at Berchtesgaden, in the Bavarian Alps, and is regarded as Germany's oldest gentian distillery. It holds rights to dig the roots of yellow gentian on mountain pastures that now lie within the Berchtesgaden National Park, and the roots are traditionally distilled in small huts up on the mountain before the spirit is brought down. Enzian, German for gentian, is a clear, earthy, bitter spirit distilled from the fermented roots rather than flavoured with them.

name: Hierbas Ibicencas
description: Hierbas from Spain.
funFact: The only Hierbas bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after eating, or over ice in summer. The dulce version is thick and sweet; the seca is drier and closer to a straight herbal anise.

composition.summary: Anise spirit macerated with Balearic herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Anise-flavoured spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Rosemary, thyme, fennel, lemon verbena, juniper, orange leaf

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated; sprigs often left in the bottle

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 20–40% depending on style

composition.process: Leaving the herbs in means the liqueur keeps changing on the shelf, which producers treat as a feature.

originStory: Hierbas Ibicencas is the herbal liqueur of Ibiza, made by steeping local plants such as thyme, rosemary, fennel, lemon verbena and juniper in an anise spirit, and islanders made it at home for generations, each family with its own blend. It is now a protected geographical indication, and sprigs of the herbs are often left in the bottle. The island's commercial producers bottle versions of that household recipe, and it is usually served cold after a meal.

name: Travarica Badel
description: Travarica from Croatia.
funFact: The only Travarica bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, poured on arrival with dried figs or cheese. The herbs are usually left in the bottle, so the last glass is noticeably more medicinal than the first.

composition.summary: Grape or fruit rakija macerated with wild Mediterranean herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Lozovača or fruit rakija

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Sage, rosemary, juniper, mint, wormwood, St John's wort

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, sometimes redistilled

composition.process: Herbs are picked in early summer when the oils are highest and steeped for weeks in the sun.

originStory: Travarica, from trava, herb, is the herbal rakija of Croatia's Adriatic coast, especially Dalmatia, where grape brandy is steeped with local plants such as sage, rue, fennel, mint and carob, and families made it at home from their own grape spirit. Badel, the Zagreb drinks company that counts 1862 as its beginning and carries the date in its name, bottles a commercial travarica in that tradition. The company took its modern shape after the Second World War from several older firms.

name: Branca Menta
description: Fernet-Branca from Italy.
funFact: One of 2 Fernet-Branca bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Shot glass or small chilled rocks glass
serve.how: Pour a small measure neat as a digestif after a heavy meal; the menthol-and-bitter-herb blast is the point, so take it in confident sips rather than nervous ones. A light chill softens the eucalyptus edge for newcomers, but true believers drink it room temperature. For the Argentine experience, pour an ounce or two over ice and top generously with cola for a fernet con coca.

composition.summary: A ferociously bitter Milanese amaro built from twenty-seven herbs and spices.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape spirit infused with twenty-seven herbs, roots and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Botanicals are macerated and infused, then blended to recipe

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak casks before bottling

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 39% ABV

composition.process: Myrrh, saffron and menthol-heavy botanicals are steeped until the result tastes like medicine that won.

originStory: Fratelli Branca introduced Branca Menta in the 1960s as a sweeter, mint-flavoured companion to Fernet-Branca, the bitter that Bernardino Branca, a self-taught herbalist, created in Milan in 1845 and sold with his sons. One story told about it is that the opera singer Maria Callas suggested adding mint to fernet. It keeps the bitter herbal base of the original, with peppermint oil added, and is still made in Milan by the Branca family company.

name: Amaro Sfumato Rabarbaro
description: Amaro from Italy.
funFact: One of 6 Amaro bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat after a meal at room temperature, which is how Italy drinks it. Lighter amari take ice and soda well; heavy ones do not. In cocktails they swap in for vermouth to add bitterness without more alcohol.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit or wine macerated with bitter herbs, roots and peel, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, sometimes a wine base

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, cinchona, rhubarb, wormwood, citrus peel, spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated or infused, then sweetened and rested

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Varies; some rest in oak for years

composition.process: Bitterness comes from roots and barks, sweetness from sugar syrup, and the balance between them defines the house style.

originStory: Amaro Sfumato Rabarbaro comes from Cappelletti, a family firm in Aldeno, in Trentino in the Italian Alps, founded in 1909 by Giuseppe Cappelletti and also known for its wine-based aperitivo. Rabarbaro amari, flavoured with Chinese rhubarb root, are an old northern Italian style, and Sfumato, smoky, takes its name from the smoky edge that sets it apart from other rhubarb bitters. It is made from rhubarb, alpine herbs and sugar on a spirit base, and is drunk as an after-dinner amaro.

name: Amaro Braulio
description: Amaro from Italy.
funFact: One of 6 Amaro bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat after a meal at room temperature, which is how Italy drinks it. Lighter amari take ice and soda well; heavy ones do not. In cocktails they swap in for vermouth to add bitterness without more alcohol.

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Varies; some rest in oak for years

composition.process: Bitterness comes from roots and barks, sweetness from sugar syrup, and the balance between them defines the house style.

originStory: Amaro Braulio was first sold commercially in 1875 by Francesco Peloni, a pharmacist in Bormio, in the Valtellina high in the Lombard Alps, working from a recipe of mountain herbs, roots and berries such as gentian, juniper and wormwood. It takes its name from the Braulio, the mountain and valley above the town, and it is still made at the Peloni family's premises in Bormio, where it is aged for two years in Slavonian oak casks.

name: Meletti Amaro
description: Amaro from Italy.
funFact: One of 6 Amaro bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Neat after a meal at room temperature, which is how Italy drinks it. Lighter amari take ice and soda well; heavy ones do not. In cocktails they swap in for vermouth to add bitterness without more alcohol.

components.label: Botanicals

components.label: Distillation

components.label: Aging

originStory: Meletti is the family firm Silvio Meletti founded in Ascoli Piceno, in the Marche, in 1870, first to make an anise liqueur, the Anisetta Meletti that remains its best-known product. The family also gave its name to the Caffè Meletti on the city's Piazza del Popolo, an elegant café that became a local landmark. Its amaro, built on herbs, spices and citrus with a light, floral character, came later, and the company is still run by Meletti descendants.

name: Pelinkovac Badel
description: Pelinkovec from Croatia.
funFact: The only Pelinkovec bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or long with tonic and lemon, which cuts the bitterness enough to make it an aperitif. It is drier than Jägermeister and should not be treated as a substitute.

composition.summary: Wormwood and herbs macerated in spirit with minimal sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Wormwood, gentian, bitter orange, liquorice root

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

composition.process: Restraint with sugar is what keeps it on the bitter side of a liqueur.

originStory: Pelinkovac takes its name from pelin, wormwood, the bitter herb at its heart, and it is a dark, bittersweet liqueur long popular in Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia, where it is drunk as an aperitif or after a meal. Badel, the Zagreb drinks company that counts 1862 as its beginning, is today one of its best-known producers, making it from wormwood and other herbs macerated in spirit and sweetened. The company took shape after the Second World War from several older Zagreb firms.

name: Pernod Absinthe
description: Absinthe Verte from France.
funFact: One of 3 Absinthe Verte bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Absinthe glass with a slotted spoon
serve.how: Three to five parts iced water dripped slowly over a sugar cube on a slotted spoon. The louche should build gradually. No flames — burning the sugar is a 1990s invention that scorches the herbs.

composition.summary: Wormwood, anise and fennel distilled, then steeped with herbs for colour.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral or wine-based spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, green anise, fennel; petite wormwood and hyssop for colouring

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then a second cold steep for natural colour

composition.process: Artificially coloured absinthe stays green forever, which is the giveaway.

originStory: Henri-Louis Pernod founded his absinthe distillery at Pontarlier, near the Swiss border, in 1805, after starting in Couvet, Switzerland, in 1797 with a recipe linked to Dr Pierre Ordinaire, and Pernod Fils became the most prestigious absinthe of the Belle Époque. France banned absinthe in 1915 and the company turned to anise. After the European bans were lifted, Pernod brought absinthe back, and in 2013 it reformulated it to come closer to the pre-1915 recipe, with a grape spirit base.

name: La Fée Parisienne
description: Absinthe Verte from France.
funFact: One of 3 Absinthe Verte bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Absinthe glass with a slotted spoon
serve.how: Three to five parts iced water dripped slowly over a sugar cube on a slotted spoon. The louche should build gradually. No flames — burning the sugar is a 1990s invention that scorches the herbs.

composition.summary: Wormwood, anise and fennel distilled, then steeped with herbs for colour.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral or wine-based spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, green anise, fennel; petite wormwood and hyssop for colouring

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then a second cold steep for natural colour

composition.process: Artificially coloured absinthe stays green forever, which is the giveaway.

originStory: La Fée, the fairy, was launched at the end of the 1990s by the British entrepreneur George Rowley, working with the French absinthe historian Marie-Claude Delahaye, founder of an absinthe museum at Auvers-sur-Oise, as absinthe began to return to European shelves. Its name recalls la fée verte, the green fairy, the nickname absinthe earned in nineteenth-century Paris, and its eye logo became a familiar emblem of the revival. The Parisienne is the brand's classic green absinthe, made in France.

name: St. George Absinthe Verte
description: Absinthe Verte from USA.
funFact: One of 3 Absinthe Verte bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Absinthe glass with a slotted spoon
serve.how: Three to five parts iced water dripped slowly over a sugar cube on a slotted spoon. The louche should build gradually. No flames — burning the sugar is a 1990s invention that scorches the herbs.

components.label: Base

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, green anise, fennel; petite wormwood and hyssop for colouring

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then a second cold steep for natural colour

composition.process: Artificially coloured absinthe stays green forever, which is the giveaway.

originStory: St. George Absinthe Verte was released at the end of the 2000s, after US regulators began approving absinthe again, making it one of the first absinthes legally made in the United States since the ban of 1912. Its creator, Lance Winters, St. George's master distiller, had been working on the recipe for some eleven years. St. George Spirits itself, now based in Alameda, California, was founded in 1982 by the German-born Jörg Rupf, who began by making fruit brandies in the European manner.

name: Ricard
description: Pastis from France.
funFact: One of 3 Pastis bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour one part pastis into a tall or small tumbler and top with about five parts very cold water — the drink blooms milky yellow on contact. Add an ice cube after diluting if you like, but never drop ice into neat pastis or the oils will clump. Sip unhurried, aperitif-style, noticing star anise and licorice mellowing into gentle sweet herbs; it should taste like a Marseille terrace at golden hour.

composition.summary: A Provençal aperitif of star anise and licorice root steeped in neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit with star anise, licorice root and herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Built by maceration and blending, not by redistillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; sweetened and bottled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–45% ABV

composition.process: Licorice root is the tell — it gives pastis the roundness absinthe never had.

originStory: Paul Ricard, a Marseille native, launched his pastis in 1932, billing it as the real pastis of Marseille, in the space absinthe had left after it was banned in 1915. His anise and liquorice aperitif, diluted with cold water until it turns cloudy, became one of France's most popular drinks. The Vichy regime banned pastis during the war, and it returned at full strength only in 1951. In 1975 Ricard merged with its old rival Pernod to form Pernod Ricard.

name: Pernod Anise
description: Pastis from France.
funFact: One of 3 Pastis bottlings catalogued here.

Sip unhurried, aperitif-style, noticing star anise and licorice mellowing into gentle sweet herbs; it should taste like a Marseille terrace at golden hour.

composition.process: Licorice root is the tell — it gives pastis the roundness absinthe never had.

originStory: Pernod's anise grew out of the absinthe house Henri-Louis Pernod founded at Pontarlier in 1805. When France banned absinthe in 1915, the company turned to an aniseed spirit made without wormwood, and that drink, bottled at a lower strength than its predecessor, became Pernod as most drinkers now know it. It is a pale yellow-green and turns cloudy with water. In 1975 the company merged with its great Marseille rival, Ricard, to create Pernod Ricard.

name: Henri Bardouin Pastis
description: Pastis from France.
funFact: One of 3 Pastis bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour one part pastis into a tall or small tumbler and top with about five parts very cold water — the drink blooms milky yellow on contact. Add an ice cube after diluting if you like, but never drop ice into neat pastis or the oils will clump. Sip unhurried, aperitif-style, noticing star anise and licorice mellowing into gentle sweet herbs; it should taste like a Marseille terrace at golden hour.

composition.summary: A Provençal aperitif of star anise and licorice root steeped in neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit with star anise, licorice root and herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Built by maceration and blending, not by redistillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; sweetened and bottled

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–45% ABV

composition.process: Licorice root is the tell — it gives pastis the roundness absinthe never had.

originStory: Henri Bardouin is made by Distilleries et Domaines de Provence in Forcalquier, in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, a house that dates itself to 1898 and is known for liqueurs and aperitifs drawn from the plants of the surrounding hills. Its pastis is unusually complex for the style, built from dozens of herbs and spices beyond anise and liquorice, many of them from Haute-Provence. Pastis became the classic aperitif of southern France after absinthe was banned in 1915.

name: Ouzo 12
description: Ouzo from Greece.
funFact: One of 2 Ouzo bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour two fingers into a small tumbler and add cold water or an ice cube to taste, watching it cloud ghostly white as the anise oils louche. Greeks sip it slowly over a long afternoon, never as a shot, always with a little food on the table. Take small sips and notice the licorice sweetness up front giving way to fennel and a faint citrus lift.

composition.summary: A Greek anise spirit made by distilling alcohol with aniseed and botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral alcohol, sometimes with grape distillate in the blend

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled in copper pots with aniseed, fennel and spices

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; rested briefly then bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 37.5–48% ABV

composition.process: Distilling the aniseed rather than merely flavouring it is what earns the name.

originStory: Ouzo 12 was first made in 1880 by the Kaloyannis brothers, distillers in Constantinople, and its name, the story goes, comes from the cask customers liked best, number 12, which the brothers then used for the whole brand. It went on to become one of the best-known ouzos in Greece. Ouzo is a protected name reserved for Greece and Cyprus, and the origin of the word itself is disputed, between an Italian shipping mark, uso Marsiglia, and the Turkish word for grape.

name: Ouzo Plomari
description: Ouzo from Greece.
funFact: One of 2 Ouzo bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour two fingers into a small tumbler and add cold water or an ice cube to taste, watching it cloud ghostly white as the anise oils louche. Greeks sip it slowly over a long afternoon, never as a shot, always with a little food on the table. Take small sips and notice the licorice sweetness up front giving way to fennel and a faint citrus lift.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral alcohol, sometimes with grape distillate in the blend

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled in copper pots with aniseed, fennel and spices

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; rested briefly then bottled clear

components.label: Strength

composition.process: Distilling the aniseed rather than merely flavouring it is what earns the name.

originStory: Ouzo Plomari was first distilled in 1894 by Isidoros Arvanitis in Plomari, a harbour town on the island of Lesbos that is one of the most celebrated homes of ouzo, and it carries the town's name. Lesbos has a long ouzo tradition built on local aniseed, and Plomari's distilleries made the town's name a byword for the spirit across Greece. Ouzo itself is a protected name that may only be used for spirits made in Greece and Cyprus.

name: Yeni Rakı
description: Rakı from Turkey.
funFact: One of 2 Rakı bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a couple fingers into a tall narrow rakı glass, add an equal measure of cool water to summon the milky 'lion's milk' cloud, then a cube of ice if you wish. Keep a second glass of plain water alongside, Turkish-style, and alternate sips. Drink it slowly across a long meze table — rakı is a conversation spirit — noticing the raisin sweetness beneath the anise and the warm spice on the finish.

composition.summary: Turkey's anise spirit, distilled from grapes and raisins.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh grapes or sun-dried raisins, fermented into a wash

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled in copper pots with aniseed on the final run

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, though many brands rest it before bottling

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: The suma — grape distillate — is run again over aniseed, which is what makes it rakı.

originStory: Yeni Rakı was introduced in 1937 by Tekel, the Turkish state monopoly on alcohol and tobacco, and the state went on making it for nearly seven decades. Its name means new rakı. Rakı is an aniseed spirit that turns milky white when water is added, which is why Turks call it lion's milk, and it is traditionally served with meze. When Tekel's spirits business was privatised in 2004, Mey İçki took over the brand, and Diageo bought Mey in 2011.

name: Tekirdağ Rakı
description: Rakı from Turkey.
funFact: One of 2 Rakı bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a couple fingers into a tall narrow rakı glass, add an equal measure of cool water to summon the milky 'lion's milk' cloud, then a cube of ice if you wish. Keep a second glass of plain water alongside, Turkish-style, and alternate sips. Drink it slowly across a long meze table — rakı is a conversation spirit — noticing the raisin sweetness beneath the anise and the warm spice on the finish.

composition.summary: Turkey's anise spirit, distilled from grapes and raisins.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh grapes or sun-dried raisins, fermented into a wash

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled in copper pots with aniseed on the final run

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, though many brands rest it before bottling

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: The suma — grape distillate — is run again over aniseed, which is what makes it rakı.

originStory: Tekirdağ is a port town on the Sea of Marmara in Turkish Thrace, and its name has long been attached to rakı, the aniseed-flavoured grape spirit that Turkey drinks with meze and fish. Tekirdağ Rakısı was for decades a label of Tekel, the state spirits monopoly, and its character is often credited to the artesian water of nearby Çorlu. When Tekel's spirits business was privatised the brand passed to Mey İçki, now part of Diageo, and like all rakı it turns milky white when water is added.

name: Arak Touma
description: Arak from Lebanon.
funFact: One of 2 Arak bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: 38-45°F, well chilled with water and ice
serve.how: Mix roughly one part arak with two parts cool water in a small tumbler, then add ice — always in that order, since ice added first can crystallize the anise oils into a film. Watch it swirl milky white, the classic louche of the Levant. Sip it alongside food rather than alone, letting small sips reset your palate between bites of mezze; notice the grape sweetness underneath the licorice.

composition.summary: A Levantine grape spirit redistilled with aniseed until it clouds with water.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fermented grapes, typically local varieties like obeideh

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled repeatedly, aniseed added on the final pass

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Traditionally rested in porous clay amphorae

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–53% ABV

composition.process: Adding aniseed only to the last distillation keeps the perfume clean rather than heavy.

originStory: Arak Touma is a Lebanese arak, grape spirit distilled again with green aniseed in the Levantine manner, and its makers have not published how the label began.

name: Arak Massaya
description: Arak from Lebanon.
funFact: One of 2 Arak bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: 38-45°F, well chilled with water and ice
serve.how: Mix roughly one part arak with two parts cool water in a small tumbler, then add ice — always in that order, since ice added first can crystallize the anise oils into a film. Watch it swirl milky white, the classic louche of the Levant. Sip it alongside food rather than alone, letting small sips reset your palate between bites of mezze; notice the grape sweetness underneath the licorice.

composition.summary: A Levantine grape spirit redistilled with aniseed until it clouds with water.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fermented grapes, typically local varieties like obeideh

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled repeatedly, aniseed added on the final pass

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Traditionally rested in porous clay amphorae

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–53% ABV

composition.process: Adding aniseed only to the last distillation keeps the perfume clean rather than heavy.

originStory: Massaya was founded in 1998 by the brothers Sami and Ramzi Ghosn at Tanaïl, in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, on a family estate they had been forced to abandon during the civil war. They had returned in the early 1990s and brought in partners from two French wine families, the Bruniers of Vieux Télégraphe in Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Dominique Hébrard, formerly of Cheval Blanc. Arak was part of the plan from the start: the house distils it three times in copper alembics heated with vine wood, rests it in clay jars from the potters of Beit Chabab, and bottles it in distinctive blue glass.

name: Anís del Mono
description: Anís from Spain.
funFact: The only Anís bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Seco neat and cold; dulce over ice or with a splash of water, which turns it cloudy. It is also drunk with coffee as a carajillo, and in some regions poured directly into it.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit distilled or macerated with green anise and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green anise seed, sometimes star anise and fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sweetened to dulce or seco

composition.process: Anethole from the anise is what clouds the liquid when water is added, the same effect as in ouzo and pastis.

originStory: The brothers Josep and Vicenç Bosch began making Anís del Mono in Badalona, just north of Barcelona, in 1870. Why the label shows a monkey is disputed: one story credits a pet at the factory, another reads it as a jab at the Darwin controversy, and the monkey is often said to wear the naturalist's face. In 1897 the firm ran one of Spain's first poster competitions, won by the painter Ramon Casas. The faceted bottle, registered in 1902, is still scraped with a spoon or stick as a percussion instrument in Spanish Christmas carols.

name: Chinchón Dulce
description: Chinchón from Spain.
funFact: The only Chinchón bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Dry over ice as an aperitif, sweet after a meal, and the 74% version with considerable respect and a great deal of water. Spaniards also add it to coffee as a carajillo.

composition.summary: Locally grown anise distilled in copper alembics.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Anise grown around Chinchón

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, distilled with the seed

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 35% to 74% depending on style

composition.process: Distilling with the seed rather than adding oil afterwards is what earns it protected status.

originStory: Chinchón Dulce is the sweet style of the aniseed spirit of Chinchón, the hill town south-east of Madrid whose name is a protected designation for anís, and the history of this particular label has not been published.

name: Zibib Sudanese
description: Zibib from Sudan.
funFact: The only Zibib bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Poured over ice or cut with two parts water, which turns it milky white. Egyptians drink it with mezze rather than after a meal, and it stands up well to strongly spiced food.

composition.summary: Grape or raisin spirit redistilled with aniseed.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grapes, raisins or dates

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Aniseed, sometimes mastic

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the anise, usually twice

composition.process: Anethole precipitating out of solution when water is added is what produces the cloud.

originStory: Zibib, named from zabib, the Arabic word for raisin, is the name used in Egypt for the local aniseed spirit of the arak family, and no documented history has been found for a Sudanese bottling of it.

name: Mastika Peshtera
description: Mastika from Bulgaria.
funFact: The only Mastika bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or with a splash of water, which turns it cloudy. It is a before-dinner drink in the Balkans, taken with salty meze rather than at the end of a meal.

composition.summary: Grape or grain spirit distilled with anise and mastic resin.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape or grain spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mastic resin, anise, sometimes fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with botanicals, then sweetened

composition.process: The resin gives a pine-and-cedar note that separates it immediately from a plain anise spirit.

originStory: Peshtera Mastika is the aniseed spirit of Vinprom Peshtera, a distiller in the town of Peshtera at the foot of Bulgaria's Rhodope Mountains, and the company has not published a detailed account of how it began.

name: Aalborg Taffel Akvavit
description: Taffel Akvavit from Denmark.
funFact: The only Taffel Akvavit bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Freezer cold, in small measures, with the meal. Danish tradition is a beer alongside and a toast before each glass, with eye contact — skipping the eye contact is the part visitors get wrong.

composition.summary: Grain spirit redistilled with caraway and citrus, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Caraway dominant, plus citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Bottling unaged and clear is what distinguishes it from the oak-rested Norwegian styles.

originStory: Aalborg Taffel Akvavit goes back to 1846, when Isidor Henius, a young immigrant distiller, set up in the Danish city of Aalborg and began producing a cleaner, more refined spirit than the local farm brandy. Flavoured with caraway, it was meant for the dinner table, which is what taffel means, and its red label became a familiar sight at Danish lunches. Henius's business became part of De Danske Spritfabrikker, formed in 1881, which made Aalborg the name most associated with Danish akvavit. The brand is now produced in Norway.

name: O.P. Anderson
description: Dill Aquavit from Sweden.
funFact: The only Dill Aquavit bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: From the freezer, in small measures, with food rather than before it. Dill aquavit belongs with crayfish and new potatoes in a way the caraway styles do not — it is a summer spirit.

composition.summary: Grain or potato spirit redistilled with dill as the lead botanical.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain or potato neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Dill leading, with fennel, coriander and citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Dill's aromatics are fragile, so it goes in later and gentler than caraway would.

originStory: O.P. Anderson was introduced in 1891 at the Gothenburg Exhibition by the city firm O.P. Anderson & Son, at first under the name Gammal Fin 1ma Aquavit before it took the company's name. It is seasoned with caraway, anise and fennel and rested in oak barrels for about eight months, which gives it a pale straw colour. Usually described as the oldest Swedish akvavit brand still on sale, it is now produced by the Nordic drinks group Anora.

name: Moutai
description: Sauce-Aroma Baijiu from China. China's most famous baijiu.
funFact: Moutai: China's most famous baijiu

serve.how: Room temperature in a very small cup, with food, and shared. Chinese banquet custom is to toast rather than sip. The umami depth needs food alongside it; drunk alone it can be overwhelming.

composition.summary: Sorghum solid-state fermented with wheat qu in stone pits, distilled seven times.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Red sorghum and wheat qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Seven distillations across a year-long cycle

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware jars, then blended

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 53%

composition.process: 53% is considered the point where water and ethanol molecules bind most tightly, and the style is bottled there deliberately.

originStory: Moutai takes its name from Maotai, a town on the Chishui River in Guizhou, where three private distilleries, Chengyi, Ronghe and Hengxing, were making sauce-aroma liquor from local sorghum before the People's Republic was founded. By the company's account the spirit won a medal at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco, and in 1951 the three distilleries were merged into the state-owned Kweichow Moutai. Served at state banquets for decades, including the dinner for Richard Nixon's visit to China, it became the country's most famous baijiu.

name: Wuliangye
description: Strong-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: One of 2 Strong-Aroma Baijiu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with food. The fruit-and-funk profile is intense on its own but cuts through rich, oily Sichuan food remarkably well. Toast rather than sip.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in aged mud pits, distilled and blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, often with rice, wheat, corn and glutinous rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation in steamer stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The older the mud pit, the more complex the microbial population, and the higher the value of the spirit.

originStory: Wuliangye, from Yibin in Sichuan, traces its recipe to the Chen family, who are said to have refined a mixed-grain spirit there during the Ming dynasty, and the distillery still works fermentation pits it dates to that era. The spirit received its present name in 1909, when the local scholar Yang Huiquan proposed Wuliangye, meaning five-grain liquor, at a Yibin banquet, for its blend of sorghum, rice, glutinous rice, wheat and corn. In 1950 eight Yibin distilleries were merged into one state enterprise, which took the Wuliangye name in 1959.

name: Luzhou Laojiao
description: Strong-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: One of 2 Strong-Aroma Baijiu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with food. The fruit-and-funk profile is intense on its own but cuts through rich, oily Sichuan food remarkably well. Toast rather than sip.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in aged mud pits, distilled and blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, often with rice, wheat, corn and glutinous rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation in steamer stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The older the mud pit, the more complex the microbial population, and the higher the value of the spirit.

originStory: Luzhou Laojiao, in the Sichuan river city of Luzhou, dates its oldest fermentation pits to 1573, in the Ming dynasty, and has kept them in use ever since; its premium label, Guojiao 1573, is named for that year. The mud-lined pits are central to the strong-aroma style, which was first called Lu aroma after this distillery before it became the most widely made kind of baijiu in China. The modern company was formed in 1950, and its brewing techniques were included in China's first national list of intangible cultural heritage.

name: Fenjiu
description: Light-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Light-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food, or lightly chilled if it is your first baijiu. Its cleaner profile also makes it the style most usable in cocktails, where it behaves a little like a funky gin.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in stone jars with barley and pea qu.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, with a barley and pea qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, two fermentations

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware, typically shorter than other styles

composition.process: Stone jars keep the ferment isolated from soil microbes, which is why the style stays clean.

originStory: Fenjiu comes from Xinghua, or Apricot Blossom, village in Fenyang, Shanxi, and takes its name from the nearby Fen River. Liquor-making in the area is very old, and tradition ties the village to a Tang-dynasty poem by Du Mu in which a herd boy points a traveller towards Apricot Blossom village to find a wine shop. Fenjiu is the model of the light-aroma style, fermented in earthenware jars buried in the ground rather than in mud pits, which gives a cleaner, more delicate spirit, and Beijing erguotou and Taiwanese kaoliang belong to the same family.

name: Erguotou Red Star
description: Erguotou from China.
glassware: Small cup or straight from the bottle
funFact: The only Erguotou bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with street food. It is a working drink and treated as one; nobody in Beijing contemplates their erguotou. It also mixes surprisingly well with sour or citrus flavours.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented and distilled, with only the middle cut kept.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation, middle fraction only

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimal

composition.process: Discarding the head and tail of the run is exactly what the name describes, and why it is cleaner than its price suggests.

originStory: Beijing's Red Star distillery was formed in 1949, when a dozen distilleries around the city were merged into one state enterprise, by the company's account in part to supply the celebrations for the founding of the People's Republic. Its spirit is erguotou, Beijing's own light-aroma baijiu. The name means second pot head: by the usual account, three brothers at the Yuanshenghao distillery in the 1680s found that their finest spirit ran while the second pot of cooling water sat atop the still. Red Star erguotou went on to become one of the most familiar spirits in northern China.

name: Kinmen Kaoliang
description: Kaoliang from Taiwan.
funFact: The only Kaoliang bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. At 58% it is not a sipping spirit; Taiwanese custom is to drain the cup on a toast and refill.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented with wheat qu and solid-state distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum grown on Kinmen

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation and distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Stored in granite tunnels cut into the island

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 38–63%, with 58% the signature

composition.process: The granite tunnels hold a stable cool temperature year-round, which is why they are still used.

originStory: Kinmen Kaoliang began in 1952 on Kinmen, the island group off the Fujian coast held by Taiwan, when the garrison commander Hu Lien set up an army-run distillery there, with the local distiller Yeh Hua-cheng overseeing its technical side. It took the name Jiulong River Distillery once a new plant was finished, and from 1956 became the Kinmen Distillery. Kaoliang is the Chinese word for sorghum, and the spirit is a light-aroma baijiu. Now owned by the Kinmen County government, the company remains an important source of revenue for the islands.

name: Xifeng
description: Feng-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Feng-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. It is a good bridge for anyone who finds strong-aroma too pungent and light-aroma too plain.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in annually rebuilt earth pits, then basket-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with barley and pea qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation and distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Wax-sealed wicker baskets rather than earthenware jars

composition.process: Rebuilding the pits each year is the opposite of the strong-aroma approach and deliberately so.

originStory: Xifeng comes from Fengxiang County, near Baoji in Shaanxi, an old seat of government in the Wei River valley with a long tradition of liquor-making. The name joins xi, west, with the first syllable of Fengxiang. Xifeng is the model of feng aroma, a baijiu style of its own: it is fermented in mud pits like strong-aroma spirits but aged in jiuhai, large containers woven from rattan and sealed on the inside, which gives it a fruity, earthy character between the strong and light styles.

name: Jinmailang Sesame
description: Sesame-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Sesame-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food. The sesame note is genuinely reminiscent of the oil, and it pairs remarkably well with northern Chinese dishes that already use it.

composition.summary: Sorghum, wheat and bran fermented in brick-lined pits.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with wheat, bran and barley qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, in brick and mud pits

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The sesame note comes from the fermentation, not from any sesame — none is used.

originStory: Jinmailang Sesame is a sesame-aroma baijiu, a style first developed at the Jingzhi distillery in Shandong in the mid-twentieth century and named for a toasted note that comes from the process rather than from sesame, and no history of this particular label has been published.

name: Iichiko
description: Mugi Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Mugi Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with cold water
serve.how: On the rocks, or mizuwari with cold water at about one to one. Barrel-aged versions drink comfortably neat and are often mistaken for a light whisky in a blind pour.

composition.summary: Barley fermented with barley koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Barley

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Barley or rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, often under vacuum for a lighter result

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Vacuum distillation lowers the boiling point and produces a markedly cleaner, fruitier spirit.

originStory: Iichiko was launched in 1979 by Sanwa Shurui, a company founded in 1958 in Usa, in Ōita Prefecture on the island of Kyushu, which had turned from sake to shochu as competition from the big sake brewers grew. It is a mugi, or barley, shochu, light and clean in style, and its name is a local dialect phrase meaning roughly that's good. The name and the nickname shitamachi no Napoleon, the downtown Napoleon, were chosen through a public call in a local newspaper, and the brand's monthly posters, put up without a break since the 1980s, became well known across Japan.

name: Kurokirishima
description: Imo Shochu from Japan.
funFact: One of 2 Imo Shochu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Tumbler, or a ceramic kurojoka for warming
serve.how: Oyuwari — cut with hot water, hot water poured first — opens the aroma and is the traditional Kagoshima serve. On the rocks in summer. Never chilled to the point of numbness; the earthiness is the point.

composition.summary: Sweet potato fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Kogane sengan and other Kagoshima sweet potatoes

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or barley koji, black or white

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%, sometimes 20%

composition.process: Black koji, revived from Okinawan awamori production, gives a richer and sweeter result than white.

originStory: Kirishima Shuzo was founded in 1916 by Kichisuke Enatsu in Miyakonojō, in Miyazaki Prefecture, near the Kirishima volcanic range on the border with Kagoshima. The company built its name on imo, or sweet potato, shochu, and in the late 1990s launched Kurokirishima, made with black kōji, the mould long used for Okinawan awamori. Kuro means black, and the brand did much to make black-kōji shochu a mainstream style across Japan.

name: Satsuma Shiranami
description: Imo Shochu from Japan.
funFact: One of 2 Imo Shochu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Tumbler, or a ceramic kurojoka for warming
serve.how: Oyuwari — cut with hot water, hot water poured first — opens the aroma and is the traditional Kagoshima serve. On the rocks in summer. Never chilled to the point of numbness; the earthiness is the point.

composition.summary: Sweet potato fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Kogane sengan and other Kagoshima sweet potatoes

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or barley koji, black or white

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%, sometimes 20%

composition.process: Black koji, revived from Okinawan awamori production, gives a richer and sweeter result than white.

originStory: Satsuma Shuzo was founded in 1936 in Makurazaki, a fishing port at the southern tip of Kagoshima, in the old province of Satsuma, the heartland of sweet potato shochu. Its flagship, Satsuma Shiranami, takes a name meaning white waves. In the late 1970s the company's advertising promoted the local custom of cutting shochu six parts to four with hot water, and the campaign is credited with helping to spark Japan's shochu boom of the following decade, when shochu from the south reached drinkers across the country.

name: Takara Jun
description: Kome Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Kome Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp, warm or on the rocks
serve.glass: Wine glass, or warmed in a choku
serve.how: Warmed gently in winter, on the rocks in summer, or neat at room temperature. Kuma shochu is traditionally pre-mixed with water and warmed in a ceramic flask overnight before serving.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Both the base and the koji are rice, which is why it sits so close to sake on the palate.

originStory: Takara Shuzo released Jun in 1977. The Kyoto company traces its roots to a sake brewery in Fushimi founded in 1842 and was incorporated under the Takara name in 1925. Jun is a kōrui shochu, made by continuous distillation into a clean, light spirit rather than in a pot still, the type that became the usual base for chūhai, the shochu highballs that spread through Japanese bars in the early 1980s. Jun has remained one of Takara's flagship labels since its launch.

name: Lento Kokuto
description: Kokuto Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Kokuto Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with water
serve.how: On the rocks, or with cold water. Despite the base it is not sweet, since the sugar ferments out entirely. It sits somewhere between a light rum and a shochu, which is exactly what it is.

composition.summary: Brown sugar fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Amami kokuto, unrefined brown sugar

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji, which is legally required

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

composition.process: The rice koji requirement is what keeps it classified as shochu rather than as rum.

originStory: Lento is made by Amami Ōshima Kaiun Shuzo in Uken, on the southern Japanese island of Amami Ōshima, a distillery founded in 1954 as Toda Shuzo. It is a kokutō shochu, distilled from brown sugar and rice kōji, a style that only the Amami Islands are permitted to make, under an arrangement that followed their return to Japanese rule after the Second World War. Lento is rested in tanks exposed to classical music, a process the distillery calls acoustic ageing, and its name is the musical term for slowly.

name: Zuisen Awamori
description: Awamori Kusu from Japan.
funFact: The only Awamori Kusu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or on the rocks
serve.how: Neat at room temperature in a small cup, or on the rocks. Okinawans traditionally cut it with water and let it sit overnight before serving, which softens it noticeably.

composition.summary: Awamori aged three years or more in clay pots by fractional topping.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Long-grain Thai rice with black koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware; traditional systems run far longer

composition.process: Clay is slightly porous, so the spirit oxidises slowly in a way glass or steel would not allow.

originStory: Zuisen was founded in 1887 in Shuri, the old royal capital of Okinawa, and takes its name from a spring near the Zuisen Gate of Shuri Castle. Awamori is Okinawa's rice spirit, made from long-grain Thai rice and black kōji, and kusu is the term for awamori aged at least three years. The Battle of Okinawa destroyed much of the island's awamori heritage, including its old kōji strains, but a strain collected from Zuisen before the war was later found preserved at the University of Tokyo, and in 1999 the distillery released an awamori made with it.

name: Jinro Chamisul
description: Andong Soju from South Korea. The world's best-selling spirit by volume.
funFact: Jinro Chamisul: The world's best-selling spirit by volume

serve.how: Room temperature in a small cup, poured for others rather than yourself, which is fixed Korean etiquette. It is strong and clean, and deserves to be sipped rather than shot.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with nuruk and distilled in a traditional soju gori.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Nuruk, a Korean wild-culture starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in an earthenware soju gori

composition.process: Nuruk carries a wilder mix of moulds and yeasts than Japanese koji, which gives a more rustic result.

originStory: Jinro was founded in 1924 by Jang Hak-yeop in Yonggang, in what is now North Korea, and was re-established in the South after the Korean War. Chamisul, launched in 1998, was filtered through bamboo charcoal and presented as softer and cleaner than older soju; its name means real dew. Like most mass-market soju it is a diluted style, blended from neutral spirit and water, a method that spread after rice was restricted for distilling in the 1960s. A toad is the brand's emblem, and industry rankings have long listed Jinro as the largest-selling spirit brand in the world by volume.

name: Chum Churum
description: Andong Soju from South Korea.
funFact: One of 3 Andong Soju bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in a small cup, poured for others rather than yourself, which is fixed Korean etiquette. It is strong and clean, and deserves to be sipped rather than shot.
