funFact: New England imported Caribbean molasses and distilled it locally, so rum was cheaper than beer in eighteenth-century Massachusetts.

steps: Put the sugar in a warmed heatproof glass and add a splash of hot water to dissolve it.
Add the spirit and stir once.
Top with hot water and stir again.
Garnish and drink while hot.

originStory: The Rum Toddy is the colonial New England toddy, rum distilled locally from Caribbean molasses stirred with sugar and hot water and finished with nutmeg, a household winter habit that no one is credited with inventing.

name: Whiskey Sling
description: Bourbon, lemon, sugar and water with nutmeg over the top. A toddy served cold, which is all a sling has ever been.
funFact: The 1806 newspaper definition of a cocktail — spirits, sugar, water and bitters — describes it explicitly as a bittered sling, which makes the sling the parent form.

steps: Shake the bourbon, lemon juice, syrup and water with ice.
Strain into a tumbler over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface.
Serve without a straw.

originStory: The sling is one of the oldest American mixed drinks, spirit with sugar and water and a grating of nutmeg, served hot or cold. When a newspaper in Hudson, New York, printed the first known definition of the cocktail early in the nineteenth century, it called the cocktail a bittered sling, which makes the sling the older form. Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide prints a hot whiskey sling of whiskey and boiling water under nutmeg, and no single creator is recorded.

name: Brandy Sling
description: Cognac with lemon, sugar and water, nutmeg grated over the top. The sling in its brandy form.
funFact: Slings were drunk hot in winter and cold in summer from the same recipe, which is why the old books often print no temperature at all.

steps: Shake the cognac, lemon juice, syrup and water with ice.
Strain into a tumbler over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg over the top.
Serve cold, or build the same measures with hot water in winter.

originStory: Slings, spirit sweetened and diluted with water and topped with nutmeg, were common in American taverns by the eighteenth century, and brandy slings were among the standard versions. Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide makes the brandy sling exactly as the brandy toddy, with nutmeg grated on top. The origin of the word is uncertain, and the name later passed to grander drinks such as the Singapore Sling.

name: Gin Sour
description: Gin, lemon and sugar. The plainest sour there is, and the shape almost every gin drink in the canon is built on.
funFact: Two of spirit, three-quarters of citrus, half of sugar is the ratio nearly every sour resolves to — the Daiquiri, the Sidecar and the Margarita are the same arithmetic in different bottles.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The sour first appears in a bar book in Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide, widely regarded as the first American book of mixed drinks, in brandy, gin and Santa Cruz rum versions, made like the fix of spirit, sugar, water and lemon but without the fruit. The gin sour is one of those originals. The template went on to become the backbone of a whole branch of cocktails, from the daisy and the fizz to the Sidecar and the Margarita.

name: Rum Sour
description: Aged rum with lemon and sugar. Sits between a Daiquiri and a Whiskey Sour, and lands closer to the whiskey than you would expect.
funFact: The only difference from a Daiquiri is lemon in place of lime, which sounds trivial and changes the drink completely — lemon reads richer, lime reads sharper.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

originStory: The rum sour is as old as the sour in print: Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide notes that a Santa Cruz sour is made with rum from St Croix, then a Danish island in the Caribbean, in place of the gin. Made with lemon rather than the lime of the later Cuban Daiquiri, it shows how the same structure took on different citrus in different places. No individual is credited with the rum sour.

name: Applejack Sour
description: Apple brandy with lemon and sugar. A Jack Rose without the grenadine, and considerably drier for it.
funFact: Laird's has distilled applejack in New Jersey since the 1700s and holds licence number one, the oldest commercial distilling permit in the United States.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Applejack Sour puts the apple brandy of New Jersey, long made by Laird and Company, holder of US distilling licence number one, on the old sour template of spirit, lemon and sugar, and no one is credited with it.

name: Gin Crusta
description: Gin, maraschino, lemon and bitters in a sugar-rimmed glass lined with a single whole lemon peel.
glassware: Small wine glass with a sugared rim
funFact: The crusta is defined by the peel — one lemon rind cut in a single piece and pressed inside the glass, which is where the name comes from.

steps: Peel a lemon in one continuous spiral and press it inside a small wine glass.
Rim the glass with lemon and caster sugar.
Shake the gin, maraschino, curacao, lemon juice and bitters with ice.
Strain into the prepared glass and serve.
recipe.garnish: A whole lemon peel inside a sugared rim

originStory: The crusta appears in Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide in brandy, whiskey and gin versions, and Thomas wrote that it was said to have been invented by Santina, a celebrated Spanish caterer, usually identified today as Joseph Santini of the Jewel of the South in New Orleans. The name is usually explained by the crust of sugar on the rim of the glass, above a whole lemon peel lining the inside. The gin version has always been rarer than the brandy original.

name: Whiskey Crusta
description: The crusta built on rye. Same lemon-lined glass, same sugared rim, a heavier drink underneath it.
glassware: Small wine glass with a sugared rim
funFact: Joseph Santini created the original Brandy Crusta in New Orleans around 1850, and it is the drink the Sidecar and the Margarita both descend from.

steps: Line a small wine glass with a single long lemon peel.
Rim it with lemon and caster sugar.
Shake the rye, maraschino, lemon juice and bitters with ice.
Strain into the prepared glass and serve.
recipe.garnish: A whole lemon peel inside a sugared rim

originStory: Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide printed the crusta in brandy, whiskey and gin versions, making the whiskey one exactly like the brandy with whiskey in its place, and credited the form to a New Orleans caterer called Santina, now usually identified as Joseph Santini. Its name refers to the crust of sugar on the glass's rim. The whiskey crusta never matched the fame of the brandy one, which bartenders often cite as an ancestor of the Sidecar.

name: Brandy Julep
description: Cognac, sugar and mint churned through crushed ice. The julep as it was made before bourbon claimed it.
funFact: The julep was originally made with cognac or peach brandy; bourbon only became standard after phylloxera cut off the French supply in the 1870s.

steps: Press the mint gently with the sugar in a julep tin — bruise it, do not tear it.
Add the cognac and pack the tin with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the outside of the tin frosts.
Cap with more crushed ice and crown with a dense mint bouquet.

originStory: The julep is first described in America early in the nineteenth century, as a morning dram of spirit with mint taken by Virginians, and in its early days it was often made with cognac or peach brandy rather than whiskey. Its name comes, via Arabic and French, from the Persian gulab, rosewater. Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide made its mint julep with cognac and its brandy julep the same way without the fancy fruit, and bourbon became the standard only as American whiskey rose.

name: Champagne Julep
description: Mint and sugar under champagne over crushed ice. Lighter than any julep has a right to be.
funFact: Jerry Thomas prints it in 1862, which puts champagne juleps in American bars decades before the Kentucky Derby made the bourbon version a fixture.

steps: Press the mint with the sugar in a julep tin.
Fill the tin with crushed ice.
Pour the champagne slowly over the ice so it does not foam over the rim.
Stir once, gently, and crown with mint.

originStory: The Champagne Julep is one of the grander variations of the julep, which nineteenth-century American bars made on almost any base, mint and sugar under sparkling wine and crushed ice, and no individual is credited with it.

name: Remsen Cooler
description: Scotch and soda over a long unbroken spiral of lemon peel. Named for a whisky brand nobody drinks any more.
funFact: The cooler is defined by the continuous citrus spiral hung inside the glass — the same construction as a Horse's Neck, which is a cooler under another name.

steps: Peel a lemon in one continuous spiral and hang it inside a Collins glass.
Fill the glass carefully with ice, holding the spiral against the side.
Add the Scotch and top with cold soda water.
Stir once and serve.

originStory: The Remsen Cooler is printed in William Boothby's American Bar-Tender of 1891, which says it was introduced by William Remsen, a retired naval officer and popular member of the Union Club in New York, and Boothby made it with Old Tom gin, a long lemon peel and soda. By 1922 Robert Vermeire's London guide made it with Remsen's Scotch whisky instead, and Scotch became the usual base, so the drink carries two competing stories.

name: Klondike Cooler
description: Rye with orange peel and ginger ale over ice — a cooler named for the gold rush of 1897.
funFact: The Klondike rush drew a hundred thousand prospectors north in two years; barely a few hundred struck it rich, and the drink outlasted almost all of them.

steps: Hang a continuous orange peel spiral inside a Collins glass.
Fill with ice, keeping the spiral pressed against the side.
Add the rye and top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and serve.

originStory: The Klondike Cooler takes its name from the Yukon gold rush at the end of the nineteenth century, a whiskey cooler of orange juice and ginger ale over a long orange peel, and who first made it is not recorded.

name: Harvard Cooler
description: Applejack, lemon and sugar lengthened with soda. The Harvard's long, cold cousin.
funFact: Cooler, rickey, fizz and Collins are separated by fine distinctions of sweetener, citrus and garnish that Victorian bar books took entirely seriously.

steps: Shake the applejack, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wheel.

originStory: The Harvard Cooler is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as applejack or calvados shaken with lemon or lime juice and sugar and lengthened with soda water in a long tumbler. It shares its name with the Harvard, the brandy and vermouth cocktail named for the university, but not its recipe, and its creator is not recorded.

name: Bombo
description: Rum, water, sugar and nutmeg. The plainest rum drink in the colonial Atlantic, and the one sailors actually drank.
funFact: Bombo, sometimes bumbo, was the currency of colonial election campaigns — George Washington's agents handed out gallons of it during his 1758 run for the Virginia House of Burgesses.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in a little of the water in the bottom of the vessel.
Add the rum and the remaining water and stir.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface.
Serve at ambient temperature, or over ice in the heat.

originStory: Bombo, or bumbo, was a plain mix of rum, water, sugar and nutmeg drunk by sailors, soldiers and colonists across the eighteenth-century Atlantic, from the Caribbean to the American colonies. It was common enough in Virginia that candidates treated voters to it, and George Washington's papers from his first successful campaign for the House of Burgesses record rum bought for that purpose. The origin of the name is uncertain, and no single creator is recorded.

name: Blackstrap
description: Dark rum with molasses and hot water. Colonial, cheap and unapologetically heavy.
funFact: Blackstrap molasses is the third boiling of cane syrup with nearly all the sugar removed, which is why it tastes bitter and mineral rather than sweet.

steps: Stir the molasses into a little hot water until it has fully dissolved.
Add the rum and stir again.
Top with the remaining hot water.
Serve hot, in a warmed mug.

originStory: Blackstrap is a cheap colonial New England mix of rum and molasses, both plentiful in a region whose distilleries turned Caribbean molasses into rum, and no creator or date is on record.

name: Shandygaff
description: Ale and ginger beer, half and half. The Victorian ancestor of the shandy, and sharper than the lemonade version that replaced it.
funFact: Dickens uses the word in 1868 and Wodehouse never stopped; the ginger-beer version predates the lemonade shandy by a good half-century.

steps: Chill both the ale and the ginger beer thoroughly.
Pour the ginger beer into a pint glass first.
Add the ale slowly, down the side of the tilted glass, to control the foam.
Do not stir — the pour does the mixing.

originStory: Shandygaff, beer or ale mixed with ginger beer, is recorded in English from 1853, and the origin of the word is obscure. The shorter word shandy, first recorded in 1888, began as an abbreviation of it, and the lemonade version that most people now order came later. H. G. Wells gave the drink a cameo in The History of Mr Polly, where a shandygaff is mixed from beer and ginger beer in a round-bellied jug.

name: Green Swizzle
description: Rum, lime and falernum swizzled green with a wormwood bitters, and immortalised by a Wodehouse character who claimed it changed his life.
funFact: The original green came from a Barbadian wormwood bitters that is now effectively lost, which is why every modern version reaches for Chartreuse instead.

steps: Fill a tall glass with crushed ice.
Add the rum, lime juice, falernum, Chartreuse and bitters.
Spin a swizzle stick between your palms until the outside of the glass frosts over.
Top with more crushed ice and crown with mint.

originStory: The Green Swizzle was a fixture of Caribbean bars in the early twentieth century, found in Trinidad, Barbados and Grenada, and a Trinidad cookery handbook of 1907 is among its earliest records. Its green came from wormwood bitters, with falernum as the sweetener, not from the crème de menthe of some later versions. P. G. Wodehouse gave it lasting fame in 1924, when Bertie Wooster sang its praises after a visit to the West Indian section of the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley.

name: Zoom
description: Spirit, honey and cream shaken cold. Three ingredients, and it works with brandy, whisky or gin equally well.
funFact: The Savoy prints it as a template rather than a fixed recipe — the base spirit is left to the drinker, which is unusual for a book that specifies everything else.

steps: Loosen the honey with a splash of warm water so it will combine.
Add the cognac, honey syrup and cream to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe and grate nutmeg over the top.

originStory: The Zoom is a short interwar drink of spirit, honey and cream with the base left to the drinker, brandy, whisky or gin, and neither its creator nor the reason for its name is recorded.

name: Scaffa
description: Layered liqueurs and spirit served at room temperature, with no ice and no dilution whatsoever.
funFact: The scaffa is the only classical drink category defined by being served warm and undiluted — a deliberate refusal of everything ice brought to bartending.

steps: Pour the maraschino into a small glass.
Float the green Chartreuse over the back of a barspoon.
Float the brandy last and add a dash of bitters on top.
Serve at room temperature, without ice and without stirring.
recipe.garnish: None — the layers are the presentation

originStory: The scaffa is an old class of drink served without ice and at room temperature, spirit and liqueur built straight into the glass with bitters. Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide prints a brandy scaffa of brandy and maraschino with two dashes of bitters, and Leo Engel's London guide of 1878 gives the same, close to the layered pousse-cafés it resembles. The meaning of the name has never been explained.

name: Cardinale
description: A Negroni with dry vermouth in place of sweet. Drier, paler, and sharper at the finish.
funFact: The name is usually traced to the Hotel Excelsior in Rome, where a cardinal is said to have asked for his Negroni without the sweetness.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Cardinale is usually credited to Giovanni Raimondo at the bar of the Hotel Excelsior in Rome in the 1950s, though it was once attributed to Harry's Bar in Venice. His version is said to have used Riesling with the gin and Campari, where later recipes, the IBA's among them, settled on dry vermouth. The name is generally put down to its cardinal-red colour, though some accounts link it to a visiting cardinal.

name: Pirlo
description: Still white wine with Campari poured through it and a splash of soda. Brescia's own aperitivo, older than the Venetian spritz.
funFact: The name comes from the Brescian dialect verb pirlare, to spin — the Campari corkscrews down through the wine as it is poured, which is the whole trick.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice and add the white wine.
Pour the Campari slowly into the centre so it spirals down through the wine.
Add a small splash of soda.
Do not stir it flat — the descending swirl is the point.

originStory: The Pirlo is the traditional aperitivo of Brescia, still white wine with a red bitter and a splash of soda, a cousin of the Venetian spritz whose name is usually explained from the Brescian dialect after the way the bitter spirals down through the wine, and no creator or date is recorded.

name: Hugo
description: Prosecco, elderflower, mint and lime over ice. The Alpine answer to the Aperol Spritz, and lighter than any of them.
funFact: Roland Gruber mixed the first one in Naturns in 2005 and used lemon balm syrup; elderflower only replaced it once the drink spread beyond South Tyrol.

steps: Put the mint and lime wedges in a large wine glass and press them once, gently.
Add the elderflower syrup and fill the glass with ice.
Pour in the prosecco, then top with soda water.
Stir once from the bottom and serve with the mint standing proud.
recipe.garnish: A mint sprig and a lime wedge

originStory: The Hugo was invented in 2005 by Roland Gruber at the San Zeno bar in Naturns, in South Tyrol, as a light aperitif of prosecco with mint. His original used lemon balm syrup; elderflower syrup or liqueur replaced it as the drink spread through the Alps and into Germany and Austria. Gruber has said the name was a chance choice, and that he first thought of calling it Otto.

name: Kaisermelange
description: Black coffee whisked with an egg yolk and honey, laced with brandy. A Viennese coffee house order, not a bar one.
funFact: Viennese coffee houses run to dozens of named preparations, each with a fixed ratio of coffee to milk to foam — ordering simply a coffee marks you out immediately.

steps: Whisk the egg yolk with the honey until pale and smooth.
Pour a little of the hot coffee in slowly while whisking, to temper the yolk.
Add the brandy and the rest of the coffee, whisking as you go.
Serve in a warmed glass without straining.

originStory: The Kaisermelange, the emperor's mélange, is one of the many named coffees of the Viennese coffee house, black coffee whisked with an egg yolk and honey and laced with brandy, and no one has recorded who first made it.

name: Kafi Luz
description: Weak coffee with a serious measure of fruit brandy. The house drink of central Swiss village taverns.
funFact: It is traditionally poured pale on purpose — the coffee is there to carry the Träsch, the pear-and-apple brandy of central Switzerland, rather than the other way round.

steps: Stir the sugar into the hot coffee until it dissolves.
Add the Trasch and stir once more.
Serve in a small handled glass, hot.
Refills are poured into the same glass without rinsing it.

originStory: Kafi Luz is a farmhouse and tavern habit of central Switzerland around Lucerne, pale weak coffee poured over sugar with a fruit brandy such as Träsch or plum schnapps, and it has no recorded creator.

name: Eierpunsch
description: Hot white wine beaten with egg yolks, sugar and vanilla until thick. The richest thing at a German Christmas market.
funFact: Christmas market stalls sell it in the same returnable ceramic mug as Glühwein, and the deposit on the mug is often larger than the drink.

steps: Whisk the yolks, sugar and vanilla in a bowl until pale.
Heat the wine to just below a simmer, never letting it boil.
Pour the hot wine onto the yolks in a thin stream, whisking constantly.
Return to a low heat and whisk until it thickens enough to coat a spoon.
Pour into a warmed mug and serve at once.

originStory: Eierpunsch, egg punch, is a German winter drink of white wine beaten with egg yolks, sugar and vanilla over gentle heat and sold beside Glühwein at Christmas markets, a household and market tradition with no recorded creator.

name: Maibowle
description: White wine infused with sweet woodruff and topped with sparkling wine. Made once a year, in May, when the herb is young.
funFact: The woodruff has to be picked before it flowers and wilted for a day first — fresh green leaves give nothing, and too much of it turns the punch bitter.

steps: Wilt the woodruff for a day, then tie it in a bunch by the stems.
Hang it in the white wine with the cut ends clear of the liquid and steep for no more than 30 minutes.
Lift out the herb and stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Chill thoroughly, then add the sparkling wine just before serving.
recipe.garnish: A woodruff sprig and a few strawberries

originStory: Maibowle, the May punch of Germany, is traced to a wine flavoured with sweet woodruff that the Benedictine monk Wandalbert of Prüm Abbey mentioned in 854. The herb is picked in spring before it flowers and wilted briefly so that its scent develops, then steeped in white wine that is topped with sparkling wine. It is still made in late April and May, especially for May Day, and across the border in Belgium the town of Arlon makes a version called Maitrank.

name: Diesel
description: Lager and cola, half and half. Ordered without irony in every German pub, and darker than either half suggests.
funFact: The same mix goes by different names depending on the beer and the region — Krefelder with Altbier, Colaweizen with wheat beer, and Diesel almost everywhere else.

steps: Chill both thoroughly.
Pour the cola into a tilted pint glass first.
Add the beer slowly down the side to keep the head from running over.
Serve without stirring.

originStory: Diesel is the German pub name for lager mixed half and half with cola, one of several beer and soft-drink mixes that go by regional names such as Krefelder with Altbier and Colaweizen with wheat beer, and no one is credited with the mix or its name.

name: Kaffekask
description: Coffee and brännvin in the same cup, measured by whether you can see a coin at the bottom.
funFact: The traditional measure is a coin dropped in the empty cup: pour coffee until it disappears, then pour spirit until you can see it again.

steps: Drop a small coin into the bottom of the cup if you are doing it properly.
Pour hot coffee until the coin is no longer visible.
Add brannvin until the coin comes back into view.
Sweeten if you like, and drink it hot.

originStory: Kaffekask is a Swedish rural custom of coffee laced with brännvin in the same cup, especially associated with the north of the country and close kin to the Norwegian karsk, and it has no recorded creator or date.

name: Svařák
description: Czech mulled wine: red wine warmed with cloves, cinnamon and citrus, and poured by the litre at winter markets.
funFact: Czech svařák is usually poured far less sweet than German Glühwein, and market stalls heat it in open vats rather than sealed urns.

steps: Combine everything in a wide pan.
Heat slowly to steaming and hold it there for 20 minutes without boiling.
Taste and add sugar only if it needs it.
Ladle into warmed mugs, spices and all.

originStory: Svařák is the everyday Czech name for svařené víno, mulled wine, sold from stalls at the Christmas markets of Prague and other towns as part of the central European family of spiced hot wines, and it has no recorded creator or date.

name: Hriatô
description: Caramelised sugar, pork fat and borovicka, drunk hot. A mountain drink that makes no apology for any of that.
funFact: It comes from the shepherding regions of Liptov and Orava, where the fat was the point — it was a working drink for cold weather, not a novelty.

steps: Melt the sugar in a small pan until it caramelises to a deep amber.
Add the lard and let it melt into the caramel.
Pour in the water carefully — it will spit — and stir until smooth.
Take it off the heat, add the spirit, and serve hot with a slice of bread.

originStory: Hriatô, whose name means warmed, is a winter drink of the Slovak mountain regions of Liptov, Orava and Spiš, honey or caramelised sugar heated with bacon or butter and a local spirit, traditionally served around Christmas, with no recorded creator.

name: Šumadijski Čaj
description: Serbian tea, which contains no tea. Rakija heated with sugar and honey until it looks entirely innocent.
funFact: The name is the joke: it arrives the colour of tea, in a tea glass, and is drunk in tea-sized sips for reasons that become clear quickly.

steps: Caramelise the sugar in a small pan until amber.
Add the water and stir until the caramel dissolves again.
Pour in the rakija and warm it through without letting it boil off.
Stir in the honey and serve hot in a small glass.

originStory: Šumadijski čaj, Šumadija tea, is a winter drink from the plum country of central Serbia that contains no tea, rakija heated with sugar or honey and served hot in a tea glass, a folk tradition with no recorded creator.

name: Arak Limonana
description: Frozen mint lemonade with arak poured through it. The drink Tel Aviv runs on between May and October.
funFact: Limonana is a coined word — limon plus nana, lemon plus mint — invented for an Israeli advertising campaign in the 1990s that sold a drink which did not exist yet.

steps: Blend the lemon juice, mint, syrup and ice until slushy and bright green.
Pour into a tall glass.
Pour the arak over the top and watch it turn the surface milky.
Serve with a spoon and a straw.

originStory: Limonana, from the Hebrew limon, lemon, and nana, mint, is a word coined in Israel in the 1990s for an advertising campaign promoting bus advertising, in which well-known faces endorsed a drink of that name that turned out to be fictional. The frozen lemon and mint drink that followed became a fixture of Israeli summers, and adding arak, the anise spirit of the Levant, turned it into a bar drink, though no one is credited with that combination.

name: Poktanju
description: A shot glass of soju or whisky dropped into a glass of beer, and drunk in one go. The bomb drink.
funFact: Poktanju is the dropped version and somaek the poured one — the distinction matters at a Korean table, where the pouring itself carries a full set of manners.

steps: Pour the beer into a glass, leaving room at the top.
Rest a filled shot glass on the rim, or drop it in from a height.
Let it settle for a second — it will foam hard.
Drink it down in one, which is not optional.

originStory: Poktanju means bomb liquor in Korean, a shot of soju or whisky dropped into a glass of beer, and it became a fixture of South Korean social life in the second half of the twentieth century. Accounts of how it started differ, crediting office workers of the boom years, officers back from training in America or a meeting of prosecutors, police and journalists in Chuncheon, and none is settled.

name: Subak Soju
description: A hollowed watermelon filled with its own blended flesh and soju, and served back in the rind.
funFact: It is sold that way in Korean pubs — the emptied melon comes to the table as the vessel, with ladles, and is shared between four or more people.

steps: Cut the top off the watermelon and scoop out the flesh, keeping the shell whole.
Blend the flesh smooth and strain out the seeds.
Stir the juice together with the soju and pour it back into the shell.
Add ice and serve with a ladle and several glasses.
recipe.garnish: The watermelon lid, set back on top

originStory: Subak soju, subak being Korean for watermelon, is a party serve of Korean pubs and summer gatherings in which a hollowed watermelon is filled with its own flesh blended with soju and shared at the table, and no creator or date is recorded.

name: Arak Attack
description: Balinese arak with orange juice and a red float. The cheapest drink on Bali and the one most travellers meet first.
funFact: Balinese arak is distilled from palm sap or rice and varies wildly by producer, which is why the orange juice is doing more work than it appears to be.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the arak and top with orange juice.
Stir once to combine.
Trickle the grenadine down the inside so it settles at the bottom.

originStory: Arak Attack is a tourist-bar pun on Bali's own spirit, the island's palm or rice arak mixed with orange juice under a red float, and neither the person who coined the name nor the date is recorded.

name: Arrack Sour
description: Ceylon coconut arrack with lime and sugar. A sour built on a spirit made from the sap of a flower.
funFact: Sri Lankan arrack is distilled from the sap of unopened coconut flowers, tapped by climbers who move between treetops on ropes strung across the canopy.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Arrack Sour applies the classic sour of spirit, lime and sugar to Sri Lankan arrack, distilled from the sap of unopened coconut flowers that tappers collect high in the palms, and no individual creator or date is recorded.

name: Bandera
description: Three glasses in a row — lime, blanco tequila and sangrita — arranged in the colours of the Mexican flag.
funFact: It is not a shot to be thrown back: the order is meant to be sipped in rotation, and the sangrita is the chaser, never the mixer.

steps: Line up three shot glasses left to right.
Fill the first with lime juice, the second with blanco tequila, the third with sangrita.
Sip from each in turn rather than drinking any of them down.
Refill whichever empties first.

originStory: The Bandera, Spanish for flag, is a serving custom of Mexico's tequila country rather than one bar's recipe, three glasses of lime juice, blanco tequila and sangrita set side by side in the green, white and red of the flag and sipped in turn, with no recorded creator.

name: Batida
description: Cachaça blended with fruit and sweetened condensed milk until it is thick enough to stand a straw in.
funFact: Batida simply means shaken, and the form takes any fruit at all — coconut, passion fruit, tamarind, cashew fruit — with condensed milk as the constant.

steps: Put everything in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth and thick.
Pour into a tall glass without straining.
Serve with a wide straw.

originStory: Batida, from the Portuguese for beaten or shaken, is a Brazilian family of cachaça drinks blended or shaken with fruit or coconut and often sweetened with condensed milk, a popular tradition rather than the invention of any one bar, with no recorded creator.

name: Ponche a la Romana
description: Sparkling wine poured over pineapple ice cream. Chile drinks it at New Year and at every national holiday.
funFact: The name points at Rome and the drink has nothing to do with it — the Chilean version fixed on pineapple ice cream and never looked back.

steps: Put two scoops of pineapple ice cream in a wide chilled glass.
Pour the sparkling wine slowly over the top so it foams up but does not spill.
Let it sit for a moment until the ice cream starts to soften at the edges.
Serve with both a spoon and a straw.

originStory: Ponche a la romana is a Chilean party drink of sparkling wine poured over pineapple ice cream for New Year and the national holidays, its name echoing the iced punch à la romaine of grand nineteenth-century dinners, and no creator or date is recorded.

name: Papelón con Limón y Ron
description: Raw cane sugar dissolved in water with lime, poured over ice and cut with rum.
funFact: Papelón is unrefined cane sugar sold in solid cones; it has to be dissolved in warm water first, and it tastes nothing like white sugar syrup.

steps: Dissolve the grated papelon in the warm water and let it cool completely.
Add the lime juice and stir.
Fill a tall glass with ice and pour the mixture over.
Add the rum and stir once more.

originStory: Papelón con limón is an everyday Venezuelan drink of papelón, unrefined cane sugar sold in hard cones, dissolved in water and sharpened with lime, and adding rum turns the household refreshment into a long drink with no recorded creator.

name: Rum and Ting
description: Overproof white rum with Ting, the Jamaican grapefruit soda. Two ingredients, no ceremony.
funFact: Ting is made with real grapefruit juice and is bracingly bitter, which is the only reason it can stand up to 63 percent rum.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum.
Top with cold Ting.
Stir once and add a squeeze of lime if the soda is very sweet.

originStory: Ting, a sparkling grapefruit soda, was first produced in Jamaica in 1976 by Desnoes and Geddes, so Rum and Ting can be no older than that. Paired with Jamaican white overproof rum, it became one of the island's everyday highballs, the kind of order that needs no recipe, and nobody is credited with first mixing the two.

name: Ponche de Crème
description: Trinidad's Christmas drink: eggs, condensed milk, rum and a heavy hand with the Angostura.
funFact: Angostura bitters have been made in Trinidad since 1875, and in a Ponche de Creme they are a measured ingredient rather than a dash.

steps: Beat the eggs with the lime zest until completely smooth and pale.
Whisk in both milks, then the rum, then the bitters.
Strain through a fine sieve to catch the zest and any thread of egg.
Chill for at least a day before serving — it thickens and settles as it rests.
Serve cold, over one cube of ice, with nutmeg over the top.

originStory: Ponche de crème is the Christmas eggnog of Trinidad and Tobago, eggs, milk, rum and spice seasoned with the Angostura bitters made in Port of Spain, a family recipe rather than an invention, with no recorded creator.

name: Springbok
description: Green crème de menthe under a layer of Amarula, poured to the colours of the national rugby jersey.
funFact: Amarula is made from the fruit of the marula tree, which grows wild across southern Africa and is harvested from the ground rather than picked.

steps: Pour the crème de menthe into a shot glass.
Rest a barspoon just above the surface, curve up.
Pour the Amarula slowly over the back of it so it floats in a clean layer.
Serve without disturbing the line between them.

originStory: The Springbok shooter layers green crème de menthe under Amarula, the South African cream liqueur made from marula fruit, in the green and gold of the national rugby team named for the antelope, and no creator or date is recorded.

name: Sour de Maracuyá
description: A Pisco Sour rerouted through passion fruit. Sharper, more floral, and harder to stop at one.
funFact: Peruvian pisco is never diluted or aged in wood after distillation, so the fruit in a sour has nothing to hide behind.

steps: Dry-shake everything but the bitters, without ice, for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe and let the foam settle.
Drop three dashes of Angostura onto the foam.
recipe.garnish: Three drops of Angostura bitters on the foam

originStory: The Sour de Maracuyá reworks the Pisco Sour, usually credited to the American bartender Victor Morris at his bar in Lima, with passion fruit, one of many local-fruit versions served in Peru, and no individual is credited with this one.

name: Attention
description: Absinthe, gin, violet and dry vermouth in equal parts. Pale lilac, and considerably stranger than it looks.
funFact: The Savoy prints a whole run of equal-parts absinthe cocktails from the years just after it came back to European bars, and this is the prettiest of them.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Attention is a pale lilac drink of absinthe, gin, crème de violette and dry vermouth in equal parts, and neither its creator, its first printing nor the meaning of its name is recorded.

name: Bennett
description: A Gimlet with bitters in it. That one addition changes the whole balance of the drink.
funFact: Two dashes of Angostura is the entire difference between this and a Gin Rickey served up, which is a fair summary of how the old books drew their distinctions.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 prints the Bennett as Old Tom gin with fresh lime juice and two dashes of Angostura, and says it was very popular in Chile, where it was named after a well-known landowner of that country. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 kept it with dry gin, and neither book gives Bennett's first name or the bartender who made it.

name: Colony
description: Gin, grapefruit and maraschino. Named for the Manhattan restaurant where being seated badly was a public event.
funFact: The Colony's headwaiter Gene Cavallero was famous for seating people by status rather than reservation, which made the front room the most contested real estate in the city.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Colony is named for the Colony, the New York restaurant that became one of the city's most fashionable dining rooms under its proprietor Gene Cavallero and is said to have served its regulars discreetly during Prohibition. The drink, gin with grapefruit and maraschino, is usually dated to that period and sometimes credited to the bartender Marco Hattem, though the attribution is uncertain and no exact date is recorded.

name: Commodore
description: Rye with lemon, grenadine and orange bitters. A sour with a red tint and a dry finish.
funFact: Real grenadine is pomegranate syrup, not red sugar water, and in a drink this simple the difference between the two is the whole drink.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints the Commodore as Canadian whisky with lime or lemon juice, a little syrup and orange bitters, while other books of the period use the name for quite different drinks. No single creator, bar or date is attached to it, and the name, a naval rank, was one of many military and naval titles borrowed by drinks of the time.

name: Duchess
description: Absinthe with both vermouths, in thirds. No base spirit at all — the absinthe is the base.
funFact: Absinthe was banned across most of Europe and America when this was written down, which is exactly why the drinks that used it read as daring rather than quaint.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: Jacques Straub's Drinks, published in Chicago in 1914, prints the Duchess as absinthe with French and Italian vermouth in equal thirds, shaken, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 carried it to London. It is one of a handful of classic drinks in which absinthe is the base rather than a seasoning, and its creator and the reason for the name are not recorded.

name: Earthquake
description: Gin, whisky and absinthe in equal measure. The name is a warning, not a flourish.
funFact: Toulouse-Lautrec drank a version of this made from cognac and absinthe and called it tremblement de terre, which the London version borrowed and then made worse.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Earthquake is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as equal parts gin, whisky and absinthe, with a joking note on the name and a warning about its strength. It is often compared with the tremblement de terre of cognac and absinthe that legend attributes to the painter Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec. No creator is recorded for the London drink.

name: Fourth Degree
description: Gin with both vermouths and a rinse of absinthe. A Perfect Martini with the corners taken off.
funFact: Splitting the vermouth between dry and sweet is what bartenders call perfect, a term that predates the Martini and applies to any drink built this way.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 describes the Fourth Degree as a Martini in the Continental style with a dash of absinthe, gin with dry and sweet vermouth in equal measure, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints it the same way with four dashes of absinthe. The origin of the name is not recorded.

name: Gin and It
description: Gin and Italian vermouth, at room temperature and without ice. The Martini before refrigeration reached the bar.
funFact: It is served warm on purpose — the drink dates from London bars that had no reliable ice, and chilling it turns it into something else entirely.

steps: Pour the gin and the sweet vermouth straight into a small glass.
Stir them together briefly with a barspoon.
Add no ice and do not chill the glass.
Drop in a cherry and serve.

originStory: Gin and It is British bar shorthand for gin and Italian, the sweet vermouth that Turin houses such as Martini and Cinzano exported in the nineteenth century, a plain pairing traditionally poured without ice and with no recorded creator or date.

name: Grand Slam
description: Swedish punsch with both vermouths. Sweet, spiced and almost entirely forgotten.
funFact: Swedish punsch is built on Batavian arrack shipped from Java, which is how an Indonesian spirit ended up defining a Scandinavian liqueur.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Grand Slam is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as Swedish punsch with French and Italian vermouth. Its name is the card players' term for taking every trick, from whist and bridge. Swedish punsch, built on the Batavia arrack that the Swedish East India Company began importing from Java in the eighteenth century, was a fashionable bottle in the bars of the period. Its creator is not recorded.

name: Hoop La
description: Equal parts Lillet, Cointreau, brandy and lemon. A Corpse Reviver with brandy where the gin should be.
funFact: It shares its skeleton exactly with the Corpse Reviver No. 2 — four equal parts, one of them citrus — which is the most reliable template in the whole Savoy book.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Hoop La is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as equal parts lemon juice, Kina Lillet, Cointreau and brandy, and the same formula appears elsewhere in the book under other names, the Frank Sullivan and the Odd McIntyre, after two American newspaper writers of the day. It shares its four-equal-parts structure with the Corpse Reviver No. 2. Its creator is not recorded.

name: Maiden's Blush
description: Gin with curaçao, grenadine and lemon. Named for its colour, which is the palest possible pink.
funFact: The Savoy prints two different drinks under this name, one with curaçao and one with absinthe, and gives no hint as to which came first.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 gives a Maiden's Blush of gin and grenadine with a dash of an absinthe-style spirit as a recipe of Frank Newman of Paris, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints two drinks under the name, one of gin with curaçao, grenadine and lemon, the other built with absinthe. The name was a period term for a pale pink, the colour the grenadine gives.

name: Moonlight
description: Kirsch, grapefruit and sugar. Three ingredients, dry as a bone, and nothing like as sweet as cherry brandy suggests.
funFact: Kirsch is distilled with the cherry stones left in, which is where its faint bitter-almond edge comes from and why it is not a sweet liqueur.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Moonlight is a dry short drink of kirsch, grapefruit juice and a little sugar, and its creator, first printed source and the reason for its name have not been recorded.

name: Nineteen Twenty
description: Kirsch, gin and sweet vermouth in thirds. A Martini with cherry stones running through it.
funFact: Drinks named for years cluster around 1920 in the old books, and almost all of them were invented in Europe by American bartenders who had just left home.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints a Nineteen-Twenty of kirsch, gin and French vermouth with a teaspoon of groseille syrup and a dash of absinthe, named, by all appearances, for the year, and the same book has a Nineteen-Twenty Pick-Me-Up of absinthe and gin. The version with sweet vermouth has no recorded source, and no creator is named for any of them.

name: Prince of Wales
description: Rye, maraschino and pineapple under champagne, and attributed to a king who liked his drinks complicated.
funFact: The recipe is credited to Edward VII from his years as Prince of Wales, a period he spent building a reputation that made the attribution entirely plausible.

steps: Muddle the pineapple with the maraschino and bitters in a shaker.
Add the rye and ice, and shake hard.
Double-strain into a chilled flute.
Top with champagne and add an orange twist.

originStory: The Prince of Wales is credited to Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, the future Edward VII, by an anonymous biography of 1901 written by a member of the royal household, which says he composed a cocktail of rye whisky, pineapple, maraschino, bitters, lemon peel and a little champagne. He was heir to the throne for nearly sixty years and well known for his love of society and entertaining, and the attribution has stayed with the drink ever since.

name: Soul Kiss
description: Dubonnet, dry vermouth, rye and orange juice. Low, aromatic and easier than its name suggests.
funFact: Dubonnet was created in 1846 to make quinine palatable to French soldiers in North Africa, which is a strange origin for something this gentle.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: Jacques Straub's Drinks, published in Chicago in 1914, already prints several Soul Kiss cocktails, one of them rye with Dubonnet, French vermouth and a spoonful of orange juice, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 carries a close version with Canadian whisky. Neither book names a creator or explains the name. Dubonnet's own story credits Joseph Dubonnet with creating his quinine aperitif in Paris for French soldiers in North Africa.

name: Southern Bride
description: Gin, grapefruit and a bar spoon of maraschino. The Colony's shape with the proportions moved.
funFact: Maraschino is measured in barspoons rather than ounces for good reason — it is made from whole crushed Marasca cherries, stones included, and takes over a drink quickly.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Southern Bride is a short gin drink of grapefruit juice with a touch of maraschino, close kin to the Colony, and its creator, first printed source and the meaning of its name have not been documented.

name: Whist
description: Applejack, rum and sweet vermouth. Named for the card game bridge was built out of.
funFact: Whist ruled English card tables for two centuries before bridge displaced it, which dates the naming convention as precisely as anything in the book.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Whist is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book as calvados with Bacardi rum and Italian vermouth, and Craddock's note calls it a drink known in the West Indies for countless years, a kind of West Indian sundowner. It shares its name with the card game, but neither its creator nor the reason for the name is recorded.

name: Improved Holland Gin Cocktail
description: Genever with maraschino, absinthe and bitters. The Old Fashioned before anyone thought to call it old.
funFact: Improved meant one thing precisely in the old books: a plain spirit-sugar-bitters cocktail with maraschino and absinthe added, and nothing else.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The later, revised edition of Jerry Thomas's bar guide prints an improved gin cocktail made like his improved brandy cocktail, with gum syrup, bitters, maraschino, absinthe and a twist of lemon, and Holland or Old Tom gin in place of the brandy. The improved cocktails dressed up the plain mix of spirit, sugar, water and bitters, and Holland gin, or genever, was then a common gin in American bars. Drinkers who preferred the plain version later began asking for their cocktails the old-fashioned way.

name: Fancy Brandy Cocktail
description: Brandy, curaçao, sugar and bitters served in a sugar-rimmed glass. Fancy meant the rim, and nothing more.
funFact: Jerry Thomas separates plain, improved and fancy versions of the same drink; fancy adds only a sugared rim and a fine lemon twist, and costs more.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.
recipe.garnish: A lemon twist over a sugared rim

originStory: The Fancy Brandy Cocktail is printed in Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide, widely regarded as the first American book of mixed drinks, as the plain brandy cocktail strained into a fancy wine glass with a piece of lemon peel on top and the rim moistened with lemon. Thomas used fancy for dressed-up versions of standard drinks, and the grades of plain, fancy and later improved show how carefully bartenders of the period told one variation from another.

name: Absinthe Cocktail
description: Absinthe, water, sugar and bitters, stirred cold. The absinthe drip served as a cocktail rather than a ritual.
funFact: New Orleans drank more absinthe per head than any American city, and the Old Absinthe House on Bourbon Street still has the marble fountains it was dripped from.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The later, revised edition of Jerry Thomas's bar guide prints the Absinthe Cocktail as a pony of absinthe with two dashes of anisette and one of Angostura, lengthened with a stream of iced water, shaken and strained, the slow drip turned into a cocktail. New Orleans, with its French heritage, was the American city most closely tied to absinthe, though no individual creator is recorded.

name: Rum Old Fashioned
description: Aged rum, sugar and bitters. The template holds with any brown spirit, and rum takes to it better than most.
funFact: Demerara sugar syrup rather than plain is the one change worth making — it meets the molasses in the rum instead of sitting on top of it.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Rum Old Fashioned applies the original cocktail of spirit, sugar, water and bitters, which drinkers began ordering the old-fashioned way as bartenders added liqueurs, to aged rum, a common choice in the modern revival, and no one is credited with it.

name: Morning Glory
description: Brandy and Scotch together, with curaçao, absinthe and bitters. Built to be drunk in the morning, which explains a great deal.
funFact: Nineteenth-century bar books have a whole category of morning drinks, and the honest reading is that they were hangover cures with better names.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The later, revised edition of Jerry Thomas's bar guide prints a Morning Glory Cocktail of brandy and whiskey together, stirred with gum syrup, curaçao, bitters and a dash of absinthe and topped with seltzer, one of several morning drinks of the period. Later books used the name for a fizz as well. Its creator and the place where it was first mixed are not recorded.

name: Artillery
description: Gin and sweet vermouth with two dashes of Angostura. A Gin and It with the bitters that make it a cocktail.
funFact: The 1806 definition — spirits, sugar, water and bitters — means a drink without bitters is technically not a cocktail at all, which is the joke this one is built on.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Artillery is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as dry gin and Italian vermouth, one of the many gin and vermouth combinations of the period. No creator or date is recorded, and the military name follows the period habit of naming drinks after weapons and regiments.

name: Diki Diki
description: Applejack, Swedish punsch and grapefruit. Named for a Filipino chief the Savoy's bartender had read about.
funFact: Swedish punsch turns up all over the Savoy book and almost nowhere since — it was the fashionable bottle of the 1920s and then simply stopped being ordered.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: Robert Vermeire wrote that he introduced the Diki-Diki at the Embassy Club in London in February 1922, and he printed it that year in Cocktails: How to Mix Them as calvados with Swedish punsch and grapefruit juice. He named it after Diki-Diki, whom his book describes as the ruler of an island in the southern Philippines. Harry Craddock carried it into the Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930.

name: Deshler
description: Rye and Dubonnet with curaçao and Peychaud's. Named for a boxer who never lost a fight he was paid to win.
funFact: It is named for the featherweight Dave Deshler, and it is one of very few pre-Prohibition drinks that calls for Peychaud's outside New Orleans.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Deshler appears in Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks, published in New York in 1916, as rye and Dubonnet with Peychaud's bitters, a little Cointreau and twists of orange and lemon. Accounts of its name differ: some tie it to the featherweight boxer Dave Deshler, others to the Deshler Hotel in Columbus, Ohio, and none is settled.

name: Frisco
description: Rye with Bénédictine and lemon. Three ingredients, and the Bénédictine does most of the talking.
funFact: Bénédictine's label still carries D.O.M. for Deo Optimo Maximo, a monastic dedication kept on a bottle that a nineteenth-century wine merchant invented the backstory for.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Frisco is a short rye drink of Bénédictine and lemon that carries San Francisco's nickname, and no bartender or bar there has a documented claim to it.

name: Barbary Coast
description: Gin, Scotch, crème de cacao and cream. Named for the stretch of San Francisco you did not walk down alone.
funFact: The Barbary Coast was the city's saloon district until the 1917 vice raids closed it, and the drink outlived the neighbourhood by a century.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Barbary Coast is named for the old saloon and red-light district of San Francisco, which drew sailors and gold seekers from the second half of the nineteenth century until reformers closed it down early in the twentieth. The drink, gin and Scotch with crème de cacao and cream, is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, but its creator and first appearance are not recorded.

name: Suissesse
description: Absinthe shaken with egg white and anisette until it turns pale green and thick. A New Orleans breakfast.
funFact: Absinthe louches — turns cloudy — when water hits it, because the anise oils fall out of solution; egg white takes that cloud and makes it a texture.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until the tin is painful to hold.
Strain into a small chilled tumbler, no soda.
Rest a mint sprig on the foam.

originStory: The suissesse, French for a Swiss woman, is an absinthe drink shaken with egg white and anisette that New Orleans adopted as its own. Stanley Clisby Arthur's Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em recorded the city's absinthe drinks in 1937, and the suissesse has remained a fixture of French Quarter brunch. Who first made it is not recorded.

name: Café Brûlot
description: Coffee, brandy, spice and citrus peel set alight at the table and ladled while still burning.
funFact: The showpiece is the peel: a whole orange rind is studded with cloves and lowered on a fork so the burning brandy runs down it in a spiral of flame.

steps: Stud the orange spiral with the cloves and set it aside.
Warm the brandy, curaçao, sugar, cinnamon and lemon peel in a wide brûlot bowl or pan.
Light the spirit carefully and lower the clove-studded peel into the flame on a long fork.
Ladle the burning brandy over the peel until the flame dies down.
Pour in the hot coffee to extinguish it and serve in demitasse cups.
recipe.garnish: None — the peel is the theatre

originStory: Café brûlot is a New Orleans tableside coffee of brandy, spices and citrus peel set alight and ladled, and Antoine's, the French Quarter restaurant, credits its creation to Jules Alciatore, son of the founder, in the 1890s. The name comes from the French brûler, to burn, and the full name on some menus is café brûlot diabolique. It became a showpiece of the city's old Creole restaurants, served from special bowls with long ladles.

name: La Louisiane
description: Rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe. The house drink of a Bourbon Street restaurant that closed decades ago.
funFact: Restaurant de la Louisiane printed it as its house cocktail, and it sits between the Vieux Carré and the Sazerac in a city that produced remarkably few bad ideas.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: La Louisiane was the house cocktail of the Restaurant de la Louisiane, one of the old Creole restaurants of the French Quarter, and Stanley Clisby Arthur recorded it in 1937 in Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em, describing it as out of the ordinary as the dishes on the restaurant's menu. Rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe place it in the same family as the Vieux Carré and the Sazerac.

name: Gun Shop Fizz
description: A whole bottle of Peychaud's stretched across twenty drinks with fruit, wine and soda. Bitters as the base spirit.
funFact: Kirk Estopinal built it at Cure in New Orleans around the idea that bitters could be a base rather than a seasoning; it uses roughly four ounces per batch.

steps: Muddle the lemon, orange and cucumber with the syrup in a shaker.
Add the Peychaud's, the red wine and ice, and shake briefly.
Pour unstrained into a Collins glass.
Top with soda and add more crushed ice to fill.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cucumber slice

originStory: The Gun Shop Fizz was created by Kirk Estopinal at Cure, the New Orleans cocktail bar on Freret Street, and it turns the usual logic of a drink upside down by using Peychaud's bitters as the base rather than as a seasoning, with citrus, fruit and soda. It shows how far modern bartenders pushed the old New Orleans bitters, though the drink's date and the story behind its name have not been widely published.

name: Milk Punch
description: Spirit, citrus and hot milk curdled on purpose, then strained clear. It comes out looking like water and keeps for months.
funFact: Curdling is the whole technique: the milk solids trap the harsh compounds and the tannins, and straining them out leaves a punch that is clear, silky and effectively stable.

steps: Steep the lemon peels in the sugar for two hours to draw out the oils.
Add the spirits, water and lemon juice and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Heat the milk to just below a simmer and pour the punch into the milk — this way round, never the reverse.
Leave it to curdle for an hour, then strain slowly through a coffee filter until it runs clear.
Bottle it and let it rest; it improves for weeks and keeps for months.

originStory: The earliest known recipe for milk punch appears in an English cookbook of 1711, and the drink became an eighteenth-century favourite, prized because it could be bottled and kept. Its secret is curdling: milk is added to spirit, citrus and spice so that it splits, and straining off the curds leaves a clear, stable punch. Benjamin Franklin recorded his own version in 1763, and the technique returned to bars in the modern cocktail revival.

name: Brandy Milk Punch
description: Brandy, milk, sugar and vanilla, shaken cold. New Orleans drinks it before noon and does not apologise.
funFact: It shares only a name with the clarified English punch — this one is opaque, shaken to order, and belongs firmly to brunch.

steps: Add everything to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds until it is properly cold.
Strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg heavily over the top.

originStory: Brandy milk punch is the New Orleans brunch version of the old milk punches of Britain and America, brandy, milk, sugar and vanilla shaken cold and dusted with nutmeg rather than clarified, and no creator or date is recorded.

name: Claret Cup
description: Bordeaux lengthened with soda, citrus, cucumber and borage. The drink of an English summer afternoon on a lawn.
funFact: Cucumber and borage in a wine cup are not garnish — the whole style is built around cooling the drink and the drinker, which is what cup meant.

steps: Stir the sugar into the curaçao and brandy until dissolved.
Add the claret, lemon slices and cucumber ribbons and chill for an hour.
Set a large block of ice in a bowl and pour the mixture over it.
Top with cold soda water just before serving and float borage flowers if you have them.

originStory: Claret cup is one of the long wine cups of Victorian England, red Bordeaux lengthened with soda and citrus and scented with cucumber and borage for garden parties and summer picnics, and recipes fill the period's books without naming any inventor.

name: Champagne Cup
description: Champagne stretched with brandy, curaçao and fruit over a block of ice. A cup rather than a cocktail, and served by the bowl.
funFact: Cups are always built over one large block rather than cubes — a block melts slowly enough that the bowl is still drinkable an hour into a garden party.

steps: Combine the brandy, curaçao, maraschino and fruit and chill for an hour.
Set a large block of ice in a punch bowl.
Pour the chilled mixture over it, then add the champagne slowly.
Top with soda water and stir once, gently, from the bottom.

originStory: Champagne cup is one of the light cups that Victorian and Edwardian hosts mixed by the bowl for dances and garden parties, sparkling wine stretched with a little brandy and liqueur over fruit, and no creator is recorded.

name: Badminton Cup
description: Claret with cucumber, sugar and soda. Named for the Gloucestershire house, not the game — and the game is named for the house too.
funFact: Badminton House gave its name to both the cup and the sport, which the Duke of Beaufort's guests are said to have invented indoors on a wet afternoon.

steps: Put the cucumber slices, sugar and a grate of nutmeg in a bowl.
Pour the claret over and leave it to steep, cold, for one hour.
Strain out the cucumber and pour over a block of ice.
Top with cold soda water and serve.

originStory: Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide prints it simply as Badminton: half a peeled cucumber steeped with sugar and a little nutmeg in a bottle of claret, then lengthened with a bottle of soda water. The name is usually traced to Badminton House in Gloucestershire, seat of the Dukes of Beaufort, which also gave its name to the game, and no creator of the cup is recorded.

name: Chatham Artillery Punch
description: Rye, brandy and rum under champagne. A militia punch with a reputation for ending evenings early.
funFact: The Chatham Artillery is a Savannah militia unit founded in 1786, and the punch's reputation rests on its habit of tasting like fruit and drinking like three spirits.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the lemon juice, then stir in the cooled tea.
Add the three spirits and refrigerate for at least a day — it needs the rest.
Set a block of ice in a punch bowl and pour the mixture over it.
Add the champagne last, at the table, and grate nutmeg over the surface.

originStory: An account published in the Augusta Chronicle placed the creation of Chatham Artillery Punch in the 1850s, when the Republican Blues returned to Savannah from a drill in Macon and were welcomed by the Chatham Artillery, a militia unit founded in 1786. A competing legend links it to George Washington's visit to the city, but the original recipe and creator are unknown. It gained national fame after Southern journalists meeting in Savannah in 1870 wrote about it.

name: Mike Collins
description: The Collins built on Irish whiskey. Same lemon, same soda, a softer spirit underneath.
funFact: The Collins family is named once per base — John for whiskey, Tom for Old Tom gin, Mike for Irish, Pedro for rum, Pierre for cognac, Sandy for Scotch.

steps: Shake the whiskey, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

originStory: The Mike Collins is the Irish whiskey member of the Collins family of tall lemon, sugar and soda drinks, its nickname part of a naming habit that gave each spirit its own Collins, and no creator or date is recorded.

name: Colonel Collins
description: The bourbon Collins, named for the rank the South gives anyone who owns a distillery.
funFact: Kentucky colonel is an honorary commission the state governor still hands out, and it has been given to distillers, astronauts and Muhammad Ali alike.

steps: Shake the bourbon, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

originStory: The Colonel Collins is the bourbon member of the Collins family, its name a nod to the honorary Kentucky colonel that the state's governor still confers, and like the other spirit-named Collinses it has no documented inventor.

name: Applejack Rickey
description: Apple brandy, lime and soda, with no sugar at all. A rickey is defined by what is missing.
funFact: The rickey was made at Shoomaker's in Washington for the lobbyist Joe Rickey, and the original was bourbon; gin only took over later.

steps: Squeeze half a lime into a tall glass and drop the shell in.
Fill with ice and add the applejack.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once. Add no sugar — that would make it a Collins.

originStory: The Applejack Rickey applies the rickey's rule of lime and soda with no added sugar, a rule born at Shoomaker's bar in Washington, to American apple brandy, and no individual is credited with this version.

name: Gin Buck
description: Gin, lemon and ginger ale. A buck is a rickey with ginger in place of soda, and lemon in place of lime.
funFact: Buck, mule and rickey are the same drink separated by mixer and citrus, and the names have been used interchangeably for a century by everyone except bartenders.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the gin and the lemon juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and hang a lemon wedge on the rim.

originStory: Jacques Straub's Drinks of 1914 defines the Gin Buck as a gin rickey made with ginger ale instead of seltzer, and the buck, a spirit topped with ginger ale and sharpened with citrus, was a standard in British and American bars of the early twentieth century. The origin of the name is uncertain, and the mule, made with ginger beer, is a later and more famous relative.

name: Whiskey Buck
description: Bourbon with lemon and ginger ale. The buck template on American whiskey.
funFact: Ginger ale outsold every other American soft drink through the 1920s, largely because it was the one mixer that could hide bathtub spirits.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the bourbon and lemon juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and garnish with lemon.

originStory: The Whiskey Buck is the American whiskey member of the buck family of spirits topped with ginger ale and sharpened with lemon, and no creator or date is recorded for it.

name: London Buck
description: Gin and ginger ale with a squeeze of lemon. The buck named after the gin rather than the spirit type.
funFact: London dry describes a production method rather than a place — it can legally be made anywhere, and most of the biggest brands are not made in London.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the gin and lemon juice.
Top with ginger ale.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wedge.

originStory: The London Buck is the gin buck under the name of the London dry style, which describes a way of making gin rather than a place, and its name is bar shorthand with no recorded creator or date.

name: Mexican Mule
description: Tequila, lime and ginger beer in a copper mug. The Moscow Mule with agave underneath.
funFact: The copper mug was a marketing device from the start — it was the vodka distributor's idea in the 1940s, and it does genuinely keep the drink colder.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the tequila and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.
recipe.garnish: A lime wedge and a mint sprig

originStory: The Mexican Mule swaps tequila into the Moscow Mule, the ginger beer and lime highball that Smirnoff's John G. Martin and Jack Morgan of the Cock 'n' Bull, among others, are credited with launching in America with its copper mug, and no individual is credited with the tequila version.

name: Kentucky Mule
description: Bourbon, lime and ginger beer. The mule with the vanilla and oak of a Kentucky barrel behind it.
funFact: Bourbon must be aged in new charred oak, which is why it gives up so much vanilla so fast and why the barrels are then sold on to Scotland.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the bourbon and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish.
recipe.garnish: A lime wedge and a mint sprig

originStory: The Kentucky Mule is the bourbon version of the Moscow Mule, the ginger beer and lime highball launched in America to sell Smirnoff vodka in a copper mug, and no individual is credited with putting bourbon in it.

name: Nacional
description: Rum, apricot and lime from the Hotel Nacional, which has been pouring it since 1930.
funFact: The Hotel Nacional opened in 1930 and its bar survived the revolution intact — the drink is still on the menu, in the same room.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Nacional, or Hotel Nacional Special, comes from the Hotel Nacional de Cuba in Havana, which opened at the end of 1930, during American Prohibition. Charles H. Baker's The Gentleman's Companion credited it to Wil P. Taylor, who managed the hotel in the early 1930s, while other accounts name the American bartender Eddie Woelke, and the hotel still serves it.

name: Isle of Pines
description: Rum, grapefruit and mint from the Cuban island now called Isla de la Juventud.
funFact: The Isle of Pines was disputed between Cuba and the United States until 1925 and is where Fidel Castro was imprisoned before the revolution he later won.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Isle of Pines, white rum shaken with grapefruit, mint and sugar, is a Havana-style sour named after the island off Cuba's southern coast now called the Isla de la Juventud, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.

name: Gin Blossom
description: Gin, apricot eau-de-vie and dry vermouth, stirred and given a long stretch of orange peel.
funFact: Julie Reiner built it at the Clover Club in Brooklyn, and the eau-de-vie is doing something a liqueur cannot — it brings apricot without bringing sugar.

steps: Stir all ingredients with ice until very cold.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Cut a long strip of orange peel and express it over the surface.
Drop the peel in and serve.

originStory: The Gin Blossom is credited to Julie Reiner, who served it at the Clover Club, the bar she opened in Brooklyn's Cobble Hill in 2008 after making her name at the Flatiron Lounge in Manhattan. She built it as a stirred drink in the Martini mould, gin with vermouth and orange bitters. Its trick is the eau-de-vie, an unsweetened apricot brandy that brings the scent of the fruit without the sugar a liqueur would add, so the drink stays dry.

name: Industry Sour
description: Green Chartreuse and Fernet-Branca with lime and sugar. Made by bartenders, for bartenders, at the end of a shift.
funFact: Joaquín Simó built it at Death and Co, and the name is literal — it is the drink the trade orders when the guests have finally gone home.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Industry Sour, Fernet-Branca and green Chartreuse shaken with lime and sugar, is named for the bar trade, which calls itself the industry, and published credits for its creation disagree, so who first made it is not settled.

name: Trident
description: Aquavit, Cynar and dry sherry with peach bitters. A Negroni rebuilt from Scandinavian and Italian parts.
funFact: Robert Hess designed it as a deliberate Negroni analogue — same equal-parts skeleton, three substitutions, and nothing of the original left in the glass.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Trident is the work of Robert Hess, the Seattle drinks writer and educator who published as DrinkBoy, and it dates from around 2000. Hess built it as an experiment in rebuilding the Negroni from different parts, keeping the classic's equal measures of spirit, bitter and fortified wine and swapping each one: aquavit for gin, Cynar for Campari and dry sherry for vermouth. It was created to use Fee Brothers' peach bitters, which still finish it.

name: Slope
description: Rye, sweet vermouth and apricot. One of the Brooklyn drinks named for the neighbourhoods around the bar that made them.
funFact: Milk and Honey's staff named a whole run of Manhattan variations after Brooklyn neighbourhoods — Red Hook, Greenpoint, Bensonhurst, Carroll Gardens and this one.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Slope is credited to Julie Reiner, the New York bartender behind the Flatiron Lounge in Manhattan and the Clover Club in Brooklyn, and it is a Manhattan variation of rye with Punt e Mes and a little apricot liqueur. It takes its name from Park Slope, and it belongs with the drinks named after Brooklyn neighbourhoods that New York bartenders made in the 2000s, beginning with the Red Hook at Milk & Honey.

name: Fort Washington Flip
description: Applejack and maple with a whole egg. A flip built entirely out of things that grow in the northeast.
funFact: Chad Solomon named it for the Manhattan neighbourhood, and it is one of the few modern drinks to take the whole-egg flip seriously rather than as a novelty.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled glass.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface and serve.
