originStory: The Fort Washington Flip, applejack and maple syrup shaken with a whole egg, is a modern American take on the old whole-egg flip, and the bartender who created it and the reason for its name are not reliably recorded.

name: Coffee Flip
description: Cold coffee, port and a whole egg. The Coffee Cocktail with the coffee it was always missing.
funFact: The classic Coffee Cocktail contains no coffee at all — it is port, brandy and egg, and it earned the name purely from how it looks in the glass.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled glass.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface and serve.

originStory: The Coffee Flip, cold coffee and tawny port shaken with a whole egg, has no recorded creator, and it adds real coffee to the old Coffee Cocktail of port, brandy and egg, which Jerry Thomas admitted was named only for how it looked in the glass.

name: Scorpion
description: Rum and brandy with orgeat and citrus, blended and served for several people out of one bowl.
funFact: Trader Vic's version is a bowl drink with a gardenia floating in the middle, and the flower is specified in the original recipe as seriously as the rum is.

steps: Put everything in a blender with crushed ice.
Blend on high for five seconds only — it should stay loose, not slushy.
Pour into a scorpion bowl or a large tiki mug.
Float a gardenia in the centre if you can get one.
recipe.garnish: A gardenia, or a mint sprig and an orange wheel

originStory: The Scorpion is one of Victor Bergeron's signature drinks, served at the Trader Vic's restaurants that grew out of his Oakland bar, and his books of the 1940s print it, including a version for a group served in a bowl. That bowl of rum, brandy, orgeat and citrus, with a gardenia floating in the middle, became one of the emblems of the tiki era. When Bergeron first mixed it, and why he called it the Scorpion, are not recorded.

name: Q.B. Cooler
description: Three rums with honey, ginger, lime and orange. The drink the Mai Tai was reverse-engineered from.
funFact: Trader Vic tasted this at Don the Beachcomber's, could not get the recipe, and built the Mai Tai partly out of what he thought was in it.

steps: Flash-blend everything but the soda with a scoop of crushed ice for five seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tall tiki mug.
Add the soda water and top with more crushed ice.
Crown with a dense mint sprig.

originStory: The Q.B. Cooler comes from Don the Beachcomber, the Hollywood bar that Ernest Gantt, later known as Donn Beach, opened in the 1930s and from which the tiki drink grew. Its rums, honey, ginger and citrus became part of the Mai Tai quarrel: a longtime colleague said Beach's claim to the Mai Tai really meant that Trader Vic's drink was modelled on the Q.B. Cooler, and drinks historians still argue over how alike the two are. The initials are usually said to stand for the Quiet Birdmen, a fraternity of aviators.

name: Ancient Mariner
description: Two rums with grapefruit, lime and allspice. A modern tiki drink built to look like an old one.
funFact: Jeff Berry created it in the 1990s while reconstructing lost Don the Beachcomber recipes, and named it for the Coleridge poem rather than any bar.

steps: Flash-blend everything with a scoop of crushed ice for five seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug.
Fill to the top with more crushed ice.
Garnish with mint and a lime wheel.
recipe.garnish: A mint sprig and a lime wheel

originStory: Jeff Berry, the tiki historian known as Beachbum Berry, created the Ancient Mariner in 1994 and published it in his first book, the Grog Log, in 1998, while he was tracking down the lost recipes of Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic. He built it to taste like a drink from those original Polynesian bars, with Demerara and Jamaican rums, grapefruit, lime and allspice. The name borrows the title of Coleridge's poem, and the drink has become a modern tiki standard.

name: Brace Up
description: Brandy, absinthe, egg and lemon shaken to a froth. Thomas files it under morning drinks, which tells you what it was for.
funFact: The 1862 book groups a whole shelf of these under recuperatives, and every one of them contains raw egg — the Victorian bar's entire theory of the morning after.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until the tin frosts over.
Strain into a small tumbler.
Grate nutmeg heavily over the top and drink it standing up.

originStory: The Brace Up survives in a later edition of the bar guide by Jerry Thomas, the New York bartender whose book was the first widely circulated American bartender's guide; it is not in his first edition. It shakes brandy with a whole egg, lemon, sugar and a touch of anise, and its name reads like an instruction to pull yourself together. Thomas gathered many of his recipes from other bars, so who first mixed it is not recorded.

name: Jersey Cocktail
description: Hard cider with sugar and bitters. A cocktail by the 1862 definition, built on cider instead of spirit.
funFact: It qualifies as a cocktail on the original terms — a base, sugar, water and bitters — and proves the definition never actually required a distilled spirit.

steps: Stir the syrup and bitters together in the bottom of a rocks glass.
Add ice.
Pour the cider over slowly so it keeps some of its bubble.
Twist a lemon peel over the top and drop it in.

originStory: The Jersey Cocktail appears in Jerry Thomas's How to Mix Drinks of 1862, the first widely circulated American bartender's guide, among cocktails built on the old formula of a base, sugar and bitters. Thomas fills the glass with cider, mixed with sugar and bitters and finished with lemon peel, and the drink is generally taken to be named for New Jersey, whose orchards supplied much of the cider and applejack drunk in the northeast. Its inventor is not recorded.

name: Hot Spiced Rum
description: Rum, butter, sugar and spice under boiling water. The buttered rum before anyone shortened the name.
funFact: The butter is not a garnish or a modern flourish — Thomas prints it in 1862, and it is what keeps the drink from tasting thin.

steps: Put the sugar, butter, cloves and cinnamon in a warmed mug.
Add a splash of boiling water and mash it into a paste.
Pour in the rum and stir.
Top with the rest of the boiling water and grate nutmeg over.
recipe.garnish: Grated nutmeg and a cinnamon stick

originStory: Hot rum drinks were a winter staple of colonial New England, where rum distilled from Caribbean molasses was the everyday spirit. Jerry Thomas fixed this one in print in 1862: Jamaica rum, sugar, a spoonful of allspice and cloves, a piece of butter as large as half a chestnut and a tumbler topped up with hot water. The name simply describes the drink, and the Hot Buttered Rum most people now order is the same idea with the butter promoted to the title.

name: Champagne Cobbler
description: Champagne over crushed ice with curaçao and fruit. The cobbler template applied to the most expensive bottle in the room.
funFact: The cobbler was the drink that sold the straw — it was among the first served with one, because crushed ice made it impossible to drink any other way.

steps: Fill a goblet with crushed ice.
Add the curaçao and syrup and stir once.
Pour the champagne slowly over the ice so it does not foam over.
Pile fruit and mint on top and add a straw.
recipe.garnish: Seasonal fruit and a mint sprig

originStory: Jerry Thomas's How to Mix Drinks of 1862 printed a Champagne Cobbler alongside sherry, catawba, hock and claret versions, applying the cobbler of wine, sugar and fruit over shaved ice to sparkling wine. The cobbler family had swept American bars in the decades before, and Charles Dickens put the sherry version in Martin Chuzzlewit. Thomas says the Champagne Cobbler should be sipped through a straw, and the cobbler helped make the straw a bar fixture. Its creator is not recorded.

name: Port Cobbler
description: Port, sugar and fruit churned through crushed ice. Sweeter and heavier than the sherry version, and older.
funFact: Cobblers were the most-ordered American drink of the 1840s, and the sherry version in particular was what a nineteenth-century bar sold most of.

steps: Muddle the orange slices with the syrup in the bottom of a goblet.
Fill the glass with crushed ice.
Add the port and churn with a barspoon until the glass frosts.
Cap with more ice, pile fruit on top and add a straw.
recipe.garnish: Berries, an orange slice and mint

originStory: The Port Cobbler is the nineteenth-century American cobbler of wine, sugar and fruit churned over crushed ice made with port, one of many variations on the far more famous sherry cobbler, and no creator is recorded for it.

name: Gin Smash
description: Gin, mint and sugar over crushed ice. A julep in a short glass, which is the only difference there has ever been.
funFact: The old books separate smash from julep purely by glass size — a smash is a short drink and a julep a long one, and nothing else about them differs.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in a rocks glass.
Add the gin and fill with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the outside of the glass frosts.
Cap with more ice and crown with mint.

originStory: The smash is a nineteenth-century American drink, and Jerry Thomas's How to Mix Drinks of 1862 gives brandy, gin and whiskey versions, describing it as simply a julep on a small plan. The difference was size: spirit, sugar and mint over shaved ice in a short glass rather than a tall one, which is why old bar books treat the two as one family. The smash faded in the twentieth century and returned with the classic-cocktail revival.

name: Santina's Pousse Café
description: Brandy, maraschino and curaçao floated in three clean bands. Named for the New Orleans bartender who worked out how to do it.
funFact: Layering works on sugar content rather than alcohol — the sweeter a liqueur, the denser it is, which is why the syrups always go in first.

steps: Pour the curaçao into a narrow pony glass.
Rest a barspoon just above the surface, curve upward, and pour the maraschino over the back of it.
Float the cognac last, the same way.
Serve without a stirrer — disturbing the layers ruins the drink.
recipe.garnish: None — the three bands are the drink

originStory: Joseph Santini, who ran a celebrated bar on Gravier Street in New Orleans in the 1850s, is remembered for two drinks: the Brandy Crusta and this pousse-café. Jerry Thomas printed it in 1862 as Santina's Pousse Café, crediting the proprietor of Santina's Saloon, a celebrated Spanish café in New Orleans, and the misspelling has stuck. Its brandy, maraschino and curaçao are now usually floated in three bands, and layering works on density, which follows sugar rather than alcohol, so the sweetest liqueur goes in first.

name: Pousse Café
description: Five or more liqueurs floated in bands, poured heaviest first. Entirely about the pour and not at all about the taste.
funFact: The name means push the coffee — it was served after dinner, alongside coffee, and the more bands a bartender could hold apart the better their reputation.

steps: Pour the grenadine into a tall narrow glass — it is the densest and goes first.
Float each of the others in turn over the back of a barspoon, in the order given.
Pour slowly enough that the stream never breaks the layer beneath.
Serve upright and do not move it quickly.

originStory: Pousse-café is French for coffee-pusher, and the name first belonged to any small after-dinner drink taken with or after coffee. In nineteenth-century New Orleans and New York it came to mean something more theatrical: liqueurs and spirits floated in separate coloured bands, poured slowly so that each settled on the one below. Jerry Thomas's guide of 1862 already printed several, including Santina's from New Orleans, and the drink became a test of a bartender's steady hand.

name: Angel's Kiss
description: Crème de cacao under a float of cream, with a cherry balanced on top. A pousse-café with only two bands.
funFact: It is the simplest drink in the pousse-café family and the one people actually learn on — two liqueurs are hard enough to keep apart.

steps: Pour the crème de cacao into a narrow glass.
Float the cream over the back of a barspoon so it sits in a clean band.
Balance a cherry on the surface of the cream.
Serve without a straw.

originStory: The Angel's Kiss in its modern form, crème de cacao under a float of cream, is the simplest of the layered pousse-café drinks, and older books such as the Savoy Cocktail Book give the name to a four-band drink and print this two-band one as the Angel's Tip, with no creator recorded.

name: Widow's Dream
description: Bénédictine shaken with a whole egg and cream. Rich, herbal and almost a dessert.
funFact: Bénédictine's recipe is genuinely secret — the company says three people know it, and holds that only one of them travels at a time.

steps: Dry-shake the Bénédictine and egg without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until cold.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Float the cream over the back of a spoon and grate nutmeg over.

originStory: The Widow's Dream is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as a liqueur glass of Bénédictine shaken with a whole egg and topped with cream. Bénédictine was launched at Fécamp in Normandy in the 1860s by the merchant Alexandre Le Grand, who presented it as the revival of a lost recipe from the town's old Benedictine abbey, a story historians doubt. The cocktail's creator is not recorded, and neither is the widow of its title.

name: Rock and Rye
description: Rye infused with rock candy and fruit. Sold as a cold remedy for most of the nineteenth century, and taxed as one.
funFact: It was marketed as medicine to dodge liquor law, and bottles carried a label claiming it cured colds — which is how a cocktail ended up behind a pharmacy counter.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: Rock and rye began in nineteenth-century American saloons as rye whiskey sweetened with crystallised rock candy, often with orange, lemon or other fruit added to the bottle. It was widely sold with claims that it eased coughs and colds, and bottled versions sat on pharmacy shelves as well as behind bars. No single inventor is recorded, and several small producers have since revived the bottled style.

name: Barbados Rum Punch
description: One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak. The rhyme is the recipe.
funFact: The rhyme is taught to Barbadian children and printed on tea towels, and it scales to any quantity because the ratio is the entire specification.

steps: Combine the lime, syrup, rum and water in a jug and stir.
Add the bitters and stir again — Angostura is not optional here.
Pour over ice in short glasses.
Grate nutmeg heavily over each one.
recipe.garnish: Grated nutmeg and a lime wheel

originStory: Barbados is one of the places where rum began: planters there were distilling spirit from sugar-cane molasses by the mid-1600s, and English visitors called it kill-devil. Punch, a mix of spirit, citrus, sugar, water and spice that English sailors are thought to have picked up in India, became the island's way of drinking it. The traditional Barbadian rhyme is a mnemonic for the proportions rather than a list of ingredients, which is why the recipe scales to any size of bowl.

name: Caudle
description: Hot spiced wine or ale thickened with egg and oatmeal. Half a drink, half a meal, and given to the sick for six hundred years.
funFact: Caudle and posset are sisters — a posset is curdled with wine, a caudle thickened with grain, and both were served to women after childbirth well into the 1800s.

steps: Simmer the oatmeal in the water until it thickens into a thin gruel.
Beat the yolks with the sugar and nutmeg.
Warm the wine and whisk it into the gruel, then temper in the yolks off the heat.
Return to a very low heat and stir until it coats a spoon. Do not let it boil.

originStory: Caudle is one of the oldest drinks in English cookery, a warm mixture of wine or ale thickened with grain or egg yolks and sweetened, with recipes surviving from medieval cookbooks. Its name comes through Old French from the Latin for warm. For centuries it was a drink of the sickroom and the lying-in chamber, served to new mothers and to the visitors who came to see the baby. Its relative the posset was a richer dish of milk curdled with wine or ale.

name: French 76
description: The French 75 with vodka. Cleaner, colder and with nothing in the way of the champagne.
funFact: The 75 family is numbered by artillery calibre, and the variants that followed kept the joke going by picking bigger guns.

steps: Shake the vodka, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with champagne so it does not overflow.
Express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.

originStory: The French 76 is a vodka version of the French 75, the gin, lemon and Champagne drink named after the French army's 75mm field gun of the First World War, with its number moved one step on, and no creator or bar of origin is recorded.

name: French 125
description: The French 75 rebuilt on cognac, which is what many argue it should have been all along.
funFact: Whether the original took gin or cognac has been argued for a century; the cognac version at least puts a French spirit in a French drink.

steps: Shake the cognac, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Strain into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with champagne.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: The French 125 rebuilds the French 75, named after the French army's 75mm field gun, on cognac instead of gin, a spirit some early recipes for the original already used, and who first gave the cognac version its own name is not recorded.

name: Agavoni
description: A Negroni with tequila in place of gin. Same equal thirds, more earth underneath.
funFact: Blanco tequila carries the vegetal edge of cooked agave straight through, which is exactly what Campari's bitterness has something to hold on to.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Agavoni, also called the Tequila Negroni, keeps the Negroni's equal measures of Campari and sweet vermouth and swaps gin for blanco tequila, its name a contraction of agave and Negroni, and its creator and date are not recorded.

name: Tequila Sour
description: Tequila, lemon and sugar with egg white. The sour template on agave, and a Margarita's plainer cousin.
funFact: Lemon rather than lime is what separates this from a Margarita — swap the citrus and the drink stops tasting Mexican and starts tasting like a whiskey sour.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Let the foam settle before garnishing.
recipe.garnish: An orange slice and a cherry

originStory: The Tequila Sour applies the old bar template of spirit, citrus and sugar, here with lemon and often egg white, to the agave spirit of Jalisco, and nobody has a documented claim to the first one.

name: Mezcal Sour
description: Mezcal, lime and agave syrup under an egg-white foam that carries the smoke straight up.
funFact: The smoke is not added — mezcal agave is roasted in earth pits lined with hot stones, and the flavour comes from a week underground.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until very cold.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dust the foam with chilli salt.
recipe.garnish: A dusting of chilli salt on the foam

originStory: The Mezcal Sour applies the classic sour of spirit, citrus and sugar to Oaxaca's mezcal, whose smoke comes from agave hearts roasted in earthen pits, and no single bartender is credited with the first one.

name: Toreador
description: Tequila with apricot brandy and lime. One of the first tequila drinks to reach a London bar book.
funFact: Tequila barely appears in English cocktail books before the 1930s, and when it does it is usually spelled wrong and described as a Mexican brandy.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Toreador is printed in the Café Royal Cocktail Book, compiled by W. J. Tarling for the United Kingdom Bartenders' Guild and published in London in 1937, alongside the Picador, another drink named for the bullring. Both belong to the handful of tequila drinks in British bar books of the period, when the spirit was still a rarity outside Mexico. Pairing tequila with apricot brandy and lime made a drink in the style of the era's fruit-brandy sours.

name: Matador
description: Tequila, pineapple and lime. The easiest agave drink there is, and Trader Vic's answer to the Margarita.
funFact: Pineapple and agave share a green, faintly vegetal note, which is why the pairing works far better than the fruit-juice shortcut it looks like.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Matador, tequila shaken with pineapple and lime, has no recorded creator, and it is a different drink from the Matador of tequila, curaçao and dry vermouth printed in London's Café Royal Cocktail Book before the Second World War.

name: Brave Bull
description: Tequila and coffee liqueur over ice. A Black Russian with agave instead of vodka.
funFact: Swap the tequila for vodka and it is a Black Russian; swap it for bourbon and it has no name at all, which is a fair comment on how these drinks get named.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice.
Add the tequila and the coffee liqueur.
Stir briefly to combine and chill.
Twist a strip of lemon peel over the top and drop it in.

originStory: The Brave Bull is the tequila relative of the Black Russian, tequila poured over ice with coffee liqueur, its name a nod to the fighting bulls of the bullring, and who first made it, and where, is not recorded.

name: Chapala
description: Tequila with orange, lime, grenadine and a drop of orange flower water. Named for Mexico's largest lake.
funFact: Orange flower water is measured in drops and turns up in only a handful of classics — this one, the Ramos Gin Fizz, and almost nothing else.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Chapala, tequila with orange, lime, grenadine and a few drops of orange flower water, is named after Lake Chapala in Jalisco, Mexico's largest lake, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.

name: Berta's Special
description: Tequila, honey, lime and soda with an egg white. From a Taxco cantina that has been open since the 1930s.
funFact: Bertita's still stands on the square in Taxco, and the drink is one of very few pre-war Mexican cocktails whose bar of origin is still trading.

steps: Dry-shake the tequila, honey, lime, egg white and bitters without ice.
Add ice and shake hard until cold.
Strain into a tall glass over fresh ice.
Top with soda water and stir once.

originStory: Berta's Special is linked to Bar Berta, a cantina on the main square of Taxco, the silver-mining town in Guerrero, beside the church of Santa Prisca. Its house drink of tequila with lime and honey, lengthened with soda, is known locally simply as a Berta and was taken up by visitors to the town. When the bar first poured it, and who the Berta of its name was, are not reliably recorded.

name: Picador
description: Tequila, Cointreau and lime, shaken and served up with no salt. The Margarita as a London bar first wrote it down.
funFact: It appears in British books in the 1930s under this name, which puts a Margarita in print in London before the drink had settled on its Spanish one.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Picador appears in the Café Royal Cocktail Book, compiled by W. J. Tarling for the United Kingdom Bartenders' Guild and published in London in 1937. Its tequila, triple sec and lime use the same proportions as the Margarita, years before the Margarita became famous under its own name. Drinks historians cite it as evidence that the formula existed before the many bartenders and socialites who later claimed to have invented the Margarita. A picador is the mounted lancer of the bullfight.

name: Cadillac Margarita
description: A Margarita made with reposado and finished with a float of Grand Marnier poured over the back of a spoon.
glassware: Rocks glass with a salted half-rim
funFact: The float is the whole point — stirred in it disappears, but sitting on top the Grand Marnier hits first and the tequila arrives underneath it.

steps: Salt half the rim of a rocks glass, so the drinker can choose.
Shake the tequila, Cointreau, lime and agave with ice.
Strain into the glass over one large cube.
Float the Grand Marnier over the back of a barspoon.
recipe.garnish: A lime wheel and a salted rim

originStory: The Cadillac Margarita is the premium Margarita of reposado tequila with a float of Grand Marnier, named after the American car that became shorthand for the top of the range, and it has no recorded creator.

name: Changuirongo
description: Tequila and whatever soda is cold. Mexico's everyday highball, and deliberately unfussy.
funFact: Grapefruit soda makes it a Paloma and cola makes it a Charro Negro; with anything else it just keeps this name and nobody minds.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the tequila.
Top with whatever cold soda is to hand.
Squeeze a lime wedge in and drop it in the glass.

originStory: The Changuirongo is Mexico's everyday tequila highball, tequila topped with whatever soda is to hand, a cantina standby in Jalisco whose colloquial name has no documented origin.

name: Jack and Coke
description: Tennessee whiskey and cola. Probably the single most-ordered mixed drink in the world.
funFact: Jack Daniel's is charcoal-mellowed through ten feet of sugar maple before barrelling — the Lincoln County Process, and the reason it is not legally a bourbon.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the whiskey.
Top with cold cola and stir once.
Squeeze a lime wedge over it if the bar has one.

originStory: The Jack and Coke pairs two Southern American brands, Jack Daniel's Tennessee whiskey from Lynchburg and Coca-Cola from Atlanta, and no one is credited with first pouring them together.

name: Rum and Coke
description: Rum and cola without the lime. Add the lime and it becomes a Cuba Libre, which is a different order.
funFact: The lime is the whole distinction — bartenders treat Cuba Libre and rum and coke as two drinks, and customers almost never do.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and serve, with no lime.

originStory: Rum and cola without the lime has no recorded inventor, while the version with lime is the Cuba Libre, which by most accounts began in Havana around the turn of the twentieth century, and the Andrews Sisters' wartime hit Rum and Coca-Cola made the pairing famous across the United States.

name: Whiskey Ginger
description: Whiskey and ginger ale. The buck without the lemon, and the order people give when they want something easy.
funFact: Ginger's heat reads as a continuation of the spice already in rye, which is why the pairing works better with rye than with bourbon.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the whiskey.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and hang a lime wedge on the rim.

originStory: The Whiskey Ginger, whiskey lengthened with ginger ale, has no recorded inventor, and with a squeeze of lemon or lime it becomes a buck, an older and better documented family of highballs.

name: Vodka Cranberry
description: Vodka and cranberry juice. A Cape Codder without the lime, and the most-ordered vodka drink there is.
funFact: Cranberry juice is almost never sold unsweetened — the fruit is far too sour to drink straight, which is why the bottle usually says cocktail on it.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the vodka.
Top with cranberry juice.
Stir once until the colour is even.

originStory: The Vodka Cranberry is the Cape Codder without its lime, a pairing the Ocean Spray cranberry growers' cooperative promoted from the mid-twentieth century and later named after the cranberry bogs of Massachusetts, and it has no single inventor.

name: Vodka Soda
description: Vodka and soda water. The least of all possible drinks, ordered on purpose.
funFact: It is ordered as much for what it leaves out as for what it contains — no sugar, no juice, and nothing to disguise a bad vodka either.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the vodka.
Top with cold soda water.
Squeeze a lime wedge in and drop it in the glass.

originStory: The Vodka Soda is the plainest of highballs, vodka lengthened with soda water, with no inventor or birthplace, and it became a standard order as vodka spread through American bars after the Second World War.

name: Vodka Tonic
description: Vodka and tonic. The Gin and Tonic with the botanicals taken out, which leaves the quinine exposed.
funFact: Without gin's botanicals there is nothing standing between the drinker and the tonic, so the brand of tonic matters more here than in almost any other highball.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the vodka.
Top with cold tonic, poured down a barspoon to keep the bubble.
Squeeze a lime wedge in.

originStory: The Vodka Tonic is the Gin and Tonic with vodka in the gin's place, a highball that followed vodka into Western bars after the Second World War, and it has no recorded creator.

name: Tequila and Tonic
description: Blanco tequila and tonic. Spain drinks it more than Mexico does, and it works better than it sounds.
funFact: Quinine's bitterness meets cooked agave's vegetal edge rather than fighting it, which is why the drink took hold in Spain where the gin-tonic culture was already built.

steps: Fill a large copa glass with ice.
Add the tequila.
Top with cold tonic.
Garnish with a grapefruit peel rather than lime — it suits the agave better.

originStory: Tequila and Tonic is a simple highball of blanco tequila and tonic water, made wherever the agave spirit of Jalisco is poured, and no bartender or bar has a documented claim to it.

name: Dog's Nose
description: Porter with a measure of gin dropped into it. Dickens printed the recipe in 1836.
funFact: The Pickwick Papers describes it as warm porter, moist sugar, gin and nutmeg, which makes it one of the earliest English drink recipes published in a novel.

steps: Warm the porter gently — not hot, just off the chill.
Stir in the sugar until it dissolves.
Add the gin and stir once.
Grate nutmeg over the top and serve in a tankard.

originStory: Dog's Nose is an old English mixture of beer and gin, and one of its earliest appearances in print is in Charles Dickens's The Pickwick Papers, serialised from 1836. In the novel a temperance society's report records a tailor's fondness for it, describing the drink as warm porter, moist sugar, gin and nutmeg. The origin of the name is not documented, and the mixture belongs to the long English pub habit of strengthening beer with spirit.

name: Flaming Dr Pepper
description: A lit shot of overproof amaretto dropped into beer. Tastes, improbably, like Dr Pepper.
funFact: It contains no Dr Pepper and no cola of any kind — the resemblance comes from amaretto's almond meeting the malt, and it is genuinely close.

steps: Fill a shot glass three-quarters with amaretto and float the overproof rum on top.
Pour the lager into a separate glass, leaving room.
Light the float, let it burn for a second, then drop the whole shot glass into the beer.
Drink it down immediately, while it is still foaming.

originStory: The Flaming Dr Pepper takes its name from the soft drink first served in Waco, Texas, though it contains none: amaretto under a lit layer of high-strength spirit, dropped into beer, is meant to recall the soda's flavour, and the almond against the malt comes surprisingly close. The best-known claim to have invented it comes from Dave Brinks of the Gold Mine Saloon in New Orleans, a claim that has not been independently confirmed.

name: Blow Job
description: Layered coffee liqueur and Baileys under whipped cream, drunk hands-free. The name is the gimmick and so is the delivery.
funFact: It belongs to a run of 1980s layered novelty shots that were designed around how they are drunk rather than how they taste.

steps: Pour the coffee liqueur into a shot glass.
Float the Irish cream over the back of a barspoon so it sits in a clean band.
Cap with a swirl of whipped cream.
Serve on a napkin, to be taken without hands.

originStory: The Blow Job is an innuendo-named American novelty shot of coffee liqueur and Irish cream under whipped cream, traditionally lifted without using hands, and nobody has a documented claim to inventing it.

name: White Gummy Bear
description: Vodka, peach schnapps, sour mix and lemon-lime soda. Tastes exactly like the sweet it is named for.
funFact: The whole family of sweet-shop shots works by hitting one recognisable confectionery note hard enough that nobody looks for a second one.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The White Gummy Bear is a modern American shot of vodka, peach schnapps, sour mix and lemon-lime soda named after the sweet it imitates, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.

name: Chocolate Cake Shot
description: Vodka and hazelnut liqueur, chased by a sugared lemon wedge. The lemon and sugar is what makes it taste of cake.
funFact: There is no chocolate in it at all — the illusion comes entirely from hazelnut meeting sugared citrus, and it collapses if you skip the lemon.

steps: Shake the vodka and Frangelico with ice until very cold.
Strain into a shot glass.
Coat a lemon wedge heavily in caster sugar.
Drink the shot, then bite the lemon immediately.

originStory: The Chocolate Cake Shot, hazelnut liqueur and vodka chased with a sugared lemon wedge, contains no chocolate and takes its name from the cake-like taste the combination leaves, and it has no recorded creator.

name: Melon Ball
description: Midori, vodka and pineapple. Bright green, and one of the drinks that made melon liqueur a 1980s fixture.
funFact: Midori launched in America at Studio 54 in 1978, which is roughly the most 1970s fact available about any bottle behind a bar.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: A melon ball on a pick

originStory: The Melon Ball, Midori with vodka and pineapple, has no recorded creator and rose with the melon liqueur itself, which Suntory launched in the United States with a party at Studio 54 in New York in the late 1970s.

name: Ferrari Shot
description: Equal parts Fernet-Branca and Campari. Bitter twice over, and an industry handshake more than a drink.
funFact: San Francisco drinks more Fernet-Branca per head than anywhere outside Argentina, and the bar trade there adopted this as its shift-drink shorthand.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Ferrari Shot, equal parts Fernet-Branca and Campari, is a bartenders' pour associated with San Francisco's devotion to Fernet, its name usually explained by its red colour, and it has no recorded inventor.

name: Sourtoe Cocktail
description: A shot of whisky with a mummified human toe in it. The toe must touch your lips; the rules are posted on the wall.
funFact: The Downtown Hotel has run it since 1973, keeps the toes in salt, and fines anyone who swallows one — which has happened more than once.

steps: Pour a shot of whisky.
Add the toe.
Drink it down fast or slow — the only rule is that your lips touch the toe.
Return the toe to the salt. Swallowing it carries a fine.
recipe.garnish: The toe, which stays with the bar

originStory: The Sourtoe Cocktail began in 1973 in Dawson City, Yukon, when Captain Dick Stevenson, a local riverboat captain, turned a preserved human toe into a club initiation. The toe, the story goes, had belonged to a rum-runner of the 1920s who lost it to frostbite. The ritual is now run at the Downtown Hotel's Sourdough Saloon, where the rule is that the toe must touch the drinker's lips, and after a guest deliberately swallowed one in 2013 the fine for doing so was raised to 2,500 Canadian dollars.

name: Blue Motorcycle
description: Five white spirits with blue curaçao and lemon-lime soda. A Long Island with the cola swapped for the blue.
funFact: The Long Island family is defined by five spirits in equal quarter-ounces, and every variant in it changes only the mixer and the colour.

steps: Shake everything but the soda with ice.
Strain into a tall glass packed with fresh ice.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a straw.

originStory: The Blue Motorcycle is one of the many offshoots of the Long Island Iced Tea, swapping the cola for blue curaçao and lemon-lime soda over the same five-spirit base, and its own creator is not recorded.

name: Trash Can
description: The Long Island's five spirits with blue curaçao, finished by upending a can of energy drink into the glass.
funFact: The can is inverted into the glass and left standing there, draining slowly as the drink goes down — which is where the name comes from.

steps: Fill a pint glass with ice.
Add all six spirits and liqueurs and stir once.
Open a small can of energy drink and upend it into the glass.
Leave the can standing in the drink and serve it that way.
recipe.garnish: The inverted can, left in the glass

originStory: The Trash Can is a recent American party drink built on the Long Island Iced Tea's five spirits with blue curaçao, served with a can of energy drink upended into the glass, and it has no recorded creator.

name: Banana Daiquiri
description: Rum, lime and banana blended with ice. A Floridita fruit daiquiri, and the one that travelled worst and furthest.
funFact: La Floridita built frozen fruit daiquiris around a commercial blender in the 1930s, which put Havana ahead of every American bar on the technology.

steps: Put the rum, banana, lime and syrup in a blender.
Add the crushed ice and blend until smooth and thick.
Pour into a chilled coupe without straining.
Garnish with banana and lime.
recipe.garnish: A banana slice and a lime wheel

originStory: The Banana Daiquiri is one of the blended fruit daiquiris that grew from the frozen Daiquiri made famous at Havana's El Floridita by Constantino Ribalaigua Vert in the 1930s, and no one is recorded as the first to add banana.

name: Strawberry Daiquiri
description: Rum, lime and strawberries blended to a slush. The drink that taught America what a daiquiri was, wrongly.
funFact: The frozen version so completely displaced the original that bartenders now have to specify a daiquiri up when they mean the three-ingredient drink.

steps: Blend the rum, strawberries, lime and syrup until smooth.
Add the crushed ice and blend again until thick.
Pour into a chilled glass.
Notch a strawberry onto the rim.

originStory: The Strawberry Daiquiri descends from the frozen daiquiris of Havana's El Floridita, blending strawberries into the rum, lime and sugar original, and it became a fixture of American restaurants and resort bars without any recorded creator.

name: Frosé
description: Rosé frozen solid, then blended with strawberry and lemon. It only works because the wine is frozen first.
funFact: Bar Primi in New York put it on in 2016 and it was everywhere within a summer; the trick is that rosé never freezes hard, so it blends into a slush rather than a block.

steps: Pour the rosé into a shallow tray and freeze overnight — it will go slushy, not solid.
Scrape it into a blender with the strawberries, lemon juice and syrup.
Blend until smooth, adding a little more frozen wine if it loosens.
Pour into chilled wine glasses and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: A strawberry and a lemon twist

originStory: Frosé, a contraction of frozen rosé, is credited to Bar Primi in New York, which put a blended frozen rosé on its menu in the summer of 2016. It spread across the United States within a season, helped by photographs shared online and by rosé's rising popularity. The method relies on alcohol lowering the wine's freezing point, so rosé left in a freezer sets into a slush rather than a solid block and blends easily with fruit and lemon.

name: Amaretto Stone Sour
description: Amaretto with sour mix and orange juice. The gateway drink of a thousand bad decisions, and genuinely good.
funFact: A stone sour is any sour with orange juice added, so the name describes a whole family — this is simply the one everybody orders.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: An orange slice and a cherry

originStory: The Amaretto Stone Sour is amaretto in a stone sour, the American sour lengthened with orange juice and sometimes called a California sour, and no bartender is credited with it.

name: Brandy Ice
description: Brandy, crème de cacao and vanilla ice cream blended smooth. A dessert that arrives in a glass.
funFact: Ice cream drinks blend rather than shake because there is no water to dilute — the ice cream is the chill, the sugar and the body all at once.

steps: Put the ice cream, brandy and crème de cacao in a blender.
Blend just until smooth — over-blending turns it to soup.
Pour into a chilled wine glass.
Grate nutmeg over the top.

originStory: The Brandy Ice, brandy and crème de cacao blended with vanilla ice cream, is an American after-dinner drink in the line of the Brandy Alexander, with the cream swapped for ice cream, and no creator or bar of origin is recorded.

name: Bombardino
description: Hot advocaat and brandy under whipped cream. Drunk on Italian ski slopes and almost nowhere else.
funFact: Order it calimero and you get coffee in it; order it bombardino sporco and you get whisky instead of brandy. The Alps have a vocabulary for this.

steps: Warm the advocaat gently in a pan — it must not boil or it will split.
Stir in the brandy off the heat.
Pour into a warmed heatproof glass.
Cap with whipped cream and dust with cocoa.

originStory: The Bombardino comes from Livigno, a ski town in the Italian Alps near the Swiss border, and its origin story is told in more than one way. In the most often told version a man from Genoa running the Mottolino mountain hut served the hot mix to skiers coming in from a blizzard, and one of them said it was like a little bomb, which gave it its name. Another account credits Aldo Del Bò, a local ski-lift manager, in 1972. Either way, it spread from Livigno to ski resorts across northern Italy.

name: Campari Spritz
description: Prosecco, Campari and soda. Sharper and more bitter than the Aperol version, and older.
funFact: Campari is roughly twice the strength of Aperol and considerably more bitter, so the same three-two-one build gives a completely different drink.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Add the Campari, then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda.
Stir once from the bottom and hang an orange slice on the rim.

originStory: The Campari Spritz is the Veneto's spritz of sparkling wine, bitter liqueur and soda made with Campari, the Milanese bitter that is stronger and sharper than Aperol, and like most spritz variations it has no recorded creator.

name: Rabarbaro Spritz
description: Prosecco with rhubarb amaro and soda. Darker and earthier than any citrus spritz.
funFact: Rabarbaro is made from Chinese rhubarb root that is smoke-dried before it is macerated, which is where the faint tarry note underneath comes from.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice.
Add the rabarbaro, then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda.
Stir once and garnish with an orange half-wheel.

originStory: The Rabarbaro Spritz swaps the usual orange bitter in the Veneto's spritz for rabarbaro, the Milanese style of rhubarb-root amaro best known through Rabarbaro Zucca, and the serve has no recorded creator.

name: Braulio Spritz
description: Prosecco with the Alpine amaro of the Valtellina. Pine, mint and gentian instead of orange.
funFact: Braulio is made in Bormio from mountain herbs gathered in the Stelvio valleys, and it tastes far more of a forest floor than of a citrus grove.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice.
Add the Braulio, then the prosecco.
Top with soda.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon twist rather than orange.

originStory: The Braulio Spritz puts Braulio, the alpine amaro of Bormio named after the Braulio valley where its herbs were first gathered, in place of Aperol or Campari, and the serve has no recorded creator.

name: Limoncello Spritz
description: Prosecco, limoncello and soda over ice with mint. The southern Italian answer to the Venetian spritz.
funFact: Sorrento lemons are grown under chestnut-pole pergolas and are thick-skinned by design — limoncello is made from the peel alone, never the juice.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice and add the mint.
Pour in the limoncello, then the prosecco.
Top with a splash of soda.
Stir once and hang a lemon wheel on the rim.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a mint sprig

originStory: The Limoncello Spritz is a recent southern Italian take on the Veneto's spritz built on limoncello, the lemon-zest liqueur whose birthplace Capri, Sorrento and the Amalfi Coast all claim, and it has no single creator.

name: Prairie Oyster
description: A whole raw egg yolk in brandy with Worcestershire, vinegar and pepper. Swallowed in one, unbroken.
funFact: The yolk is meant to stay intact all the way down, which is the entire ordeal — the drink is a Victorian hangover cure and reads as one.

steps: Pour the brandy, Worcestershire, vinegar and hot sauce into a small tumbler.
Slide the yolk in whole, taking care not to break it.
Season the top with salt and cracked pepper.
Swallow it in one, without chewing and without looking.

originStory: The Prairie Oyster belongs to the Victorian and Edwardian tradition of morning-after restoratives, and its name is a joke: the whole raw yolk, swallowed unbroken, stands in for an oyster on a prairie about as far from the sea as one can get. Harry Craddock printed a version in the Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and P. G. Wodehouse's valet Jeeves, whose own restorative is a similar mixture, gave the type its most famous fictional outing. Its creator is not recorded.

name: Bull Shot
description: Vodka and cold beef consommé with Worcestershire and pepper. A Bloody Mary made of stock instead of tomato.
funFact: It was invented at the Caucus Club in Detroit in 1952, and served hot as often as cold — the hot version is a different drink and a better one in winter.

steps: Roll everything between two tins with ice rather than shaking, so it does not foam.
Strain into a tall glass over fresh ice.
Season the top with celery salt and cracked pepper.
Serve with a lemon wedge.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wedge and cracked pepper

originStory: The Bull Shot is usually credited to the Caucus Club in Detroit, where it is said to have been created in the early 1950s by mixing vodka with cold beef bouillon in place of the Bloody Mary's tomato juice. It became a fashionable lunchtime and brunch drink of the late 1950s and 1960s, a savoury sibling of the Bloody Mary, served hot as well as cold. Canned beef consommé made it easy for any bar to reproduce.

name: Ojen Cocktail
description: Spanish anise liqueur with Peychaud's and soda. New Orleans drank it at Carnival for a century.
funFact: Ojén came from Andalusia and New Orleans bought so much of it that when the distillery closed in the 1990s the city's last cases were rationed by the bottle.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: Ojén is an anise liqueur named after the Andalusian town near Málaga where it was first distilled, and New Orleans took it up so thoroughly in the nineteenth century that it became one of the city's Carnival drinks, poured at Mardi Gras gatherings as the Ojen Frappé or the Ojen Cocktail. When the Spanish producer stopped making it late in the twentieth century, the city's bars made their remaining bottles last as long as they could, and the Sazerac Company, based in New Orleans, later revived the liqueur for its home market.

name: Vodka Martini
description: Vodka and dry vermouth, stirred. The Martini with the botanicals taken out, which is either the point or the problem.
funFact: Ian Fleming had Bond order his shaken, which is why half the world does — bartenders stir it, because shaking clouds the drink and over-dilutes it.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.
recipe.garnish: An olive or a lemon twist

originStory: The Vodka Martini spread in the 1950s, when vodka was rising fast in American and British bars and many drinkers wanted a Martini without gin's botanicals; early versions were sometimes called the Kangaroo. Ian Fleming, writing in London, helped make it famous by having James Bond order his vodka Martinis shaken and not stirred, a phrase the films turned into a catchphrase. Bartenders still mostly stir it, since shaking clouds the drink and adds more water. No single bartender is credited with the first one.

name: Fifty-Fifty
description: Equal parts gin and dry vermouth. The Martini as it was actually poured before the ratio started climbing.
funFact: Martini ratios have gone one way for a century — one to one in 1900, six to one by 1950, and effectively neat gin by 1980.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Fifty-Fifty, equal parts gin and dry vermouth, is printed under that name in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, but the proportions were not new: Martini and Martinez recipes of the late nineteenth century often used as much vermouth as gin, or more. Over the following decades the gin share kept climbing until the dry Martini became almost neat spirit, which is why the even split now reads as a revival. Bartenders of the classic-cocktail revival brought it back as the 50/50 Martini, often with orange bitters, as a lighter and more aromatic drink.

name: Tuxedo No. 2
description: Gin and dry vermouth with maraschino, absinthe and orange bitters. The Tuxedo with everything turned up.
funFact: It is named for the Tuxedo Club in New York, which also gave the dinner jacket its American name — the club came first and both borrowed from it.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.
recipe.garnish: A lemon twist and a cherry

originStory: The Tuxedo takes its name from the Tuxedo Club at Tuxedo Park, the private enclave founded by New York society in the 1880s, where the drink is said to have first been mixed; the same club is credited with giving the tailless dinner jacket its American name. A close relative of the early Martini, it was built on gin and dry vermouth seasoned with a few dashes of liqueur and bitters. As bar books multiplied, so did Tuxedo recipes, and later guides numbered them to tell the versions apart. Who first mixed it at the club is not recorded.

name: Reverse Manhattan
description: The Manhattan with its proportions turned around — two of vermouth to one of rye. Lighter, and a longer evening for it.
funFact: Reversing a spirit-forward drink is a modern habit with an old justification: vermouth in 1890 was a fresher, better product than most of what was sold in the century after.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Reverse Manhattan flips the classic's proportions so that sweet vermouth is the base and rye the accent, the same move as the Reverse Martini, and no individual is credited with the first one.

name: Sherry Julep
description: Sherry, sugar and mint churned through crushed ice. The gentlest drink in the julep family by a distance.
funFact: Juleps were made on whatever the bar had — cognac, peach brandy, rum, gin and sherry all appear in the nineteenth-century books, and bourbon is the latecomer.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in a julep tin.
Add the sherry and pack with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the tin frosts over.
Cap with more ice and crown with mint.

originStory: The Sherry Julep applies the nineteenth-century American julep of spirit, sugar and mint over crushed ice to sherry, the wine of the fashionable sherry cobbler, and its creator is not recorded.

name: Vermouth Cassis
description: Dry vermouth and blackcurrant liqueur lengthened with soda. The French café order, also known as a Pompier.
funFact: Pompier means fireman, and the drink is named for them — a low-strength order for someone who might be called back to work.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the vermouth and the cassis.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and hang a lemon twist on the rim.

originStory: Vermouth Cassis, dry French vermouth with crème de cassis and a splash of soda, is a French café aperitif also known as a Pompier, French for fireman, a nickname whose reason is not documented, and it has no recorded creator.

name: Cynar Negroni
description: A Negroni with Cynar in Campari's place. Less bitter orange, more artichoke and earth.
funFact: Cynar is built on artichoke leaves and thirteen other botanicals, and it is noticeably lower in both bitterness and alcohol than Campari — so the same build drinks softer.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Cynar Negroni puts Cynar, the Italian artichoke amaro launched in the years after the Second World War, in Campari's place in the Negroni's equal measures with gin and sweet vermouth, and no creator is recorded for the swap.

name: Dukes Martini
description: Frozen gin poured into a frozen glass over a vermouth rinse. No ice, no stirring, and a two-drink limit.
funFact: The house limit of two is real and enforced. The bar keeps its gin in the freezer, so the drink is never diluted at all — which is exactly why two is the number.

steps: Keep the gin in the freezer and the glass in the freezer with it.
Splash a little vermouth around the frozen glass and tip out what does not cling.
Pour the frozen gin straight in. Add no ice and do not stir.
Cut a strip of lemon peel over the surface at the table and drop it in.
recipe.garnish: A lemon peel, cut at the table

originStory: Dukes Bar, in a hotel tucked into St James's in London, built its reputation on a Martini served without ice: gin and glasses kept in the freezer, the glass rinsed with vermouth and the gin poured in at the table. Salvatore Calabrese, who ran the bar in the 1980s, is credited with making the frozen style its signature, and his successors kept it. The bar's lore holds that Ian Fleming drank there and that it shaped Bond's taste in Martinis. Because the undiluted drink is so strong, staff decline to serve any guest more than two.

name: Connaught Martini
description: Stirred at the table from a trolley, with a choice of five bitters and a strip of Amalfi lemon.
funFact: The trolley is the drink. It is wheeled over, the bitters are chosen in front of you, and the whole thing is stirred and poured at the table rather than at the bar.

steps: Chill the glass thoroughly before the trolley arrives.
Stir the gin and vermouth with ice until very cold.
Strain into the chilled glass and add the chosen bitters on top.
Cut a wide strip of Amalfi lemon peel over the surface and discard it.
recipe.garnish: A lemon peel, expressed and discarded

originStory: The Connaught Martini belongs to the Connaught Bar in Mayfair, which opened in its present form in 2008 inside the Connaught hotel, in a room designed by David Collins. Under Agostino Perrone the bar turned the Martini into table-side theatre: a trolley is wheeled to the guest, the spirit is chosen, a selection of the bar's own bitters is offered, and the drink is stirred and poured in front of the guest. The ritual has become the bar's signature and one of the most recognisable Martini services in London.

name: Havana Cocktail
description: Apricot brandy, Swedish punsch and gin with lemon. A Savoy drink named for a city it has nothing to do with.
funFact: Savoy drinks named for places are usually named for the guest who ordered them or the ship they arrived on, which is why so few of them taste like anywhere.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Havana Cocktail is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, the collection compiled at the American Bar of the Savoy hotel in London. Despite its name it contains no rum: apricot brandy and gin are joined by Swedish punsch, a Scandinavian liqueur built on Batavia arrack that was a common bar ingredient between the wars. Craddock did not explain the name, and many Savoy drinks were named after people, places or events now forgotten. Punsch's later disappearance from English-speaking bars left the drink obscure for decades.

name: Thistle
description: Scotch and sweet vermouth with Angostura. A Rob Roy by another name, and the older one.
funFact: The thistle became Scotland's emblem from a legend about barefoot Norse raiders standing on one and giving away a night attack with the noise.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Thistle is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and it is effectively the same drink as the Rob Roy, which was created at the Waldorf Hotel in New York in 1894 and named after an operetta. The Thistle takes its name from Scotland's national emblem, which legend links to Norse raiders who are said to have given away a night attack by crying out after stepping barefoot on thistles. Its creator is not recorded.

name: Flying Scotsman
description: Scotch, sweet vermouth, sugar and bitters. Named for the train, and sweeter than a Rob Roy.
funFact: The Flying Scotsman ran London to Edinburgh from 1862 and in 1934 became the first locomotive officially recorded at a hundred miles an hour.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: Harry Craddock printed this drink in The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as the Flying Scotchman, a sweetened Scotch and vermouth cocktail named after the famous express train between London King's Cross and Edinburgh. The service had been running since the 1860s, and the locomotive given the same name became a national celebrity: in 1934 it was the first steam locomotive officially recorded at one hundred miles an hour. The drink is a sweeter relation of the Rob Roy, and its creator is not recorded.

name: Pineapple Fizz
description: Rum, pineapple and sugar shaken and topped with soda. One of the Savoy's plainest and best fizzes.
funFact: Pineapple was still expensive enough in 1930 to signal something — English country houses had rented single fruits as table centrepieces within living memory.

steps: Shake the rum, pineapple juice and syrup hard with ice.
Strain into a tall glass over fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge.

originStory: The Pineapple Fizz appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, one of the simplest fizzes in the book: rum, pineapple and sugar shaken and lengthened with soda. The fizz family itself is American, taking shape in the later nineteenth century as sours lengthened with soda water. Pineapple had long been a status symbol in Britain, and in the eighteenth century the fruit was so rare and costly that it was sometimes hired rather than bought, to decorate a dinner table. The drink's creator is not recorded.

name: Carroll Gardens
description: Rye with Punt e Mes, an Italian amaro and a touch of maraschino. The richest of the Brooklyn variations.
funFact: The Brooklyn variations all replace the original's Amer Picon, which stopped being imported to America in the 1970s and sent a generation of bartenders looking for substitutes.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Carroll Gardens is credited to Joaquín Simó, who created it at Death & Co in New York in 2008, one of the drinks named after Brooklyn neighbourhoods that followed the Red Hook from Milk & Honey. It pairs rye with Punt e Mes, Amaro Nardini and a touch of maraschino, an Italian accent on the old Brooklyn formula. Like the rest of the series it works around the original Brooklyn's Amer Picon, a French bitter aperitif that is not sold in the United States.

name: Cobble Hill
description: Rye, dry vermouth and Amaro Montenegro with muddled cucumber. The only Brooklyn variation that tastes green.
funFact: Cucumber in a stirred whiskey drink was a genuinely odd idea in 2007, and it is the reason this one still gets made when the others have faded.

steps: Press the cucumber gently in the bottom of a mixing glass.
Add the rye, vermouth and amaro with ice and stir until cold.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe so no cucumber comes through.
Float a thin cucumber slice on top.

originStory: The Cobble Hill was created by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey in New York, one of the run of Brooklyn-cocktail variations named after Brooklyn neighbourhoods that began at the same bar with the Red Hook. Ross, the Australian-born bartender also known for the Penicillin and the Paper Plane, built it on rye with dry vermouth, the floral Amaro Montenegro and muddled cucumber, which gives it a cool, green note none of the other variations share.

name: Bushwick
description: Rye, sweet vermouth, Amer Picon and maraschino. The closest of the variations to the Brooklyn it descends from.
funFact: Amer Picon has not been sold in America since the 1970s, so every bar making this either has a smuggled bottle or a house substitute, and they will tell you which.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Bushwick is usually credited to Phil Ward at Death & Co in New York, one of the drinks that bartenders there named after Brooklyn neighbourhoods in the 2000s, and it stays closest to the drink they all descend from. The original Brooklyn, a pre-Prohibition mix of rye, vermouth, maraschino and Amer Picon, faded because the French bitter is not sold in the United States. Bars making the Bushwick track down a bottle of Picon, use a house-made version or substitute an amaro.

name: La Última Palabra
description: The Last Word rebuilt on mezcal. Same equal quarters, and the smoke changes everything about it.
funFact: The Last Word's equal-parts structure is unusually forgiving of a base swap, which is why it has produced more successful variations than almost any other classic.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: La Última Palabra, Spanish for the last word, rebuilds the equal-parts Last Word of gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino and lime on mezcal instead of gin, and no single bartender is credited with naming it.

name: Coffee Grog
description: Hot coffee with rum, butter and spice, and a flamed orange peel dropped in at the end.
funFact: Don the Beachcomber built a batter of butter, brown sugar and spice and kept it behind the bar by the tub, so the drink was a scoop and a pour rather than a build.

steps: Mash the butter with the sugar and spices into a paste.
Drop a spoonful into a warmed mug and pour the hot coffee over it, stirring until it melts.
Add the rum and stir once more.
Hold a strip of orange peel over a flame, squeeze it so the oils catch, and drop it in.

originStory: The Coffee Grog, hot coffee with rum, a spiced butter batter and a flamed citrus peel, is a hot drink in the tiki style, and the bar that first served it is not reliably recorded.

name: Sonic
description: Whisky with half soda and half tonic. Named for the two mixers rather than anything faster.
funFact: Splitting the mixer halves the tonic's sweetness while keeping its bitterness, which is the whole reason a Japanese bar reaches for two bottles instead of one.

steps: Fill a tall glass with a single long ice spear, or with hard clear cubes.
Add the whisky and stir once to chill it.
Pour the soda and tonic together down a barspoon.
Lift once from the bottom and serve without garnish.

originStory: The Sonic is a Japanese bar term joining soda and tonic, for a whisky or shochu highball lengthened with an even mix of soda water and tonic water, and no bar or bartender is credited with coining it.

name: Pomada
description: Menorcan gin and cloudy lemonade. The drink of the island's summer fiestas, poured by the jug.
funFact: Menorcan gin is distilled from wine rather than grain, a habit left behind by the British navy during its eighteenth-century occupation of the island.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the gin.
Top with cloudy lemonade.
Stir once. At a fiesta it is mixed by the jug and poured from horseback height.

originStory: Pomada is the drink of Menorca's summer fiestas, gin from Mahón mixed with cloudy lemonade, and its roots go back to the island's British occupation in the eighteenth century, when Royal Navy sailors created a demand for gin and local distillers began to make it. Menorcan gin, distilled from wine alcohol with juniper, has its own protected geographical indication as Gin de Mahón. In Ciutadella the mix is called gin amb llimonada, while elsewhere on the island it is pomada, a name that comes from the Xoriguer distillery's own bottled version.

name: Agua de Sevilla
description: Cava with brandy, triple sec and pineapple under a cap of whipped cream. Seville drinks it in the heat.
funFact: It is a bar drink rather than a home one, and the whipped cream is not optional — served without it, in Seville, it is simply a different order.

steps: Shake the brandy, triple sec and pineapple juice with ice.
Strain into a large wine glass over fresh ice.
Top with cold cava and stir once, gently.
Cap with whipped cream and dust with cinnamon.

originStory: Agua de Sevilla is a Seville bar drink of cava enriched with brandy, orange liqueur and pineapple under whipped cream, a local summer speciality whose creator and date are not recorded.

name: Zurracapote
description: Red wine macerated for days with peaches, cinnamon and lemon. Rioja's fiesta punch, and not a sangría.
funFact: The difference from sangría is time: sangría is mixed and drunk the same day, and zurracapote is left to macerate for two or three before anyone touches it.

steps: Combine everything in a large jar or bucket and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Cover and leave somewhere cool for two to three days.
Taste and add sugar only if the fruit has not done enough.
Strain or serve with the fruit, over ice, in tumblers.
recipe.garnish: A slice of the macerated peach

originStory: Zurracapote is a fiesta wine punch of La Rioja, red wine or clarete left to macerate with peaches, lemon, sugar and cinnamon, made by local festival clubs there and in neighbouring regions as far as Cuenca, and its beginnings are not documented.

name: Sangría Blanca
description: White wine with peach, citrus and brandy over ice. Sangría without the tannin, and easier in the heat.
funFact: White sangría is the version served across most of northern Spain, where the local wine is white and using a Rioja red for punch would be an odd thing to do.

steps: Combine the wine, brandy, triple sec and fruit in a jug.
Chill for at least four hours so the fruit gives up its flavour.
Add ice and top with soda water just before serving.
Pour into tumblers, making sure everyone gets fruit.

originStory: Sangría Blanca is the white-wine version of sangría, the Spanish wine punch named from sangre, blood, for the colour of the red original, made lighter with dry white wine, peach, citrus and brandy, and it has no recorded creator.

name: Kir Breton
description: Cider with blackcurrant liqueur. The Kir made with what Brittany actually grows.
funFact: The original Kir uses Burgundy's aligoté, and every French region has since made the same drink from whatever it presses — cider in Brittany, and it is the better version.

steps: Pour the cassis into the bottom of a wine glass.
Add the cold cider slowly so it does not foam over.
Do not stir — the pour combines it.
Serve without ice.

originStory: The Kir Breton is Brittany's version of the Kir, the Burgundian aperitif of white wine and crème de cassis named after Félix Kir, the post-war mayor of Dijon, made instead with the region's dry cider.

name: Trou Normand
description: A shot of calvados taken between courses, on the theory that it makes room for the rest of the meal.
funFact: Trou normand means the Norman hole, and the modern restaurant version replaces the neat shot with apple sorbet drowned in calvados.

steps: Pour a small measure of calvados.
Drink it in one, between courses, standing if the table is that sort of table.
For the modern version, put a scoop of apple sorbet in a glass and pour the calvados over it.
Either way, return to the meal immediately.

originStory: The trou normand, the Norman hole, is the Normandy custom of taking a small glass of calvados partway through a long meal, on the old belief that it makes room for the courses still to come, a regional habit with no inventor that restaurants now often serve as apple sorbet doused in calvados.

name: Bacardi Cocktail
description: Rum, lime and grenadine. A Daiquiri with grenadine, and the only cocktail a court has ruled on the recipe of.
funFact: In 1936 the New York Supreme Court held that a Bacardi Cocktail must be made with Bacardi rum, which remains the only time a court has specified a cocktail's brand.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: Bacardí, the rum house Facundo Bacardí Massó founded in Santiago de Cuba, made its name with a lighter, filtered rum, and the cocktail named after it began as a Daiquiri of Bacardí, lime and sugar. The red version, coloured with grenadine, grew up in American bars. Its popularity led to a legal fight, and after the repeal of Prohibition the New York Supreme Court ruled that a drink sold as a Bacardi Cocktail had to be made with Bacardí rum, a rare case of a court tying a cocktail to a brand.

name: New York Sour
description: A whiskey sour with a float of red wine sitting on top of it. The two layers are meant to be drunk together.
funFact: It is generally traced to 1880s Chicago rather than New York, and was called a Continental Sour and a Claret Snap before the name that stuck.

steps: Shake the whiskey, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a rocks glass over one large cube.
Pour the red wine slowly over the back of a barspoon so it sits on the surface.
Serve without stirring — the layers combine as you drink.

originStory: Despite its name, the New York Sour is usually traced by drinks historians to Chicago in the 1880s, where a bartender is said to have finished a whiskey sour with a float of claret, and it circulated under other names, among them the Continental Sour, before settling on New York. The red wine is poured gently over the back of a spoon so that it sits as a separate layer, and the two parts are meant to be tasted together. The original bartender's name is not recorded. It is now an International Bartenders Association official cocktail.

name: Spicy Fifty
description: Vodka with elderflower, honey and lime, and a slice of red chilli shaken through it.
funFact: Salvatore Calabrese built it at Fifty St James in London, and it is one of very few modern drinks the IBA has taken into its official list.

steps: Put the chilli slices in the shaker and press them once — no more.
Add everything else with ice and shake hard.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe so no chilli comes through.
Float a single thin slice of chilli on the surface.

originStory: Salvatore Calabrese, the Italian bartender long based in London, created the Spicy Fifty around 2005 as the signature drink of Fifty, a members' club in St James's that opened that February. It drew on the chilli-heavy cooking of the chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten, and the name joins the club's with the kick of fresh red chilli. Vanilla vodka, elderflower, honey and lime make up the rest of the drink. In 2020 the International Bartenders Association added it to its list of official cocktails in the New Era category.

name: Špricer
description: White wine and sparkling water, half and half. Slovenia's everyday drink, and ordering it is not a compromise.
funFact: It is poured at weddings, on building sites and in wine bars without any change in status — the same glass, the same ratio, no apology for diluting good wine.

steps: Pour the wine into a plain tumbler.
Add an equal measure of cold sparkling water.
Ice is optional and often left out entirely.
Serve immediately, while it still has its bubble.

originStory: The špricer is Slovenia's everyday mix of white wine and sparkling water, the same drink as the Austrian Gespritzter, the Hungarian fröccs and the Croatian gemišt, with a name from the German spritzen, to spray, and no recorded inventor.

name: Southside Fizz
description: The Southside lengthened with soda. Gin, lime and mint, made long.
funFact: The 21 Club and Chicago's South Side both claim it, and the Prohibition story that the rougher South Side gin needed mint to hide it is almost certainly invented.

steps: Shake the gin, lime, syrup and mint hard with ice.
Double-strain into a tall glass over fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Crown with a mint sprig.

originStory: The Southside Fizz is the long version of the Southside, the gin, citrus, sugar and mint sour whose origin is disputed. One story links it to the Southside Sportsmen's Club on Long Island, another to Chicago's South Side, where Prohibition gangs are said to have needed mint and sugar to make rough gin palatable, a tale often dismissed as legend. New York's 21 Club made the Southside one of its house drinks and serves it with a splash of soda, which effectively makes it a fizz.

name: Army and Navy
description: Gin, lemon and orgeat. The almond does all the work that sugar would otherwise do.
funFact: Orgeat is an almond syrup thinned with orange flower water, and it brings texture as well as sweetness — which is why the drink tastes fuller than three ingredients should.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Army and Navy, gin with lemon and orgeat, was in print by 1948, when David Embury included it in The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks. The name is often linked with the Army and Navy Club in Washington or with the annual Army-Navy football game, but neither connection has been documented, and no creator is recorded. Orgeat, an almond syrup traditionally scented with orange flower water, does the work that plain sugar would in most sours and adds body as well as sweetness, which gives the drink its fuller texture.

name: Honeysuckle
description: Rum, lime and honey. A Daiquiri with honey instead of sugar, and rounder for it.
funFact: Honey will not dissolve in a cold drink and has to be loosened with warm water first — the step every recipe assumes and no recipe prints.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Honeysuckle is the Daiquiri of rum and lime made with honey in place of sugar, a close relative of the gin-based Bee's Knees, and no creator is recorded for it.

name: Petite Fleur
description: Rum, Cointreau and grapefruit in equal parts. Small, sharp and almost forgotten.
funFact: Equal-parts drinks were the house style of the 1930s because they were easy to teach and easy to pour fast, not because anyone thought thirds were ideal.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

originStory: The Petite Fleur, French for little flower, is an equal-parts mix of white rum, Cointreau and grapefruit juice in the old house style of equal measures, and no creator or date is recorded for it.

name: Ideal Cocktail
description: Gin and dry vermouth with grapefruit and maraschino. A Martini with fruit in it, which is less alarming than it sounds.
funFact: Grapefruit was a novelty ingredient in 1930s London — commercial cultivation had barely started, and it appears in the Savoy far more often than in any book before it.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Ideal Cocktail is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, one of the early Martini variations that added fruit and a touch of liqueur to gin and vermouth. Here a spoonful of grapefruit juice and a few dashes of maraschino make the drink brighter and slightly bitter. Who named it the Ideal, and why, is not recorded, and it is rarely seen today outside classic-cocktail bars.

name: Marmalade Cocktail
description: Gin shaken with a spoonful of orange marmalade and lemon. The bitterness of the peel is the whole point.
funFact: Craddock recommends it before lunch specifically, on the grounds that the bitterness in the peel is an appetiser rather than a flavour.

steps: Stir the marmalade into the gin in the shaker until it starts to break up.
