Add the lemon juice and ice and shake hard for 15 seconds.
Double-strain to catch the shreds of peel.
Garnish with a strip of orange peel.

originStory: The Marmalade Cocktail appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, written as a recipe for a party of six: gin, lemon juice and a couple of spoonfuls of orange marmalade shaken together. Craddock noted that its bittersweet taste made it especially suitable as an aperitif before lunch. Marmalade, made from bitter Seville oranges, was a fixture of the British breakfast table, and the idea of shaking it into a gin drink returned decades later in Salvatore Calabrese's Breakfast Martini.

name: Shamrock
description: Irish whiskey with dry vermouth, green Chartreuse and crème de menthe. Green, herbal and stronger than it looks.
funFact: Green Chartreuse and crème de menthe in the same glass is a lot of mint, which is why the measures are so small and why the drink survives at all.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Shamrock appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, an Irish whiskey and dry vermouth drink tinted green with small amounts of green Chartreuse and crème de menthe, and named for the three-leafed plant that is Ireland's emblem and the symbol of St Patrick. It comes from a period when Irish whiskey was still widely poured in British and American bars, before the industry's long decline in the twentieth century. Its creator is not recorded, and it is most often made today around St Patrick's Day.

name: Blarney Stone
description: Irish whiskey with absinthe, curaçao and maraschino. The Savoy's most crowded Irish drink.
funFact: Kissing the Blarney Stone at Cork's Castle Blarney is supposed to grant eloquence, which is a reasonable claim to make about this much whiskey too.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.
recipe.garnish: An orange twist and an olive

originStory: The Blarney Stone, Irish whiskey seasoned with absinthe, curaçao and maraschino, is an old-style Irish whiskey cocktail named after the stone at Blarney Castle near Cork that visitors kiss for the gift of eloquence, and its creator is not recorded.

name: Habushu
description: Okinawan awamori with a habu pit viper coiled in the bottle, usually sweetened with honey and steeped with herbs. The snake is the point: it is left in the flask for months, and the spirit takes on a faintly savoury, medicinal weight the base rice spirit does not have on its own.
funFact: Producers chill the snake until it is torpid, then lower it into the flask — where the alcohol fixes it mid-strike. The open jaws in a display bottle are set by the ethanol, not by taxidermy.

serve.how: Poured neat at room temperature in very small measures, usually as a tonic at the end of a meal rather than a drink you sit with. Honey-sweetened bottlings are the gentler introduction.

composition.summary: Long-grain rice awamori infused with a whole habu viper, honey and herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Awamori distilled from Thai indica rice with black koji

components.label: Infusion
components.detail: One whole habu pit viper, steeped for months

components.label: Sweetening
components.detail: Honey and up to a dozen herbs in most commercial bottlings

composition.process: The viper is steeped whole rather than for flavour extraction alone — the practice is tonic and totemic as much as culinary, and Okinawan makers sell it on longevity rather than taste.

originStory: Habushu is an Okinawan liqueur of awamori, the rice spirit of the Ryukyu Islands, steeped with a habu pit viper and usually sweetened with honey and herbs, and when the practice began on Okinawa is not documented.

name: Sodabi
description: Benin's palm-wine distillate, made by fermenting the sap of the oil palm and running it through simple pot stills. It is the spirit poured on the ground in Vodun ceremony before anyone drinks, which makes it ritual equipment as much as a drink.
funFact: It carries the name of Bonaventure Kpodji Sodabi, a Beninese soldier who learned distilling in France during the First World War and brought the method home around 1919.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature, in small measures, and traditionally with a first splash poured to the ground for the ancestors before the glass reaches a mouth.

composition.summary: Fermented oil-palm sap, pot distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap tapped from the oil palm, fermented into palm wine

components.label: Fermentation
components.detail: Wild yeasts, one to three days in the heat

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot stills, frequently improvised

composition.process: Sap ferments within hours of tapping, so distillation happens close to the tree. Strength varies widely between producers because almost none of it is standardised.

originStory: Sodabi is Benin's palm-wine spirit, and the most widely cited account of its name credits the Sodabi brothers of Allada, two Beninese men who learned to distil while serving in French colonial regiments in the First World War. After returning home in 1918 they tried fermented bananas and pineapples before settling on palm wine, and the method spread through Benin and Togo in the 1930s despite a colonial ban. A popular story that an Englishman exclaimed so that be on tasting it is generally dismissed.

name: Klekovača
description: Plum rakija redistilled over juniper berries, the Balkan answer to the question of what happens when a fruit brandy meets a gin botanical. The juniper does not mask the plum so much as sit alongside it, resinous and cold.
funFact: The name comes from kleka, the local word for juniper — and it is shared with a mountain in western Bosnia, which is why bottles and maps sometimes confuse people.

serve.how: Room temperature or barely cool, never iced, in a small tulip glass before a meal. Chilling it hard flattens the juniper, which is the entire reason the drink exists.

composition.summary: Šljivovica redistilled with juniper berries.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plum rakija, usually from Požegača plums

components.label: Botanical
components.detail: Wild juniper berries, macerated then redistilled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often rested in glass demijohns rather than wood

composition.process: Redistilling rather than simply macerating keeps it clear and stops the juniper turning bitter, which is what separates it from the many home infusions that share the name.

originStory: Klekovača is a western Balkan plum brandy distilled or redistilled with juniper berries, named from kleka, a local word for juniper, and it comes from a rural tradition with no single recorded origin.

name: Chinguirito
description: Mexico's contraband cane spirit, distilled from raw sugarcane juice or piloncillo on the Veracruz coast. For most of its history it was defined less by how it was made than by the fact that making it was a crime.
funFact: The Spanish Crown banned it in 1631 to protect brandy shipped from Spain, and the ban held for 165 years. When the Crown finally legalised it in 1796 it promptly taxed it to pay for coastal fortifications.

serve.how: Neat in a small tumbler, or lengthened with lime and soda in the coastal style. The modern artisanal bottlings reward drinking it the way you would a rhum agricole blanc.

composition.summary: Fresh sugarcane juice or piloncillo, fermented and pot distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pressed cane juice, or piloncillo dissolved in water

components.label: Fermentation
components.detail: Open vats with wild yeast

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or clay pot stills

composition.process: Because it was illegal for so long the method was never standardised, and the surviving recipes are regional rather than national. Small Veracruz producers have revived it since the 2010s.

originStory: Chinguirito is the cane spirit of colonial New Spain, distilled from sugarcane juice, molasses or piloncillo, and its history is largely a history of prohibition. The Spanish Crown banned cane spirit in its American colonies for much of the colonial period to protect sales of brandy shipped from Spain, and chinguirito was made in secret along the Gulf coast around Veracruz and elsewhere. The Crown finally legalised it, and began taxing it, at the end of the eighteenth century. The origin of the name has not been documented.

name: Chuchuhuasi
description: Amazonian bark macerated in cane aguardiente, usually cut with honey. It is sold by the jar in the markets of Iquitos and Pucallpa, closer to a household remedy than a bar bottle, and it tastes like one.
funFact: The bark comes from Maytenus laevis, a rainforest tree whose name in Quechua means roughly trembling back — a reference to the rheumatism it was long steeped to treat.

serve.how: A small measure at room temperature after eating, taken as a digestif. Market versions are steeped for weeks and vary enormously between sellers.

composition.summary: Maytenus laevis bark steeped in cane aguardiente with honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cane aguardiente from the Peruvian Amazon

components.label: Botanical
components.detail: Chuchuhuasi bark, steeped for weeks to months

components.label: Sweetening
components.detail: Wild honey, sometimes with cinnamon or clove

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation, so nothing is stripped out — the tannin from the bark is what gives it the dry, drying grip on the finish.

originStory: Chuchuhuasi is the bark of an Amazonian tree and, in Peru, the drink made by steeping that bark in cane aguardiente with honey, sold in Amazon cities such as Iquitos, and no date or originator is recorded.

name: Yaa Dong
description: Thailand's roadside macerations — roots, bark and herbs steeped in lao khao rice spirit and sold by the shot from big glass jars. There is no single recipe; every stall keeps its own, and the jar you are pointed at depends on what you say is wrong with you.
funFact: The name means roughly preserved medicine, and it is sold as one — stalls organise their jars by complaint rather than by flavour, which is why a chaser is usually handed over with the glass.

serve.how: One small shot at room temperature, taken quickly, with a chaser of soda or a slice of fruit. It is a street-stall drink rather than a sipping spirit, and it is not built to be lingered over.

composition.summary: Roots, bark and herbs macerated in lao khao rice spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Lao khao, unaged Thai rice spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Dozens of roots, barks and dried herbs, varying by stall

components.label: Sweetening
components.detail: Palm sugar or honey in many recipes

composition.process: Maceration for weeks in glass jars, topped up rather than emptied, so a long-running jar is never quite the same drink twice.

originStory: Yaa dong, roughly steeped medicine in Thai, is the roadside custom of steeping roots, bark and herbs in lao khao rice spirit in big glass jars, each vendor keeping its own blend, with no recorded beginning.

name: Pox
description: The Maya ceremonial spirit of the Chiapas highlands, distilled from maize, sugarcane and wheat bran. It is still poured in Tzotzil ritual, and the bottles that reach bars outside Mexico are a recent and slightly awkward second life for it.
funFact: Pox means medicine in Tzotzil, and it is pronounced posh. It is still used in ceremonies at the church of San Juan Chamula, where it sits alongside candles and copal rather than behind a bar.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature in a small cup. It is softer and sweeter than mezcal and does not need the ceremony of salt or citrus that agave spirits attract.

composition.summary: Maize, sugarcane and wheat bran, fermented together and pot distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cracked maize with piloncillo or cane juice

components.label: Adjunct
components.detail: Wheat bran, which drives the bread-dough note

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or clay pot stills in highland Chiapas

composition.process: The maize is the ritual ingredient and the cane is the fermentable — which is why it reads sweet rather than starchy, and why it sits closer to a light rum than to a corn whiskey.

originStory: Pox, pronounced posh, is the ceremonial spirit of the Maya communities of the Chiapas highlands, distilled from maize and sugarcane and offered in churches such as San Juan Chamula's, and when distilling began there is not documented.

name: Ruby Port
description: The youngest and brightest of the Port family, bottled early to preserve its deep red color and primary fruit. An approachable gateway into fortified territory.
funFact: Port is fortified mid-fermentation with 77% grape spirit, which stuns the yeast and locks in the wine's natural sweetness.

serve.how: Serve slightly cooler than room temperature in a port glass, pouring around three ounces — its 20% strength makes a little go a long way. No decanting required for this young style; just swirl and enjoy the deep purple color with its rush of plum, raspberry, and chocolate. It is the friendliest entry into Port, so keep it simple and pair it with dessert.

composition.summary: Douro field blend of Touriga Nacional and friends, fortified young and bottled early.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão

components.label: Region
components.detail: Terraced schist slopes of the Douro Valley, Portugal

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified mid-fermentation with 77% grape spirit, halting the yeast

components.label: Aging
components.detail: A short rest in large vats; bottled young to keep fruit

composition.process: Spirit goes in while sugar remains, stunning the yeast and locking bright primary fruit into the wine.

originStory: Port took shape in the seventeenth century, when English merchants shipping wine from Portugal's Douro valley found that adding grape brandy kept it sound on the voyage, and in 1756 the Marquis of Pombal made the Douro one of the first legally demarcated wine regions in the world. Fortification happens during fermentation: grape spirit of about 77 per cent is added to stop the yeast and keep the wine's natural sugar. Ruby is the youngest and simplest expression of the style, aged only a few years in large vats so that it keeps its colour and fresh fruit.

name: Tawny Port
description: Port that traded youthful fruit for decades in wooden casks, slowly fading to amber and gaining nut and caramel powers. Serve slightly chilled for maximum effect.
funFact: The age statement on a tawny Port — 10, 20, 30, or 40 years — refers to the average age of the blend, not the youngest wine in the bottle.

serve.how: This is the Port that genuinely wants a chill — half an hour in the fridge sharpens its caramel and hazelnut beautifully. Pour three ounces into a port glass, swirl, and watch for the amber rim that decades in cask have painted. Sip slowly and notice how dried fig and orange peel emerge as it warms in your hand; an open bottle keeps for a month or more.

composition.summary: Same Douro red varieties as any Port, but aged to amber in wooden casks.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz and other Douro reds

components.label: Region
components.detail: Douro Valley fruit, traditionally aged in Vila Nova de Gaia lodges

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified mid-fermentation, then handed over to oxygen

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Years to decades in seasoned oak pipes; blends carry age statements

composition.process: Slow oxidative aging in small wooden pipes fades the color and trades fruit for walnut and caramel.

originStory: Tawny Port is the Douro's long-aged style, the same fortified wine as ruby but left for years in small oak casks, where slow oxidation fades the colour from red to amber and brings out nutty, caramel flavours. The Douro was demarcated in 1756, among the first wine regions to be legally defined, and its shippers, many of them British houses with Portuguese lodges in Vila Nova de Gaia, blended aged tawnies as their house styles. Indicated-age tawnies, labelled 10, 20, 30 or 40 years old, describe the average character of the blend rather than the age of its youngest wine.

name: Vintage Port
description: The final boss of fortified wine, made only from a single declared harvest and built to outlive its buyers. Requires decanting, patience, and ideally an heir.
funFact: Vintage Port is made only in exceptional years 'declared' by each house — roughly three per decade — and spends just two years in barrel before decades of bottle aging.

serve.how: Stand the bottle upright for a day, then decant carefully off its heavy sediment an hour or two before serving — this ritual is mandatory, not optional. Serve at cellar temperature in port glasses and give it time; the cassis, violet, and dark chocolate unfurl slowly with air. Traditionally the decanter passes to the left around the table, and a mature bottle deserves an unhurried evening.

composition.summary: A single declared Douro harvest of Touriga Nacional and its blending partners.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Touriga Nacional at the core, with Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz

components.label: Region
components.detail: The best quintas of the Douro Valley, one harvest only

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Foot-trodden in lagares by many houses, then fortified mid-ferment

components.label: Aging
components.detail: About two years in wood, then decades in bottle

composition.process: A house declares the vintage only in exceptional years, bottling unfiltered so the wine keeps evolving for generations.

originStory: Vintage Port is the Douro's single-harvest wine, made only in years that a house judges exceptional and formally declares, which historically has happened only a few times a decade. After about two years in cask it is bottled unfiltered to age for decades in glass, throwing a heavy sediment that makes decanting necessary. The style depends on bottles that can be laid on their side, and it developed in the eighteenth century as shippers began to bottle and cellar their best years, a practice that built the reputation of port's old British houses.

name: Amontillado Sherry
description: A sherry with two lives: it begins under protective flor like a fino, then loses its yeast shield and ages exposed to air. The result is amber, nutty, and quietly complex.
funFact: Edgar Allan Poe made this style infamous in his 1846 tale 'The Cask of Amontillado,' in which a wine lover is lured to his doom by the promise of a taste.

serve.how: Serve cool but not cold in a copita — the narrow tulip concentrates the hazelnut and orange-peel aromatics. Pour small (two to three ounces), swirl, and sip slowly; an open bottle keeps for weeks in the fridge, so there's no rush. Notice the two lives in one glass: fino's saline snap up front, oxidative nut and tobacco depth behind.

composition.summary: Palomino from Jerez, aged first under flor yeast and then exposed to air.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino Fino, grown on the chalk albariza soils of Jerez

components.label: Region
components.detail: The sherry triangle: Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María, Sanlúcar

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Biological aging under flor, then refortified so the yeast dies

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Years in a solera, first protected, then oxidative

composition.process: Refortifying kills the flor blanket mid-life, handing the wine over to oxygen for its second, nuttier existence.

originStory: Amontillado takes its name from Montilla, the town south of Córdoba whose wines it was originally meant to resemble: amontillado means in the style of Montilla. In the bodegas of Jerez it describes a sherry that begins under flor, the protective yeast that shapes fino, and then, once the flor dies away or is ended with further fortification, continues to age in contact with air, gaining colour and nutty depth. The style was well established by the nineteenth century, when Edgar Allan Poe made a cask of it the bait in his tale The Cask of Amontillado.

name: Cream Sherry
description: An oloroso sweetened into plush, toffee-toned comfort, long the gateway sherry of grandmotherly sideboards. Modern bartenders have quietly rediscovered its charms over ice.
funFact: The style was created for the British market, and the term 'cream' was popularized in Bristol as a plusher successor to the older blend known as 'Bristol Milk.'

serve.temp: 55-60°F lightly chilled, or over one large cube
serve.how: Serve it slightly chilled in a copita after dinner, or take the modern bartender's route: a big ice cube in a rocks glass with an orange twist. The chill and slight dilution wake up the toffee and walnut notes and trim the sweetness. Sip slowly and let it warm in your hand; raisin and brown sugar keep unfolding.

composition.summary: Oxidative Palomino oloroso, sweetened with Pedro Ximénez, blended for the British market.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino base, sweetened with Pedro Ximénez or Moscatel

components.label: Region
components.detail: Jerez de la Frontera, Andalucía, Spain

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Dry oloroso blended with sweet wine after aging, not before

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oxidative solera aging before the sweetening blend goes in

composition.process: Sweetening happens at the end: a fully dry, oxidatively aged oloroso is blended with syrupy PX to order.

originStory: Cream sherry was created in the cellars of John Harvey & Sons in Bristol, a city that had long imported sweet sherry blends known as Bristol Milk. From the 1860s Harvey's sons developed a richer blend sweetened with Pedro Ximénez, and the company's story holds that a visiting lady, offered it after the familiar Bristol Milk, declared that if that was milk, this must be cream. Harveys Bristol Cream became the firm's flagship and, from the late 1920s, a major export to the United States.

name: Fino Sherry
description: Bone-dry sherry raised beneath flor, a living blanket of yeast that guards it from air. Emerges pale, saline, and almond-tinged — the driest creature in the bodega.
funFact: The flor yeast that shapes fino consumes the wine's glycerin and residual sugar as it protects it, which is why fino tastes so strikingly dry and lean.

serve.how: Serve fino cold from the fridge in a copita, treating it like a crisp white wine — and finish the bottle within a few days, as the flor's protection is gone once opened. Pour small measures and keep the bottle on ice at the table. Taste for the bracing, bone-dry salinity: green almond, sea spray, and a sourdough tang that makes it the world's greatest aperitif.

composition.summary: Palomino from the albariza chalk of Jerez, aged entirely beneath a yeast blanket.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino Fino, on the white albariza chalk soils

components.label: Region
components.detail: Jerez de la Frontera and El Puerto de Santa María

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified only to about 15%, low enough for flor to live

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Years in a solera, never touching oxygen, then bottled

composition.process: The living flor blanket seals the wine from air while eating its glycerin and sugar, leaving it lean and saline.

originStory: Fino is the driest and palest style of sherry, and its character comes from flor, a layer of yeast that grows naturally on the surface of young wine in the cool, humid bodegas of the Jerez region. Under flor the wine is shielded from air while the yeast consumes glycerine and residual sugar, leaving it lean, saline and almond-scented. Fino rose to prominence in the nineteenth century as shippers came to value the flor-aged wines, and in the twentieth century Jerez became the first official denominación de origen in Spain.

name: Manzanilla Sherry
description: Fino's coastal cousin, aged only in one seaside town where ocean air keeps its yeast blanket thriving. Drinkers swear they taste salt spray and chamomile in every sip.
funFact: Manzanilla may only be aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where humid Atlantic air keeps the flor yeast alive and vigorous year-round.

serve.how: Pour it well chilled into a copita and drink it fresh — buy small bottles and finish them within days, as its delicate coastal character fades fast once open. Serve as the opening act of a meal with salty snacks in hand. Notice the seaside signature: chamomile and green olive over an almost briny, sea-salt finish.

composition.summary: Palomino aged under flor exclusively in the seaside town of Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino Fino, from the same albariza vineyards as fino

components.label: Region
components.detail: Sanlúcar de Barrameda only, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified low; humid Atlantic air keeps flor thick year-round

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera aging in coastal bodegas built with high, ventilated walls

composition.process: Sanlúcar's damp ocean air feeds a heavier, more persistent flor than inland Jerez, which is why it tastes of salt spray.

originStory: Manzanilla is the fino of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the town at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, and by law it can only be aged there. The town's damp Atlantic air keeps the flor yeast thick and active all year, which gives manzanilla a lighter, more saline character than the finos of Jerez. Its name, which is also the Spanish word for chamomile, has been explained both by the wine's aroma and by the village of Manzanilla in Huelva, and the question has never been settled. It has its own denominación, separate from Jerez.

name: Oloroso Sherry
description: Fortified high from the start so no yeast can shield it, this sherry ages in open combat with oxygen. Decades later it emerges dark, walnut-rich, and structurally imposing.
funFact: Oloroso means 'fragrant' in Spanish; the style is fortified above 17% precisely so that flor yeast cannot survive on its surface.

serve.how: Serve at cool room temperature in a copita — chilling too hard mutes its walnut-and-leather depth. Pour a couple of ounces, swirl generously, and sip it like you would an aged whisky; an open bottle holds for a month or more. Notice the paradox of a dry sherry that smells sweet: all that toffee and dried fruit on the nose resolves into a savory, structured palate.

composition.summary: Palomino fortified high enough to kill flor, then aged openly against oxygen.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino Fino, from the albariza chalk of Jerez

components.label: Region
components.detail: Jerez de la Frontera, Andalucía, Spain

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified above 17% from the start, so flor never forms

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Decades of oxidative solera aging; the wine concentrates as it evaporates

composition.process: Fortifying past 17% at the outset denies flor any chance to grow, committing the wine to a life of oxidation.

originStory: Oloroso, Spanish for scented, is the sherry made to age without flor. In the bodegas of Jerez the cellar master selects fuller-bodied young wines and fortifies them to around 17 per cent or more, too strong for the protective yeast to survive, so the wine ages in contact with air from the start. Over years in the solera, the system of stacked casks that blends older and younger wines, it darkens and gains walnut and dried-fruit depth. Olorosos are naturally dry, and they are the base of sweetened blends such as cream sherry.

name: Palo Cortado Sherry
description: The bodega's happy accident: a wine that set out to become fino but lost its flor and drifted toward oloroso richness. It keeps amontillado's finesse and oloroso's body.
funFact: Its name means 'cut stick,' after the chalk mark cellar masters slash across casks whose flor has unexpectedly died, rerouting the wine to oxidative aging.

serve.how: Serve just cool in a copita and give it a real swirl — this rarity carries amontillado's aromatic finesse on oloroso's rich frame, and both deserve airtime. Pour small, sip slow, and revisit as it warms in the glass. Track the shape-shift from bright citrus peel and sea salt into hazelnut and toffee on the long finish.

composition.summary: Palomino that began as fino, lost its flor unexpectedly, and turned oxidative.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Palomino Fino, selected from the finest albariza parcels

components.label: Region
components.detail: Jerez de la Frontera and El Puerto de Santa María

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Flor dies unbidden; the cask is refortified and rerouted

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Long oxidative solera aging, often decades in the bodega

composition.process: A cellar master chalks a cut mark on the butt whose flor has failed, sending it down the oxidative path.

originStory: Palo cortado is the sherry that does not follow its plan. It begins as a fine young wine destined for fino or amontillado, but for reasons cellar masters have never fully explained, the flor fades and the wine starts to develop more like an oloroso while keeping some of its original finesse. The name, cut stick, comes from the chalk marks used in the bodegas of Jerez: a single vertical stroke, or palo, marks a cask headed for the fino style, and when the wine changes course the cellar master strikes a line across it. True palo cortado is rare.

name: Pedro Ximénez Sherry
description: Grapes sun-dried to near-raisins before pressing yield a black, syrupy elixir of fig and molasses. Less a beverage than a dessert that happens to pour.
funFact: PX can exceed 400 grams of sugar per liter, and in Spain it is famously poured straight over vanilla ice cream.

serve.how: Serve small, slightly cool pours in a copita — an ounce or two is dessert in itself — or go full Spanish and pour it straight over vanilla ice cream. Swirl and watch the black syrup coat the glass in slow legs. Sip in tiny amounts and let fig, molasses, and espresso saturate the palate; a bottle lasts for months in the fridge.

composition.summary: Pedro Ximénez grapes sun-dried to raisins, pressed into black syrup in Andalucía.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Pedro Ximénez, much of it grown in neighbouring Montilla-Moriles

components.label: Region
components.detail: Jerez, with fruit historically dried in Montilla-Moriles

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Grapes sun-dried on esparto mats, pressed, then muted with spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera aging in old butts, deepening to opaque black

composition.process: Spirit is added almost immediately to stop fermentation, preserving nearly all the raisined sugar in the pressed juice.

originStory: Pedro Ximénez is both a grape and the sweetest of sherry's styles. Legend holds that the grape was brought to Andalusia in the sixteenth century by a soldier named Pieter Siemens, returning from the Rhine or the Canary Islands, though the story is unproven. The grapes are laid out to dry in the sun until they are close to raisins, then pressed, and the thick, dark wine can carry well over 400 grams of sugar per litre. Its heartland is Montilla-Moriles, but Jerez bodegas age it in their soleras too, and in Spain it is often poured over vanilla ice cream.

name: Dry Vermouth
description: The pale, herbal French counterpart to Italy's sweet style, crisp with alpine botanicals and citrus. Best known as the whispering partner in a Martini.
funFact: The dry French style was developed around 1813 by Joseph Noilly, whose Noilly Prat remains the benchmark bartenders reach for in a classic Martini.

serve.how: Vermouth is wine, so keep the open bottle in the refrigerator and finish it within a month or two. Pour a small measure into a chilled small wine glass — no ice needed if the bottle is cold — and add a twist of lemon peel, expressing the oils over the surface. Sip it slowly as an aperitif and pick out the chamomile and alpine herbs that usually hide inside your Martini.

composition.summary: Neutral white wine from southern France, fortified and steeped with alpine botanicals.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Neutral whites: Clairette, Piquepoul and Ugni Blanc in the French style

components.label: Region
components.detail: Marseillan and the Lyon region; the French dry tradition

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Wine fortified, then infused with wormwood, chamomile and citrus peel

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Noilly Prat weathers its base wine outdoors in oak for a year

composition.process: Leaving the base wine exposed to sun, wind and sea air oxidizes it before the botanicals ever go in.

originStory: Dry vermouth was born in Lyon in 1813, when the herbalist Joseph Noilly created a pale, dry formula that became the first French vermouth, a counterpart to the sweet red style of Turin. Noilly is said to have modelled it on the way wine changes during long sea voyages, and his son Louis and son-in-law Claudius Prat later moved production to Marseillan on the Mediterranean coast, founding Noilly Prat in 1855. Chambéry's Dolin followed with its own dry and blanc styles, and French dry vermouth became the classic partner for gin in the dry Martini.

name: Sweet Vermouth
description: Wine aromatized with wormwood, spices, and bittersweet botanicals in the Italian style. Equally content stirred into a Negroni or served alone over ice with an orange slice, as Turin intended.
funFact: Modern sweet vermouth was born in Turin in 1786 at the shop of Antonio Benedetto Carpano, and the word 'vermouth' comes from 'Wermut,' German for wormwood.

serve.temp: Chilled bottle, served over one large cube
serve.how: Do it as Turin intended: pour two to three ounces over a large ice cube in a rocks glass and garnish with a fat orange slice or expressed peel. A splash of soda turns it into a proper low-proof aperitivo highball if you like. Sip slowly and trace the bitter orange, clove, and cola notes as the ice slowly opens it up — and keep the bottle in the fridge once opened.

composition.summary: Neutral white wine, fortified and aromatized with wormwood, spices and caramel in Turin.

components.label: Grapes
components.detail: Neutral white base wine; the red color comes from caramel, not grapes

components.label: Region
components.detail: Turin and Piedmont, home of the Italian rosso style

components.label: Vinification
components.detail: Fortified, infused with wormwood and spices, sweetened with sugar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Little or none; house botanical recipes matter more than time

composition.process: Wormwood — Wermut in German, hence the name — is macerated with dozens of spices to build a bittersweet profile.

originStory: Modern vermouth began in Turin in 1786, when Antonio Benedetto Carpano, working in a liquor shop near the royal palace, sold a sweetened wine flavoured with wormwood and other botanicals and called it vermouth, after Wermut, the German for wormwood. It quickly found favour at the Savoy court, and Turin became the capital of the sweet Italian style, home to Martini & Rossi, Cinzano and Carpano's own Antica Formula. Through the nineteenth century Italian vermouth crossed to American bars, where it became essential to the Manhattan and later to the Negroni.

name: Lion's Tail
description: Bourbon soured with lime and sweetened with Jamaican allspice. A London book's American drink, and the reason allspice dram sits behind modern bars.
funFact: "Twisting the lion's tail" was American slang for provoking the British, whose royal arms carry a lion — which is why a drink printed in a London book in 1937 is almost certainly the work of an American bartender that Prohibition had driven across the Atlantic.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lime twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: The Lion's Tail is printed in the Café Royal Cocktail Book, compiled by W. J. Tarling and published in London in 1937, one of the few bourbon drinks in a British bar book of the period. Its name borrows a nineteenth-century American expression: twisting the lion's tail meant provoking Britain, whose royal arms bear a lion, which has led drinks historians to suspect an American contributor working in London after Prohibition. The drink was largely forgotten until Ted Haigh revived it in his book Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails, just as allspice dram was returning to American shelves.

name: Million Dollar Cocktail
description: Gin, sweet vermouth and pineapple shaken to a thick foam with egg white. The Singapore Sling's older, richer sibling from the same bar.
funFact: Somerset Maugham put it in his 1926 story The Letter, which did more for the drink than any bartender — though cocktail historian David Wondrich disputes the Raffles origin entirely and argues it was first poured at the Shanghai Club.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 10 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard for a further 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Let the foam settle before serving.

originStory: The Million Dollar Cocktail is traditionally credited to Ngiam Tong Boon, the Hainanese bartender at the Long Bar of the Raffles Hotel in Singapore in the early twentieth century, who is also credited with the Singapore Sling, although the documentary evidence for both attributions is thin and drinks historians have questioned them. Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book, which carried it to a wider audience in London. Its egg white gives it a thick foam that set it apart from most gin and vermouth drinks of the period.

name: Maximilian Affair
description: Mezcal met elderflower and Punt e Mes in Boston. Smoke, blossom and bitter orange, with the lemon holding them apart.
funFact: Misty Kalkofen improvised it at Green Street in 2008 when Ron Cooper, who founded Del Maguey mezcal, walked into the bar unannounced. The name is a joke about France's 1860s adventure in Mexico — French elderflower, Mexican mezcal.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and discard it.

originStory: The Maximilian Affair is credited to Misty Kalkofen, who created it in 2008 while tending bar at Green Street in Cambridge, Massachusetts, part of the Boston bar scene that helped bring mezcal into American cocktails. The name nods to France's intervention in Mexico, when Napoleon III installed the Austrian archduke Maximilian as emperor: French elderflower liqueur meets Mexican mezcal, with Italian Punt e Mes as a third party and lemon to hold them together.

name: East India Cocktail
description: Brandy laid over curaçao, maraschino and raspberry. An 1880s after-dinner drink built like a sweetmeat.
funFact: Harry Johnson printed it in 1882 and then changed his own sweetener by 1890; Harry Craddock dropped the maraschino altogether in 1930 and poured in pineapple juice instead. Three books, three different drinks, one name.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The East India Cocktail first appears in Harry Johnson's Bartender's Manual of 1882, where Johnson, a German-born New York bartender, noted that it was a great favourite with the English living in the different parts of East India. His brandy-based recipe used curaçao, maraschino, a fruit syrup and bitters, and the drink drifted as it was copied: Johnson adjusted it in later editions, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 printed a version with pineapple juice. Who first mixed it, and where, is not recorded.

name: Up-to-Date
description: Amontillado sherry stood up to rye in equal measure, with Grand Marnier closing it. Nutty, dry and far older than it tastes.
funFact: It comes from Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks — the last book to record New York bartending before Prohibition closed the bars, written by the head bartender of the Hotel Wallick on Times Square.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon peel over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: The Up-to-Date comes from Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks, published in New York in 1916 by the head bartender of the Hotel Wallick on Times Square. Ensslin's book was one of the last American bar guides before Prohibition closed the country's saloons, and it is also the first known printing of the Aviation. The Up-to-Date's pairing of whiskey and sherry in equal measure was largely forgotten until the classic-cocktail revival, when bartenders rediscovered sherry as a mixer and went back to Ensslin's pages for recipes.

name: Old Hickory
description: Two vermouths and two bitters, and nothing else. The lowest-proof drink in New Orleans and one of the best-balanced.
funFact: Stanley Clisby Arthur recorded in 1937 that it was Andrew Jackson's favourite drink while he and the pirate Jean Lafitte were winning the Battle of New Orleans in the winter of 1814. Jackson's nickname was Old Hickory.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds — it is low-proof, so it takes dilution well.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Twist a lemon peel over the top and drop it in.

originStory: The Old Hickory is recorded in Stanley Clisby Arthur's Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em, published in 1937, where Arthur tells the story that it was a favourite of General Andrew Jackson, nicknamed Old Hickory, during the defence of New Orleans against the British in the winter of 1814 and 1815. The anecdote is unverified, and Arthur's book is known for colourful stories, but the drink itself, built entirely on two vermouths and two bitters, is a genuine New Orleans classic and one of the lowest-strength drinks in the city's canon.

name: Cherry Blossom
description: Cherry brandy and cognac cut with curaçao and lemon. Japan's own contribution to the Savoy era, built to look like the flower it is named for.
funFact: It was created by Tasaburo Tao at Bar Paris in Yokohama, the port city where Japanese cocktail culture actually began — the same city that produced the Bamboo a generation earlier.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Cherry Blossom is generally credited to Tasaburo Tao of Bar Paris in Yokohama, who created it in the 1920s, and it is one of the earliest Japanese cocktails to win fame abroad, appearing in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book in London in 1930. Yokohama, the treaty port where foreign residents and hotel bars introduced Western drinking to Japan, had already produced the Bamboo, created at the city's Grand Hotel by Louis Eppinger. Tao's drink was built and coloured to recall the sakura, the cherry blossom of the Japanese spring.

name: Yokohama
description: Gin and vodka under orange and grenadine, with one dash of absinthe doing all the talking.
funFact: A single dash of absinthe carries a drink that is otherwise mostly orange juice — which is why the recipe survives in the old books exactly as written, with the absinthe measured in dashes rather than fractions.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without garnish.

originStory: The Yokohama Cocktail was in print by 1930, when Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book, and it is named after the Japanese treaty port where Western-style hotel bars first took root in Japan. It is an unusual drink for its time, combining gin with vodka, still rare in British and American bars, along with orange juice and grenadine. Its creator is not recorded, and whether it was devised in Yokohama itself or simply named after the city by a bartender elsewhere is unknown.

name: Joy Division
description: A Martini given Cointreau and three dashes of absinthe. Bright, herbaceous and considerably less austere than the name suggests.
funFact: Phil Ward built it at Death & Co in 2008 by taking a 2:1 gin Martini and adding half an ounce of Cointreau — a reminder that most modern classics are an existing drink plus one idea.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: Phil Ward created the Joy Division at Death & Co in New York's East Village in the late 2000s, before he left to open Mayahuel, his agave-focused bar. He started from a dry gin Martini and added Cointreau and a few dashes of absinthe, a small change that makes the drink brighter and more aromatic without hiding the gin. Its name borrows that of the Manchester post-punk band.

name: Paper Tiger
description: A Negroni that swapped gin for spiced dark rum. Same bitter architecture, warmer floor.
funFact: It holds the Negroni's equal-thirds structure exactly and changes only the base — the cleanest way to prove that the Negroni is a template rather than a recipe.

ingredients.amount: cubed, plus a large cube to serve

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange peel over the top and drop it in.

originStory: The Paper Tiger is a modern Negroni variation that keeps the equal measures of Campari and sweet vermouth and swaps gin for spiced dark rum, and its creator and first bar are not recorded.

name: Brainstorm
description: Irish whiskey with a quarter-ounce each of dry vermouth and Bénédictine. Small, dry and pre-Prohibition.
funFact: It is one of the few pre-Prohibition cocktails built on Irish whiskey rather than rye — a category that all but vanished from American bars for most of the twentieth century and only came back in this one.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: The Brainstorm is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930: Irish whiskey stirred with two dashes each of Bénédictine and French vermouth and finished with orange peel. It is one of the few classic cocktails built on Irish whiskey rather than rye or bourbon, from a period when Irish whiskey was still widely poured in American and British bars. Who created it, and where its name came from, is not recorded.

name: Fog Horn
description: Gin, lime and ginger beer over ice. A Moscow Mule that predates the Moscow Mule and never needed a copper mug.
funFact: The Waldorf Astoria put it on the map decades before vodka arrived in America — the gin-and-ginger build the Moscow Mule would later borrow wholesale.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the gin and lime juice.
Top with ginger beer and stir once, gently, to combine.
Garnish and serve with a straw.

originStory: The Fog Horn, gin and lime lengthened with ginger, is an early member of the buck family, the highballs of spirit, citrus and ginger ale or ginger beer that took shape in American bars around the turn of the twentieth century. It is recorded among the drinks of the original Waldorf-Astoria bar in New York, whose recipes were collected by Albert Stevens Crockett, and it predates the Moscow Mule, which applied the same structure to vodka, by decades. Its creator is not recorded, and neither is the reason for its name.

name: Blue Train
description: Gin, lemon and curaçao, named for the overnight sleeper to the Riviera. The blue arrived later than the drink did.
funFact: The original was a plain gin-lemon-triple sec sour; the blue curaçao was added decades later so the drink would match the name of the Calais–Mediterranée express it honoured.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Flame an orange peel over the surface if you have one.

originStory: The Blue Train is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, a gin sour with Cointreau and lemon named after the Calais-Mediterranean Express, the luxury overnight sleeper to the Riviera known as Le Train Bleu for its blue-and-gold carriages. The train was a symbol of the 1920s smart set, celebrated in a Diaghilev ballet and an Agatha Christie novel. Craddock coloured the drink with a dash of blue vegetable extract, the job blue curaçao does in most later versions, and its creator is not recorded.

name: Prince Edward
description: Scotch and Drambuie held together by Lillet Blanc. A Bobby Burns that traded its vermouth for something lighter.
funFact: It is a Bobby Burns with Kina Lillet where the Italian vermouth should be — the same substitution that made the Vesper and the Corpse Reviver No. 2 taste the way they originally did, before Kina Lillet was reformulated in 1986.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir until cold and properly diluted, about 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and drop it in.

originStory: The Prince Edward is a Scotch cocktail built like a Bobby Burns, with Drambuie and Lillet in place of the vermouth, and which Prince Edward it honours, and who first mixed it, are not recorded.

name: La Perla
description: Manzanilla sherry and reposado tequila in equal measure, sweetened with pear. Saline, dry and unlike anything else on the shelf.
funFact: Jacques Bezuidenhaut built it at Tres Agaves in San Francisco in 2005, and it did more than any other drink to put dry sherry back behind American bars — manzanilla is aged under a living cap of flor yeast that keeps air off the wine entirely.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

originStory: La Perla is credited to Jacques Bezuidenhout, the South African-born bartender based in San Francisco, who paired reposado tequila with manzanilla sherry and a measure of pear liqueur. It is usually linked to Tres Agaves, the tequila-focused restaurant and bar where he worked in the city, and it became one of the best-known sherry cocktails of the American revival. Its saline edge comes from the manzanilla, aged under flor, a living cap of yeast that keeps air away from the wine.

name: Ferrari
description: Fernet-Branca and Campari, half and half, and nothing else. Two amari that were never meant to meet.
funFact: The name is for the colour, not the car — though it is also the drink bartenders hand each other at the end of a shift, which is how a two-ingredient pour with no history became a fixture without ever appearing in a book.

ingredients.amount: cubed, or none if taken as a shot

steps: Add both amari to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir briefly — about 15 seconds, as there is nothing here to dilute far.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass, or into a shot glass neat.
Serve with no garnish.

originStory: The Ferrari, equal parts Fernet-Branca and Campari, joins two of Milan's best-known bitters in a bartenders' pour that rarely reaches a printed menu, and it has no recorded creator or date, its name usually explained by its racing-red colour.

name: Boomerang
description: Rye, dry vermouth and Swedish Punsch, with a dash of lemon to stop it closing up. Craddock at his most obscure.
funFact: Swedish Punsch is a rum-and-arrack liqueur that Sweden has been making since 1733, and it was common enough in 1930 that the Savoy Cocktail Book used it without explanation. It then vanished from English-speaking bars for seventy years.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well for about 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve.

originStory: The Boomerang appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, a whisky drink made there with Canadian Club, dry vermouth and Swedish punsch, sharpened with dashes of bitters and lemon. Swedish punsch traces its beginnings to 1733, when the Swedish East India Company's ships began bringing Batavia arrack to Gothenburg, and it was common enough in London bars between the wars that the Savoy used it without explanation. It then all but vanished from English-speaking bars for decades, and the Boomerang's creator is not recorded.
